Pick of the Week
NIGHT TIME (2:29)
[Grand Canyon, BMI—Feldman,
Goldstein, Gottehrer]
RHYTHM OF LOVE
(1:56)
[Grand Canyon, BMI—Feldman,
Goldstein, Gottehrer]
STRANGELOVES (Bang 1000)
The
Strangeloves
should
rapidly jump
into
the
winner’s
circle with
this top-drawer follow-up to their last-time-out smasheroo of “Cara-Lin.”
The top
lid here, “Night Time,”
is
a pulsating, hard-driving rhythmic
romantic blueser about a lad who wants
to spend the PM hours with
his gal. “Rhythm Of Love”
is a plaintive, afterhours, soulful romancer.
BABY COME ON HOME
(3:13)
[Keetch Caesar &
Dino, BMI—Berns]
(NO, NO, NO) CAN'T STOP LOVIN’ YOU NOW
[2:20)
[Cotillion-DeFaith, BMI—Burke]
SOLOMON BURKE (Atlantic 234)
The vet pop-r&b songster is a natural to create plenty of sales excite-
ment on
the basis
of
this
latest
Atlantic money-maker dubbed “Baby
Come On Home.” The side
is an extremely slow-shufflin’ blues-drenched
chorus-backed weeper about an unhappy guy who
is spending his time
carrying the torch for his ex-gal. “(No, No, No)
Can’t Stop Lovin’ You
Now,”
is a lively, contagious warm-hearted pledge
of devotion.

SEARCHERS (Kapp 729)
The
Searchers
are
currently
clicking
in
their
native England
with
“Take Me For What I’m Worth” and
there’s no reason why the
lads
can’t
duplicate
that
success
on
this
side
of
the foam. The
side
is
a
rollicking,
fast-moving
ditty
about
an
average
type
guy who
serves

on
his
gal
that

“Too

close

MGM SINGING STRINGS (MGM 13448)
Here’s a top-drawer
flick theme from the soon-to-bow “Dr. Zhivago”
tabbed “Laura’s Theme” which should attract both Top 40 and middle-

is enhanced by a
fine wordless chorus. Watch

is labeled “The Old And The New.”

HOLLYWOOD:
“Amen,” a huge Xmas season
sin-
gle a year ago by the Impressions on
ABC-Paramount, appears
to
be hap-
pening
all
over
again
on
the West
Coast.
It’s
in the form
of a magnifi-
cent
choral
album
titled
“Amen”
which
was
cut
by
the
Van
Nuys
Baptist
Choir
and
released
a
few
weeks ago by Liberty. Usually album
sales by a local church choir are con-
fined
to
that
area
in
which
they’re
recorded.
But
this
one
is
showing
strong
sales
in
such faraway
places
as Bakersfield and Phoenix. The song
is
a
standard
spiritual,
recorded
by
Belafonte and others
prior
to
its
re-
introduction
in
the
multi-prize
win-
ning film “Lilies of the Field.” A num-
ber
of instrumental
singles
did
little
to
appease
consumer demand
for
a
vocal treatment similar to one offered
in the film. Jester Hairston, who sang
it for
Sidney
Poitier
(who
admitted
that he
“couldn’t hold a note with
a
handcuff”)
cut a
single version prior
to
the
national
release
of
the movie
but, for some reason,
it was never re-
leased.
Epic
wisely
did
issue
the
pundtrack version with Hairston and
it was one
of
label’s most successful
albums
of
’64.
It
wasn’t
until
the
Impressions got hold of the song and
ABC-Paramount released the first sin-
gle vocal version,
(a year and a half
after the
film opened)
that the song
became
a
national
chart
breaker.
Whether
the
new
treatment
can
spread
past
Phoenix
and
maintain
sales into the new year
is a question
that won’t
be
answered
for
another
few weeks. The album
is
altogether
an excellent one and the “Amen” cut
is the finest version we have yet heard
of
this
spirited
spiritual.
.
.
.

market by speaking directly to young
attempts

people

Early Mag
Start
Capitol has been one
of
the
pion-
eers,
as
well,
in
the magazine
field.
As far back as March, 1943 when the
firm was in its infancy, Dave Dexter,
former
Chicago
editor
of Downbeat,
edited
a
four
page
semi-monthly
periodical called “The Capitol” which
was distributed at no charge through
record
dealers.
Its
circulation
sky-
rocketed
to
900,000
a month during
the war years and was undoubtedly
the largest pop music publication
in
U.
S.
history. In 1945
it became the
“Capitol News,”
a 7X9
sixteen page
two-color
slick with news and photos
of bands, artists and openings with a
price
tag
of
fifteen
cents
an
issue.
Dexter describes
it as “a little Down-
beat”. Despite its phenomenal success
in
the
circulation
department,
the
journal
showed
only
a
small
profit
margin and was abandoned in 1955, a
few
years
after
Dexter
joined
the
repertoire
department
with
Capitol.
He
is
presently
an
executive A&R
producer for the label. A house organ
called ‘Capitol World”, edited by then
publicity
chief
Marilyn
Hammond,
was begun in 1949 and covered deejay
events and changes. That too was dis-
continued about the same time as the
“Capitol
News”.
With
Hondas,
stereo
sets
and
al-
bum giveaways added a incentive
to
an expanding circulation Teen Set
is
already
one
of
the
most
successful
merchandising tools devised by Capi-
tol
in
years.
As
yet
the
label
has
not been informed
of the
total
sales
for Volume
III and IV but estimates
more
than
200,000
sold
in
the
past
three months.

BRIGHT LIGHTS AND COUNTRY MUSIC—
Bill Anderson—Decca DL 4686/74686
Bill Anderson and the Po’ Boys, who recently
rode high on the country charts with their tear-
jerkin’
smash,
“Bright
Lights
And
Country
Music,” have dubbed this package with the same
name and can expect similar reaction in the C&W
sales market.
In addition to the
title track, the
LP also features Anderson’s latest single release,
“Golden
Guitar,”
and
a
smattering
of
country
favorites, including “The Wild Side Of Life” and
“Mountain Dew,” making up a delectable morsel
for the bluegrass-oriented buyer.
MAXWELL
STREET—Jimmy
Davis—Elektra
Records EKL 303/EKS 7303
Street singing seems
to be disappearing from
the American scene, but one place where it is still
thriving is in Chicago in the Maxwell Street flea
market area, and one of the most expressive
of
the
blues-performers who
regularly
work
the
street
is Jimmy Davis. In this LP, which
is
set
to
his
powerful
singing
and
rhythmic
guitar
playing,
the chanter
sings
such tunes
as “Two
Trains Running,” “I Got My Eyes On You,” and
“Alberta.” Could be a big one.
I
LIKE
IT
THIS WAY—Lisa
Kindred—Van-
guard VRS 9196/VSD 79196
Lisa Kindred comes on strong with this collec-
tion of folk-blues tunes. Able support is given to
the songstress by the sounds of bass, 6- and 12-
string guitar, drums and a fretted dobro. Songs
included in the package are “Candy Man,” “I Like
It This Way,” and “Baby, Did You Hear Me.” An
excellent addition to the Vanguard catalog.
IN A MOOD—Arthur
Prysock—Old Town LP
2010
Arthur Prysock has
captivated
audiences
for
many years and his latest set is possibly his finest
effort. In the package the blues chanter backed by
sweet
orking
sings
such
tunes
as “My Funny
Valentine,” “My
First
Love,”
and
“Don’t You
Ever
Feel
Sorry.” The album
should
score big
with good music spiners and the adult audience.
THE BEST OF ESQUIVEL—RCA Victor LPM/
LSP 3502
By the time Juan Garcia Esquivel was
18, he
was arranging, conducting, and composing for his
own 22 piece orchestra. Esquivel’s ork sound
is a
combination of exotic instruments
set to unique
arrangements and
original recording techniques.
Examples of this can be heard on this LP which
ranges
from
pop
(“Take
The
‘A’
Train”)
to
classical (“My Reverie”) to Latin (“Malaguena”).
Plenty of good listening.
THE NEW BEER BARREL POLKA—Will Glahe
—London SP 44069
Accordion
soloist and
band-leader
Will
Glahe
makes
his
Phase
Four
Stereo
debut
with
this
vivid musical portrayal of the sights and scenes
of Bavaria and neighboring Austria. The
infec-
tious jollity of the polka and the nostalgic strains
of the Viennese waltz combine
to transport the
listener to this beautiful corner of Europe. High-
lighted by
“Beer
Barrel
Polka,” “The
Skater’s
Waltz,” and “Auf Wiederseh’n Sweetheart,” this
LP should do very well with stereo fans.
MADE
IN
HOLLYWOOD—Surrey
Strings—
Surrey S/SS 1011
For the listeners who enjoy the relaxing sound
of warm, sweeping strings, set to ultra-pleasant,
moody
melodies,
this
package
by
the
Surrey
Strings
should
satisfy many an
appetite. Long-
time favorites in the vein of the romantic ballad
make up the
bill of fare, with themes from some
of Hollywood’s
finest motion
pictures
highlight-
ing the assortment. With
lovely tracks running
from beginning to end, the LP incorporates such
sturdies as “Unchained Melody” and “Song From
Moulin Rouge.”
LATIN AU GO GO—Louie
Ramirez—Atco
33-
179/SD 33-179
Louie Ramirez and his orchestra should capture
a large audience with
this package
of mambos,
cha-chas and boleros. The youthful, driving sound
is sparked by Ramirez, who is an ace on the vibes
and
timbales
and
his
partner,
Torrens,
a
top
percussionist.
The
band’s
arrangements,
all
written by
the
leader,
are unusual for a Latin
band because of their jazz orientation. Top tracks
include “Monton
Simon,” “Con La Bembapara,”
and “Alma Con Alma.”
LA GUAPACHOSA—Sonora Santanera—Colum-
bia EX 5151
Latin
music,
from
the
soft
and
swaying
rhythm of the guaracha to the
torrid, pulsating
beat of the cumbia is the keynote of this package
by Sonora
Santanera. Whether for
listening
or
for dancing, the album is a captivating presenta-
tion
of
tropical tempos
and
should
gain
favor
with Latin enthusiasts. Featured tracks in the LP
include “Cobarde Y Mentirosa” and “La Cumbia
Del Torero,” in addition to “Nunca Digas Que Te
Quise.”
JAZZ PICK
MILES
DAVIS PLAYS
JAZZ
CLASSICS —
Prestige 7373
The Miles Davis
Quintet, vintage
1956,
is an
aggregate
of musicians
of
outstanding
stature.
Featuring Davis on trumpet with John Coltrane
on tenor sax, 88’er Red Garland, Paul Chambers
on bass and Philly Joe Jones on drums, the group
shines with professionalism. The eight tracks on
this disk were culled from some two dozen cut by
the group and represent some of the top work of
contemporary jazz leaders. A
special hurrah for
“Tune Up” and “Airegin” in an overall top notch
LP.
JAZZ BEST BETS
THE NIGHT OF THE COOKERS, VOL.
1 —
Freddie Hubbard—Blue Note 4207
Trumpeter Freddie Hubbard leads a good group
of musicians in this solid sounding disk, cut ‘live’
at
the
Club La
Marchal.
This
first
of
a
two-
volume
set, the disk has a pair of powerful cuts
with
“Pensativa,”
a
romantic
Latin
tune,
and
“Walkin’,” a funky finger snapping outing. The
live audience
cooks with the
artists and
lots
of
jazzophiles should join them in digging this solid
scene.
SOULERO—Eddie
Higgins
Trio—Atlantic
SD
1446
The Eddie Higgins Trio
is showcased on
this
LP
of
highly
varied
jazz
tracks.
'The
Chicago-
based
outfit takes great pains to add something
extra
to
its
interpretations
of
each
of
these
tunes, and that something extra
is
soul. Dig the
swinging title track, or the boys’ rendition of the
“Django”
standard,
or what
they
do
with
the
Foster melody
of
“Beautiful
Dreamer,”
to
see
what that little extra does. LP should be a delight
for jazz
buffs.
CLASSICAL PICKS
BARTOK/MIRACULOUS
MANDARIN
SUITE
— Ormandy/Philadelphia Orchestra — Columbia
ML 6189
This potent reading of Bartok’s second and last
ballet should give great satisfaction to the many
fans of the composer and/or Eugene Ormandy. In
addition to this stirring emotion-provoking piece,
the LP offers effective readings of “Deux Images
(Two
Pictures)” and “Two
Portraits,” both by
Bartok. The high professionalism of the reading
should create a large audience for this disk.
BEETHOVEN/THE
MIDDLE
QUARTETS —
Fine Arts Quartet—Concert—Disc SP 506/3
The Fine Arts Quartet, known for its renditions
of chamber music, has an outstanding outing in
these
interpretations
of
Beethoven’s
quartets
“Opus 59 No.
1,
2, 3,” “Opus 74” and “Opus 95.”
The
group, which
hails from
the
University
_ of
Wisconsin,
effectively reads
these
highly varied
pieces in a manner that brings out the differences
in the periods that they were written, and these
readings should find great favor with devotees of
this form of music.

ALBUMS REVISITED
iiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiii
Roy Orbison's
ROY ORBISON'S
BREATEST HITS
IgIfliliiiiiiiiPESM
MIS! Mi IJLiil’Ili
By
and
large,
when
most
trade-
sters are asked to mention “catalog”
merchandise they usually note classi-
cal, Broadway cast or soundtrack al-
bums.
There
are,
of
course,
glaring
exceptions
to
this
catalog
rule-of-
thumb. “Roy Orbison’s Greatest Hits”
is one such exception. In the 3% years
since the Monument LP was released
it has sold in excess of 650,000 units.
The
disk was
an
immediate
best-
seller,
reaching
the
charts
shortly
Greatest
Hits
after
its
release.
Its
early consumer
acceptance
kept
the
album
on
the
charts for the next 86 weeks. But that
is only the first phase of the story.
In
the
past twenty months,
since
the
set has dropped
off
the
lists,
it
has
sold
over
250,000
copies.
These
thoroughly
impressive
figures
are
complimented
by
a
hefty
European
sale
of
100,000
pieces.
Interestingly
enough,
the
album
presently
sells
almost as well in stereo as
it does in
mono, which seems to suggest a more
sophisticated
audience
than
tradi-
tional rock
’n’ roll buyers.
Although the chanter
is no longer
associated with Monument,
the
LP’s
prospects
are
still
quite
rosy.
The
label projects a 100,000 plus
sale for
1966. Future
sales,
it was noted, will
be
considerably
in
excess
of
this
figure
if
Orbison
has
single
hit
on
either
of his two
affiliations. In any
event, the package
will certainly not
suffer a cut-out death for many years
to come.
Epic Rushes Release Of
On Mike Douglas Album
NEW YORK—Due to the roaring suc-

Musicor Names Spinosa Veep;
Makes Strides On Tape Front;
Inks A Bevy Of New Artists
NEW YORK—Chris Spinosa has been
appointed vice-president in charge
of
sales for Musicor Records,
it was an-
nounced
last week by Art Talmadge,
sales manager, when Musicor became
completely independent of other disk-
ery
ties.
Prior
to
joining
the
firm,
Spinosa operated his own label, Vesu-
vius
Records,
which
was
then
dis-
tributed
through
MGM
Records.
Earlier,
he was
active
in
the
retail
field.
Musicor has signed a non-exclusive
releasing
arrangement
with
Muntz
Stereo Pak for tape cartridge release
of
the
entire
Musicor
catalog.
The
Muntz
cartridges
are
primarily
de-
signed
for
use with
automobile
car-
tridge
players.
The Muntz arrangement is the sec-
ond cartridge releasing deal signed by
Musicor.
Previously,
the
firm
had
made
a
separate
non-exclusive
ar-
rangement with Music Tapes of Chi-
cago. Music Tapes, on the other hand,
has the exclusive rights to the Musi-
cor
catalog
for
reel-to-reel
pre-re-
corded tape releases.
A brace of newly signed talent will
be
in
evidence
as
Musicor
kicks
off
the new year, a year,
in which, says
Art Talmadge, “The firm should enjoy
the highest sales level in
its history.”
Newest
signing
involves
chanter,
Ry
Cooper, an alumnus
of the New
Christy
Minstrels.
Cooper’s
first
re-
lease
is
set for Jan. During the pre-
Christmas period, another new pactee,
TV’s Shari Lewis, enjoyed play with a
holiday-styled
single.
More
Lewis
product
is also in the works.
The label’s Jan. LP release features
the first Musicor album by the newly
signed Three Suns. Upcoming shortly,
are new albums and
singles by both
the Platters and the Bitter End Sing-
ers. Also in the works is a first LP by
Eartha
Kitt.

Execs
Resign

Record’s
execu-

as-

resigned

3,

vice

The Okeh label will continue, though,
and recording plans are being formu-
lated
to
assign
the
Okeh
artists
to
other members of the Epic and Okeh
producing staff.

! Tito Schipa
Dies
NEW YORK—Tenor Tito Schipa,
76,
who
sang
with
major
opera
com-
panies for more than 30 years, died of
a
heart
ailment
in
New
York
on
Thursday Dec.
16. During his career
I
he was
featured
in
such
operas
as
“Tosca” and “Manon.”
|1
The
Italian tenor was
also a com-
poser and toured in concert halls after
leaving
opera.
He
wrote
“Angela
Mia,” the theme for a Janet Gaynor-
Charles
Farrell
film,
in
addition
to
penning a number of recital songs as
well as an operetta, “Princess Liana.”
A native of Lecce, Italy, he studied
1
piano,
composition
and
voice.
He
I
toured
Europe
and
South
America
before
joining
the
Chicago
Civic
;
Opera in 1919, where he remained for
5
13 years.
ti
He
is survived by his wife, Teresa
(0
Borgna,
two
daughters,
a
son,
a
brother and a niece.

Organizational Changes At
Capitol’s Canadian Setup
HOLLYWOOD—Lloyd W. Dunn, pres-
ident
of
Capitol
Records
(Canada)
and vice president of Capitol Records,
has
announced
two
organizational
changes in the firm’s Canadian setup.
Effective
Jan.
3,
Geoffrey
F.
Racine
will
become
executive
vice-president
of
electrical
and
musical
Industries,
and
G. Edward Leetham
will become
vice
president and
general manager
of Capitol Records in Canada.
In accepting his new
position, Ra-
cine
will
relinquish
his
position
as
executive vice president. In the posi-
tion, he will be responsible for future
Capitol ventures in Canada.
Racine has been an executive with
the
Capitol
organization
for
more
than
ten
years.
In
1958,
he became
vice president and director of opera-
tions, CRDC, and later vice president
of Capitol Record Club. He was sub-
sequently
appointed
vice
president
and general manager in 1961.
In
G. Edward Leetham’s new posi-
tion,
he
will
be
responsible
for
the
complete
operation
of
the
Canadian
setup.
Leetham joined
Capitol
in 1962 as
vice
president and
director
of
sales
and merchandising. Prior to his affilia-
tion with the company, he served as
advertising and public relations man-
ager of John Inglis Company.
The
new
vice
president
has
ap-
pointed
E.
Taylor
Campbell
as
di-
rector
of
sales.
Campbell
has
been
with
Capitol
since
its
inception
in
Canada and
served most recently as
national sales manager.
Also aiding Leetham
will
be Paul
White, who
is
in charge of advertis-
ing,
sales
promotion
and
director
of repertoire; Brian O’Shea, treasurer
and
controller;
and Harold
F.
Burr,-
director of operations.
In
announcing
the
changes, Dunn
said
that
the
new
organizational
structure will enable Capitol Records,
Inc.
“to maintain
close and
effective
executive
coordination
in Canada
of
the many activities there.”

TJB
Continues With
Red Hot-Album Sales
NEW YORK—Herb
Alpert
and
the
Tijuana
Brass, who
copped
the
top
spot
in
the Cash Box
poll
for being
the
biggest
album
selling
band
of
1965,
are making
a powerful
bid
to-
ward
retaining
the
title
for
1966
as
they continue as one of the strongest
LP movers in the current crop.
The
group
first
broke
out
as
al-
bum sellers in 1963 with their “Lonely
Bull”
LP,
which
followed
up
their
smash
single by the same name. The
package has become
a
rarity
in
the
business
by
recently
jumping
back
on
the
charts, where
it
is
presently
bulleting
at
the
44
spot.
Three
other TJB
albums
followed
that
release
and
all
three
are
also
firmly entrenched on
the
best-selling
lists. The second album by the group,
“South Of The Border,”
is
at the 31
position,
while
the
latest
sets,
“Whipped
Cream
And
Other
De-
lights” and “Going
Places,” are both
in the top five, at 3 and 4 respectively.
The
TJB,
who
just
completed
a
weekend engagement
at
the HIC
in
Honolulu,
have been
set
for
a
solid
month of bookings in February. Prior
to
the
kickoff
of
one-nighters,
the
group
will
do
three
concerts
at the
Theatre
in
the Round
in
Salt Lake
City.
After
that
they
will
perform
in such cities as Seattle, Spokane, San
Diego,
Sacramento,
Miami
Beach,
New
Orleans and Houston.

Little
Stevie Wonder
Little
Stevie Wonder has not been
on
the
charts
for
over
a
year,
but
with
his
current Tamla
outing “Up
Tight”
(#50
on
this
week’s
chart),
he returns to his winning ways.
Stevie was born in Saginaw, Michi-
gan, and though blind, he began play-
ing the
piano and harmonica
at
the
age of five. The musician got his first
break when
he
visited
the home
of
Ronnie
White,
a
member
of
the
Miracles,
to
play
with
Ronnie’s
kid
brother
Gerald. When
Ronnie
heard
Stevie
sing and play the harmonica,
he sent for Brian Holland, talent scout
and A&R director of Tamla Records.
Holland was
so
impressed
with
the
youngster
that he
signed him
to an
exclusive recording contract. This re-
sulted
in
the waxing
of
several
hits
including
“Fingertips,”
and
“High
Heeled Sneakers.”
Jackie
Lee
Jackie Lee, who is currently scoring
on both pop and r&b charts with
his‘
Mirwood outing of “The Duck,” leads
a double
life—his other personality
is
Earl Cosby, half of the team
of Bob
and
Earl.
Born in California, Jackie attended
high school in Los Angeles, where he
sang in the men’s chorus. He also was
a
soloist
in
the
local
First
Baptist
Church.
He got his big break
in 1958 when
he
dropped
into
the
Cotton
Club
in
Los Angeles
to
see
his friend Bobby
Day, who was then singing with the
Hollywood
Flames. Day
invited him
to try out for the group and after his
first song he was made a permanent
member.
In 1961 he
left the group and with
Bobby
Garrett formed
the
duo
Bob
and Earl under the wing of producer
Fred Smith. When Smith joined Ran-
dall
Wood,
who
was
then
forming
Mira
Productions, Bob and
Earl mi-
grated with him.
Jackie’s waxing
of
“The Duck”
is
the
first
big
hit
for
the Mirwood
label. The
chanter, who
is
also a writer,
is currently making
personal
appearances
at
clubs
throughout the U.S. as a result of his
chart riding deck.
Santa had to work overtime
to
fill
the
large Xmas
stocking
that was
left
hanging
at WDGY-Minneapolis,
Saint
Paul.
It
all
began when
the
station ran a Christmas stocking con-
test
and
offered
to
fill
the
largest
stocking
entered
with
prizes.
Hun-
dreds
of
entries poured
in, and
sta-
tion management began
to worry as
the
12 and
15
footers
started
arriv-
ing.
The
biggest
of
them
all,
the
Grand
Prize
winner,
measured
820
feet
long and
12
feet
in
circumfer-
ence. Made of nylon net, it was nearly
as
long as
three
football
fields. The
winning
stocking makers,
three
col-
lege freshmen from the Minneapolis,
St.
Paul
area,
said
it
all
started
as
a joke, but ended up with an invest-
ment
of $150
in materials and about
300
hours
in
sewing
it.
The
outlet
filled the giant stocking with balloons,
each containing a
dollar
bill, with
a
prize guarantee of at least $500.
There
is a new
station and a new
sound
in
Cleveland. WIXY-Cleveland
recently made
its
debut
on
the
fre-
quency
that
was
formerly
used
by

tinue on the FM

format. After a

of

concluded

its

ming
should
appeal
to young
adults
18 to 45 years of age. The music that
will
be heard
will be anything from

Streisand
to
the

and

Beatles.
In

the
format that will be used on the new
outlet, program director Gerry Spinn
said
that many
people
in
the
radio
audience
grew up
listening
to

and
roll.
Spinn

to

have
changed a bit and they demand more
variety in their music.

Driving on New Year’s Eve, always
a hazardous
undertaking, was made
a
little easier this year for people in
the
Detroit area. WJBK-Detroit was
selected by the Chemstrand Company
as one
of two
stations
in the nation
to present the company’s special four-
hour New Year’s Eve program, “Mu-
sic To
Stay Awake
By.” The

from

was

from
11:00 PM
Dec.
31
to
3:00 PM
on Jan.
1; George Toles was host. In

to
lively
music,
the
show
carried
traffic
bulletins
and weather
reports,
all aimed
at keeping motor-
ists
aware
of
conditions
that might
have affected their driving. A unique
feature was an hourly salute to other
cities
in the country.

Francisco

ity A1 Collins doesn’t believe in glass

cai’-
peted studios. The deejay, along with

ranean studio, the Purple Grotto. The

mont

GrilS Appointed
To Kapp A&R
Post
NEW YORK — Vet
record
producer
Hy
Grill
has
been
appointed
pop
singles A&R producer-exec for Kapp
Records,
it was announced by Dave
Kapp, president of the
firm.
Grill has been with the organization
since January
1965, and
part
of
his
duties has been to work closely with
various Kapp-owned publishing firms.
During the year he also produced for
such
artists
as
Jimmy
Sedlar
and
Hugo Winterhalter.
In
his new
post.
Grill
will
supervise
the A&R
op-
erations for practically all the single-
oriented
artists
and
will
also
be
in
charge of their albums. He will con-
tinue
to
be
active
in
the
publishing
wing and will act as A&R consultant
to
the
firm’s
affiliated Congress and
Four
Corners
labels.

NEW YORK—Decca
Records begins
the
operation
this week
(3)
of
its
Honolulu
branch,
which
will
be
lo-
cated
at 345 Kamakee,
Honolulu.
In
making
the
announcement,
Sydney
N. Goldberg, vice president and gen-
eral
sales
manager
of
Decca
Dis-
tributing
Corporation,
stated
that
the new operation
will be under
the
direction
of
L.
C.
Gilman,
a
Decca
veep.
Goldberg
also
stated that the new
branch
will
carry
a
complete
inven-
tory
of
the
entire
Decca,
Coral,
Brunswick
and
Vocalion
catalogs,
which
is
standard
procedure
for
all
company
owned
branches.
The
new
branch
will
also carry
a
full
line
of
Decca phonographs, 18 models in
all,
plus a
full
line
of accessories.
As
is
the
case
in
a
number
of
Decca branches throughout the coun-
try, the new branch in Honolulu will
also
carry
two
additional
record
labels, Electra and Listen and Learn.
Fellowship To Be Launched
By ‘Friends Of Bob Burton’
NEW YORK—Some of the associates
of Bob Burton, the
late president
of
BMI,
have
banded
together
into
a
unit known as “The Friends Of Bob
Burton.” The
purpose
of
the
group,
which
is mainly composed of writers
and
publishers,
is
to
raise
$100,000
to
establish
the
Robert
J.
Burton
Memorial
Fellowship
at
Columbia
Law
School.
The fellowship will be awarded an-
nually
for
study
and
research
on
copyright
or
other
law
affecting
music,
art,
literature,
or other prod-
ucts of the mind, or in laws affecting
communications. The award
is
to be
made
by
the
Faculty
of
Law
on
recommendations
of
the
Faculty
member primarily responsible for
in-
struction in copyright.
The group has already raised $60,-
000
but
still
requires
another
$40,-
000 to reach their goal. In the event
the full sum of $100,000
is not raised,
a lesser sum could be used to establish
a
Memorial
Fund
which
would
be
used from
time
to
time
for
specific
research
projects
in
the
fields which
most interested Burton.
Interested
supporters
should
mail
their checks
to “The Friends Of Bob
Burton,”
P.O.
Box
734,
Radio
City
Station, New York, New York 10019.
Checks
should
be made
payable
to
Columbia
University.
Pledges
may
be made
now, with payment
in
full
now or paid over a three year or up
to
five year period. All contributions
are tax
deductible.

phony
Orchestra,

Strauss’

concert
will

the

of
his
debut
in
the
same
hall
with
orchestra
10
years ago.
He had been under contract to RCA
Victor
since

13th
birthday,

Camden
label.
Next

will

Symphony

in

world
tour
under

frequent

Orchestra

ist. Baldwin
is headquartered
in Cin-
cinnati.
Blue Note Partner: Most
Of The Cover Art
Is His
NEW YORK — There
is
a
“house”
photographer
at
Blue
Note
Records
who
also happens
to
be
a
co-owner
of
the famed
and
old
(since
1939)
jazz
label.
He’s
Francis
Wolf,
whose
photo-
graphs have adorned more than
250
Blue Note
covers, more than half of
the
label’s
catalog
of
12"
albums.
His
interest
in photography
dates
back
to pre-War days
in
his
native
Europe, and
while he
can
display
a
number
of
striking
candids
done
strictly for pleasure, he spends most
of
his
photo
work
these
days
on
Blue
Note
covers.
Today,
he
con-
siders
himself
a
“professional
ama-
teur.”
A Wolf Cover
Photo
Wolf,
whose
partner
in
the
Blue
Note
operation
is
A1
Lion,
claims
that a certain style in cover artwork
creates an important identity among
buyers,
especially when
they’re
so-
phisticated jazz
buffs.
Wolf
takes—using
most
often
a
Rolleiflex — photos
that
tie-in
with
either
the
musical
contents
or
the
title
of
an
LP.
Sometimes
natural
candids, other times modernistic
(see
cut above), the covers have included
Stanley
Turrentine
looking
over
a
bouquet of roses in “Dearly Beloved,”
Dexter Gordon comfortably seated in
a handsome
cab
in
“Doin’
Alright”
and Jackie McLean perched on
steel
girders
in “One Step Beyond.” He
is
at home
in both
outdoor and
studio
settings.
Most of the cover designs to Wolf’s
photos
are done by
Reid
Miles, and
the
product
of
both
men’s
achieve-
ment have been recognized by various
photo
awards.

S-Month-Old Single
Sparks New Sales Life
NEW YORK—Mercury Records could
well have a left field hit via an unusu-
ally ‘old’ single. The deck, which went
into
release
last
Aug.,
is
an
r&b-
oriented item called “I Dig You Baby”
by Lorraine
Ellison.
The record was only kept active by
the
label because
of
its
promise
as
evidenced by minimal
sales and
air-
play
in
several important
cities. But
the deck never really started to move
in
any
meaningful
quantity
and,
many times, came
close
to a cut-out
death. The label’s patience apparently
will now be rewarded. In the past sev-
eral weeks,
it has begun
to rack up
healthy sales in such significant mar-
kets as Los Angeles, Chicago, Miami,
Atlanta,
etc.
Interestingly
enough,
the record is now garnering both pop
and
r&b
airplay.
Morris
Diamond,
Mercury’s
national
promotion
direc-
tor,
reports
that
“I Dig You Baby”
has
presently
hit
the
40,000
sales-
mark
and
predicts
widespread
na-
tional acceptance for the recording in
the immediate future.

sociation.
The

will prepare the ballots on which each

of NARM

best sellers of his

Miami Beach.
The NARM Awards will be given in

movie
sound
track album, male vocalist, female vo-
calist,
country
and
western
artist,
folk
artist, most promising male vo-
calist, most promising female
vocal-
ist, best
selling vocal group, comedy
album,
instrumentalists,
orchestra,
children’s
line,
and
economy
price
product.

of

that
will help prepare the

Bartel,
John
Billinis,
Hess
Budin, John
T. Edgerton, Jack Geld-
bart,
Sanford
Goldman,
Jay
Jacobs,
Stanley Jaffee, Sam Morrison, Charles
Murray,
David
Press,
Charles
Sch-
lang, Herbert
Seigal,
Cecil H.
Steen,
Manuel
E.
Swatez, and Fred Traub.
The chairman of the NARM Awards
Banquet
will
be
Charles
Schlang
(Mershaw
of America,
Albany, New
York),
and
the
general
convention
chairman will be Jack J. Geldbart (L
and F Record Service, Atlanta).

Ri-Fi's Velona
Returns To Italy
NEW YORK—G. Velona, head of the
international
dept,
of
Ri-Fi
Records,
has returned to Italy following a trip
to the U.S. While here, he had busi-
ness conferences with the label’s U.S.
attorney,
Richard
Roemer,
and
a
number of labels.
Ri-Fi has risen to the top ranks of
Italy’s indie operations after only five
years of operation. The firm owns two
factories and a printing plant, which
supplies
labels, LP
jackets,
covers,
etc.
It also has a wide sales and dis-
tribution set-up. Its top artist is Mina.
Many of the
label’s performers have
appeared
at the San Remo
Festival,
and the upcoming event at the end of

BMI Report Details Music Boom Since '39
NEW YORK—“Concert Music USA,
1966,” the 12th revised edition of the
brochure that BMI
first compiled
in
1951
has been made
available
to
in-
dividuals,
educational
institutions,
symphony orchestras, and other inter-
ested groups. The brochure highlights
the continuing boom in America’s in-
terest in performing and listening to
music.
Some of the facts contained in the
brochure are as follows;
The growth of
all phases of music
in the U.S. has been phenomenal since
1939, and
an
increase
of 857%
has
been
registered
in
the
dollar volume
of
sales
of
records,
musical
instru-
ments, performing
rights
and
other
aspects
of American
music
interest
during that period. This rate
is 25%
faster than
the
country’s Gross Na-
tional Product growth
of 683%
dur-
ing
the same
time.
The number of American symphony
orchestras
has
more
than
doubled,
from
about
600
in
1939
to
1,401
in
1965, and
is more than
half
of the
world’s 2,000 symphony orchestras.
The 284 orchestras surveyed in the
sixth annual Orchestra Program Sur-
vey conducted by BMI and the Ameri-
can Symphony Orchestra League
in-
creased their average number of non-
summer
concerts by 12.1%
last
sea-
son. Summer concerts were tabulated
for the
first time in the survey’s
six-
year
history,
in
recognition
of
their
growing
importance
on
the
musical
scene. The survey
also noted a great
growth in young people’s concerts and
touring
concerts,
bringing
concert
music to new audiences.
Sales
of
musical
instruments,
ac-
cessories
and
sheet
music
have
in-
creased more than 819%, reaching an
estimated $830,000,000 in 1965; since;
1950, the industry’s
retail
sales have
approximately doubled every 10 years.
Record
sales have increased 1,344%,
to
$693,000,000,
since
1940.
Since 1950, there has been an 85%
increase in the number of people who
play musical
instruments.
In 1965, an average of 13,795 hours
of concert music per week were pro-
grammed by 994 responding AM and
FM radio
stations, or an average
of
13.9 hours per station per week.
There are now 754 opera-producing
groups in this country.
More
than
12,000,000
Americans
play musical instruments and receive
musical
instruction
in
schools
and
with private teachers, compared with
2,500,000 in 1947.
There are more than 63,000 instru-
mental music organizations in
all the
schools in the United States, with
6,-
000 orchestras, 49,000 bands and 8,000
“stage” bands.
According
to
the
American
Sym-
phony League,
this country supports
1,401 symphony orchestras, more than
half
the
world’s
total.
This
figure
does not include the 300 youth sym-
phony
orchestras
maintained
under
the training programs of many adult
symphonic
groups.
Community
orchestras,
operating
on annual budgets under $100,000, re-
main
the
largest
group,
at
1,060.
They are followed by 287 college and
university
orchestras.
Professional
musicians staff the nation’s 29 metro-
politan
orchestras
(budgeted
from
$100,000
to
$500,000)
and
our
25
major orchestras
(with budgets over
$500,000).
Yet
88%
of
the
75,000
community-orchestra
players
are
amateurs.
Classical music accounted for 15%
of
America’s
$514,740,000
long-play-
ing
record
sales,
over
half
of
the
world’s phonograph record market, in
1964. The quality and variety offered
on
515 LP monaural and
296
stereo
labels
listed
in
the
Schwann
Long
Playing Record
Catalog
for Novem-
ber, 1965, contrast favorably with the
concert music available on only 20 or
so
78-rpm
labels
in
1939—and
at
roughly half the 1939 cost per minute
of music.
There
were
37,000,000
amateur
musicians
in
the
United
States
in
1965,
nearly
4.25%
more
than
the
previous
year—a
growth
rate
2.4
times that of the over-all population.
In
1936, by
comparison,
there were
only
14,300,000
amateur
musicians,
and in 1950, only 19,000,000.
The retail value of new musical^ in-
struments,
sheet
music
and
musical
accessories
reached
$744,000,000,
up
10.5% from the previous year, nearly
nine times
the
1940
figure and
over
three times that of 1950.
In 1950, one of every 7.8 Americans
4 years old or more played a musical
instrument
or
received
instrumental
instruction; the 1964 ratio was one of
every
4.8,
making
self-made
music
second only to reading among the na-
tion’s leisure-time participative activi-
ties.
There
are now more than
12,000,-
000
school-age
instrumentalists — al-
most half of them studying piano—as
against
only
3,000,000
in
1950.
This
increase of 300%
is nearly five times
the 71% increase in the over-all 4-to-
21
population
during
1950-64.
Ap-
proximately 85%
of
all band and or-
chestra instruments are purchased for
use by school-age youngsters.
More
than
26%
of
American
schools have
increased
their musical
instruction
schedule during
the
past
five
years;
over 97%
of
elementary
and 95%
of
secondary
schools now
provide
time
for
music
instruction,
with band instruction—the most pop-
ular
course—^being
offered
by
two-
thirds
of
the
secondary
institutions.
Eight per cent of the nation’s school
systems
provide
rhythm-band
train-
ing in kindergarten, to introduce chil-
dren
to instrumental
music.
In the fall of 1964, it was estimated
that elementary, junior high and high
schools had more than 63,000
instru-
mental music organizations, including
6,000 orchestra and 49,000 bands
(in
addition
to
8,000
supervised
“stage”
[or jazz] bands). All of these figures
have doubled since World War
II, as
a
consequence
of
interest
generated
through classroom music
instruction.
These figures do not include the num-
erous
ensemble
and
chamber
music
groups
found
in
almost
all
school
music programs.
Those interested in obtaining copies
should write
to
the
Public
Relations
Department,
Broadcast
Music,
Inc.,
589
Fifth
Avenue, New York, New
York
10017.

Sebastiao Bastos, president of SOM/MAIOR, the new label which specializes
in the Modern Popular Music (successor of Audio Fidelity do Brasil), told us
about the company. First of all, he calls our attention to the fact that although
the releases in Brazil of the US Decca label are being distributed by Discos
Chantecler,
the
contract
of
representation was
signed
with SOM/MAIOR.
Bastos
is proud of his catalogue, which
is a good premonition for the future
of his new
label. First releases by the
label are “Spotlight on Earl Grant,”
“Eartha Kit canta en Espanol,” “Carmen Cavallaro—Hollywood,” “Brenda Lee
—Top Teen Hits” and “Dance The Tango,” with The
Castillians. Second
re-
leases are “Spring Into Spring” by Quartette Tres
Bien, “Hit City
’65” by
the Surfaris, “Stay Awhile” by The Kingston Trio, “Discotheque Dance Party”
by Peter Duchin, and “The Very Thought Of You” by Rick Nelson. Under pro-
duction are “Theme Song of the TV Series ‘The Virginian.’ ” With such a good
selection
of US numbers and
artists and
the known
active
distribution
of
Chantecler,
it is very possible that American music will take back its place of
preference with the Brazilian public. Besides
this, SOM/MAIOR
is busy pre-
paring its new releases in the purist Bossa-Nova style.
The same
start could be used for news about Aloysio de Oliveira and his
label Elenco. The label’s album “Vinicius & Caymmi No Zum Zum,” recorded
during a show in that night-club in Rio,
is in very good position on the local
charts. Performers on the new LP
include
Vinicius De Moraes and
Dorival
Caymmi and feminine vocal group Quarteto Em Cy and instrumental group of
Oscar De Castro Neves. A single has been released from that LP. It is called
“Broto Maroto” b/w “Tern Do De Mim,” by Vinicius and the Quarteto Em Cy.
Another big, big name of MPM, Sylvia Telles, has a new album, which was
made especially for export. The popular lark sings music
of the great Tom
Jobim
in an album called “The Music Of Mr. Jobim By Sylvia Telles”;
this
disc was produced by Aloysio for Kapp Records. She sings several number in
English,
with
versions
already
popularized by
people
like Andy
Williams,
Tony Bennet, Astrud Gilberto, as well as two numbers new to the brazilian
public:
“All
That’s Left
Is To Say Goodbye” and
“Bonita.” We
still think
“Bonita” will hit the charts in the US.
MPB-4 is not a code;
it is the name of a new vocal group from the Elenco
coast. The four young men from Niteroi (Musica Popular Brasileira Quarteto)
appeared in several shows in Sao Paulo and Rio and appear now with
a good
single on Aloysio, “Samba Lento” b/w “Sao Salvador.”
Giro Monteiro, one
of the most popular and
authentic
sambistas, and an
old-timer who adhered
to
the MPM, reached
the
top
of
his long recording
career in the Elenco release “De Vinicius
e Baden Especialmente Para
Ciro
Monteiro.” The idea for it was born when Vinicius De Moraes met with Baden
Powel in Paris a few months ago. Good numbers on the disc are “Formosa,”
“Tempo Feliz,” “Amei Tanto,” and “Tome Meu Cora^ao.”
Marcos
Nobili, who
is acting production manager at Discos Rge, has
told
us about the latest releases of the company: After her success with “Zorba The
Greek,” Dalida has waxed a good single, “Bon Soir Mon Amour”
(II Silenzio)
b/w “Le Printemps Sur La
Colline”
(Le

In

first

is being plugged by RGE as
a candidate for top positions. Tito Batista makes his disc bow on RGE with a
single, interpreting two numbers by Zeketi, who introduced him to the A&R

Crianga” b/w
“Choro

to the “To-
night Show” in New York at the
special request of Johnny Carson and the
NBC producers, where they again scored a terrific success, interpreting “Tema
Para 4” and the big hit “Girl From Ipanema.” Based on their unprecendented
success, the new manager of the group, Monte Kaye, is planning to take them
back to
the
States for a period
of three
years.
.
.
. An album
cut by Os
Cariocas in the U.S. during their recent tour
is being released by Mercury.
This
is surely another Brazilian album that will hit the
charts. The
success
of these
talented
Brazilian
artists, which
scores some more
points
for the
Brazilian Popular Modern Music and opens new doors for the
international
market,
is deserved. Our heartiest congratulations
to Severino and the boys.

Eastern Flashes
MOVIN’ and GROOVIN’—As
usual,
things
are
hoppin’
at Runyon
Sales.
Louis Wolburg huddled with Herb Kaufman of Carol Vending, Brooklyn, Jack
Rowan of Koenig Music Co., Kingston, and Steve Nekos of Nekos Vending Co.,
Kingston.
.
.
. Four years ago the first 25 cent coin-op car wash opened up
in
Ardmore, Oklahoma. Now there are three thousand spread
all over the coun-
try, California alone accounting for more than 200. The coin car wash business
IS now big enough to attract the interest of the Bank of America’s Small Busi-
ness dept., and banks go where the money
is. A BOA magazine has issued a
report on the industry that predicts even more expansion, saying, “Coin-oper-
at^ car wash units may someday become as common as coin-operated washers
and dryers in apartment houses.”
.
.
. Instead of having their regular monthly
meeting last December, the Westchester Operators Guild held a gala bash for
we ops and their wives at the Roger Smith Hotel, White Plains, NY. Seymour
Poliak, secretary of the WOG, says that a good time was had by
all and that
all but one member firm was represented.
.
.
. All four trucks are
rolling
at
Musical
Distributors, making
deliveries
of the Wurlitzer
3000,
reports Max
Gulden and Dave Freed. Business
is up in Manhattan and Brooklyn, so things
are
cookin’
while
vacationing
chief Harold Kaufman
is
with
his
family
in
Acapulco. Max and Dave also said that a 3000 had been rented to 20th Century
Fox, where it will share scenes with Sammy Davis in his forthcoming picture,
also starring Simone Signoret, Peter Lawford and Frank Sinatra,
Jr.
TRAVELER’S TWIST—If
it’s lonely in a strange town, and the wanderer
longs for a spot of fun, then—rejoice! You are not forgotten. Wurlitzer’s Bob
Bear canvassed the distributor network and came up with a
list of ‘fun places’
across the country that feature a Wurlitzer Discotheque. Here are some: Los
Angeles—Nicola’s; Denver— Adducci’s Center Restaurant & Lounge; Pennsau-
ken, N.J.—The Hampton House;
Ithaca, NY—Ithaca Bowl;
Rochester, NY
Guys & Dolls; Syracuse, NY—^The Holiday Bowl; Utica, NY—The Candlelight
Lounge; Cincinnati—The Kasbah
(Terrace Hilton Hotel); Columbus—Nation-
wide Inn; Dayton—The Tropics; Erie, Pa.—City Pub and Gino’s Cafe; Amaril-
lo, Texas—.Ah Go Go Lounge; Black Gold, Pioneer Supper Club; Portsmouth,
Va.—The Plaza Lounge; Houston, Texas—The Coachman;
Selah, Washington
—T & T Tavern; Appleton, Wise.—Club Terrace, Colonial
Inn. Ready?
Set?
Go-Go
YOU MAY SWING WHEN READY, GRIDLEY—With guitars
at
full vol-
ume and drums a-crashing. The New Beats sang their current hit, “Run Baby
Run” on a most unusual stage—the forward gun turret of Admiral Dewey’s
flagship, the cruiser Olympia. While they sang, the cameras ground away, un-
der the direction of Fran Williams, head of Deborah Television Productions,
Philadelphia. Williams
is now making films for use on audio-visual units and
is presently talking contracts with David Rosen, manufacturer of the Filmo-
theque-Discotheque machine. “Right now the record companies are on the side-
lines, waiting and watching to see what we can
do,” said Williams,
“I think
they’re going to like what they see.”
HERE & THERE—Tel-A-Sign prexy A. A. Steiger stopped by the big city
last week for a sales confab with the firm’s New York staffers Bill Gersh and
Jack Mitnik to discuss progress of the Scopitone film unit in this territory.
.
.
.
Eric Bernay, head man at A-1 Record
Sales, coinrow one
stop, reporting on
those singles currently hot with his
ops,
cites the following bust-out
sellers:
‘Spanish Harlem’ by King Curtis on Atco, ‘The Duck’ by Jackie Lee on Mir-
wood, ‘C.C. Rider’ by Bobby Powell on Whit and ‘Jenny Take A Ride’ by Mitch
Ryder and the Detroit Wheels on New Voice.
.
.
. NY Ops: keep your eye on a
red hot item from the Challenge label by the Knickerbockers called ‘Lies.’ The
single
is a smash in most parts of the country and just breakin’ big in New
York. Oughta make some noise
in the cash box
too.
.
.
. M.
L. Miller,
sales
exec at Gotham Educational Equipment Co. in New Rochelle, says their ‘Ellip-
tipool’ table
is enjoying fine sales
in the home market these days, citing
it as
a natural for the recreation room. Art Frigo, the inventor of the elliptical pool
table, has left Gotham to accept a position with Minnesota Mining and Mfg.,
Miller advises. The Gotham exec
is also pleased with the picture of the game
appearing in the December issue of Esquire Magazine.
Jersey Jottings
Jim Newlander, promotion exec out at Rowe Mfg.’s Whippany, N.J. branch,
advises that the factory force there
is presently operating at peak production,
attempting to fulfill the demands of Rowe’s distributors for vending equipment.
Woefully, Jim reports that the production staff had to come in to work a full
day last Friday (New Year’s Eve)
to get as many machines
as possible
off
the
line and out to the
distribs. But how
else could you
close a prosperous
year ? A particularly popular unit with vending ops these days
is Rowe’s ‘All-
Purpose’ vender, Newlander advised.
.
.
. Art Daddis, out at United Billiards
in Newark, says production is right on schedule and his United 6-pocket tables
should be in the hands of distributors all across the country by next week.
.
.
.
Bert Betti at Betson Enterprises closed
off a great year with equipment and
pool table
supply
sales. A big mover for Betson these
last weeks has been
ChiCoin’s
Bel-Air puck
shuffle
alley. Drawing considerable
operator
interest
on the Betson showroom
floor
lately has been American
Shufflboard’s
12
ft.
bank-shot table, a game which has been a perennial favorite for several years.
.
.
. New Year’s wishes have been extended to Jersey ops by Runyon’s Morris
Rood who says 1966 will definitely be a happy one for the Rowe
distrib with
the factory’s new ‘Band Stand’ phono and ‘Wall-Ette’ wallbox
(sales thus far
have been
terrific, Morris declared).
.
.
. Big
’66 plans are being mapped out
at American Shuffleboard by Nick Melone, Sol Lipkin and Gene Daddis, who
are closing out a really big ’65.

Gayles
Is Bang’s GM
DICK CURK:
IS FIT TO SURVIVE
NEW YORK—Juggy Gayles has been
named by Bang label chief Bert Berns
to
the
post
of general manager and
director
of
sales and promo
for
the
label. Gayles, a 30-year veteran in the
music
business,
has
left
an
album
production
post
at
Atlantic-Atco
to
assume
his new
affiliation.
The
first
records
that
Gayles
is
working on at Bang are new releases
by the Strangeloves and The Exciters,
“Night Time” and “A
Little
Bit Of
Soap,” respectively. Bang is currently
hitting with the McCoys’ “Fever” and
their LP, “Hang On Sloopy.”
Gayles’ career in the music business
dates
back
to
the
1930’s
when
he
worked promoting such
hits
as “You
Go To My Head,” “The Trolley Song”
and “White Christmas.” He organized
his own music publishing firm. United
Music, in 1947, and over the next five
years published a flock of hits includ-
ing
“The
Hucklebuck,”
“Somewhere
Along The Way” and
“I Won’t Cry
Anymore.”
In
the
1950’s, he became
a promo
man
for
the
Jubilee
label, where he
worked on hits like Della Reese’s “And
That Reminds Me” and Don Rondo’s
“White
Silver Sands.” He
joined the
Carlton
label
as
sales manager, and
was
associated
with
hits
by
Anita
Bryant
and
Jack
Scott.
With
Time
Records, he helped kick
off big LP’s
by Morgana King and Carmen McRae.
Last year, Gayles was hired by 20th
Fox
to
organize
their
new
budget
label.
Movietone.
He
later
joined
Atlantic-Atco.
NEW YORK—In
this
fast-stepping
record industry, survival of more than
a year with any idea
is considered a
major
accomplishment.
Successes
of
a
thirteen
year
duration
can
be
counted on the finger of one hand.
That’s
what
makes
Dick
Clark’s
continuous success with his “American
Bandstand” TV show such a miracle
in
the
fickle
record
industry.
The
Saturday ABC-TV’er has seen dozens
of
trends
go
by
including
calypso,
twist and
a
host
of
others and has
seen many child star disk names be-
come
mature,
top-drawer
attractions
through the
years. And even though
the music business
is nothing
like
it
was when Clark got started on Band-
stand,
the
MC-deejay’s
sensitive
an-
tenae have been able to sense what the
teenagers like and want and Clark has
continued to make it a practice to give
them the music and performers they
want.
This is one of the reasons Clark has
such a successful advertising consult-
ancy division which advises ad agen-
cies
and
manufacturers
about
teen
tastes and
desires.
But the consultancy division is only
one of Clark’s many successful enter-
prises. Another TV venture,
the
five
times a week “Where The Action Is”
TV Show is currently the second high-
est rated daytime TV show and the
#1
daytime show
on
the ABC
net-
work.
It
is
estimated
that
the
“Ac-
tion” show reaches between 18 and 20
million viewers a week
all across the
country.
Clark uses and exposes ap-
proximately 12
different teen acts a
week
on
his
Action
and
Bandstand
shows.
“Where
The
Action
Is”
will
also
become
a
touring
in-person show
in
the spring when it covers the country

i-/ V-/ Jr
.
Anthony and The Imperials actually
broke in their “adult” act New Year’s
Eve

In

Record Number
(47) Won
RIAA Awards
In
1965
NEW YORK—An
all-time
high
of
forty-seven
records,
eleven
singles
and
thirty-six albums, were
certified
for Gold Record Awards during 1965,
according to an announcement by the
Record Industry Association of Amer-
ica.
The
eleven
singles
are
the
greatest number
certified
in any one
year since RIAA’s authentication pro-
gram was initiated in 1958.
To
qualify
for
an
RIAA-certified
Gold
Record
Award,
a
single
must
have amassed a
sale
of
at
least one
million
copies;
an album must have
accumulated a minimum of $1 million
in factory sales. Sales figures are sub-
jected to audit by an independent firm
of certified public accountants in order
to qualify for an RIAA Award.
Capitol
and MGM
led
the
singles
parade
of
goldies
with
three
each.

singles awards went
to “Down-
town,” Petula Clark (Warner Bros.);

'Christmas Candy' Promo
For Sweet-Toothed
Listeners
NEW
YORK—During
the
holiday
season Capitol Records came up with
a
sugarsweet
gimmick
to
test
the
appeal
of one
of
its Christmas
LP’s,
a package
called “Christmas Candy”
by
Eddie
Dunstedder.
Marking
the
first time that the label has ever pur-
chased a substantial amount
of East
Coast EM time, the promo campaign/
contest kicked
off on
station WPIX-
FM with
cuts from the album being
played
at
various
times
throughout
the day. Listeners were asked to name
as many of the grooves as they could
identify and mail their answers on to
the firm. The grand prize for the win-
ner was
a brand new
Capitol
stereo
phonograph,
plus
a
2-pound
box
of
Whitman’s candy and
a copy
of
the
album.
An
additional
50
runnerup
listeners were
also awarded boxes of
Whitman’s
candy
and
copies
of
the
Dunstedder “candy.”
The
station claimed that the event
was
one
of
their
most
successful
stunts ever staged. Sponsored jointly
by Capitol Records, the Whitman Co.
and
the
outlet,
the
stunt
reportedly
drew over 1500 postcards and
letters
of response.
Shown smiling
in the photo above,
left
to
right,
are
station
personality
Charlie Whitaker, grand prize winner
Mrs. E. Rowe and Capitol promo man
Tom Rogan.

Carl
Davis Forms
Production
Firm
CHICAGO—Recording producer
Carl
Davis,
formerly A&R head
at Okeh
Records, has recently formed his own
independent production company, Carl
Davis & Associates. Gerald Sims, who
was
associated
with
Davis
at
Okeh,
is associated with him in the new firm.
Davis
is
currently
contracted
to record Mary Wells, Gene Chandler,
Dee Dee Sharp, Chubby Checker, the
Orlons, Brooks O’Dell, and the Diplo-
mats. Other popular recording artists
are under consideration at this time,
according to Davis.
Carl Davis & Associates
is located
in suite 5716 in the Marina City Tower
in Chicago.

ASCAP Adds To
Award Panel
NEW YORK— WNEW-New York air
personality William
B. Williams and
Professor Donald
E. Brown,
director
of the School of Music of Barrington
College, Rhode
Island, have been ap-
pointed
to serve on ASCAP’s
special
awards
panels,
according
to
an
an-
nouncement by Stanley Adams, presi-
dent of the performing rights society.
Williams, emcee
of the “Make Be-
lieve Ballroom” show since 1957,
is a
native
of
Babylon, Long
Island. He
will join ASCAP’s popular-production
awards
panel, whose
other members
are T. Edward Hambleton, co-founder
and co-director of New York’s Phoenix
Theatre, and producer of many shows;
the
Honorable Hayden
Proctor,
As-
sociate Justice of the Supreme Court
of New
Jersey;
and
Dr.
Marshall
Stearns, Associate Professor
of Eng-
lish
at Hunter
College,
jazz
expert
and author of the book, “The Story Of
Jazz.”
Professor
Brown
is
a
native
of
Lowell
Massachusetts.
He
attended
the
New
England
Conservatory
of
Music and was graduated from Bar-
rington
College
in
1947.
In
1950 he
received
the
degree
of
Bachelor
of
Music from
Westminster
Choir
Col-
lege, and in 1954 a Master of Sacred
Music
degree from
the Union
Theo-
logical
Seminary. He
has
completed
resident
studies toward
his doctorate
at Boston
University.
In
addition
to
serving
as music
director
in
several
churches. Professor Brown has given
many organ recitals. He is a colleague
of the American
Guild
of
Organists,
an
executive
vice
president
of
the
National
Church
Music
Fellowship,
and
a member
of
the
College Music
Society, the American Association
of
University Professors and the N.E.A.
He will be joining ASCAP’s Stand-
ard Awards Panel, which
consists
of
Donald Engle, director of the Martha
Baird
Rockefeller
Fund
for
Music,
Inc., formerly a manager of the Phila-
delphia
Symphony
Orchestra;
Dr.
Frederick
Fennell,
conductor
of
the
Miami Symphony
Orchestra;
Walter
Hendl, director of the Eastman School
of Music
at the
University
of Roch-
ester, formerly associate conductor of
the Chicago Symphony; and Dr. Louis
G. Worsen,
director
of music
in
the
Philadelphia public schools.

DAVE. DEE, DOZY, BEAKY, MICK & TICK
(Fontana 1537)
This crew of newcomers are currently scoring in their native England
with “You Make It Move” and there’s no reason why they can’t duplicate
that success on this
side of the foam. The tune
is a rhythmic romantic
pounder about a love-sick guy who really wants his ex-gal to return to
him. “No Time”
is a hard-driving, fast-moving ditty with an infectious
repeating riff.

of

penned tune which
is featured in the Beatles best-selling “Rubber Soul”
LP. Both
the

“Jailer Bring Me
Water.”

HOLLYWOOD:
Back in November we devoted sev-
eral paragraphs to Columbia Records’
Ben Bagley projects—a winsome dedi-
cation
to the seldom recorded works
of
America’s
great
composers.
It’s
gratifying to hear from Bruce Lund-
vall, of Columbia’s A&R staff in N.Y.
that another such album was released
last month.
It’s titled “More Cole Por-
ter
Re-visited”
and
Lundvall
notes
that the
sales on the
first Porter
al-
bum
“are
not overwhelming by any
means. But they are consistent week
after week and ultimately
I think we
will profit nicely by this release.” He
adds
“the
interest
in Bagley then
is
our ever prevalent interest in explor-
ing new
ground. The
opportunity
of
expanding the existing show market,
reaching the new “in” crowd, the “col-
lectors” and perhaps beyond,
is
cer-
tainly
reason
enough
for
these
ven-
tures.”
Again,
let
us
say
that we
don’t
think
you’ll
find
these
titles
on
the
best
seller
charts. But we
earnestly
hope
they’ll
sell well enough for the
project
to
continue.
Incidentally,
our
first
introduction
to
Bagley
was
through
a
memorable
show
titled
“Shoestring
Review”
which
he
pro-
duced. As we recall, anyone fortunate
enough
to have
attended
a perform-
ance
was
handed
a
souvenir
shoe-
string as he entered the
theater—an
obvious
but
canny
allusion
to
the
show’s
slender
circumstances.
Since
we
attended
alone
it
took
several
months before we finally found much
use
for
the
singular
gratuity.
.
.

Publish Rodgers Fact Book
NEW YORK—A new
reference
vol-
ume,
the
“Richard
Rodgers
Fact
Book,”
is now
available
to
libraries,
schools, newspaper a id magazine edi-
tors, and radio and television program
directors.
The 582-page book contains factual
information concerning all of Rodgers’
productions to date, and includes cast
listings,
songs,
lengths
of Broadway
runs,
touring
companies,
excerpts
from opening night
reviews, and
re-
vivals.
Film
and
television
produc-
tions are also covered
in the book, as
well as a general bibliography, a dis-
cography, and an index.
Professionally
interested
agencies
or
individuals may
obtain
the
book
without
cost from
the Lynn
Farnol
Group,
Inc.,
50
Rockefeller
Plaza,
New York, New York 10020.

Grammy Balloting
Deadline This Week (18)
NEW YORK—This
Tuesday
(18)
is
the
deadline
date
for
the mailing
o.
all ballots in the first round of voting
for this year's Grammy Awards.
All
active
members
of
NARAS
(National Academy of Recording Arts
and
Sciences)
received
their
ballots
and
lists
of
eligible
records
directly
after New
Year’s
Day.
Listings
in-
cluded more than 4,100 entries, a new
high
in
NARAS
history,
spread
through 47
categories, including pop,
classical,
jazz,
country
and
western
as well as engineering, composing, ar-
ranging,
album
cover
art
and
liner
notes.
NARAS’
president,
Francis
M.
Scott,
again
reminded
the
voting
members of the necessity for selective
choices.
“Your
vote,”
he
stated,
“is
the
voice
of
the
record
industry’s
knowledgeable,
professional
creators
and interpreters.” He then emphasized
the
necessity
for having “knowledge
of
every
record
you
vote
for,”
and
wound up by emphasizing
that “you
need
not
make
an
entry
in
every
category.
.
.
. Your vote
is
solicited
only where you can cast
it in fairness
to yourself, the competing artists, and
your fellow members.”
Final
nominees,
based
on
current
voting,
will
be
announced
in
mid-
February
after
all
ballots have been
tabulated by
the
accounting
firm
of
Haskins
and
Sells.
The
eventual
Grammy
winners
will
be
announced
at
simultaneous
presentation
awards
in New
York, Los
Angeles,
Chicago
and
Nashville
the
evening
of
Tues-
day, March
15.
Academy 'Prelims' See
The Big 3 In The Lead
NEW YORK—The
Big
3
(Robbins-
Feist-Miller) was awarded five out of
10 nominations in the two music cate-
gories
to lead the publishing
field
in
the recently announced Golden Globes
Awards
of

Hollywood
Foreign

In

clicked

for
‘The

the
theme from “The Sandpiper” film and
“Forget Domani,” the lead song from
“The Yellow Rolls-Royce.”
Other “Best Song” nominations
in-
cluded
“The

Of
Cat
Ballou”
published
by
Colgems,
“Sweetheart
Tree” from
“The
Great
Race”
pub-
lished

East

Music
and
the
title song “That Funny Feeling” pub-
lished by
T. M.
Music.
Big
3 also drew three nominees
in
the “Best Score” category with nods
to Johnny Mandel’s music from “The
Sandpiper,” Riz
Ortolani’s scoring of
“The Yellow
Rolls-Royce” and Mau-
rice Jarre’s “Dr. Zhivago”
score. The
other
two
nominees
selected
in
the
“Best
Score”
category
were
“Battle
Of
The
Bulge”
published
by
Union
Music
and
“The
Great
Race”
score
published by East Hill.
Final
award
winners
will
be
an-
nounced
January
31
at
the
Golden
Globes banquet with the event set for
telecasting
on
the
Andy
Williams
Show.
Following
the
Golden
Globes
outing. The Big
3
will be eyeing the
Academy Awards race with the pub-
bery
particularly
grooming
“The
Shadow Of Your
Smile”
as
a
“Best
Song”
candidate.

HARM Awards
Voting
Underway
PHILADELPHIA—Ballots
for
the
annual awards of the National Asso-
ciation of Record Merchandisers have
gone out to the regular members
(rec-
ord rack merchandisers)
of the asso-
ciation. This
is in pi’eparation for the
presentation
of
the NARM Awards
at the NARM awards banquet, which
will
be
held
Wednesday,
March
9,
1966,
at
the La Ronde
of
the
Fon-
tainebleau Hotel, Miami Beach, Flor-
ida. This is the highlight of the social
calendar
at
the
Eighth
Annual
NARM Convention, which convenes at
the Fontainebleau on Sunday, March
6 .
Excluding
kiddie
and
low-priced
lines, Columbia-Epic
leads the nomi-
nees with 12, followed by Victor
(11),
Capitol
(10),
Warner
Bros.-Reprise
(9), MGM/Verve
(7), Decca, London-
Parrot
and
Mercury-Smash-Philips,
with
6
each, UA
(5),
Atlantic-Atco
and
Liberty-Imperial-Dolton,
3
each,
Motown, Vanguard, A&M, 2 each, and
1
each
for Parkway,
Philles,
Vista,
Kapp, Starday, Musicor, Scepter, Ca-
det and Hickory.
In making the announcement, Jules
Malamud,
executive
director
of
the
association, stated that voting was on
the basis of actual sales in the 30,000
outlets
serviced
by
the
record
mer-
chandisers of NARM
in
all 50 states
of the
country.
Ballots
are returned
directly
to
an
independent
agency,
and are tabulated there. No prior an-
nouncement
of
the winners
is made
until the evening of the Awards Ban-
quet.
Charles H.
Schlang
(Mershaw
of America, Inc., Albany, New York)
will serve as chairman of the awards
banquet.

tions

Capitol Expands C&W Dept.
(Continued from page 6)
throughout the
South. A member
of
the Country Music Association, he
is
regarded
as
an
expert
in
the C&W
field.

Tal-
lant said that Capitol had been care-
fully studying the C&W market and
planning the expansion move for the
past year.
“Growth
of
the
market
has
been
evident
for
some
time,”
he
said.
“Large Northern
cities such
as
C!hi-
cago
with WJJD, Los
Angeles with
KGBS
and New
York
with WJRZ,
have been highly successful and have
shown that C&W is not just music for
one section of the country or for small
towns.
Sales
have
been
another key
factor.
Today,
top C&W
artists
like
Buck
Owens,
sell
better than many
pop
stars.

kets in an attempt to get airplay for

on

Last week this CB rep had the pleasure of having a chat with Goar Mestre,
head
of Proartel TV program producing company
related
to
Channel
13
in
Buenos Aires and other stations in several Latin American countries. One of
the
points touched was
the amount
of
difficulties met by
the
exchange
of
programs between
other
countries
and
Argentina,
since
here
the
electrical
current is 50 cycles and in other places the 60 cycle system that
is used does
not allow the direct use of video-tape; the film used does not have good quality
of image and sound, which makes
it impractical. However, some improvements
in this field may be expected in the future, according to Mestre.
The latest news from RCA
is that Juan Ramon’s latest “Tu Eres Eso,”
is
selling
wonderfully,
which
puts Ramon among
the
top
artists
in
the
teen
market.
Other
reports from RCA
include
a new
single by Johnny
Tedesco
(a cover in Spanish
of “Eve Of Destruction”), another one by tango music
celebrity Anibal Troilo (“Cancion De Ave Maria”), one by Los Playeros (“Mia
y Tuyo”), Gianni Morandi’s famous “Si Fa Sera”—also selling well—and Rita
Pavone’s “Supercalifragilistic,” backed by “Plip,” also a single with good sales
potential.
The promotion department
of Phonogram
is
really busy
these
days:
the
release of the first Verve LP’s “Astrud Gilberto,” “Count Basie-Sammy Davis,”
several local outings “Ovacionados-Los Quilla Huasi,” “Verano Con Los Clau-
dios,”
a new
single by Cesar
Isella,
recently
exited from
Los
Fronterizos
provide the work. There
is
also an album tagged “Cita Con Las
Estrellas,”
featuring
artists
like
Luis
Bravo,
Sheila, Herve
Vilard,
France
Gall, Dusty
Springfield and
others,
which
is
providing
songs
for
air
play
at
all
local
stations, and
is believed to reach good sales marks.
CBS’
press
department
is
planning
ahead
with
the
new
programs
of
“Cancionisima,”
its TV’er on Channel 11, turned into a firm promotional
spot.
One of the top stars of the program
is recently inked Nancy Li, who’s already
cutting her second single
after the
success of “La Playa.” The
lark made a
special appearance on TV
13’s “Escala
Musical,” and has
olfers from
other
programs. Folk singer Jorge Cafrune started a five-month tour of the prov-
inces, and plans to appear even in the smallest places. His new album, devoted
to “El Chacho,” is due this month.
Jorge Closas, head of Iberia Airlines’ public relations department, has been
busy
lately working with
record
companies,
arranging
releases
with
slight
shades of the Iberia colors. Among the latest are “Flying By Iberia,” cut for
RCA by Pablo del Rio, “Tangos Around The World” (Roberto Pansera-Poly-
dor), and singles by Los Cinco Latinos (Music Hall) and now Claudio (Odeon
Pops), titled “Maja De Goya.” Now, Closas
is planning “Clasicos De
Iberia,”
which feature works by well known Spanish classical music composers.
Famous
has
released
a new album by
Colombian
artists Bovea
and
the
Vallenatos, featuring twelve tunes penned by Rafael Escalona and a single by
the Yardbirds, under an arrangement with EMI of London. Also coming from
England
is
an album by Frank
Ifield,
with
titles
like
“Love
Walked
In,”
“Stardust,” “Forever Mine,” among others.
Lagos
Publishers, now working
also
in the international

the
release of “Tu Sei Quello,” by
local star Juan Ramon, teen group Los TNT
and original recorder Orietta Berti. “Tu
Sei
.
.
.” comes from

is selling well in the JR version.
Maestro Lucio Milena has finished the music for the
film “Muchachos Im-
pacientes,” and
is completing “Demetrio, Silbame La Marcha Nupcial,” with
Drinque Farias and Zulma Faiad. He has also been recording and arranging
with Pepito Perez, Rosamel Araya
(Disc Jockey), Roberto Yanes (CBS) and
Atilio Marinelli, among others.
We have just received a letter from publisher Gigi Gallo, now working with
GTA in Italy, who reports several recordings made by his brother Tullio for
this company. Among them appears the main theme from “Blindfold,” written
by Argentine musician Lalo
Schifrin, who
is currently
in
the
States. Other
local arrangers like Alberto Corvini and Pocho Gatti are expected by Gallo in

Surco
is preparing

are Sonny &

first, and the music from “Killer Joe,” also on Atlantic. There

a wonderful set of three records cut by the Fine Arts Quartet, with Mozart’s
Quartets
^’or Strings. The box also contains a booklet with explanatory texts.

Industry Jumps On
NEW YORK—Not
since
the
twist
craze exploded
six years ago has the
music industi*y been captivated by any
fad as much as ‘Batamania’ which, at
presstime, has stimulated the release
of fifteen separate records.
All
of
the
recordings,
of
course,
were springboarded into existence by
ABC-TV’s
twice-weekly
“Batman”
show. The
program,
w'hich
portrays
the
daring-do
exploits
of
the famed
comic book crime-fighter and his teen-
age
sidekick,
Robin,
has
registered
impressive figures in the early ratings
race
and
has
been
the
recipient
of
across-the-board praise from the con-
sumer press. The fascination of “Bat-
man” is far more than kid-deep. Audi-
ence
composition
data
reveals
that
the
stanza
is
watched by
the
very
same
sophisticated
adults who
have
made camp
an
integral
part
of
the
contemporary
sub-culture.
The main-theme
of the Greenway-
20th
Century-Fox
production
was
penned by Neal
Hefti and published
by Miller Music. In addition to Hefti,
who has released his own composition
on
the RCA
Victor
label,
there
are
five
covers
of
the
tune
:
A1
Caiola
(United Artists), the Gallants (Capi-
tol),
the
Riddlers
(Mike),
Labert
Ellis (A&M) and the Marketts (War-
ner Bros.). Nelson Riddle, who scored
the “Batman” background, is also re-
ported slicing the theme for 20th Cen-
tury-Fox with a lineup of other labels
racing
to
cut
still more
versions
of
the
selection. Meanwhile back at the
Big
3, the pubbery
is
setting follow-
up
plans
for
record
exploitation
of
more Batman music via development
of new tunes from
the Riddle
score.
But
that’s only part
of the
story.
Nine other manufacturers have rush-
released
decks
utilizing
the Batman
title but not the Miller theme. These
independent
versions
include
entries
by
the
Spotlights
(Smash),
Jan &
Dean (Liberty), Robin & the Avengers
(Ardent),
the
4
Of
Us
(Hideout),
Ricky
&
the
Riddlers
(Panorama),
Scotty McKay (Claridge), Gate Wes-
ley-Billy
LaMont
(Atlantic),
Gene
Simmons
(Hi)
and
the
Campers
San Remo Convenes
NEW YORK—This week the eyes of
the international music industry
will
be focused on San Remo, Italy, where
the
16th
annual
song
festival
will
convene
(27-29). This week’s interna-
tional cover (page 55) pictures all the
artists who will participate. In addi-
tion, a two page spread (pages 58-59)
includes the names and addresses
of
key publishers who will be in attend-
ance.
Vee-Jay
Issues
Notice To Trade
NEW YORK—In a signed
letter
re-
ceived by Cash Box last week, James
Bracken,
president
of Vee-Jay
Rec-
ords, made_ the following
statement:
“Upon advice of counsel and our
ac-
countants,
due
to
existing
financial
difficulties, we
filed a petition for an
arrangement
in
the
United
States
District
Court,
Chicago,
111.
These
proceedings were
instituted with
the
expectation that the corporation could
be
reorganized
on
a
sound
financial
basis, and that the equities inherent in
a going business
could be preserved
for the benefit of our customers and
our creditors.”

which Pepper will handle along with

“has

of Capitol’s hit records these past few

NEW YORK—Following an

Shown

sicurrently represented

Kurf-z Takes Over
Cameo/Parkway
Post
NEW YORK—Phil Landwehr, manag-
ing director
of Cameo/Parkway Rec-
ords,
announced
last week
that
the
duties formerly performed by Herman
Kaplan, who
has
resigned from
the
company,
have
been
taken
over
by
George
Kurtz,
administrative
vice-
president of Premier Albums.
Kurtz
will
supervise
the
coordina-
tion
of day-to-day
activities between
the firm’s Philadelphia and New York
offices. “It is my intention to develop,”
Kurtz
stated,
“a
closer
liaison
be-
tween our people in Philadelphia and
sales manager Jerry Shifrin than has
existed in the past. The rapid growth
of C/P and its new ‘open door’ policy
makes
this
imperative.”
Kurtz
has
assumed this new function in accord-
ance with Premier’s management con-
tract with Cameo/Parkway.
Kaplan
stated that he
will
shortly
announce his future plans.

New
York’s
recent
transit
strike
not
only
crippled
public
transporta-
tion but caused a critical blood short-
age, as blood donors were unable
to
get
to
the
city’s
blood
centers.
To
combat
the
shortage,
WMCA-New
York ran
a campaign
that provided
nearly
125
pints
of
blood.
Through
its public
affairs department director
David C. Horowitz, the outlet arranged
for the American Red Cross
to pro-
vide special buses to shuttle donors to
blood centers throughout the five bor-
oughs
of New York. Announcements
were aired urging listeners to donate
a pint of blood during the
crisis, and
informing
them
about
the
“Blood
Bus”
routes. As
a
special
incentive
for giving blood during this time
of
need, those participating in the cam-
paign
were
awarded
the
station’s
gold-and-black Good Guy sweatshirts.
Now featured on a weekly series on
ABC-TV,
Batman
and
Robin
are
making their way back to the hearts
of
all Americans. Taking advantage
of
the
craze,
KHJ-Hollywood
along
with
Greenway
Productions,
20th
Century-Fox TV and the ABC
Tele-
vision network
is promoting
a “Bat-
man
Secret Number”
contest. Every
hour the station reveals new clues to
the unlisted number of the batphone
hotline to the batcave. The
first win-
ning postcard sender
will join Adam
West and Burt Ward

HOLLYWOOD:
The
Academy
of
Motion
Picture
Arts and Sciences, way back in 1934
A.D.,
officially
recognized
the
sig-
nificance
of
the
popular
song’s
con-
tribution
to
films
when
it
added
that
category
to
its
list
of
annual
awards.
The
first
Oscar
went
to
Con Conrad and Herb Magidson
for
“The
Continental”
from
the
Fred
Astaire-Ginger
Rogers
musical
“The
Gay
Divorcee.”
Through
the
years,
right up
to
this 38th running of the
annual Oscar
derby, the
selection
of
the ten contenders and
five nominees
have been made by the music branch
of
the
Academy,
a
group
of
some
250
motion
picture
tunesmiths
and
lyricists, most of whom reside in the
L.
A.
area.
This
group
has,
on
occasion, been accused of being some-
what provincial
in
their
selection
of
the
nominating
songs.
If
true,
it
could
be
the
reason
why,
for
the
second
successive
year,
the
Beatles’
effort
has
been
scratched
from
the
entries
in
the
Oscar
derby.
Last
year
it was “A Hard
Day’s Night”
which was
left in the paddock. This
year
it’s
“Help”,
which,
by
Ringo,
is not listed in the top ten contenders.
In any
event,
it’s
.just
possible
that
this year’s award will go to two N. Y.
based
writers,
Burt
Bacharach
and
Hal David, who composed
the smash
title song from “What’s New Pussy-
cat”.
At
this
writing
insiders
are
favoring
“The
Shadow
of
Your
Smile”
from
“The
Sandpiper”
with
“Pussycat”
as
the
strong
second
choice.
It
should be
recalled
that
at
battling each other with two opposing
tunes (“Pussycat” and “Cat Ballou”).
The
five
nominating
songs
will
be
announced, we
hear,
on
Feb.
21
at
which time
the
entire Academy
will
vote
on
the
songs
selected
by
the
music branch. Which brings us back
to
the
total
neglect
of
the
Beatles
who,
one
of
these
years,
should
be
recognized
by
the
Academy.
The
Oscar
is
probably
the
only
major
award
they
haven’t
received
as
yet.
And
don’t you
agree
that
this year
the
music
branch
of
the
Academy
could have used just a
little “Help”?
.

ONE STOP IN FULL GEAR—New York’s
latest
one-stop
operation, King
Karol, opened shop recently at 444 West St. According to Ben Carol, the firm
is “a one-stop
in the
old sense
in that we are dedicated
to
service.” In
this
regard, Carol says, every thing possible
is done to obtain any kind of record
for his customers. Inventory
is valued at over $1 million,with all disks appear-
ing on
trade
paper
charts
in
stock. The company
has two
delivery
trucks
(one
of them
is shown
above)
that
provide
free
delivery anywhere
in
the
Metropolitan area. Because of its location near the exit of the Lincoln Tunnel,
the company expects a large
clientele from New Jersey. Customers can
also
make use of a parking lot across the street, use of which
is free. The one-stop
is under the direction of Phil King (right, top right photo), who
is assisted by
Tom Morrow and Stan Gruber.

Braverman-Mirisch
LOS ANGELES—Norman Greer has

first became known in music circles in
1956 as personal press agent for Pat
Boone.

Allan
Roberts
Dies
NEW YORK—Allan Roberts, 60 year
old composer, died in Hollywood, Fla.
of a heart condition on Jan.
14. The
composer, who was born and educated
in
Brooklyn,
N.Y.,
began
his
song-
writing career while he was an audi-
tor for a New York
hotel. He wrote
special
material
for
night
club
per-
formers and went on to gain contracts
with
various motion
picture
studios.
Some
of
the
songs
he has penned
are
“Me,
Myself
and
I
Are
All
In
Love With You,” “You Always Hurt
The One You Love,” “Put The Blame
On Marne,” “Good, Good, Good,” and
“What’s The Good Word,
Mr.
Blue-
bird.” The pictures for which he has
written scores include “Gilda,” “Down
To Earth,” and “Thrill Of Bluebird.”
Roberts,
who
was
a
member
of
ASCAP,
is
survived
by
his
widow
and two sons.

David & Jonathan

other artists, David and Jonathan de-
cided
to wax
a song
written by
the
Beatles
;
the
result
is
their
Capitol
chart rider “Michelle” (number 45 on

Both
lads
are

NEW YORK—Lyricist Fred Wise, 50,
died suddenly last week
(18)
in New
York
City.
In addition
to penning
a
vast amount
of
songs,
36
of which
were
recorded
by
Elvis
Presley,
he
was a practicing psychologist.
Wise was born
in New York City
and graduated from Columbia Univer-
sity. Before he began writing
songs,
he worked
in
the
publicity
dept,
at
MGM. A member
of ASCAP for 25
years, he was penning songs long be-
fore he became a psychologist in 1955.
He wrote many of his hit tunes with
Randy Starr.
Wise’s pennings have
included “A
Your Adorable,” “Misirlou,” “Let Me
Go Lover,”
“I Won’t Cry Anymore,”
“A
Hand
Full
Of
Stars,”
“Lonely
Blue
Boy,”
“Accidentally
On
Pur-
pose,” “Wooden
Heart,”
“Don’t Ask
Me Why,” “Rocka-Hulla Baby,” and
“Follow
That
Dream,”
and
many
others.
His earlier songs include “Nightin-
gale,” “You, You, You Are The One,”
“Roses
In
The
Rain,”
“Let’s
Har-
monize,” “Wise Old Owl,”
“Let’s Go
This a-way,” “The Robe Of Calvary,”
and
“The
Chocolate
Sundae
On A
Saturday Night.”
Wise is sui’vived by his wife, Elaine,
and his daughter. Erica.

Paur’s
recently-released
Mercury album, “Sings Of New Na-
tions,” which
also includes two songs
from Israel. The LP has been chosen
for
submission
for an award
at
the
first
World
Festival
of Negro
Arts
which
will
take
place
in
Apr.
at
Dakar,
Senegal.
The
festival
will
gather
recordings,
books,
paintings,
sculpture and
films representative
of
Negro
culture
from
all
the
nations
of the world. The de Paur Chorus
is
the first American group of artists to
be announced as appearing there and
will end
the
African
tour
with two
concerts
in Dakar on Apr.
7 and
14.

SKY HIGH — Quartette Tres Bien — Decca DL
4715/74715
The Quartette Tres Bien
serves up
a tasteful
setting of Afro-American percussion for the eight
tunes included in this package. The vibrant beat
of conga drums and bongos, the exciting rhythm
of a piano, and the solid beat of a bass are used
to produce a new kind of sound to the tracks fea-
tured. The group should find a warm reception to
the
set which includes
such songs
as “Shangri-
La,” “Fly Me To The Moon,” and “Say April.”

In Amsterdam, Phonogram organized a press-conference in the first week of
January to celebrate the simultaneous release of two LP’s by Holland’s lead-
ing cabaret-groups: Lurelei and ShafFy Chantant. Dutch singer-actor-composer
Ramses Shaffy was invited for the occasion to come to Lurelei’s own Theatre,
managed by Eric Herfst, leader of the Lurelei group. A hundred of Holland’s
leading journalists and
officials from broadcasting and theatre-world formed
the selected ensemble for which both Lurelei and Shaffy Chantant did a special

vocal repertoire in which mild, bizarre humor is prominent. The star in Lurelei
is Jasperina de Jong, outstanding lark and humorist. The satirical repertoire is
written, for the greater part, by gifted musician and poet Guus Vleugel.
