Marcos Augusto
Nobili, who
is heading
the promo
department
of Discos
RGE,
is proud and happy
to
confirm the fact that the two albums by
the
Zimbo
Trio, the best small instrumental group
of Brazil
in
1965, are being
released in the U.S. through Liberty Records. This way, the
trio will be pre-
sented
to
the
U.S.
public and
that
will
open
the
door
for
a
future
visit.
Rubinho, the drummer of the combo, considered to be the best in this country,
could not attend the latest programs of the “Teatro Record” during Christmas
and New Year because he was operated on recently
in
Curitiba, where
he,
together with
Luiz Chaves and Amilton Godoy
(piano)
were
receiving
the
“Pinheiro De Ouro” award for the best trio of the year in the State of Parana.
French music
is back
in Brazil among the
best-sellers, mainly through
the
releases of the Barclay label, represented here by RGE: Charles Aznavour,
is
being appointed by the critics as the best international attraction of the year,
while Dalida is scoring with her renditions of “Zorba Le Grec” and
“11 Silen-
zio.”
Another difficulty is arising in the record business in Brazil, which
is bring-
ing a lot of commotion within the companies and in the Association of Record
Producers. Due to the period of sacrifice we wrote about in our Review 1965,
high cost of
life,
etc., the musicians through their Union are trying
to force
a raise of 100% over the hourly price for recording
sessions. The matter
is
not yet solved and this may have great infiuence for the future of the record
business
in
Brazil.
We had a chance to talk again with Paulinho Machado De Carvalho, Presi-
dent of Emissoras Unidas who, as we had the opportunity to write before,
is
responsible not only for the presentation in this country of the biggest inter-
national names but also of the best promotion of Brazilian music
in this past
year. The big problem of bringing international attractions to Brazil, accord-
ing to radio and TV,
is the saturation of names that are
of interest to the
local
public, that
is, since
all the well-known
artists were already presented
here,
there would be
little
interest
in bringing them back
(exceptions
are
naturally Frank Sinatra, Dean Martin and a few others)
; on the other hand,
the new names, who are already top performers and recording names outside,
are practically unknown to the Brazilian public and would not gross enough
money. The only way that these well known stars can be brought here
is by
taking
advantage
of
the
artists’
tour
to
other
Latin-American
countries,
mainly Argentina. While we wait for the international stars to come, Paulinho
very wisely turned to local artists and
is giving them full support. He
is pre-
senting the biggest names of the Brazilian Popular Music
(traditional, bossa-
nova and teen-music) with the same support as were shown international per-
formers. This has given a good boost
in the
sale
of the
Brazilian produced
records and the local music and artists in general. A new TV program, in the
“Discotheque”
style for the teen
set
is being produced by Eduardo Moreira
and Bob Corte-Real, for Paulinho’s TV-Record (Channel 7 of Sao Paulo) and
is bringing new interest to the international big-beat. The new wave of Bra-
zilian compositions of that type of teen-music
is competing with the
original
on a strong basis. Note the top selling discs in this new area by the Brazilian
musicians and artists.
Cash Box—January
29,

RAMBLINGS
NEW YORK:
One of the truly exiciting new art-
ists of today
is back in New York at
a familiar Village spot, “Gerde’s Folk
City.”
The
singer-guitarist-composer
is Jose
Feliciano and even
the mere
mention
of his name
stirs the crowd
at the folkery as it did last week when
it was announced that he was coming
to perform
(1-15)
and that he has
a
new RCA-Victor LP, “A Bag Full Of
Soul.” Jose
is being billed as “Gerde’s
Favorite” and considering the
artists
who are wont to pei’form at the club
this is no small praise.
man Pat Pipolo. Along with the group
came
the
lark’s
label
debut
“Every
Now and Then.”
.
.
• The current group
at
“Harlow’s,”
the
Scoundrels,
have
a new
deck
for Kama
Sutra
titled
“La
Bola.”
.
.
. The Toys going
the
college concert route during Feb. will
break during the month
to
cut
their
next single.
.
.
.
Scott English going
on
the
road
with
the

HOLLYWOOD:
David Lean’s MGM production “Dr.
Zhivago,” comparable

The Wind”
in
scope,
story and
tech-
nical achievement,
includes
a
related
title
in Maurice Jarre’s “Lara’s Love
Theme”. It also has much of the same
sweep, brilliance and dramatic impact
that made “Tara’s Theme” a standard.
Several
versions
of
the
Jarre
song
have
already been
released with

Teddy Randazzo treatment on MGM
getting most

the

here.
An-

Sherman on Epic and Roger Williams
has just cut an instrumental for Kapp.
There

more,

pleted a lyric. The score, incidentally,

time
in
Santa Monica.

Dick Clark's Youth
Fair To Open
In
Chi.
CHICAGO—Dick
Clark,
star
of
the
“American
Bandstand”
and
“Where
The Action Is” TV’ers,
will bring his
Young
World’s
Fair
to
Chicago’s
International Amphitheatre from Apr.
22-May
1
for
ten
days
of
concerts
featuring
top
recording
stars
and
exhibits by
local
and
national
firms.
Highlighting
the
opening
night
of
the 20-concert series
(two each day),
will be Dick Clark and the entire cast
of ABC-TV’s “Where The Action
Is,”
including Paul Revere and the Raiders,
Linda
Scott,
Keith
Allison,
Steve
Alaimo
and
all
the
Action
Dancers.
Special guest stars for opening night
only will be Gary Lewis and the Play-
boys, Billy Joe Royal and the Knicker-
bockers. Stars for the remaining per-
formances
will be announced
shortly.
Clark will be master of ceremonies for
each show.
In addition to the concerts, the Fair
will present
exhibits by national and
local
firms
displaying
their products.
Exhibits will be themed around prod-
uct
and
service,
utilizing
audience
participation
displays,
contests,
give-
aways, and entertainment. There
will
also
be
educational and
instructional
clinics,
celebrity
interviews,
home-
maker
classes, Dick
Clark’s National
Skateboard
Competition
and
many
other events.
More
than
200,000
Chicago
area
young people are expected
to
attend.
HARNELL TO COLO. — Pianist Joe
Harnell, who achieved disk fame with
the
hit
version
of
“Fly Me To The
Moon,” has
signed an
exclusive
con-
tract
with
Columbia
Records.
“Fly”
was
cut
on
Kapp
Records,
his
last
disk
association.
Composer
and
ar-
ranger
as
well
as
pianist,
the
per-
former
will
contribute
original
ma-
terial for his Columbia
releases. Bob
Mersey, director of A&R,
will super-
vise the pianist’s recordings. His first
LP, “Joe Harnell Plays Golden Piano
Hits,”
will be released
in March.
In addition to his recording achieve-
ments, Harnell has been a musical
di-
rector for such
artists
as Peggy Lee
and
Marlene
Dietrich.
He
has
also
served
in that capacity for television
shows,
including
“The
Merv
Griffin
Show,”
“Play
Your
Hunch,”
“The
Phyllis
Differ
Show,” and
the
hour-
long
special
“On
the
Brink.”
Most
recently, he composed the music for a
Gene
Kelly CBS
Television Network
special titled “New York, New York”
which
will
be
shown
sometime
in
February.

TRO Ups Activities On International Scene
NEW YORK—The global look of The
Richmond Organization has been
ex-
panded with various moves
in Great
Britain,
France, and
Australia.
According to Howard
S. Richmond,
president of the TRO publishing com-
plex, Essex Music
Ltd., British
affili-
ate of TRO
International, has moved
to new
offices
in London which
will
triple the firm’s operating space. The
move by David Platz, partner and co-
founder with Richmond of The Essex
Music Group, comes only a few weeks
after the British company’s 10th anni-
versary.
The
new
Oxford
Street
head-
quarters
will
contain
latest
mecha-
nized-electronic equipment for taping
demonstrations
of
songs,
production
control,
copyright
data and
account-
ing
procedures.
The
move
also
in-
volves an increase
in
staff personnel.
The
British
firm
initiated
the
Leslie
Bricusse-Anthony Newley show score
activities
(“Stop
The
World,”
“The
Roar Of The Greasepaint,”
etc.)
and
also
owns
the
score
for
the
Lionel
Bart’s
“Oliver,”
through
its
recent
acquisition of Lakeview Music, Ltd.
TRO’s French
affiliate, Editions Es-
sex, S.A.R.L., has acquired from Rudi
Revil,
the
offices
formerly
occupied
by
Revil’s
Les
Editions
Tropicales.
The new quarters are in the heart of
the
Bourse
(financial)
district
of
Paris.
Ellen Nathan heads
office and
business administration ( as “gerent”)
and Jack Robinson, who concluded
a
visit to America last week,
is profes-
sional manager.
In Australia, a substantial increase
in
activity
has
taken
place
through
the
TRO
affiliate,
Essex
Music
of
Australia,
Pty.
Ltd.,
under
general
manager, Barry Kimberley.
Since he
became associated with
the
firm
last
year,
Kimberley
has
been
working
closely with local songwriters and re-
cording
artists
in
developing
new
Australian
originated
songs
as
well
as international territory acquisitions.
One of these Australian songs, “Why
Don’t You Try To
Didgei’idoo ?” has
already attracted attention from USA
and British recording artists.
The
Essex

MICHELLE—Bud
Shank—World
Pacific
WP
1840/WPS 21840
Bad Shank wastes no time in cashing in on his
current
chart
rider
“Michelle,”
with
this LP
dubbed with the same name. Besides the flute and
saxophone playing of the
leader, the album fea-
tures trumpeter Chet Baker and a
solid rhythm
section. The combination results in a collection of
recent melodies set to a touch of jazz. With such
songs as “As Tears Go By,” and the love theme
from
“Umbrellas
Of
Cherbourg,”
the
package
could be big.
THE
VOICE AND
GUITAR
OF
DORIVAL
CAYMMI—CAPITOL T/ST 10414
In an effort that truly lives up to
its
title, the
voice and guitar of
Brazil’s
beloved
artist-com-
poser Dorival Caymmi is fully showcased through-
out this
set. Chock-full
of
self penned melodies,
Caymmi’s readings,
all in Portuguese, are imag-
inative,
attractive and
full
of joy
of
life. Even
when the tunes go
soft and romantic the
spirit
and zest of Caymmi’s percolating homeland comes
through.
Illlilll
SOUND OF THE SITAR—Ravi Shanker—World
Pacific WP 1434/WPS 21434
Those who have sampled North Indian classical
music, or Hindustani Music as
it is known in the
land of
its
origin, will appreciate
the
tracks on
this LP and for those who are not familiar with
this sound, they
will be a rewarding
experience.
The
music
of
Ravi
Shanker
is
written
in
but
skeletal form and
this gives the
artist freedom
to create. Shanker’s excellence shines through on
each of the three tracks of this LP.
WHAT’S
NEW
HARMONICATS?—Jerry
Murad’s Harmonicats—Columbia CS
9225
What’s-new
is
the
decidedly
teen-angled
ap-
proach of the vet musical team. The harmonica,
of course, has become a standby of some
of the
hottest singles around,
so the instrument
is not
exactly a stranger to these
parts. Teo
Macero’s
teen-minded
arrangements
are
given
their
full
romping due by Murad and
his hip men.
Songs
range from “A Taste Of Honey” to “Turn! Turn!
Turn!”
JAZZ PICKS
THE SLENDER THREAD—Original Soundtrack
—Mercury SR 61070
Quincy Jones, Mercury
vp-artist and now
in-
demand
as
a
film
writer
(e.g.
“Pawnbroker”),
had a shocker theme to work with
for his latest
scoring assignment. 10 excerpts from the sound-
track
score
ably underline
the
suspenseful
plot,
that
of
saving
a

suicide.
Several tracks are swingin’ jazz pieces. Much of
the music is an effective disk sound.
THE FOLK HITS—The Mike Leander Orchestra
—London PS 453
Folk
hits, meaning
the
newer
crop
of
folk-
inspired
tunes,
are
prettied up
in an
orchestral
manner that gives them an appealing poignancy.
The orchestrations hint nicely at the original con-
cepts, but a mostly sans-lyric chorus lend a sweet
pop
air
to
the
proceedings. Tunes
include
“Mr.
Tambourine Man,” “As Tears Go By,” “A World
Of
Our Own”
and
other
folk-rock
goodies. A
pleasing reprise of now familiar repertoire.

'
—Columbia CL 2437/CS 9237

of

nance

WANDA JACKSON SINGS COUNTRY SONGS
—Capitol T/ST 2438
You can take
the
girl out of the country but
you can’t take the country out of the
girl. Since
coming to prominence Wanda Jackson has trav-
elled through Europe and Orient where
she has
gathered
a
host
of new
fans,
but
as

amply

hasn’t

pretty sounds throughout the

- JAZZ BEST BET
OPUS DE FUNK—Johnny “Hammond” Smith
Prestige 7420
The
groovy,
blues
drenched funky
sounds

Backed

of
the
“Almost Like Being In Love” or any of the other
goodies on this LP for some sweet finger snapping
listening pleasure.

Don Adams
as
Don Adams
will

strong
sales
aid from Don Adams
as

Smart.

The Alan
Lorbar
ar-
rangements have
lots
of punch.

Tony Moon
Is Pickwick's
Pubbery Man
In Nashville
NASHVILLE—Joe Abend, vice-presi-
dent in charge of music publishing and
development for Pickwick Internation-
al,
has
announced
that
Tony Moon
has
been
named
to
head
a
newly-
opened Nashville
office for Pickwick’s
Barmour
and
Weiss & Barry
music
publishing firms.
Moon, who
will operate out of 806
Sixteenth
Avenue
South,
has
been
representing
Screen
Gems-Columbia
Music,
Inc.
in
a
similar
capacity for
the
past
three
years.
During*
this
period, Moon has been the recipient of
several BMI Awards for tunes that he
personnaly
brought
into
the
firm,
placed with A & R men and
artists
and
helped
to
promote
into
top
ten
status.
In
addition
to
looking
for
new
writers, material and masters, Moon
will
concentrate
on
the many
copy-
rights already in the catalogs of Bar-
mour and Weiss & Barry and on
the
C & W writers already signed.
100,000 Teens Expected
To Attend Chi Bash
CHICAGO—“Ed Pazdur’s Teen Bash,”
a
special
teen
oriented
weekend
of
concerts, exhibits and contests, sched-
uled to take place at McCormick Place
in
Chicago
on May
6-8,
is
expected
to
draw
over
100,000
teens.
It
will
feature
eight
concerts
starring
over
ten international groups.
“The
concept
of our Teen Bash
is
totally
different from any other type
of
fair
or
exposition,”
said
Pazdur.
“It is different because the big attrac-
tion
to draw
traffic
will
be
the
con-
certs
and
not
the
exhibits.
All
the
emphasis
is placed on entertainment,
fun,
prizes
and
contests,”
continued
Pazdur.
“For
example,”
he went
on
to
say, “prizes such
as
free
trips
to
England, chaperoned by their favorite
Chicago deejay,
will be given away.”
The schedule
of attractions
will be
announced
in
Feb.
after Pazdur’s
re-
turn from Europe, where he will con-
tract
the instrumental
groups.

Marcos Nobili is still giving us news from Discos RGE in the form of quickies
about the Bossa Nova activities of the company: Zimbo Trio this year already
has won two of the most important awards: “Euterpe”
(Rio de Janeiro) and
“Pinheirode Ouro
(Parana).
.
.
. The jacket for
the_ next album by Paulinho
Nogueira is ready and it was done by 8 year old Maria Julia Nogueira, Paulin-
ho’s daughter.
.
.
. Claudia, a newly pacted versatile songstress from the RGE
cast has her first 7" 33RPM disc on the market and is being requested for per-
sonal appearances (Fasano Restaurant) and TV shows (BO 66, TV TUPI).
.
.
.
Paulinho Nogueira
is happy with another award as best
soloist
of

Ouro”.

.
.
Messias, who saw
his double-compact
re-

(Bar “Ja Estao Voltando As

through Liberty Records.

is preparing material for a new
RGE release.

.
. Composer-singer-musician Adylson Godoy is very happy about

“Isabelle” in his own version b/w “Bate-Papo Moderninho,” his own penning.

Brasileira De Discos
(Philips)
left for
the U.S. the promo dept, in Rio
is in reorganization and it is Carlos Gonqalves,
who heads that department in Sao Paulo, that furnishes news from the com-
pany. Baden Powell and Vinicius De Moraes have
another number which
is
being appointed as a sure future hit called “Canto De Ossenha.”
It has such
potential that Vinicius does not want to give
it to any other artist to record
before he does it himself. However, he made an exception for the Tamba Trio,
and this number will be the srong track
of the album that the excellent in-

is

.
.
. Another LP by Nara Leao
is being
prepared for release in the next few days. Nara
is one of the most discussed
artists from Rio de Janeiro, having many fans, which she very wisely, takes
advantage of for her own promotion.
.
.
. Following the success of the Sam The
Sham & the Pharaohs’ number “Wooly Bully,” CBD
is releasing a single “Go
Go” by the group.
The PR section of Discos Odeon
is headed in Sao Paulo by Orlando Stefano
and
it is through him that we come
in contact with the latest release news of
the company: with the title “Surge Um Astro” (A Star
is born), the label has
released an album by the newly pacted chanter Agnaldo Timoteo, with versions
of international hits.
.
.
. From a show we mentioned in previous columns, with
Pery Ribeiro and Leny Andrade, accompanied by the instrumental group Bossa
Tres, recorded live in Rio de Janeiro, Odeon
is releasing a varied album of the
best MPM style. ... A champion of disc sales, Altemar Dutra, the troubadour
of the Brazilian song, has another album on the market with the title of one of
the strong numbers included, “Eu Te Agradego”.
.
.
. For the fans of the Latin-
American rhythm another album
is released by the Acapulco Serenaders titled
“Inolvidable Ritmo,” with rich and lively arrangements.
.
.
. Also considered
to be one of the recording stars of the label
is Wilson Simonal, whose fourth
album “S’lmbora” is already in the shops and is having good sales. ... A well-
liked comedy act by radio and TV artists Vitorio & Marieta, appear in an
al-
bum cut for Odeon, “Showrise,” with several comic situations of Italian immi-
grants in Brazil.
The most popular songstress at the moment
is
Elis Regina
(Philips), who
left for Europe on a long vacation tour.
Giorgio Magnani is a descendant of Italians who came to Sao Paulo. He has
embarked on a one-man fight for the creation of a new style
in the Brazilian
Popular Music
base, with
a view
to
internationalize
it. He
is
dealing
with
several
recording
companies
and
pubberies
(Edigoes RCA
is
interested
in
several
of
his compositions)
for the mass promotion
of
his material
(some
400 compositions). In a theater in Sao Paulo, Magnani presented his numbers
“La Mia Prece,” “Occhi Di Pietra” and “II Re Del Circo” for an audience who
forced the young semi-amateur artist to repeat
his numbers
as many
as
six
times. This time, Giorgio presented
his numbers
only
in
Italian, but he has
them
all prepared in Portuguese and English, which he
is preparing to show
in another theater presentation. Another innovation that he
is promoting
is a
new Afro-Brazilian rhythm which he
calls “Too-Lee-Lee”
(also prepared for
an international market), based on the rhythmic movement
of the Negro
of
the “favela” (shantytowns on the
hills of Rio).
It
is interesting
to note that
many tries at innovation are being introduced, which means that the Brazilian
popular music is constantly on the move, maintaining the strong personality
that makes it still the most original musical manifestation in the world today.

in

Levy
Buys Alegre
Line
NEY/ YORK—Morris Levy
has
an-
nounced the
acquisition of the entire
catalog
of Alegre
Records. The pur-
chase was made under the Bulk Sales
Act of New York and involves some
50 masters on the Alegre label. Alegre
has
a
roster
of
talent who
include
Pacheco and His Charanga, the
Ale-
gre
All-Stars
(consisting
of
band-
leaders, vocalists and instrumentalists
under contract to Alegre), Eddie Pal-
mieri
and
brother
Charlie
Palmieri,
etc. It is the intention of Levy to con-
tinue
to
operate
under
the
Alegre
label.
Alegre
is
said
to
be
the
first
to
come
out with
the Charangas
sound
and the Pachanga dance, which began
in New York as a result of their first
LP
by
Pacheco
and
his
orchestra.
Following the
success
of
this album,
the
Alegre
All-Stars
were
formed,
under the supervision of Charlie Pal-
mieri.
There
are
several
new
(Alegre)
albums in reserve for future release,
and Levy, president of Roulette Rec-
ords, has indicated that a sales cam-
paign
will
be
announced
involving
the new masters. Terming the market
for
this type
of music
as
constantly
expanding, and the urgency to create
more
of
this recorded music
for the
public
ever
present,
Levy
plans
to
combine a sales campaign for Alegre
Records
as
well
as
his
Tico
label
to
fulfill
the
Latin
market’s
needs
and
wants for a time. Levy said that Tico
sales
had
increased
“considerably”
over the past two
years. He
expects
$1.5
million
in
sales
in
1966
for
his
Latin
lines.
The Alegre label
will bring with
it
Richard
Marin, who
will
be
promo-
tion and sales chief for both Tico and
Alegre.
RISING HIGH—The
five young men
pictured
here
are
the
Rising
Sons,
Columbia
artists
whose
first
single
“Candy Man”
and
“Devil’s
Got My
Woman” has just been released. Con-
current
with
the
release,
the
group
will make
its
first major
nightclub
appearence at The Trip in Hollywood.
Pelsman
S. A. Trek
Morrie
(Pancho)
Pelsman,
Rou-
lette’s international operations mana-
ger for Latin America,
representing
Roulette as well as the Tico and Ale-
gre labels, will leave on Feb. 18th for
a month’s trip to South America. The
purpose
of
his
trip
is
to
visit
the
foreign
licensees
to
further
develop
the labels, as well as gather new ma-
terial
from
the
Latin-American
Licensing Corporation, of which he
is
general
manager.
Pelsman’s
travels
will take him to Mexico, San Salvador,
Panama,
Colombia,
Ecuador,
Peru,
Argentina,
Uraguay,
Brazil,
Vene-
zuela, Puerto Rico and Miami, where
he will culminate his trip.
Jackie DeShannon Renews
Liberty
Singing-Writing
Deal
LOS ANGELES—The many
faceted
talents of Jackie DeShannon will con-
tinue
to
remain
exclusively
with
Liberty Records. According to an an-
nouncement from
Phil
Skaff,
execu-
tive
vp,
she
has
just
re-signed with
Imperial
Records
as
a
recording
artist
and
continues
on
as
writer-
contractee
with
Metric
Music,
both
divisions of Liberty.
The
vocalist has had a number
of
successes on the label, including “The
Prince,”
“You
Won’t
Forget
Me,”
“Faded
Love,”
“Needles And
Pins,”
“When You Walk In The Room” and
“Lifetime
Of
Loneliness”.
However,
it was “What The World Needs Now
Is
Love,”
a
1965
blockbuster, which
afforded her star
status.
As
a
writer,
she has had
notable
success
with
many
artists,
among
them,
Brenda
Lee
(“Dum
Dum”
“Heart
In
Hand”—“So
Deep”
“Alone
With You”—“He’s
Sure
To
Remember Me”—“He’s So Heavenly”
—“Funny
Feeling”—“Up
On
A
Hill”).
The
Searchers
(“When You
Walk
In The Room”—“Till You Say
You’ll Be Mine”—“Each Time”), The
Righteous
Bros.
(“Burn On
Love”),
Marianne
Faithful
(“Come
Stay
With Me”—“In My
Time
Of
Sor-
row”). Other DeShannon tunes have
been
cut
by
Ricky
Nelson,
Helen
Shapiro, The Fleetwoods, Troy Shon-
dell,
Sonny &
Cher,
Peggy
March,
Eddie Hodges and
Patti Page.
In addition to appearing on numerous
major network TV shows in the nation,
she has starred in several motion pic-
tures
and was
featured
on
the
first
Beatles American
tour.
She
recently
returned from Vietnam, where she ac-
companied Eddie Fisher on
a
special
Christmas tour for our servicemen.

Departs, Sam Jones

NEW YORK — With

of bassist Ray Brown, Sam Jones has
joined the Oscar Peterson Trio. Jones
was
formerly
with

Cannonball
Adderly group.
The
trio,
whose
latest
Limelight
release
is “With Respect To Nat,” an
instrumental and vocal tribute to the
late
Nat
King
Cole,
has
just
re-
turned
from
a
three-week
tour
of
Japan.
For
the
remainder
of
Feb.
and
part
of
March,
the
group
will
tour
several
colleges
in
concert. On Mar.
4, they will appear in Carnegie Hall;
on March
18,
19,
20 they
will be
in

Newark,
and
Washington,
D.C., with Duke
Ellington and
Billy
Eckstine;
and
on
Mar.
20
they
will
go to Europe on a tour that will take
them
to
Germany,
Spain,
Portugal,
and the Scandinavian
countries.

ALBUM REVIEWS
Gash Box
NEW
YORK: MY PORT OF CALL—Jimmy
Roselli—United
Artists UAS
6467
Roselli,
a
fine voice with
a most loyal follow-
ing, sings a paean
to the great
city. His
bill-of-
fare says just about everything
nice
that’s been
put into words and music on the town, including
“Autumn
In New
York,”
“The
Sidewalks
Of
New York,” “Manhattan,” “Give My Regards To
Broadway” and a rarely-heard Jule Styne-Sammy
Cahn, number, “Brooklyn Bridge.” Ralph Burns
is responsible for the happy, often hip arrange-
ments. A delightful
set by a guy who obviously
leaves
his
heart
in New
York when
he’s
not
there.
RUBY AND THE ROMANTICS
GREATEST
HITS ALBUM—Kapp KL 1458
Ruby
and
the
Romantics
should
have
little
trouble
in gamering a good
sales reaction with
this album consisting of their greatest hits. With
lead singer Ruby backed by the
soft harmony of
the Romantics, the group does such melodies as
the haunting “Our Day Will Come,” “Your Baby
Doesn’t Love You Anymore,” and “My Summer
Love.”
This
one
should make
a
strong
bid
for
chart honors.
A STRING OF PEARLS—Bobby Hackett—Epic
LN 24174/BN 26174
An alumnus of the Glenn Miller band, cornet-
lst
Bobby
Hackett
serves
up
a
set
of
Miller
favorites, but he plays them with a style
all his
own. In combination with Hackett’s cornet is the
Wall-to-Wall
Strings and
Brass and
the
result
is a tasteful album that includes such Swing-Era
classics as “A String Of Pearls,” “Rhapsody In
Blue,”
and
“In
The
Mood.”
Top-notch
sounds
throughout the
offering.

IWWBS8I

IKE
COLE’S
TRIBUTE
TO
HIS BROTHER
NAT—Dee Gee LPM/ST 4001
In his debut album, Ike Cole evokes instanta-
neous memory of his brother, the late Nat “King”
Cole. The chanter sings each tune with a clarity
and
polish
that was
so
much
a
part
of
his
brother’s style. Backed by a soft, warm ork, Cole
sings many
of
the
tunes
that
his
brother was
noted
for
including
“Blue
Moon,”
“I’m
In The
Mood For Love,” and “Hi-Lili, Hi-Lo.” With his
appealing vocal personality, Ike Cole could have
himself a winner with this package.
THE McGUIRE SISTERS RIGHT NOW!—ABC-
Paramount 530
The
tried-and-true
singing
trio
take a
senti-
mental walk down Tin Pan Alley for their
first
LP outing for ABC Paramount. Theirs is the non-
gimmick approach to pop music, most refreshing
when the market
is relying heavily on acts that
are determined to be one step ahead of the others
in being different. Sturdies include “It Isn’t Fair,”
“My Melancholy Baby,” “Nevertheless” and nine
others.

&

Country singers George Jones & Melba Mont-
gomery have grouped a collection of c&w songs,

A BAG FULL OF SOUL—Jose Feliciano—RCA
Victor LPM/LSP 3503
Singer-guitarist Jose Feliciano shows the broad
range
of his talents with
this
collection of
folk,
rock and blues songs. Backed by electric guitars
and

comes on strong with such tunes as “If

Bug You,” “A Happy Guy,” and “Goin’ To
Chi-
cago
Blues.”
The
album,
which
should
garner
many fans for the talented lad, might well hit the
charts.

THE LAMP IS LOW—Bobby Gordon—Decca DL
74726
Gordon, Decca’s mood-music man of the
clari-
net
(this
is his third LP), attractively wraps-up
a bevy of our-song creations, with strings and a
harp
helping
the
nice-and-easy mood
along.
In
addition
to
the
title number,
other
appropriate
romantic songs are “Call Me Irresponsible,” “Too
Close
For
Comfort,”
“Smile”
and “My

THE SHACKLEFORDS SING—Capitol ST 2450
With a cute, comic pop-art format on the pack-
age, the folk-rock group displays enough variety
in material and approach
to make
listening an
interesting experience in the important new musi-
cal
form.
Two
good
contrasting
examples
of
their art are the humorous “Five Feet High And
Risin’ ”
and
the
wistful
“Everything
I
Touch
Turns To Tears.”
JAZZ PICKS
FEELIN’ GOOD—Gerry Mulligan—Limelight LM
82030/LS 86030
Gerry
Mulligan, for
the
first time
in a long
time,
set aside
his baritone sax long enough to
do
a
couple
of
tunes
on
the
clarinet and
this
should prove
to be a treat
to
Mulligan’s many
fans. Of course he
also works with the sax and
has
the added attraction
of strings backing his
sound.
The
selection
of
tunes
such
as
“Love
Walked
In,”
“The
Second
Time
Around”
and
“The Lonely Night (Night Lights)” leaves
little
else
to be desired
in an LP.
THE CAPE VERDEAN BLUES—Horace
Silver
Quintet—Blue Note 4220
The
three
sources
of sound that were tapped
in the molding of the tracks on
this
disk, Cape
Verdean Portuguese folk music, Brazilian samba
and good old American funk, when combined with
the musical excellence that is the playing of the
Horace
Silver
Quintet, with
the bonus
treat of
the trombone
of
J.
J. Johnson, makes a sound
that
is indescribable
in any one word. Such cuts
as the
title
track, “Nutville” and “Pretty Eyes”
should
please music
lovers
of most any
stripe.
ASCENSION—John Coltrane—Impulse A/AS 95
That master
of
the
tenor sax John
Coltrane
teamed up for this session with a group
of jazz
musicians some of whom are names in their own
right
and
others who
are
relative
unknowns,
but
all
of whom
are
highly
capable
musicians.
The bag that they go
into on
this
single
track
disk can be
called “Free Jazz”
or “New Jazz”
of “Third-stream Jazz” but no matter what name
it
is called by,
it
is an exciting,
infectious, emo-
tional experience for the
listener.
CLASSICAL PICKS
MOZART/THE
MAGIC FLUTE—Philharmonic
Chorus
and
Orchestra/Klemperer—Angel
36315
This
single
disk
selection
of
highlights from
Mozart’s renowned opera
is given a totally con-
vincing and attractive reading by
this excellent
cast
under
the
masterful
supervision
of
Otto
Klemperer. The singing and orchestral work are
striking in their
clarity. LP should find a warm
and
welcome
reception
at
the
hands
of
both
lovers of the work and of the maestro.
SCHUBERT/MASS IN E. FLAT, D. 950—Vienna
Choir Boys—Philips PHM 500-081/PHS
900-081
This,
the
last
of
the
masses
composed
by
Schubert,
about
four months
before
his
death,
is impressive
despite the conservative nature
of
its composition. The lay-out of the piece
is quite
conventional
and
its
most
striking
feature
is
the
well-knit
solo
and
choral
parts.
The
con-
stant
interchange
between
these
two
parts
is
further highlighted by the fact that at no point
is a
soloist allowed
to predominate. Disk should
be
thoroughly
enjoyed by
devotees
of
classical
masses.

Big 3 Sweeps 'Globe
7
Film Music Awards,
'Sound
7
Best Musical
NEW YORK—It was
a
clean sweep
for material copyrighted by the Big
3
(Robbins-Feist-Miller)
at
last
week’s Golden Globe film award pre-
sentation
of
the
Hollywood
Foreign
Press
Association.
The Miller arm of the firm got the
Best Song nod with “Forget Domani,”
the Riz Ortolani-Norman Newell song
from “The Yellow Rolls-Royce.” The
Robbins wing came up with the Best
Score
in Maurice
Jarre’s themes
for
“Doctor
Zhivago.”
“Zhivago,”
avail-
able as an MGM soundtrack LP, also
won three other awards for direction
(David Lean), best actor in a drama
(Omar Sharif) and screenplay
(Rob-
ert
Bolt).
RCA Victor Records got in on two
awards
with
awards
to
“Sound
of
Music” as the best comedy or musical
and Julie Andrews as the best actress
in
a comedy or musical.
The awards show was seen on last
week’s Andy Williams
telecast.

Nationwide Tour
NEW YORK—TV
star Jimmy Dean
will begin a nationwide tour late this
month.
The
tour,
which
has
a
po-
tential
gross
of
over
$500,000,
will
extend
into
September.
Dean
will
have
his
own
package
on
most
of
the engagements, including the Chuck
Cassy Singers and other c&w singers.
Dates
in Feb. and Mar. have been
planned
so
as
not
to
interfere
with
the
taping
of
Dean’s weekly
TV’er.
This
will
be made
possible
through
advance
tapings
of
his
weekly
seg-
ments
until April
1, when the
series
will begin
its summer
hiatus.
Dean’s itinerary
includes, Houston,
Oklahoma
City,
Tulsa,
Cincinnati,
Pittsburgh,
Salt Lake
City, Anaheim
and
San
Carlos,
Calif.,
Denver,
Omaha,
Wichita,
Kansas
City,
Lake
Tahoe,
Portland,
Spokane,
Spring-
field,
111. and Columbus,
Ohio.

“Michelle,” David & Jonathan’s vocal adoption of the key number from the
Beatles’ “Rubber Soul” album, was rush released by Columbia here following
up
its entrance on Britain’s Pop-50-parade.
Bovema’s sales promotor Aart Lamberts reports that sales are
still zooming
for monaural and stereo recordings by the
late organist Cor Steyn. The com-
pany had special repertoire leaflets distributed on a large
scale among
retail-
ers, underlining the artist’s exclusive ‘Magic Organ’ albums, on which buyers’

‘PnpncpH
Bovema’s Atlantic told CB that Sonny & Cher’s “Sing C’est La Vie” released
with “Just You”
is catching on very strongly in Southern Dutch provinces.
HMV artist Toon Hermans will launch
his new
’66 one man show on Mon-
day February 21 in Tilburg. Hermans, for this 10th O.M. show, will be mixing
his best parts from previous shows with newly written
acts and
songs. Per-
formances in Heerlen and Nijmegen will further be
setting the pace
for his
Amsterdam-Carre premiere.
Parlophone’s “Rubber
Soul” album
is making
a
real
Gulliver’s
Travel
in
Radio Veronica’s
single-hit 40
this week.
Stateside
hit the stands with new repertoires by the Strangeloves
(“Cara-
lin”), the Toys (“Attack”) and Johnny Thunder’s “Everybody Do The Sloopy.”
Capitol rushed out albums by Wynn Stewart and Sinatra (“The Connoisseurs
Sinatra”).
Next to its big money making “Rubber Soul” LP, the Beatles’ million sellers
album, Parlophone had records out by the Fourmost, the Roulettes and Peter
Sellers. The
latter
is doing
his comical view
of “Help” and “A Hard
Day’s
Night.”
With Carnival on
the
doorstep, Toon Hermans wrote
a
carnival
song for
“De Kemeleers” entitled “Vroag d’n Hier Ins Wat’r Vaan Mich Welt Drinke,”
(Ask The Gentleman What He Wants To Drink From Me)
recorded by Im-
perial.
On February 16th the Swingle Singers will give a performance at The Con-
cert Gebouw, Amsterdam. The concert will be organized and financed by the
vocal group
itself. Pierre Fantosme, the group’s manager, cooperated
in
this
respect with Phonogram, the Dutch company representing Philips. The Swingle
Singers are contracted to the label and for
it they have done “Jazz Sebastien
Bach,” “The Swingle Singers Going Baroque” and the famous Mozart-album.
Phonogram has started
a most intensive
sales-action by means
of
close
co-
operation with leading Dutch dealers, cinema’s and via newspapers and other
publicity.
Popular
Greek
vocal
and
instrumental
quintet
the
Athenians
are
under
Philips contract. Their first LP was released via Philips’ Phonographic Indus-
tries
in the
special Folkmusic
series. The
five musicians
started three years
ago
in small harbor-cafes at Piraeus, where they met with songstress Nana
Mouskouri, now
a
top-star
in
both
America
and
Europe.
Phonogram
has
planned a recording in Holland of The Athenians together with Mouskouri
in
February. Greek folk-music, instrumentals and vocals are tremendously popu-
lar here.
The “Ameriachi” sound of Herb Alpert’s Tijuana Brass
is clicking
in Hol-
land.
Slowly
but
surely
Alpert’s
instrumental
hits
like
“Taste
Of
Honey,”
“Whipped Cream,” “Lonely Bull” and “Tijuana Taxi” are gaining public
at-
tention rapidly. There
is a fairly good chance, John Ros of Decca Holland told
Cash Box, that “The Ameriachi craze in America may also develop into some-
thing big
in Holland during
the
next
half
year.
In
that
case,
the
planned
Tijuana tour to Europe next fall will come at the right moment.”
The Rolling Stones have a Gold hit in the Dutch market with “Satisfaction.”
Negram’s guest
last week was Jim
Bailey from Pye Records
Ltd.
Bailey
stayed for a couple of days to discuss the possibilities of releasing Pye records
for the near future. Bailey also presented, together with Kellerman and Oeges,
two special evenings for the American forces, with a one-hour Sinatra show.
This show was accepted with such great enthusiasm that Negram decided
to
work out special dealer days on which the show
will be
presented.
Pye records are doing extremely well on the Dutch charts. Perhaps by the
influence
of Radio
Caroline,
Radio
London and
Radio
Veronica,
the
Dutch
charts are coming closer to the British ones. “Michelle” for instance, now
in
top position in England, is climbing very fast in our country and reached no. 17
this week. This version by the Overlanders will certainly be able to reach the
Dutch top 10 next week.
Vogue France has decided to release an LP by the Motions, and they also
plan to release the
first big
single by the Motions, “Wasted Words.”
From the Hansa label, Marion’s “Er 1st Wieder Da”
is beginning to
sell
all
over the
country. This German
bestseller has good chances
in
Holland.
All
important deejays have decided
to
give
this record
special plugging.
In one
of our previous columns we
told
of Russian records under German
control. Critics from Holland awarded the
last edition of “Luister”
8 records
7 stars, which is the highest possible rating. Another 12 records are ready for
release
in February.
Chris Andrews was in Holland to make a special guest appearance on the
popular AVRO TV show “Moef Ga Ga,” the Dutch “Shindig.” Chris sang his
big hits “Yesterday Man” and “To Whom It Concerns.” The show was on the
air January 31st.
Another visitor to our shores was Donovan. This young man
is very famous
here for his recordings of “Catch the Wind,” “Colours,” “Universal
Soldier,”
and he
is currently scoring with his double decker “Sunny Goodge Street” and
“I’ll Try For The Sun,” both from the LP “Fairy Tale.” He appeared in “Fan-
club,” a VARA TV show with high teenage ratings. Donovan arrived at Schi-
phol
airport on February
4th,
a week
after the
release
of
his new
British
single “Superlove,” a tribute
to John and
Paul.
Brandsteder of Inelco-Holland N.V. told Cash Box of the success he has with
“The Sound of Music” campaign. In co-operation with the 20th Century Fox
film organization a family singing competition has been organized with lots of
prizes: a free trip for the whole winning family to Salzburg-Austria; Arena
television and radio
set,
etc. The campaign started
in the key
cities, and
all
the families had to sing DO-RE-MI either in English or in Dutch.
The campaign is supported by television and radio. There
is also advertising
in news and music magazines, and this campaign for the RCA Victor LP “The
Sound
of Music”
is most promising.
Peter Nero visited Holland for a whole week and what a
success!
All the
newspapers, magazines, and music periodicals paid a
lot of attention
to
this
famous American maestro. The first of three television transmissions was
re-
leased
last week, and with that recording he conquered Holland. The
second
show will be broadcast in February or March. These shows last for about one
hour. Nero also appeared as a special guest in a Rene Sleeswijk TV’er Joseph
Cusatis on drums, Barre Philips on bass and the Cosmopolitain Orchestra
of
Jos Cleber accompanied him. Also a radio recording has been done and will be
transmitted within a short time. Dolf v.d. Linden and the Metropole Orchestra
guaranteed the best possible
success
to the
radio
listeners.
It has been a great trip and we
all hope to see him
(and Stan) back soon.

January 20th was the premiere date for Holland of the Paramount Picture
“The Sons Of
Katie
Elder”
at Tuschinsky Theatre
in Amsterdam.
It
stars
John Wayne and music is composed by Elmer Bernstein. CBS recently released
a single with the title-song of the movie sung by Johnny Cash, and in the near
future CBS will also release the original soundtrack LP recording of this movie.
The Lords, CBS’ new local beat group, were well received at the press party,
organized by CBS and held at the Grand Hotel Gooiland in Hilversum. Radio
& TV
officials, members of the Dutch Press as well as
local dealers attended
this party. The group consists of 4 boys:
Bert, Eric, Freddy and Harry, and
their very
first CBS

“Belinda”
c/w
“People
Wonder,”
is

is expected

Artone, recently appointed ESP disk distributor
in Benelux, has released a
first batch
of albums from
the
catalog
this week.
Artists
featured
include
avant garde jazz players Albert Ayler, Pharaoh Sanders, Byron Allen, Ornette
Coleman, Paul Bley, Giuseppi Logan, Bob James, Ran Blake, Sun Ra and the
New York Art Quartet. Both Coleman and the New York Art Quartet appeared
in concert in Amsterdam, October 1965. The initial record release has met with
very favorable reaction.
New Artone
releases from the
Festival catalog
include
a
single featuring
Marie Laforet in “Julie Creve-coeur” b/w “A Demain My Darling,” and new
albums by Nino de Murcia, Christian Arabian and a French Free Jazz Group.
Festival recording artist Mouloudji will be seen in a Chansons feature entitled
“Sur Up Air De Paris,” in which he presents some of his former hits as well
as material from his latest album for the label, including his own song, “Chan-
son Pour X,” shown
locally over the VARA TV network
this week. To date
Artone released
5 EPs and and
2 albums by the world famous
singer movie
star from his own production
series.

first
is the

from

Netherlands
Film
Production
International
release
“10:32,” starring Linda Christian and directed by Arthur Dreifuss. The movie
introduces two recent vocal discoveries, 22-year old Daniella and
18-year

special material
composed by vet song writer Joop Portengen. In conjunction with the movie’s
first local showings, Funckler this week issued Daniella’s recordings of “Perry”
and “Beware, Beware, Beware,” as well as Eddy Jones’ etching of “My Kinda
Heaven.”

Fred White tips C.B. to the fact that Bo Diddley
is currently cutting a new
Chess LP during his appearance at Toronto’s Le Coq D’Or.
It’ll be an audience
participation session. Jerry Palmer was set for the TV coast to coaster, “She-
bang,”
(2/3). The young Gaiety
artist, currently clicking with “Walking The
Dog,” has also been signed for a P.A.
at Disneyland. The
label has just
re-
leased a second
single, featuring a
California
group,
the Dudes. Reg Ayres
and Ed Lawson, Quality men
in Winnipeg and Toronto
respectively, are
off
and running with air promotions to tie in with the new Herman’s Hermits song
in the MGM soundtracker, “When The Boys Meet The Girls.” “Listen People”
will not be released as a single, but
it is sure getting single-type action in all
areas for Quality. Ayres and Lawson have set up contests with deejays at key
stations in their areas to promote the single-in-the-album. LP’s will be offered

RAMBLINGS
NEW YORK:
The sound that has been developing
among
the
groups
playing
in
and
about Gotham, which
is coming to be
known
nationally
as the “New York
Sound,”
is
really
as
varied
as
the
people who are creating
it. From the
hard
rock
of
the
Rascals
and
the
Vagrants
(of which
the former
has
already achieved national recognition
and
the
latter
will
soon
be
known,
based on the 13 weeks of SRO crowds
that have been drawing
at the“Roll-
ing Stone” discotheque,)
to the blues
crowd
flowed
throughout
the
store
trying
to
get
close
to
the
popular
McCallum.
.
.
. Warner Bros. Marvin
Deane
(with an
‘e’)
finally completed
the
battery
for
his
family’s
“nine”
when
Jeffory
Michael
came
on
the
scene. Mother and son are doing
fine,
but Marvin
is shook.
.
.
. Wildness of
the
week
should
be “A
Happening
With Salvador Dali”
set for Philhar-
monic
Hall
(23).
.
.
. The
Medical
Missionaries
of
Mary,
who
have
“Angels” on Kapp, have
donated
all
of their profits from the deck to help
the blind people
in Nigeria.
.
.
.
Now
a
musician
is
merely
a guy
with
a
special
talent
(some
haven’t
even
that)
who
usually manages
to
maintain an unflaggingly high opinion
of
himself.
Not
that we
can
blame
him. He’s been in some big towns and
heard him some big talk. He has also
observed
the
ferns
out
front
giving
him
the
glad
eye.
In
itself
that’s
enough
to
convince
him
that
he’s
I’homme fatal. So if he starts to think
that
he’s
Vince
Chamberlain
(even
though he looks like Zorba) why spoil
the illusion?
The other night, leaving the Victor
studios where
a
world
famous
rock
group was recording, we encountered
a
lineup
of
about
40
Thunderbirds,
XKE’s and
190
SL’s with
love god-
desses to match. Even in a dim light
we could make out that at least half a
dozen of these bandboxes were likely
Rheingold queen material and several
more
could
be future
Sophias,
Tues-
days
and Ann
Margrets.
Such
gals,
we’re
told, have
also been known
to
Fontana
released
a
new
Oscar
Brown
Jr.
album,
“Finding A New
Friend,” to coincide with the opening
of Brown’s musical revue, Joy
’66, at
the
Happy
Medium
here.
Package
showcases
the bossa nova
sound
in-
troduced in the show
.
.

.

JUDY
COLLINS
DICK & DEEDEE
of

Smash & Fontana Set New Financial Peaks
CHICAGO—Smash and Fontana Records, which set a cumulative sales goal of
$6,000,000 in sales for their fourth complete year, ending Dec. 31, 1965, topped
that goal for the year and kicked
off 1966 with the largest single month
in
their
sales
history
during
the
past
Jan.,
it was
announced
last week by
Mercury
president
Irving Green.
Irwin Steinberg, the company’s executive
v.p., in amplifying on the success-
ful
sales year and
significant early 1966
start,
said
that the
Charlie Fach-
headed dual
label operation concentrates on a limited number of artists but
backs them up with intense promotional, publicity and manufacturing facilities.
In
explaining
the
yearly,
and now
the
Jan.
all-time
sales
record,
Fach
noted Roger
Miller’s
contribution spearheaded
the
pace-setting
period, with
a number of albume making vital contributions.
Based on the healthy Jan.
sales, Fach estimates that Smash-Fontana could
wind up 1966 with a projected 25% increase, which would put the diskery into
the $7,500,000-$8,000,000
category.
George Martin
In
U.S.
For Material
Hunt
NEW YORK—George
Martin,
musi-
cal
director of the
Beatles and
since
last
fall
a
partner
in
Britain’s new
AIR
production
company,
has
ar-
rivod in the U.S. for a two week stay.
His primary concern, he
told Cash
Box,
is
to
seek-out
and
bring
back
material to be cut by the
artists who
are
being
recorded
by
AIR.
AIR
brought under a single corporate roof
the
talents
of
Martin, Ron
Richard,
John Burgess and Peter Sullivan. Ac-
cording to Martin, there
is a “dearth
of great songs” around and he hopes
to pick up
suitable material for such
performers
as
Matt
Munro,
Celia
Black and David & Jonathan.
The David & Jonathan smash
sin-
ade of “Michelle” was the first master
produced
by
AIR.
Also
on
release
here
is the Peter
Sellers’
take-off
of
“A Hard Day’s Night” and “Help!”
The voices that blend on the opening
of the latter session, by the way, con-
sist
of Martin himself and David &
Jonathan. Another AIR entry
is the
St. Louis Union’s “Girl” on Parrot.
As
for
the
Beatles,
who,
Martin
noted, made their historic
initial
visit
to the U.S. just two years ago
(Feb.
7), they may soon make their first re-
cordings
in
the
U.S.
The
group,
of
course,
has
been
“recorded”
during
their
concert
appearances,
including
an unreleased date
at Carnegie
Hall.
But,
Martin
said,
the
boys
are
in-
terested
in
doing
U.S.
studio
work.
The
reason?
“They’re
always
ready
to
do
something
new,”
Martin
ex-
plained. Coupled with
a
desire
to do
something
new,
Martin
went
on,
is
their
drive
to
outdo what they have
done
before.
Martin
said
that
their
“Rubber Soul” LP was the product of
30
recording
sessions,
representing
their
finest album
collection
to
date.
While
in
the
U.S., Martin
will
do
some
appearances
on
American
TV.
They
will
have
to
be
limited
to
conservation
guest-shots,
since
Mar-
tin
had
not,
as
of
this
writing,
his
H-1
visa
as an
artist.
AIR also records such standout acts
as Manfred Mann,
P.
J.
Proby, The
Hollies and Peter & Gordon.

PICKING A WINNER — Columbia
Records has announced the winners of
the
“Lucky
Birthday
Sweepstakes”
contest,
the
drawing
for which was
held
in New
York
during
January.
Prizes
valued
at
$365,000
will
be
awarded to the winners.
In order to win a Columbia album
of his choice and become
eligible for
the
Sweepstakes
drawing,
it
was
necessary for the
contestant’s
birth-
date to be one of those selected by the
judges as lucky birthdates. The win-
ning birthdates were
listed with Co-
lumbia dealers.
Record
buyers
competed
for
the
prizes, which
included a grand prize
of: $10,000 in cash, a 1966 Ford Mus-
tang
hardtop,
a
full-length
ranch
mink
coat,
a
Suzuki
motorcycle,
a
Columbia
“360”
Stereo System
plus
365 Columbia albums, a 23" Westing-
house
color television
set,
a portable
Masterwork phonograph and
a Mas-
terwork AM/FM transistor radio.
The
drawing
to
select
the
grand-
prize
winner,
as
well
as
the
two
second-prize winners from
the
thou-
sands of contestants was held in New
York.
Present
at
the
drawing were
(left
to
right)
:
Stanley Kavan,
vice
president
and
general manager,
Co-
lumbia
Records
Sales;
Robert
Blas-
hek, vice president, D. L. Blair; Clive
Davis,
administrative
vice
president.
Columbia;
Bob
Morrison
and
Bobbe
Norris, Columbia vocalists; William P.
Gallagher,
vice
president,
Columbia;
and
Leonard
Burkat,
vice
president,
information
and
design,
Columbia
Records.
The
grand-prize
winner was
Mil-
dred
Ingram
of
Liberty,
Indiana.
Second-prize
winners
included
Mr.
Richard Boyce of Sharon
Hill, Penn-
sylvania,
and
Richard
Sardisco
of
Rosemead, California. Boyce and Sar-
disco
will
each
receive
a
1966
Ford
Mustang
hardtop.
Five
third-prize
winners
will receive a Suzuki motor-
cycle;
the
ten
fourth-prize
winners
will
each
receive
a
Columbia
“360”
Stereo System plus 100 Columbia
al-
bums;
the 25
fifth-prize winners will
receive a 12" Westinghouse television
set; the 50 sixth-prize winners will be
awarded
a
Masterwork
portable
phonograph plus 50 Columbia albums;
and 100 Masterwork AM/FM transis-
tor radios will be awarded as seventh
prizes.
In addition to the $365,000 in prizes
awarded
to
the
“Lucky
Birthday
Sweepstakes” contest winners, a 1966
Ford
Mustang
hardtop
will
be
awarded to the owners of the Special-
ty Record Shop in Richmond, Indiana,
where
Mrs.
Ingram
obtained
her
sweepstakes entry form.
Tony Cabot Forms
Record Company
NEW YORK—Tony Cabot, director of
entertainment
for
Restaurant
Asso-
ciates, as well as musical director for
the WOR-TV Cerebral Palsy Telethon
for the past 14 years, has announced
the formation
of a new record com-
pany, Mr.
C. Presents. For the firm’s
operation, Cabot will release a limited
number of singles and
will only
fol-
low these up with album
releases
if
the
reaction
to
the
singles warrant
such further exploitation.
Cabot, who
has
recorded
with
his
own
orchestra
for RCA
Victor,
will
hand pick the talent for the label. He
has
already
signed
pop
songstress
Kathy Preston to a contract and plans
to release her
first platter in March.
He
also has
several
other vocal and
instrumental
artists under considera-
tion.
Cabot’s plans
also
call
for
his
company to release masters which he
will purchase from independent
pro-
ducers and recording artists. The firm
is located in New York City.

Lombardo, Gillette Back
At Capitol; Add Duties
For Miller, Dexter
HOLLYWOOD—Capitol
Records
has
welcomed back veteran maestro Guy
Lombardo and, in an associated move,
A&R man Lee Gillette.
Voyle Gilmore, A&R vp, announced
that
Gillette had agreed to return
to
the
label
to A&R
all
of Lombardo’s
recordings.
Thus,
the
recording
of
Gillette and Lombardo
are
re-united,
having teamed on almost
12
Capitol
LP’s in previous years.
Miller, Dexter Add Duties
Gilmore also announced several ad-
ditional responsibilities that were be-
ing given to two current members
of
the A&R department.
Bill Miller and
Dave Dexter.
Miller
will now be
responsible
for
all
Capitol
of
the
World
albums
produced
and
manufactured
by
the
label. Miller started with CRI in 1945
as recording department manager and
was
promoted
to A&R
producer
in
1952.
Dexter will assume all responsibility
for the
re-exploitation and
re-use
of
all
Capitol masters
produced
in
the
past.
Gilmore
said
that
Dexter
had
been
chosen
for
the
post
primarily
because
of
his
vast
knowledge
of
Capitol’s product and artists.
Dexter has been with the
label
al-
most
since
its founding
in
1942. He
joined CRI
in
1943
as
editor
of
the
“Capitol News.” In 1946 he was given
the
responsibility of
director
of
jazz
repertoire,
a
position
he
held
until
1950 when he was made supervisor of
jazz—in
1951
he
was
promoted
to
A&R producer and in 1961 was made
executive producer. Both Dexter and
Miller will report to Gilmore.
Gilmore said that
first sessions for
Lombardo
will
take
place
in
Las
Vegas where Lombardo
is
currently
starring
in
the
Tropicana
Lounge.
Tentative
plans
call
for
Gillette
to
record two LP’s while Lombardo is in
the gambling
spa. “Both
LP’s,”
Gil-
lette
said,
“will
be
a
little
different
than
previous
Lombardo
recordings.
We have discussed a number of ideas
and have come up with
several new
concepts.”
In addition to Lombardo, Gillette
is
known as producer for
a number
of
other artists among them was the late
Nat Cole and Tennessee Ernie Ford.

Lear
DETROIT—The appointments of Ed-

Until

dent
of

One

elec-

“With

com-
bined attributes of these two men
in
solving volume
electronic
production
problems we can look forward to the
smooth, dependable product flow
it
is
now
apparent
will
be
necessary
to
meet the increasing demand for Lear
Jet Stereo 8 products.”

'Golden Language' Series
NEW
YORK—Golden
Records
has
announced the introduction of its new
“Golden Language”
series. According
to the firm, the new series is designed
to teach a foreign language to
child-
ren without
resorting
to
the
spoon-
fed vagueness
or the text-book bore-
dom which predominates
this
field.
The
company
is
inaugurating
the
new program with a series in French
and a series in Spanish. In both cases,
children
learn
the new
language by
following the adventures of an Amer-
ican, French or Mexican boy, depend-
ing
upon
which
language
is
being
studied. Each series
is made up of six
records
and
six
books.
Available
at
all
leading
department
and
record
stores, every combination record-book
costs
99^.
The
first side of each record
is pri-
marily
in
English, and the second
is
either
in
French
or
Spanish.
The
books contain the drawings and words
of the corresponding record.

Pick of the Week
NOWHERE MAN (2:40)
[Maclen, BMI—Lennon, McCartney]
WHAT GOES ON (2:44)
[Maclen, BMI—Lennon, McCartney]
BEATLES (Capitol 5587)
The Fab Four’s latest effort should, of course, zip them up the charts
with
their usual supersonic speed. The “A” side here, “Nowhere Man,”
is an easy-going, rhythmic ode
all about a real myopic fella who has a
great deal to learn. “What Goes On” is a twangy, medium-paced country-
ish
tearjerker.
TOO LITTLE TIME
(2:45)
[George Pincus, ASCAP—Liebling, Hamlisch]
TIME AND TIME AGAIN
(2:21)
[Ron-Bre, BMI—Burnett, Osborne]
BRENDA LEE (Decca 31917)
Brenda Lee should scurry up the hitsville path in no time flat with this
exciting new Decca side labeled “Too Little Time.” The tune’s a plaintive,
medium-paced, shufflin’ ode which suggests that romance should be taken
slowly and not
rushed. On the undercut the
lark
dishes-up
a winning
rendition of “Time And Time Again.”
LOVE IS ME, LOVE IS YOU
(2:22)
[Duchess, BMI—Hatch]
I’D LET YOU BREAK MY HEART ALL OVER AGAIN
(2:27)
[Francon, ASCAP—Davis, Murry]
CONNIE FRANCIS (MGM
13470)
Both Top
40
and
middle-of-the-road
stations
will want
to
add
this
new Connie Francis entry, “Love Is Me, Love Is You,” to their playlists
in
rapid
order.
Side
is
a
medium-paced,
effectively-building,
chorus-
backed romantic handclapper with
a danceable repeating
riff.
“I’d Let
You Break My Heart All Over Again” is a plaintive, tender, slow-moving
lament with a nostalgic 1930’s flavor.
YOUNG GIRL (2:18) [Lowery, BMI—Joyner, Cartney]
I JUST DON’T KNOW IF
I CAN
(2:30)
[Buffee, BMI—Gore, Bayer]
LESLEY GORE (Mercury 72553)
Lesley Gore can have one
of her biggest successes
in
quite
a while
with
this
excellent updating
of
the
years-back “Young Love”
smash.
The tune, which
is culled from the lark’s new “All About Love” LP,
is
done up
in
a
lilting, dramatic
lush
ork and
chorus-backed
style. The
coupler’s an inventive original tabbed “I Just Don’t Know If
I Can.”
(YOU’RE MY) SOUL AND INSPIRATION (3:00)
[Screen Gems-Columbia, BMI—Mann, Weil]
B SIDE BLUES (3:00)
[Righteous Enterprises, BMI—Medley, Hatfield]
RIGHTEOUS BROTHERS (Verve 10383)
The Righteous Bros, kick off their new Verve association in
fine style
with this dynamic original called “(You’re My)
Soul And
Inspiration.”
The cut’s a slow-starting but effectively-building blues-drenched romancer
with an emotional mid-deck
recitation. “B
Side Blues”
is
a low-down,
funky r&blueser.
THE LOVE YOU SAVE (MAY BE YOUR OWN (2:53)
[Tree, BMI—Tex]
IF SUGAR WAS AS SWEET AS YOU
(2:49)
[Tree, BMI—Tex]
JOE TEX (Dial 4026)
The
pop-blues
songster’s
impressive
hit-chain
(he
hit
recently with
“A Sweet Woman Like You”)
should speedily add another strong link.
This
one
will
be
called “The Love You
Save
(May Be Your Own)”
and
it’s a low-down, slow-moving soulful lament about an unhappy fella
who
really wants
to
solve
his
romantic
problems.
“If Sugar Was As
Sweet As You”
is
a happy-go-lucky
ditty about a guy who’s on cloud
nine ’cause
he’s met Miss Right.
Pick of the Week
DON’T PUSH ME
(2:15)
[Mainstay, BMI—King]
PLEASE DON’T HURT YOUR HEART FOR ME
(2:28)
[Mainstay, BMI—King]
HEDGEHOPPERS ANONYMOUS
(Parrot 9817)
The Hedgehoppers Anonymous
should have no
difficulty
in jumping
into the winner’s
circle
lickety-split with this potent follow-up
to
their
reputation-establishing
“It’s Good News Week” triumph. The top
side,
“Don’t Push Me,”
is a pulsating, hard-driving catchy ode about a deter-
mined
fella who
serves
notice
on
his
gal
that
she
should
respect
his
rights.
“Please Don’t Hurt Your Heart For Me”
is
a
laconic, low-key
teen-directed blueser.

(2:43)
] Immediate, BMI—Jagger,

ANY OLE WAY
(2:32)
[East-Time-Redwal, BMI—Redding, Cropper]
OTIS REDDING
(Volt
132)
Otis Redding should get some more
sales mileage out of the Rolling
Stones’ recent “Satisfaction” chart-topper. Tune, which was stimulated
into release by deejays playing an LP cut, is given a hard-driving throb-
bingly bittersweet reading by the
vet blues
songster. “Any
Ole Way”
is a catchy traditional pledge of devotion.

HOLLIES (Imperial 66158)

should

The

about a love-sick guy who should but can’t give his gal the gate. “I’ve

the importance of personal identity.

Simon & Garfunkel To Get
Gold Record For 'Silence'
NEWYORK — Columbia’s
(Paul)
Simon and
(Arthur)
Garfunkel
will
be awarded
a
gold
record
for
their
debut single, “The Sounds Of Silence.”
The
gold
record
symbolizes
sales
of
over
one
million
copies,
as
certified
by
the
Record
Industry
Association
of America
(RIAA).
“The Sounds Of
Silence,” an
orig-
inal
song by
Paul
Simon,
launched
the duo
to
international fame. They
have
also
recorded
two
LP’s
for
Columbia,
“Wednesday
Morning
3
A.M.” and “The Sounds Of
Silence,”
which
includes
the
award-winning
song.
Their new
single, “Homeward
Bound,”
is
currently
holding
down
#30 slot on the Top 100.
Beishuizen To C.C.G.C.
PIET BEISHUIZEN
AMSTERDAM—After
18 years with
Philips,
Piet Beishuizen, head
of
in-
ternational press and public relations,
is
leaving
the
organisation
on May
1st to join C.C.G.C.
(Committee
Col-
lective
Gramophone
Records
Cam-
paign).
For
the
last
15
years
Bei-
shuizen
has
been
at
the
Baarn
headquarters
of
the
Philips
record
group.
During
this
time
he
has
es-
tablished
himself
as
a
major
per-
sonality
on
the
international
record
scene.
This
experience
will
be
em-
ployed to the full in his new capacity.
One of Beishuizen’s
first assignments
with
C.C.G.C.
will be
to
step up
the
sales
and promotion
of
gramophone
records in Holland generally. He will
also further the image of the gramo-
phone
record
as
an
integral
part
of
home entertainment in terms of press
relations and
increased
exposure
for
the product via radio and
television.

Industry Committee To
Probe Grammy Promo Lift
NEW YORK—Drawing
attention
to
this
year’s Grammy Awards
and,
at
the same time, to the artistic achieve-
ments
of the
entire
recording
indus-
try
is
one
of
the
chief
aims
of
a
new
industry
committee.
With
the
awards now. firmly established within
the
industry
itself, new methods
of
bringing the Grammy Awards
to the
attention of the general public will be
probed by the committee of ten.
Serving in a voluntary capacity are
Bob
Altshuler
of Columbia
Records,
Marty
Ostrow
of
Cash
Box,
Bob
Austin
of
Record
World,
Christie
Barter of Capitol Records, Sol Hand-
werger
of MGM Records, Herb
Hel-
man
of RCA
Victor
Records,
Lloyd
Leipzig
of
United
Artists
Records,
Bob
Rolontz
of
Atlantic
Records,
Herm
Schoenfeld
of
Variety
and
Billboard’s
Lee
Zhito,
organizer and
head of the committee.
At
the
group’s
initial
meeting
it
probed the possibility of disk jockeys
conducting
their own Grammy nomi-
nations straw pulls, with prizes being
awarded
to those listeners who come
closest
to
the
actual
final
results.
These will be announced on March 15.
Another
suggestion
consisted
of
record
companies
preparing
two
kinds
of album
stickers:
one
indicat-
ing
that the album had been
picked
as a Grammy nominee, and the other
that
it had
actually been awarded
a
Grammy.
Sol Handwerger noted that
MGM-Verve
had
done
this
before
and that the results had been notably
gratifying.
The
importance
of
obtaining
out-
standing
press
coverage
from
the
dailies and the weekly magazines was
also stressed. Here executive director
George
Simon
noted
the
increased
coverage
in
recent
years.
Last
year,
Time
Magazine
ran
two
separate
stories
on
the
result
of
the
awards,
while Life gave Roger Miller and
his
five
Grammys
a
full-page
picture
blow-up.
Several
company
members
suggested
that
contacts
with
press
and
radio
outlets
could
be
made
through companies as well as through
the Academy in order to lend an even
greater push to the promotion which
NARAS, on
its own, has been giving
the
Grammys.
Also
noted
was
the
importance
of
publicizing
not
only
the
actual
awards
presentations
on
March
15,
but
also
the
Academy’s
annual, all-important
television
spec-
tacular,
“The
Best On
Record,”
to
be telecast this year on May 16 over
the NBC network.
Finally,
it was recommended
that
all
radio
stations
be
encouraged
to
contact
their
nearest NARAS
office
to
coordinate
any
promotions
or
to
discuss
plans
regarding
them
with
Academy
officials.

To honor Frank Sinatra’s 25th anniversary since his start in show biz, Nippon
Victor will hold a “Sinatra Fair” Feb. 21-Apr. 20 while the firm releases an
anniversary two-set album titled “The History of Frank Sinatra.” The pack-
age
will
include
his famous
hit tunes when
he was
associated with RCA
Victor, Columbia and
Capitol.
The
Philips
sales department
of Nippon Victor puts “No, No
Boy/Little
Robby” in overseas markets through the firm’s
international
sales network.
The tune was recorded by the Spiders, who have been quite popular in Japan.
Foreign artists scheduled to perform here in Apr. include Jimmy Smith and
His Trio, Herbie Mann, Marcell Amon, and Percy Faith. To honor his perform-
ance, Nippon Columbia released “The Girl From Ipanema” LP as a Feb. new
issue, which
is doing well with Latin music
lovers.
In May, Duke .Ellington
will come to Japan.
Nippon Grammaphone
decided
to
release imported
tapes
in
Mar.
with
a
concert
of America Ampex
Co.,
with which German Grammaphone has
a
contract.
Labels
on
the
imported
tapes
include
Verve, MGM
and
Archive.
Though unnecessary to add, labels releasing imparted tapes in Japan are Nip-
pon Victor, Toshiba and King Records.
Among the Feb. new releases from Teichiku Records are “I Love Jazz” by
Louis Armstrong, and the All Stars on Decca which includes “I Love Jazz,”
“Twelfth Street Rag,” “Skokiaan” and nine
others. Besides the above record,
the firm
is also pushing “Walk Away” by Brenda Lee, “California
Girls” by
The
Surfaris, “Dynamic Tangos” by The
Castillians, “Flamenco
Songs And
Dances” by Carmen Ameya and “Apaches Beat Hits” by the Fabulous Jokers.
Toshiba Records
is releasing the following recordings: “Twilight Time” by
Roger Williams. “Animals” on Odeon includes fourteen tunes in which “Halle-
lujah,
I
Love
Her
So”
are
good
enough
to
show
their
originality.
“The
Ventures A Go-Go” includes “Ten Seconds To Heaven,” “Satisfaction,” “Go-Go
Guitar” and
nine
others.
“Cliff On
Stage”
includes “Apron
Strings,” “My
Baby,” “More It” and nine others. “Looking Back” by Nat Cole boasts “Time
and The River,” “Send For Me,” and nine others. “Beach Boys’ Party”
is an
anniversary release to honor their coming to Japan. The disk includes “Tell Me
Why,” “I Get Around” and eleven other tunes.
Nippon Grammaphone
releases
Connie
Francis’
“International
Hits.”
“All
About Oscar Peterson
Vols.
I and
II”
is an
anniversary
release
to
honor
Peterson’s performance
here. The
set includes “Debut,” “But Not For Me,”
“How High The Moon,” “Summer Time” and twelve
others.
In addition the
label has “Top Tangos For You Vol. 2”
in which Alfred House and Ricardo
Santos are included together. “Have Fun With Les Players” includes “I Feel
Fine,” “You Never Can Tell,” “She’s A Woman,” “After Dark,” “The House
of the Rising Sun” and twelve others.

AUSTRALIA
CBS has already done considerable promotion for their star Claude Leveillee
and the results have really been remarkable. Many a record, whether EP
or
single has found
its way into private
collections. At the prompting
of Mirni
Smith, he, as well as many other CBS-stars got considerable plugging on radio
and TV. Danny Fisher recorded a new disk and he will sing the songs on the
TV-program “Tienerklanken”
(Teenager
sounds).
Barclay has launched the promotion for a
girl, who
is gradually becoming
known, not only in France (she is of French descent), but.elsewhere in Europe,
as the “new Piaf,” the young songstress
is Mireille Mathieu. She
is appearing
in a Brussels music-hall and will, while here, also make a TV-performance on
the Flemish network. The Belgian papers are headlining her more and more.
Current
Barclay-successes
are:
“La
Boheme”
(The
Gipsy)
by
Aznavour;
“Potemkine” by Jean Ferrat; “Ces Gens-La” (Those people) by Brel and other
songs by Aufray,
the McCoys, and
Dalida. “The Monkiss” by
the
Airdales
and the Strangeloves is enjoying a lasting success. This dance
is widely known
and popular.
Vogue
is
actively engaged
in the promotion of the
tour
of Belgium from
March
12
to
20 by the Kinks, a tour organized by Unidans
Productions
of
Jean Vanloo. Across the whole country large posters are appearing on many
walls and
the promotion
in
the papers
is
being
actively
pursued. The
Pat
Boone
single “Mai Mai Mai”
(Valentina), a big success
in San Remo,
is
to
be put on sale by Vogue with
a
special promotion
effort.
A new star
in the
Ranch-skies
is
Jean-Marie Bernard,
a
talented young
man, who hails from Luxembourg and has just recorded
his
first
disk. Both
songs
are
published by Bens
Music. “Pas De
Filles”
(No
girls)
could
well
turn out
to be
a
bestseller.
Benoit Philippe has
a
second recording “Quand
Tu Es Dans Mes Bras” (When you’re in my arms), likely to hit
it
off better
than his
first try “Lisette”. In France, Philippe received a
special promotion
from
Polydor,
which
also
distributes
all
Ranch-records
in
Belgium.
There
certainly is no lack of promotion. Both singers together during a popular TV-
program.
Intervox-Eurovox
prexy
L.
J. Van Rijmenant
returned
from
Hamburg,
where he met Gunter Gayer
of
Sikorski
Music,
Gunter
Ilgner
of
Polydor,
record manufacturer Max Kunath and Messrs. Seeger and Bokler, of the Peer
Group.
Positive deals were made for the
first German recording by Flemish
thrush Mary-Ann, newest television discovery of “Discover the Star,” who will
record
top-title
“1-2-3-4-5-6-7”.
Bizz-talks
also
included
negotiation
for
the
Eurovox background music line and tape library, as well as scheduled German
recordings with folk group “The Dockx Brothers” and Ann Soetaert.
New Eurovox-productions
this month include a
stereo single by the Fabu-
lous
Jokers
“Brazil”
b/w
“Perfidia”
(on
Arcade
records,
nationally
dis-
tributed by Cardinal Records), “A Worried Man” b/w “Cottonfields” by The
Dockx Brothers, “1-2-3-4-5-6-7” b/w “Di Di 0 Day” by Mary-Ann and “Hump-
ty Dumpty” b/w “Tantie Jane” by Mel Turner,
all on Eurovox’s own
Dino-
label, handled by Candle
Records. On
Jan.
25th, Marc Dex and
the
Ruby’s
introduced their new Dino-outing “Vaarwey Jenny” on Frans Romeyns’ teen-
television program “Tienerklanken.”
New outing on Funckler Johnny Nash’s “Let’s Move and Groove (Together)”
b/w “Understanding” and “For Your Love” by Sam and
Bill
is now starting.
Epic introduced, this week, three new records “Mr. Lonely” by Bobby Vinton
b/w “There
I’ve Said It Again” and a new group of folk-singers
(three
girls
and four young men) The Back Porch Majority with “A Song Of Hope” b/w
“Mighty Mississippi.” The third record on Epic: The Glenn
Miller Orchestra,
under the direction of Ray McKinley with “Red Roses For A Blue Lady” b/w
“Everybody
Loves
Somebody”. On Hickory
a new
record
is
the
Newbeats
“Little Child.” Also on Hickory “Love Worked A Miracle” b/w “I Love You
Because” by Bob Luman. Colpix introduces a new LP of Nina Simone “Nina
Simone at the Village Gate” including several sensational titles “House Of The
Rising Sun,” “Bye Bye Black Bird,” “Just In Time,” and and “Brown Baby.”
The original soundtrack of “Thunderball” on United Artists (The latest James
Bond
successfilm)
is
already
one
of
the
biggest
LP’s. Festival
introduces
Christian Arabian, an author, composer, interpreter of his own songs with his
LP “Chansons Vertes Et Grises” including “Do Do Do,” “Le Bal Des Affreux,”
“Guerrologie” and “Les Mages”.
Also on Festival, Les Barbecues (seven young men) playing in New Orleans
Style. They play
“Julie
Crevecoeur,” “La Bague Au
Doigt,” two
songs by
Marie Laforet, “Aline”, a smash hit of this summer and a composition of J. R.
Morton “Milemberg Joy.” Also
on
Festival
Colette Chevrot comes
out with
his third record, including a hit “L’Elephant Rose.” This title
is gaining promi-
nence
due
to
the
company’s
continued
radio
promotion.
Other
titles
of
C.
Chevrot are “L’eau Et La Pierre” and “Ce N’Est Pas Avec Des Mots.”
On the classical side, Polygram reports to us, that an important number of
new albums were released: “Brahms/Klavierkoncert nr 2-B dur
op. 83” with
Alexander Uninsky
(Klaiver Klavier) and the Philharmonic
Orchestre of the
Hague conducted by Willem van
Otterloo. The
classical record of the month
is “Telemann”
(Dxy
835750)
with
f.e.
Konzert D-Dur
fur
drei
Trompete,
Pauken, zwei Oboen,
Streiche und Continuo, Orchestre “Pro Arte” Munchen,
conducted by Kurt Redel.
In the Polygram chanson-field new releases are: Philippe Clay “Abecedaire”/
Manger Porteur b/w “Incontestablement”; Frank Fernandel: “Non, Rien Au
Monde”
b/w
“Aujourd’hui”;
Anne
Sylvestre:
“Lazare
Et
Cecile”;
Johnny
Halliday:
“Le
Diable Me Pardonne” b/w
“Tu
Oublieras Mon Nom”;
Paul
Louka: “La Femme A Jean” b/w “Adieu Louise”. The titles of Anne Sylvestre,
Johnny
Halliday, and Paul Louka
are
controlled by Primavera
Music
Pub-
lishers
Brussels.
Paul Louka had
a very
successful
appearance
in
Brussels
Music Hall “Ancienne Belgique” (Old Belgium) and we
really hope that this
talented
Belgian
artist
will
reach
the
top
in
the chanson
field.
Other new
Polygram releases are: Dutch pop-art group HET with “Ik Heb Geen Zin Om
(Continued on next column)
Aztec Services and Stadiums Pty. have combined to present what they term
as the
first all-Australian big show which kicks
off
in Melbourne on March
1st. Then
it will play Ballarat, Brisbane, Newcastle, Sydney, Adelaide, Perth,
and
will wind-up at Shepparton on March
11th. The show will feature some
of the hottest acts pn the
local pop scene at the moment: Normie Rowe and
the Playboys, Bobbie and Laurie and the
Rondells, M.P.D.
Limited, and
the
Easybeats. National publicity is being handled by Bill Gordon publicity services.
The new album by
the
Beatles, “Rubber
Soul,” which was
released
only
this week
is already a runaway best-seller for EMI.
If sales of this package
are any
indication, the group
hasn’t
lost any
of
its popularity
as
is
being
claimed in some quarters here. They also happen to have the top single across
the nation too with “Day Tripper” b/w “We Can Work It Out,” which
is
still
on top
of our national
best-seller
list,
a
position
it has enjoyed
for
several
weeks. Not bad for a group
that’s supposed
to be losing fans.
During their recent “back home” concert tour, Australia’s world renowned
group the Seekers were presented a Gold Disc from EMI to mark sales in this
country of 50,000 copies
of “The Carnival
Is Over.” This
figure
in Australia
is generally accepted as the local equal to one million sales of a single
in the
United
States.
In addition
to
this, there was the rather unique presentation
to the group, from album station 3XY, of the station’s
special DIGMO
(Des-
troying the International Garbage Music Organization) Trophy for being the
most outstanding Australian group.
Festival Records has issued an album set entitled “Nat ‘King’ Cole In The
Beginning,” which
carries many
of the
great
old
sides by
the
original
trio
such
as “Honeysuckle Rose,” “Sweet Lorraine,” “Early Morning Blues” and
“Scotchin’ With The Soda.” This should catch some solid sales with the lovers
of the early Nat Cole
Trio.
It
is almost certain that Nancy
Sinatra
will have
the next smash around
Australia with her Reprise single “These Boots Are Made For Walkin’.” The
air-play on
this
side
is
quite staggering.
We understand that the A side of the new single by local star Merv Benton
has been banned by some of the leading Top 40 stations in some of our major
cities. The
title
(we believe
it’s
a
revival)
is “You Got What
It Takes
(To
Take What
I’ve
Got)”;
the
coupling
is “Shake,
Rattle And
Roll,” and
the
record
is
on the W & G
label.
As
yet, there
is no sign
of the
local release
of the Bobby
Fuller
click on
the Mustang
label.
It
is called “I Fought The Law.”

Record retailers, of course, purchase at wholesale prices, and the 25% Fed-
eral Government
Sales Tax
is computed
at
the
wholesale
level.
While
our
money
is not the same value
as that
of the United
States
(although
there
isn’t a great deal of difference between ours and the American dollar),
it can
be
readily seen that record prices
in Australia are considerably higher than
those of the U.S.A. and for the rest of the world for that matter. The trade
has for several years been looking for a reduction
in
sales
tax, but with no
success
to
date.
It
is hoped that the Record Manufacturers Association
will
continue its appeals to the Federal Government for the much needed reduction
in Sales Tax.
EMI
is out with a whole
flock of hot new singles fi'om their various over-
seas catalogs including “As Tears Go By” by the Rolling Stones; Pinkerton’s
Assorted Colours with “Mirror, Mirror”;
“Listen People” by Herman’s Her-
mits; “Waitin’ In Your Welfare Line” by Buck Owens; “This Golden Ring”
by the Fortunes; the Exciters with “A Little Bit Of Soap”; “Lightin’ Strikes”
by Lou
Christie; and “Up Tight” by
Little Stevie Wonder.
The
latest issue
of the APRA
(Australian Performing Right Association)
bulletin indicates that we can expect the new copyright legislation to become
effective later this year. There
is wide trade interest in the proposed amend-
ments to the existing act, because
it
is of vital importance
to many
sections
of the industry, especially to record companies and music publishers who are
all of the opinion that the changes should swing their way.
It’s quite obvious
that
all
parties cannot benefit from the
alterations,
so
the new
act
will be
eagerly awaited.

Capitol f Liberty Qoing
Into Tape
Cartridges
CAPITOL
HOLLYWOOD—Capitol Records will
move
into
the
tape
cartridge
field
“within & few months,” Alan Livings-
ton,
president
of
the
label,
has
an-
nounced.
Livingston’s
disclosure
of
the
la-
bel’s move
into what
is now
essen-
tially an
area for
automobile use
of
the
cartridge was made
in
an
open
letter to the industry.
Here
is
the
entire
Livingston
an-
nouncement :
“Since the introduction of a major
market
for
the
continuous-loop
tape
cartridge
by
the
Ford
Motor
Com-
pany,
Capitol
has
consistently taken
the
position
that
it would
not
offer
its extensive catalog for this purpose
until
future
availability
and manu-
facturing
rights
to
the
cartridge by
the record industry were
established,
and
standardization
assured.
Other record companies apparently
saw fit to take a similar position. Had
this not occurred, the record industry
would have found itself at the mercy
of limited suppliers and the whims of
patent holders. We felt
it our obliga-
tion
to
accept industry leadership
in
the face of another threatened battle
of
record
systems.
Now we
are
pleased
to
announce
that,
within
a few
months,
Capitol
will
offer
its
first
release
of
eight-
track,
continuous-loop
stereo
tape
cartridges.
These
cartridges
will
be
compatible
with
Ford
Motor
Com-
pany tape decks and with those under
development
by
other
major
auto-
mobile manufacturers,
thus
assuring
standardization.
Negotiations
with
various
sup-
pliers,
prior
to
commitment,
have
enabled us to be assured of cartridge
supply at competitive
prices,
as
well
as
the
.sight
to
manufacture.
This
right to manufacture
is at a fair and
acceptable
license
rate,
and
is, with
certain suppliers, license-free
after a
reasonable number of years—thus as-
suring us of being in complete control
of
our own
product.
It
is
assumed
that similar arrangements will be
of-
fered to other record manufacturers
As
to
the
future
of
the
tape-car-
1ldust-^’
is our
beIief that
tape de<fks will have to move into the
home
in
substantial numbers
before

LIBERTY
HOLLYWOOD—Liberty Records
will
be entering the stereo tape cartridge
field
with
a
vengeance
sometime
in
April, climbing abroad the tape auto
wagon with an
initial release of sev-
enty-five stereo tape albums. A sepa-
rate division for tape has been set up
at the Liberty
offices with Ron Bled-
soe as general manager and Dick Bow-
man as national sales manager.
The
initial
release
will
include
sixty-six
albums
available
on
both
four and
eight track Fidelipak
cart-
ridge
and
nine
twin
packs
on
Lear
type eight track. The single packs will
retail
for
$6.95
and
twin
pack
for
$9.95.
Recent Product
Included in the release will be many
of the Liberty-Dolton-Imperial-World
Pacific
artists with their most recent
disk
product.
Plans
are
to
have
a
minimum of 130 titles within the year
with releases scheduled within
a few
weeks
after
disks
are
shipped.
Dis-
tribution
of
tape
will
be
through
Liberty’s
regular
outlets
with
the
possibility
that
automotive
channels
will be added in the future.
Packaging
An entirely new concept in packag-
ing will be introduced in the form of
the Trak Pak, Liberty’s own case and
track
which
can
hold
any
existing
continuous
tape
cartridge.
Both
will
be made
of an inexpensive transpar-
ent plastic material and the case will
be
dust proof
as
well
as
shock and
heat resistant. The open sides
of the
case will allow the graphic identifica-
tion
on
the
cartridge
to
be exposed
which
will
mean
identification
does
not have to be presented on the case
itself. A consumer may therefore
re-
place
any
cartridge
into
the
case
without
the
inconvenience
of
corre-
lating
cases with
cartridges.
Liberty
is
repackaging
with
adaptions
of
present disk art work reduced to cart-
ridge
size. With
the
introduction
of
the
Trak
Pak
titles
will
be
visible
from three sides and thus enhance the
merchandising of the product.
The
transparent
track
may
be
mounted
under
the
auto
dashboard
or vertically on a wall or door inside
the
car. Each
track
will
hold up
to
six cases with cartridges and may be
molded
in
various
lengths
as
neces-
sary to hold many more. The case will
be
easily
attached
to
the
track
and
can conversely be easily removed from
the
track,
hanging
individually
or
with a group. Cartridge removal from
(Continued on page 42)
