1.
Mercury’s Green To First Gonf.
With Philips’ Solleveld
NEW YORK—Irving B. Green, presi-
dent
of Mercury
Records,
planed
to
Baarn, Holland last weekend, where he
conferred with
Mercury’s world-wide
licensee and leaders of Philips Phono-
graphic
Industries
in
their
first
conference
with
C.
Solleveld,
newly-
appointed
chairman
of management
of
the
Philips
global
record
entity.
Solleveld
will helm
a meeting which
also will include Les Gould, England;
Paul
Lebbink,
Italy;
Hanz
Schrade,
Germany;
Georges
Meyerstein,
France; and Jack Haislinghaus, Ben-
elux
countries,
April
18th
and
19th.
Solleveld succeeds J. W. A. Langen-
berg, who resigned recently to accept
an important
position with
a promi-
nent
Dutch
group
of
ship-building
firms.
Solleveld joined the Philips organi-
zation in the early forties. He worked
in various commercial departments of
the
firm
until
1946,
when
he
was
made
general
sales manager
of
the
manufacturing and
selling
organiza-
tion
of
Philips
in
Indonesia. He
re-
turned later to the home office of Phil-
ips
in
Baarn
as
right-hand man
to
E.
B. W. Schuitma,
original
director
of P.P.I. Subsequently he became gen-
eral
manager
of
Phonograme,
the
Dutch sales organization. In 1961 Sol-
leveld
was
appointed
general
man-
ager of the main industry group
for
Philips in Eindhoven, Holland, where
he
dealt with tape
recorders,
profes-
sional
and
home
movie-making
and
projection
equipment,
closed
circuit
and
other TV
equipment,
and, most
recently,
the
Plumbicon
studio
color
camera.
Green
will
remain
in
Holland
at
Eindhoven
following
the
meeting
to
discuss
further
expansion
of
Mer-
cury’s
home
entertainment
products
division
in
the
tape
recorder,
car-
tridge,
and phono
industry. He
will
meet
with Herman
Koning,
general
manager
of
Philips’
phono
division,
and
A. Van
Strien, manager
of
the
tape
recorder
division.
Green’s
European
itinerary
calls
for
a
stopover
in
Geneva,
Switzer-
land,
for
talks
with
Brice
Somers,
chief
of
Mercury’s
international
di-
vision.
Final
lap
on
the
junket
will
be
London.
Discussions
regarding
cross-releasing of British and Ameri-
can artists will take place with Gould,
Jack
Baverstock,
and
others
in
the
English
Philips organization,
as well
as with
indie English record produc-
ers whose
product
is
being
used
by
Mercury’s
labels.
Tracy Departs , Sherman Top Limelight Man
CHICAGO—With
the
departure
last
week of Jack Tracy, director of A&R
for Limelight Records, Dick Sherman,
product manager of the all-jazz label,
will assume
a
fuller
control
in
a
re-
alignment
of
executive
duties
an-
nounced by Irving B. Green, president
of Mercury Records, parent company.
Tracy did not announce future plans.
Sherman
will
also continue
to
act as
product manager for Mei’cury’s new-
ly
initiated
recorded tape
division,
a
post
to
which
he
was
appointed
a
month
ago,
Green
noted.
Sherman
will assume
full responsibility for
di-
rect
relations with
artists, both
cur-
rent
and
in
any new
artist
acquisi-
tions which might occur in the future.
He
will
plan
album
releases
and
schedule the actual recording of pres-
ent and new
jazz
artists.
Recording
sessions will be supervised by Quincy
Jones
(vice president in A&R), Luchi
De Jesus and Hal Mooney.
With fifteen months of actual mar-
keting experience in the
all-jazz
line,
Sherman
stated
that
Limelight
will
continue
with
a
compact
roster
of
carefully selected top jazz names. The
present
line-up
includes:
The
Oscar
Peterson
Trio,
Les
McCann,
The
Three
Sounds,
Art
Blakey
and
the
Jazz
Messengers,
Milt
Jackson,
Ro-
land Kirk, Dizzy Gillespie, and Gerry
Mulligan.
Deluxe
packaging,
which
has
be-
come a Limelight collector’s lure, will
be
continued,
with
“important
im-
provements”
to
be
incorporated
in
forthcoming
Limelight
album
re-
leases.
Six
of
the
first
thirty Lime-
light
album
packages
were
included
in
the
recent Chicago Art
Directors’
Guild
1966
competition.
The
Polish
Jazz Federation awarded
its packag-
ing plaque
for
1965
to
the
late
Eric
Dolphy’s
“Last
Date”
Limelight
al-
bum, Sherman
added.

M. Honer, Harmonica Maker
To Expand Into Guitar Field
HICKSVILLE,
L.I.—M.
Honer,
Inc.
is entering the guitar field after 109-
years
as
a
dominant maker
of har-
monicas,
accordions,
and
other
free
reed
instruments.
The
firm,
long
known
primarily
for
its
‘Marine
Band’
harmonicas,
has
introduced
a
full
line
of
acoustic,
semi-acoustic,
and
electric
guitars. Honer
calls the
new
line,
‘Contessa’.
The compatibility of the guitar and
the harmonica, which has been shar-
|
ing substantially in the popularity of
rock,
folk-rock,
and
folk
music, was
among
the
principal
factors
in
prompting
Hohner’s
adoption
of
the
guitar. Honer will conduct an exten-
j
sive
advertising
campaign
for
the
Contessa
line.

BEHIND THE
RECORDS
BMI AWARDS
DO
TO
SATURDAY
MUSIC.
INC.
Saturday
Music,
Inc.,
was
the
worthy
recipient
of
three
BMI
Awards,
and
it
couldn't
happen to three greater songs
or more
talented
writers.
All
of the Award winning compo-
sitions are
natural
for covers,
so alert producers please take
note.
"Lover’s Concerto” by Sandy
Linzer and Denny Randell has
had
35
recordings
released
within
the
past
six
months.
Certainly
a
great
tribute
to
this
beautiful
song. The
vari-
ous versions of "Lover’s Con-
certo”
reveals
most
impres-
sively
that
many
arrangers
are so talented that cover rec-
ords are not "copies” of a
hit,

Merco Earnings Up 41 %
Sales Rise 26% In 1965
NEW YORK—Merco
Enterprise,
the
large,
Garden
City,
L.I.-based
rack-
jobber, reported earnings
of $358,343
for the year ended
Dec.
31,
1965, an
increase
of
41%
over
the
previous
year’s $255,089 figures.
The company’s sales rose to $8,143,-
131
in
1965, a jump of 41% over last
year’s
$6,543,500
take.
Earnings
per
share increased to $1.02 over .72 cents
in 1964.
Merco sells records to approximate-
ly
100
retail
record departments and
40
“junior”
sized
departments
(the
latter
in
variety
stores
and
college
book stores)
in 24
states. In addition,
the
firm’s
wholly-owned
subsidiaries
operate 29 leased record departments
in
discount
centers
in
N.Y.,
N.J.,
Conn., and Md.
Jack Grossman, president of Merco,
feels that the 1965 figures, which were
the highest
in the company’s
history,
will be surpassed
in 1966 through ex-
panded
diversification
and
the
addi-
tion
of both leased and
serviced-only
record departments.

Kaplan Post Completes
Mercury's Geo. Sales Ties
CHICAGO—With

regional manager
for
Mercury
Rec-
ords,
a
geographically
strategic
bal-
ance of coordinated
sales supervision
has been
struck by

dent
and
product
manager
Kenny
Myers.
Kaplan
joins Mercury
after an
ex-
tensive background
in
the record
in-
dustry. Most
recently
he
headed
his
own independent promotion firm, Bur-
kap
Associates,
in
Atlanta.
Prior
to
this he
operated Ponderosa
Distribu-
tors
in
Columbia,
South
Carolina,
a
one-stop owned by Pat Cohen of Rich-
mond, Virginia. Kaplan has also been
associated
with
Mobile
One-stop
in
New York
City,
upstate New
York,
and
the
Carolinas, as
well
as South-
east
Record
Merchandisers
in
Char-
lotte.
Headquartering
in Atlanta, Kaplan
will
be
responsible
for
the
distribu-
tion
points
of
Atlanta, Miami, Char-
lotte,
New
Orleans,
Memphis,
and
Nashville. His appointment will com-
plement

managers:

Bridges,
Western;
Sonny
Kirehen,
Eastern;
and
Frank
Peters, Mid-Western.

May will be the biggest month for the Japanese pop fan to witness perform-
ances by foreign artists. Theolonious Monk and his quartet arrive here at the
beginning of May at the invitation of Tokyo Concert to have a fortnight tour
through the main
cities of Japan. The
artist
is well-known here as a
pianist
and composer and
his “Blue Monk” and “Round About Midnight”
are much
appreciated by modern jazz fans
here.
Duke Ellington and his orch. arrive here on May 12 for a ten day perform-
ance tour at the invitation of the Kambara Music
office. Percy Faith and his
orch. are to arrive here on May 9 for a fortnight’s tour throughout the major
cities of Japan, at the request of Nippon Columbia Musical Enterprises.
Billy
Vaughn and his orch. will arrive on May 23 for a ten day series of perform-
ances and Pat Boone
also
arrives here
for
a
ten day performance
tour on
May
24.
John Sabron arrives here on May 22 at the invitation
of
Ishii Music
office
to participate in the Paris Festival held here on July
14, in which Ivette Jiro,
now in Japan,
is scheduled to appear.
Ros Indios Tabarajhas, noted for “Maria Elena,” arrived here on April
12
for several performances
in which the American pop
songster Ricky Nelson
is scheduled to appear.
The Nippon Hoso Kyokai Symphony
Orch., the most authorized one
here,
will
reportedly have
16 performances
overseas
in
America,
Mexico,
Brazil,
Argentina, Hawaii and other countries, between April 28 and May 31, in which
they are scheduled to participate in the International Festival in Mexico. This
is
their fourth
visit,
especially
characterized
as
the
culture
delegate
of the
Foreign Ministry this time,
in the wake of the European and American tour
of
I960, the South-East Asian tour
of
1962, and the South-East Asian and
Australian tour of 1964. The orch. consists of 116 members and
is conducted
by Hiroyuki Iwaki and Yuzo Toyama.
According
to
the AP
report,
the
Beatles
are coming
to Japan
via West
Germany at the end of June for only two performances around and in Tokyo
the
first of which
is scheduled for June 30 in Tokyo. While Tastu Nagashima,
representative of Kyodo Kikaku,
is negotiating
in London for the
other.
While the popular American TVer, “Bat Man,” was set to be broadcast here
in Japan on May 10, the theme music
is now in competition in Japan’s record
market, as five record companies released or will release more than ten disks
of
the same
tune. Nippon
Victor
released
three
“Bat Man,”
including
the

of

(65)
to March

(66)

Joe Napoli, the American
GI, who during the
last war participated in the
Battle
of the Bulge
in the Belgian Ardennes, and afterwards
organized the
famous
international
jazz-festival
at
Comblain-la-Tour
in
order
to
collect
funds to restore the war-damaged church of this
little
village, has informed
Cash Box, that this
yfear’s festival
is to be held on Saturday Aug. and Sun-
day Aug.
7. More about the origins of this festival, started in 1959 and known
to jazz-fans of five continents, can be found elsewhere in this issue.
Ardmore and Beechwood told us that they have acquired the copyrights on
the current United Kingdom
strong one by the Walker Brothers: “The Sun
Ain’t Gonna Shine Anymore.”
It should be added that the Walker
Bros, are
due
in Brussels for a TV-appearance
soon. The publishing house
also owns
rights to “Someday One Day,” by the Seekers; “Homeward Bound,” by Simon
and Garfunkel;
“Little By
Little” by Buddy; “Tiens Bon,” by Richard Anth-
ony; and two numbers by Marc Aryan “Parce Que Je T’Aime” and “C’est La
Vie.”
Jean-Claude Annoux and Theresa recently appeared at the Old Belgium
in
Brussels. Theresa acquired fame during the recent Eurovision Song Festival
in Luxembourg, where she represented Monaco. The forthcoming appearance
in Belgium of the following stars from S.A.-Grammophon
is announced: Anny
Cordy, on May
1, in Liege; Gribouille at Middelkerke. Liz Brady was engaged
by Frans Romeyns for his TV’er. She is a rising lark in Paris with tremendous
vocal qualities. Liz Brady will feature in “Tienerklanken,” a very popular TV-
series with famous and
less famous
stars.
James Brown was in Paris to present his new release “Papa’s Got A Brand
New Bag.” Among the bestsellers of the week distributed by Polydor, we
still
find: “Ganz In Weiss” by Roy Black; “Moon Over Naples” by Bert Kaempfert;
“Hundert Mann Und Ein Befehl” by Freddy. Renate Kern will be staying in
Belgium on April 21 for the program “Tienerklanken” on the Flemish TV.
News in the classical music section was provided by manager Holzapfel, who
informed us that on April 20 a large reception was organized for the presenta-
tion of a national recording album “The Flemish Music Of The 15th And 16th
Century Society.” Almost
all the pieces of music are borrowed from the fam-
ous
Archiv-series and bearing such well-known names
as
Dufay,
Ockegem,
Desprez, Lassus, and many others, altogether some 23 pieces from the patri-
mony of our once
so famous and
still highly praised
15th and
16th Flemish
songs. A very remarkable and valuable recording.
Vogue
still remains on top with “These Boots Are Made For Walkin’ ” by
Nancy Sinatra, surely the main top-tune of 1966. Frans Romeyns, talent-scout
of the “Tienerklanken” section of the Flemish TV-network last week travelled
to Paris, where he contacted several artists of the Disc A-Z label (represented
in France and Belgium by Vogue) for one of his next programs, among them
Romuald,
Danyel Gerard and
les
Troubadours. The renowned
Jean-Jacques
Debout also appears on his
list.
From Barclay the news
that
there
is
a chance
of
a
visit
to Belgium by
Sonny and Cher. From a promotion point of view this would indeed be a very
smart move. While in Paris we heard from Brillant and Helman, of the Bar-
clay group, that the duet
is now working on a
flick in the U.S.A. There
is a
possibility that they
will be
visiting Belgium
in early June, for a
p.a.- and
TV-performance.
Contacts have been
laid with the French and Flemish TV-
networks.
It
all now hinges on dates
.
.
. and
dollars!
The
Riviera-headquarters
in

released

of

Neil Christian, with on

nice.”
Christian
is to
travel to Brussels soon to feature in Tienerklanken.
Cameo-Parkway this week released an LP-album of Chubby Checker, “The
Greatest Hits.” Many the big successes
of Chubby are included on
this LP:
“Baby, Baby, Balia, Balia,” “Stoppin’ in Las Vegas,” “Loddy Lo,” “Lay Elise
Mollie” and many
others. On

with

“A Hard Day’s Night” and

’n

is

Ola and the Janglers, six young men from Sweden, on Funckler present their
first LP:
“Surprise,
Surprise” and
it contains

on United

include
Little Anthony and the Imperials with “Hurt” c/w “Never Again,” Jr. Walker
& the All Stars present “Cleo’s Mood” on Tamla Town.
Once again we find Villard on our best-seller
list with “Capri C’est Fini,”
and “Mourir Ou Vivre.” Together with another Philips-artist Michele Torr, he
put in an appearance for a few days at the Old Belgium, where both got an
excellent reception by the audience. A cocktail party attended by many jour-
nalists was arranged for them by Polygram at the Martini Terrace in Brussels.
J. Darlier of the Herman Brauer publishing house
is endeavouring
to
ar-
range a visit by Herman’s Hermits. Talks are going on with the Flemish TV.
It sure would be fine if they were successful for Herman has never before been
over here with his Hermits. His songs, though elsewhere near the top of the
hit-parade, have never quite caught on here. Perhaps a visit could change all
this. Darlier furthermore told us the company owns copyrights on “J’ai Envie
De Vivre Avec Toi”
(I Feel Like
Livin’ With You)
and “Ne Te Marie Pas
Sophie” (Don’t Get Married Sophie) by Herve Villard and on Herman’s Herm-
its song “Listen People” and the
first French spoken recording by Herman
“Je Suis Anglais”
(I’m English). Burt Blanca
is to feature in a TV-program
on April 28 and Serge Davignac has again hit a lucky streak:
his second re-
cording
is placed number two in a poll of the French radio-producers.
World Music Group
is actively pushing the titles of the Screen Gems cata-
logue: “A Groovy Kind Of Love” by the Mindbenders, “Soul And Inspiration”
by the Righteous Brothers and “The Gamma Goochee” by Gamma Goochee.
The latter is almost certain to be a big hit during the coming holiday season.
In the Acuff-Rose catalogue “I Fought The Law” by Bobby Fuller Four, just
released, looks
quite promising.
Reactions
to
the most recent Digno
Garcia
recording: “Guantanamera,” and by Luigi:
“Nadine,” both on
Palette, have
been very encouraging.
Les Cousins have just completed a tour of Argentina and the TV-networks
are negotiating with them for performances. During the coming weeks, they
will participate
in
6
different programs, one
of them
in Germany. Moreover
they have just recorded a new remarkable EP “All Right Mamma” and “Four
Sailors Back Home.”

ON COIN ROW THIS WEEK—Mike Munves was on the phone with brother
Joe as we entered
the Munves
office.
Joe’s upstate on
a
sales
tour and was
calling
in
orders. We asked Mike what
the customers
wanted.
“Everything,
everything. We’ve got so many orders in we can’t ship ’em all.” Packaged units
were lining the walls, ready
to go out. ... At United East Coast the show-
rooms were bare—all sold out and waiting
for more from Williams.
.
.
. Abe
Lipsky, UJA’s Man
of
the
Year,
is moving
plenty
of
pool
tables and
used
cigarette machines these days;
his showrooms to are getting that “sold out”
look.
.
.
. A1 d’lnzillo spread his arms and said, “What can
I
tell you? We have
a double shift at the factory, working
all night and
all day Saturdays, to get
enough ‘ElectroPooT tables out to the customers. The game was two years
in
the making and we knew
it would be popular—but we never dreamed
it would
go over like
it has. Just tremendous!” Even the demonstration table was gone
from the Albert Simon showrooms.
.
.
. Irving Green, son of Runyon Sales Co.
president Irving Green,
will be working at the New York showrooms part of
the week on a regular basis now
; the rest of the time
he’ll be on the road for
Rowe. Irving Kempner and Louis Wolburg are giving Irving some tips on the
trade, and they’re two of the best teachers around.
.
.
. There are new feminine
additions
to
the
Runyon

this

but
blonde
and

Sandy
Rasnitzky—ah,

and
remains

favorite. And

makes

good cup

to
time
our

to
the
Runyon showrooms just at the
coffee break. Louis Wolburg reminds
us
that
there
will be
a Rowe AC service class at the New York
offices Wednesday,
April 27th, starting promptly at six in the evening. The brand new Rowe Band
Stand
phonograph
will
be looked
into.
.
.
. Dave Freed and
Milt Tucker
of
Musical
Distributors were

unloading

in the showrooms now,
and quite a game

to base. Murray Kaye,
Atlantic

ace, preparing

GET TOUGH—Howard Kaye
is more
than
enthusiastic
about
the
sales
of
“Tough Guy,” the new Irving Kaye fibreglass cue—“I’m
ecstatic.
I’d say the
ratio between our cue and a wooden cue
is ten to one on
life. And you can’t
break them. You know how it is—a guy misses a shot and bangs the cue down
on the table and boom,
it goes flying
off
in forty
dix-ections. Some
opei-ators
have
to
spend twenty
dollars
a week
on
replacements. They
don’t have
to
spend anything on replacements with ‘Tough
Guy’. The demand for
it
is
so
hot—this is no con—we’ve had to set up another production line to handle
it.”
MOA DRIVES ON WITH DRIVE—Since the
first of the year, the men from
MOA have been going
all out
in
their membership drive and
president John
Wallace announced last week that one hundred new faces have come into the
MOA fold. The goal
is 250, and Wallace promises to keep up the push.

BOOTLEGGING—The romantic
picture
of
a
beat-up coupe
that sags
in
the
trunk, racing along a highway
with
a yowling
police
car behind
it, may be
amusing. Certainly
it
is
profitable. New
profits
are coming
in
because
of
a
New York state sales tax on cigarettes. Instead of moonshine, the genial boys
in the pink
shirts are now hauling smoke across the
border. North Carolina,
where most of the major tobacco
firms
are
located,
is the
central
source
of
supply for the truckloads of bootleg butts. New York state revenue losses are
running towards 30 million dollars a year and cigarette vending operators are
being hurt from both sides. All because of a tax somebody
in Albany thought
would be a good idea and would bring in
all kinds of lovely money. Nice going.

this year.

AGAC Seeks Broader Creative Membership
NEW YORK—A recruitment drive
is
on at the American Guild of Authors
& Composers (AGAC), to fill its mem-
bership rolls with rock ’n roll, & R&B
and country music composers.
According to Burton Lane, president
of
the
Guild,
a
program
placing
emphasis in these
fields will cover at
least a 12 month period. For the
first
time in the Guild’s 35 year history, a
series of ads
is being placed in music
trade papers. Augmenting this will be
brochures
outlining the
Guild’s bene-
fits
to
writers,
posters
that
will
be
hung at major recording studios and
a general education program.
Latter
approach will bring Guild speakers to
high schools and
colleges.
Lane
contends
that many
writers,
some young and
relatively
inexperi-
enced
in the music
field, are
signing
contracts
“right
out
of
the
middle
ages.” A noted composer himself
(e.g.
“Finian’s
Rainbow,”
“On A
Clear
Day”), he points to the fact that the
Guild has been able to “recover” for
its members a sum of $1 million since
1959. In 1947, the
Guild,
in negotiat-
ing a new draft
of
its uniform
con-
tract with publishers, won the right to
audit publishers books.
A system of dues payments can be
worked out. Lane said, that enables a
new member
to
“join now
and
pay
later.”
Among
the
recent
additions
to
AGAC are Brook Benton, Clyde
Otis
and
Clint
Ballard.
Also,
Richard
Rodgers recently re-entered the ranks
of the Guild’s membership.
AGAC is approaching its 35th anni-
versary.
Until
Lane
assumed
the
presidency eight years ago, the Guild
was known as the Songwriters Protec-
tive League.
Its
membership
totals
more
than
2000 writers, ranging in ages from 12
to
90
plus. The youngest member
is
Emery Deutsch, Jr., son of the popu-
lar violinist.
SIGNING TIME—Pianist Peter Serkin
(right)
recently
signed
the
contract
which
ties
him
exclusively
to RCA
Victor
Red
Seal
recordings,
while
A&R manager Roger Hall looked on.
Serkin, the son of famed pianist Ru-
dolf Serkin, already has two Red Seal
LP’s in release and
is scheduled to go
to Chicago
this summer
to complete
his
first
disk
with
orchestra.
The
pieces selected are Bartok’s
first and
second concertos and Seiji Ozawa will
be conducting the Chicago Symphony.
Max Wilcox, Red
Seal a&r producer,
supervises Serkin’s recording sessions.

HOLLYWOOD-Backed by a series of
statistics relative to the popularity of
the guitar throughout the world, Don
Blocker, general manager
of Liberty
Eecords, has
set an all-encompassing

May
2

June
10
on

all
of
which
feature

According
to
Blocker,
there
are
more than 8,000,000
guitarists
in the
U.
S. and 1,400,000 guitars were sold
in
1965.
That same
year
sales were
up 75% on
electric and 40 %> on non-
electric over
1964.
Ventures
Highlighted

of

and

Lewis
of
Decca-England
about
the
current
world-wide
licensing
agree-
ment Decca has with Monument and
which expires in Oct. Foster present-
ed Monument artists Boots Randolph

to the USA
while Weiss
continued on his swing to Oslo, Stock-
holm,
Copenhagen,
Zurich,
Berlin,

the record
situa-

as
it
applies
to
the Monument,
Sound Stage 7 and LTD International
record catalogues taking into
consid-
eration the appeal of American prod-
uct at
this time
overseas, new mar-
keting
plans,
etc.
Weiss
is now back at his
interna-
tional headquarters
in Hollywood.

The 18 songs for the

been picked and the 18 stars who will do the numbers for the TV preliminary
round. Polydor, Metronome,

will have

Reports reach us that the record industry will plan a second festival spon-
sored by the industry
itself as this festival
will, of course, use record
stars,
but is not in connection with the major record firms as in the past. This year,
401 songs were entered compared with 234 last year and the
18 songs were
picked by a jury consisting of 3 composers, 3 conductors, 3 radio station per-
sonalities, 3 journalists and 3 music students. The prelims will be held on the
21st of May in Berlin and we’ll have more news about the festival as the time
grows near for the
contest.

peop^_ we believe
in. We expect
them to Show reciprocal confidence in
us
so
that we can
create
centralized
direction
impossible
when

are accepted at random from a vari-
ety of sources.”
The new
S.A.C.
policy, which

radical departure for agencies

field,
is viewed as an-
other
step

David Platz Heads
TRO's Ini'l. Scene
NEW YORK—David
Platz, head
of
Essex Music Ltd. in London, has been
named director of international oper-
ations for the entire Richmond Orga-
nization,
according
to
Howard
S.
Richmond,
president
of
TRO,
of
which Essex
is
the
British
affiliate.
The development comes
in
the wake
of the recent Essex move to expanded
quarters.
Platz, who was born
in Germany,
came
to Essex Music
as manager
in
1955,
working
at
the
time
in
two
small, back-room
offices
in Denmark
Place,
London.
Since
that
time,
he
has
guided
the
firm,
in
cooperation
with TRO headquarters in New York,
to a number
of major
successes,
in-
cluding
13
major
awards
for
out-
standing
British
songs,
in
11
years.

undertaken
a

with

nounced

creased responsibilities. These include
a growing amount of indie disk activ-
ity and the recording and placing of
masters
with

record
labels.

as

in

London and New York productions of
“Beyond
The
Fringe.”

discs
are produced by
Essex
for
lease
to
Decca Ltd.
Well-known
British
producer,
Denny
Cordell,
has
also
recently
joined
Essex
for
the
production
of
masters.
Cordell
produced
hits
by
the Moody Blues and Georgia Fame
and the Blue Flames. Also associated

Mercury Inks Jerry Butler
NEW YORK—Jerry Butler has been

to
a
long-term
Mercury
re-
cording
pact,
it was
announced
last
week
by
label
president
Irving
B.
Green. Mercury
will
release a single
immediately after the termination of
the
songster’s
contract with VeeJay,
which expires May 31,
1966.
Mercury
begins
its
recording
ses-
sion
blueprint
immediately.
Green
added. Luchi De Jesus of the
label’s
New York A&R
staff jetted to Cleve-
land last week where he huddled with
Butler
who
was
working
in
Leo’s
Casino.
Alan
Mink,

national
promotion
manager,
will
also
fly
to
Cleveland
to correlate special promo-
tions for Butler. The songster will be
presented
in

tions
at
the

set by Queen Booking, New York; the
Pine
Gi’ill
in
Buffalo, May 9-16;

25-June
3.

Butler

H.
Stein-
berg

Myers,

vice-president and vice-president and
product manager respectively of Mer-
cury
and
Irv Nahan
and
W.
Yale
Matheson, personal manager and
at-
torney
respectively
for
Butler.
Butler’s
last
single was
a remake
of
his own
original
hit, “For Your
Precious Love,” released in Dec. 1965.
The hit was originally recorded under
the name of Jerry Butler and the Im-
pressions for VeeJay in
1958. At the
time
Butler was
singing
lead
with
Curtis
Mayfield
and
Sam
Gordon,
original members of the Impressions,
still with the group.
Green
stated
that
Butler’s
single
will
be
made
available
world-wide
sometime
in
mid-June
through
the
global
affiliates
of

in

international
Philips
organization.

fore the end of May.

CBS-lsrael To Release
Israel Song Festival LP
NEW YORK—CBS
Records
Israel
will release an LP of the Israel Song
Festival 1966, according to announce-
ment
by
Simon
Schmidt,
managing
director of CBS
Israel.
The
firm which
obtained
exclusive
worldwide
rights
for
the album,
re-
corded
it at
the Song
Festival, held
on Israel’s Independence Day, Apr. 25.
The
Israel Song Festival
is an an-
nual
event
sponsored by
the
Israeli
Broadcasting Service, Kol Israel, and
the Independence Day Committee
of
the Prime
Minister’s
Office.
Among
the CBS
artists who
par-
ticipated in the festival are the Pava-
rim, a three-guitar, folk-singing
trio,
and vocalist Edna Goren.
The disk is scheduled for release on
May
15.

NARAS L.A. To Talk
Valiant' Will Handle
Over Grammy Awards
HOLLYWOOD—It’s NARAS of Holly-
wood’s turn to talk over the associa-
tion’s Grammy awards categories this
week. On Wednesday
(11), members
of the Los Angeles chapter will gath-
er in open discussion. Meet follows a
recent assemblage, for the same pur-
pose, of the New York chapter.
Notes chapter president Dave
Pell:
“This
open
discussion among
West
Coast members is designed to unearth
not
only
gripes from
members,
but
also constructive comments regarding
the annual awards. Only by bringing
this subject directly to our voters and
hearing exactly how they feel, will we
be able to know
(1) whether they are
in accord with the current categories,
and
(2)
if they are not satisfied, how
they
feel
the
set-up
might
be
im-
proved.”
In the hope of emphasizing the pos-
itive aspect of the meeting, the notice
sent
to
the
membership
contained,
“Constructive
Criticism
Wanted,”
a
re-print of a recent Cash Box
edito-
rial. Pell states that all comments will
be noted and referred to the chapter’s
awards &
categories
committee
for
study, with eventual recommendations
to be made by the chapter’s full board
of governors to the national academy.
Richard Farina
Dies On Coast
CARMEL,
CAL. — Richard
Farina,
folksinger, was killed in a motorcycle
mishap
several hours
after the
pub-
lication of his first novel, “Been Down
So Long
It Looks Like Up To Me.”
The 29-year-old Farina was a native
of New York and the brother-in-law
of
the
well-known
folk
lark,
Joan
Baez. Farina’s wife, the former Mimi
Baez, and
he
had moved
to
Carmel
three
years
ago. They
recorded two
folk albums for Vanguard.
MPPA Now NMPA
NEW YORK—Members of the Music
Publishers’
Protective
Association,
during a special meeting held on May
3, unanimously adopted the new name
of
National Music
Publishers’
Asso-
ciation,
Inc. for the organization.
In announcing the
action. Associa-
tion president Arthur Israel, Jr. states
that “the name under which we have
written a 49-year record
of achieve-
ment and progress is one of which we
are proud. But
it
is no longer appro-
priate
in these days and in the
light
of our present
activities and accom-
plishments.” He further state that the
new title is “a more fitting and mean-
ingful designation for our Association
in
the mid
’60s and
in
the
light
of
our future plans and purposes.”

NIGHTCLUBS
'Fuller Four' Swings
In New York Debut
NEW YORK—The Bobby Fuller Four
has finally brought its unique western
flavored
rock
sound
to New
York,
with its start last week of a two-week
stint at Ondine, the somewhat nauti-
cal but very swinging discotheque.
The Mustang Records group which
clicked big with “I Fought The Law”
and followed that with
their current
chart item
“Love’s Made A
Fool Of
You,”
are
an
extremely
tight
and
highly
professional
group
and
their
long
sets, as taxing on the group as
they
are, never drag
or
lose any
of
the enthusiasm that they
start with.
Fuller
is
spotlighted
in
the
per-
formance,
and
as
a
matter
of
fact
works on a
separate
stage from
the
rest of the quartet. The free-swinging
Fuller plays lead guitar for the group
as
well
as
singing
lead,
while
the
others chime
in with
the usual rock
group
instrumentation
(rhythm
and
bass
guitar and drums)
and
lots
of
infectious vocal harmony.
After
all
is
said
and
done,
the
Bobby Fuller Four
is a group that
is
out
to
please
both
the
listeners and
dancers in the crowds that they draw
and manage to do both very well.

BRITAIN
EMI Chairman,
Sir Joseph Lockwood,
recently returned from
a 5% week
world tour which took him as far afield as the United States, Japan, Australia,
and New Zealand, culminating in Greece where a four-day conference was held
at the Columbia Graphophone Company of Greece. The conference was attended
by top executives of the EMI world wide organization including Robert Mc-
Kenzie (Greece); Glenn E. Wallichs, Alan Livingston, Lloyd Dunn and Stanley
Gortikov
(United
States);
John
Wall,
L.

(Italy)
and
Richmond (South Africa). Discussions centered around EMI’s global activities
and plans for the future were formulated. Sir Joseph also took the opportunity
on

visit to
call on A.
Campbell, managing
director
of (Jramofon
Limitet Sirketi (Turkey). Whilst in New Zealand Sir Joseph toured the newly
opened extension to the HMV factory
A1 Bennett, president of Liberty Records
in London recently
for meetings
with Sir Joseph Lockwood, L. G. Wood and G. N. Bridge of E.M.I. Records.
It
is now four years since EMI launched Liberty on its own label in this country
since when they have achieved consistent chart success and are currently at
No. 2 with “Bang Bang” by Cher. Bennett was accompanied on his London trip
by Seymour Zucker, vice president of Liberty Records, Ron Kass, director of
overseas operations, and Jerrv Thomas, international
sales manager. Bennett
also had
talks with
Philips Records
executives who
recently
took
over
the

Pacific Jazz Label
for U.K.
distribution and which gave them
chart
success via Bob Lind’s “Elusive Butterfly” issued here on Fontana.
Pursuing his publishing interests, Bennett also had meetings with M. Ricketts
and Teddy Holmes
of Chappells who for many years have
represented
the
Sheldon and Travis catalogues which were acquired in 1963 by Metric Music,
the publishing outlet of Liberty Records
Inc. An agreement was
signed
last
year between Bennett and Louis Dreyfus, chairman of Chappell & Co. whereby
Liberty
should
place
all

with

in

covered by the

Copyrights currently in the charts are “Elusive Butterfly” (Metric) and “I Put
A
Spell on You”
(Sheldon). Kenny Barker has been appointed

manager of Metric in London and is currently working on the latest Bob Lind
recording “Truly Julie’s Blues” backed with “Remember The Rain” (Fontana).
After lengthy negotiations which started in January this year Harold Davi-
son Ltd., a division of the Grade Organization, has acquired the entire share
holdings in Tito Burns Productions Ltd. one of this country’s leading theatrical

The move brings an amalgamation of many of the world’s top stars into Harold
Davison Ltd. including Bob Dylan, Dusty Springfield, Peter, Paul & Mary, the
Searchers, Peter Nero, Dionne Warwick, Vikki Carr, Roger Miller, the Rolling

Five,

MEXICO
Many of the greatest hits recorded by Javier Solis, the Mexican idol who died
three weeks ago, are enjoying good
sales. Among them are “Una Limosna,”
“Payaso,” “Lloraras,” “El Loco,” “Que Va,” “Cuatro Cirios” and some others.
The whole CBS factory is pressing only records released by Javier Solis. Inde-
pendently of that, we were informed that CBS still has three unknown LP’s re-
corded by Javier before he died.
Edgardo Obregon, who for many years has worked at CBS as a&r, resigned
his job last April 15. He was in charge of artists like Enrique Guzman, Sonia
Lopez, los 4 Brillantes, Luis Moreno, los Teen Tops, los 4 Crickets and others. It
is not known yet if Edgardo will take charge of a radio station that belongs to
his father or if he will continue as a&r but now at RCA or another label. As
we informed you last time, Paco de la Barrera resigned from RCA and now is
a&r of Orfeon Records.
There is another change, this one in the publishing
field: Enrique Marquez,
who used to work for Grever Publishing, will do the same job as promoter, but
now on the Orfeon Publishing.
On April 29, Capitol Records extended an invitation to the radio disk jockeys,
press people and friends of the record industry, to the premier of “Dimension
66” (a new music dimension in Mexico), with the performance of Nacho Mendez
(a&r, composer, singer and arranger of Capitol Records), Matilde
(singer of
Musart Records) and los Profetas (new rock and roll group).
Direct from New York arrived to Mexico City the young Mexican idol Enri-
que Guzman, who spent about two weeks in the U.S. to wax an LP at Columbia
Records in the English language. Before that, CBS released with Enrique a new
single that contains the songs “Una Chica Formal” and “Todo Es Mio,” both of
them written by Spanish composer Augusto Alguero and with the arrangements
and orchestra of Chuck Anderson.
“A La Buen De Dios”, a winning song of the past San Remo Music Festival,
has been recorded already by los Dominic on the Polydor label and by los Her-
manos Carrion on Orfeon Records, both of them in the Spanish language.
Capitol Records offered a private exhibition to disk jockeys and newspaper-
men of the premier in Mexico City of the Beatles picture “Help.” The album
was released a long time ago but the picture has just been released now.
On the Orfeon label, Maria Elena Sandoval, a popular folk lark recorded the
old Argentinian tango “Ansiedad” and the top hit “Te Amare Toda La Vida” in
a special folk arrangement.
Andy Russell sent to several radio
stations of the Mexican
capital, an EP
containing, on one

“Longing” and “Enamorado” with a small introduction spoken by himself. On

were made in Hollywood.

ERMANY^>
After a long long wait watching one English teenager after another making
the Cash Box Top 100 charts, Germany finally has a teenager that has made
it.
Drafi
Deutscher who
is now
swinging
with
his
“Marble
Breaks And
Iron Bends” has been one of Germany’s top
artists for about 2 years with
one smash
hit after the
other. “Marble Breaks”
did about %
of a
million
records in its Gennan version breaks a long fasting period. Although Germany
has had top hits like “Sailor” from Lolita, “Morgen” from Ivo Robic and of
course
the smash
success
of Bert Kaempfert and Horst Jankowski,
all
of
the
artists
have
been
adult
singers
or
instrumentalists
of - a
standard
or
ballad nature. Drafi is a rocker who
still comes up with a sound that the U.S.
teens dig and that’s a hard thing to do from shores many miles away from
the record hop and shop scene. Drafi is produced and published by Peter Meisel
here.
Speaking
of
Bert Kaempfert,
it
looks
like
his
tune
“Strangers
In The
Night” which has been not only recorded by Bert, but also Jack Jones and
Frank Sinatra, looks
like one of the big winners of the season. Bert did the
tune for his
first U.S.
film
score, “A Man Could Get Killed,” but with
talk
already going around that the tune
is a possible Academy Award winner,
it
certainly won’t be his
last
score.
Camillo Felgen from Radio Luxemburg who now has an exclusive Polydor
contract has his first release for the label.
Aberbach Music
is
still working hard on “Sha La La La Lee” with the top
versions from the Small Faces, & the Blue Flames.
Fred Jay who
did
the
lyrics
for the
top
hit “The Wedding”
and many
others while in the U.S. and presently turning out smash
hits one after the
other including the present hit “Happy You, Happy Me” for the Leismanns
here
is visiting the U.S. now for a two month trek to New York and Holly-
wood. He’ll be hot on the wires in June to Germany to find out about his tune
which has made the “German Pop Music Festival” preliminaries as one of the
18 out of over 400 tunes sent in.
CBS has just released a “My Fair Lady” package which not only contains
the music from the film in German but also the best parts of the dialog.
Philips has kicked
off their publicity campaign for the Walker Bros. here.
The U.S. boys who have made such a name for themselves in England have
failed to rack up impressive record sales in Germany, but the planned
visits
combined with
Swiss
and German TV
and
a few
night
club
appearances
should boost the stock of the talented youngsters considerably.
Teldec
really took advantage
of the 2% day Nancy Sinatra
visit
to
Ger-
many as they quickly filmed her top hits “Boots” and “How Does That Grab
You, Darling” for several TV shots. The new record is moving very well and
may well duplicate the “boots” success which topped the charts here.
Electrola has done a German production with Ray Anthony and his trumpet
of the
festival -winning “Merci Cherie” and the top
selling “Ballad Of The
Green Berets.” Both were recorded
in Cologne during a recent
visit of the
star to this country.
One of the most neglected
fields and one
of the most important
fields
in
the music business
is TV. Recently the “Golden Rose Of Montreux” world
light entertainment TV festival was held for 1 week as
it is yearly. TV pro-
ducers from 25 countries were on hand as were journalists to see the entries
of the world and decide which were
the
best. Although
local
artists from
many
countries including Julie Andrews,
Ella
Fitzgerald,
the
Beatles, Vico
Torriani and many others were represented in shows, no one from the record
business seemed to take basic interest in the festival. Errol Garner, Marianne
Faithful and Chris Andrews were personally on hand for the
festivities and
the
finals were televised Europe
-wide. This yearly Montreux Swiss
festival
is the only large festival which
restricts
itself
to
light entertainment. The
only
entries
allowed were
variety shows,
musical
reviews
or
spectaculars,
comedy shows and pop music
shows.
Ballet,
classical,
jazz and folk music,
pantomime, as well as circus and cabaret were only allowed as a portion of
a variety show and not as an entity
itself. What better way
is there for an
artist
or
a
song
to
get world wide
recognition than through
world wide
television? There
is no better place in the world to contact TV producers of
music shows, journalists, etc. than at this festival but the record industry has
neglected
this chance
to
really woo
this
all important promotion
outlet
at
their o-wn festival. How about next year?
In any case Cash Box will be on
hand to cover the event. That’s it for this week in Germany.

TALES OF TENTH AVENUE—Business
is booming this crazy spring;
the
early warm weather gave ops
’n’ distribs a chance to jump the gun on their
sales programs; then rain and cold winds slowed things down a
bit, but look
out now! Dick Greenberg at Mike Munves’ showrooms says that orders have
been so hot that most of the display machines are gone, gone, gone. “I’ve never
seen it looking so empty,” said Dick, and he further advised that orders for the
DuKane “Grand Prix” are coming in thick and fast. “We’re after the factory
to send us as many as they can,” said Dick. Joe Munves
is
off on an eastern
seaboard tour, visiting Munves customers and phoning in big orders.
.
.
. Abe
Lipsky, UJA’s Man of the Year, reports heavy action in the export markets.
An operator from British Guiana dropped in a few days ago and dropped off
a nice order for phonographs. He’s departed with the machines and Abe’s ring-
ing up a happy total on the cash register. Abe talked about the entertainment
plans for the UJA banquet and bash June 4th. The featured comic will be the
redoubtable Joe E. Lewis, king joker of Frank Sinatra’s merry band. Killer Joe
i
Piro and his dance troupe will keep everything shakin’ and breakin’ and the
J
master of ceremonies will be Jackie Phillips. The featured singer is being kept
^
under wraps for awhile, Abe said. “And by the way: we’ve had a young fellow
here from Greece, training at our showrooms and at the RCA Institute. He’s
on his way back to Greece with a large order of Wurlitbers and AMI’s. AMI’s
big in Greece.”
.
.
. Lou ‘the Redhead’ Druckman of United East Coast Corp.
says “things are poppin’ along nicely for us. We have some new equipment just
arrived and we look forward to doing good business.” The way the action has
been on the Williams line of games, the delivery trucks keep zipping up to the
'
front door, unloading new shipments, and then taking off for more.
.
.
. Over at
Runyon
Sales,
Louis Wolburg
is
keeping
a busy
pace
and
seeing
lots
of
I
satisfied customers, among them Al Kerner of Sak Trading Corporation, Jack
Hern of La Salle Music Corp. and John Tartaglia of Tartaglia Bros., in Port
Chester. Abe Green, president of Runyon Sales, is the man who secured Killer
Joe Piro and
his dance troupe for the UJA banquet. Pretty Runyon
staffer
Sandy Rasnitzky offered us coffee, but we had to dash back to the office—we’re
already
at work on the big Coin Machine section for the Cash Box Annual
Directory.
.
.
. Dave Freed at Musical Distributor’s Manhattan
office hard
at
^
work with salesman Milt Tucker on Musical’s big spring sales push. Dave savs
the response to the Wurlitzer 3000 has be«n “overwhelming,
really
terrific.
4
And we’re making the most out of our Chicago Coin line of games. They’re the
'
hottest games on the market today—and we’ve got ’em.”
.
.
. The brand new
spot on Tenth Avenue, One-Stop Coin, headed by Sandy Moore, has been open
'
for a week now, and orders are already coming
in. The new showrooms are
roomy and relaxing and Bill Wiener is prepared to do a lot of vending business.
“We look forward to an exciting time here on Coin Row,” he said, “and we’re
ready to serve and advise our customers with the best we have—and we think
we have the best.”
.
.
. Murray Kaye, the dynamic Atlantic sales ace, reports
^
that orders are piling up on his desk. “Business is good and that’s no
lie. But
the weather’s so good
I want to get out and play a little
golf. That’s no
lie,
either.”
Albert Simon
says
although
the
U.S.
Billiards
factory
is
working
overtime during the week, and putting on a special shift to work Saturdays,
the demand for “ElectroPool” has been so
great that they’re
still trying
to,
catch up on production. Al also
tells us that the Rock-OIa phonographs have
been moving strongly and that two whopping orders came in this week for the
Rock-Ola cold canned drink vendor. “Everyone who uses it says it’s a wonderful
machine, and
it’s
certainly wonderful
saleswise. We’ve had two
orders
fori
twenty-five machines
apiece
this week
alone.” That’s
the way
it looks
this
week on New York’s Coin Row.
.
.

ON THE MOVE—Upwards of two hundred Florida operators are expected to
pack their bags and converge on Daytona Beach for a three day meeting of the
Florida Amusement & Music Association at the Daytona Plaza Hotel, May 27,
^
28 and
29. FAMA president L.
J. Lougue says, “There
is a determined and
enthusiastic group of operators who want to put this association on the map.
*
We’re fortunate to be able to have MOA president John Wallace and executive
vice-president Fred Granger
available for
this meeting.
There’s a
lot
to be
done here that should have been done a long time ago, and we’re
all going to
band together and make this thing stick.”
.
.
. National Automatic Merchandis-
ing Association exec direk Thomas Hungerford announced
that the
group’s
i
membership rose to 1,550 businesses in 1965— the result of a go get ’em mem-
bership campaign which went over the one hundred fifty new faces goal to one
f
hundred seventy. Keep it up !
.
.
. Dave Rosen winged back recently from Milan
to announce that everything’s finalized for the production of his “Filmotheque-
Discotheque” movie-music machine;
they’re already rolling
off the assembly
line at the Innocenti plant. Dave making final negotiations with his distributors
for the handling of the machines and looks forward to a sales stampede. ...
,
And speaking of juke boxes (which we always do) we hear that two phono
favorites have new
single
releases:
Johnny
Nash’s “Somewhere” b/w “Big
^
City” (Johnny’s off on a one-stop promo tour for his disc) and the G-Clefs, who
open at Trude Heller’s May 15th, have “Lonely Boy.”
.
.
. We goofed last week,
saying that Godwin Distributors, Wurlitzer agent in Memphis, would hold a
formal grand opening on May 1st—’t ain’t so—it’s May 9th and May 10th, both
days all day.
.

. Mike Mulqueen advises that the regular meeting of the New
York State Operators Guild will be held at the Hotel Washington, Newburgh,
’
N.Y., on May 18th at seven-thirty in the p.m.

LIPKIN AT THE AMERICANA—American
Shuffleboard’s
Sol
Lipkin
and
Mike Bozza took their bank shot shufileboard and non-coin 6-pocket table into
the Americana Hotel in New York last week for the 60th Annual Convention
of the Boys’ Clubs of America. Five furious days of hand shaking and demon-
strating didn’t leave the boys bushed, tho, but rather exhilarated at the fervor
and enthusiasm
exhibited by Boys’ Clubs
reps
for the
organization.
“These
people are expanding every year,” Lipkin said, “thanks largely to contributions
from many prominent Americans
and
the
conscientious
public
in
general.”
Sol’s convention schedule in coming months will be taking him to Atlantic City,
Chicago and the coast. Does he get worn out? Maybe, but he loves it and does
a fantastic job for the firm. American’s
general manager Nick Melone and
wife celebrated their
silver annivesary
last month by going out on
the
big
town. Congrats to the Melones.
76

NEW YORK—Chappell
Music
is
in
for a new look. The 88-year old Louis
Dreyfus, who took over as skipper of
the
pubbery
upon

a

over
2
years
ago,
is now implementing
a
series of
moves calculated to give the firm the
modern
look
of many
of
its
more
youthful competitors.
For years, Dreyfus has owned and
operated the related British company,
known as Chappell’s, and in this
role
over the years, he became a producer
of many
hit
musicals
and
a
record
man,
as
well
as
a
successful
music
publisher and nurturer of writing and
producing
talent.
Today, Dreyfus operates both com-
panies
in
addition
to
branches
in
Paris,
Munich,
Sydney,
Toronto
and
Milan.
He
commutes
three
or
four
times a year between New York and
London
to
supervise
the vast
opera-
tions.
Despite
his
age,
the
veteran
music man keeps a
close eye on
the

ALBUM
POP BEST BETS
THE
ANITA
KERR
ORCHESTRA—Warner
Bros. W/WS 1640
After
gaining
world-wide
fame,
and many
a
musical award, through her vocal
organizing
at
the helm of the Anita Kerr Singers, Anita Kerr
has
launched an
attack on
the
orchestral
scene
and
has
immediately
displayed
another
of
her
many-faceted
talents.

Pickwick Study:
11
LONG ISLAND CITY, N.Y.—Cy Les-
lie,
president
of
Pickwick
Inter-
national,
leading
merchandiser
of
economy-priced
recordings,
has
dis-
closed
the
results
of
a
four month
survey
of
record
retail
windows
re-
vealing
that
pedestrians
spend
less
than 11 seconds considering a window
and deciding whether or not to enter
a
store.
The
survey,
which
covered
almost
1,000
stores
in
fifteen
cities,
high-
lighted,
according
to
Leslie,
many
factors that should be
of “enormous
importance
to
record
retailers
who
have window display space available.”
“Too many
retailers today tend
to
treat
their
windows
as
a
bother—
just
empty
space
they must
fill
up
with
something.
They
jump
at
the
opportunity to install often
dull, drab
‘packaged’ windows. Thus many win-
dows
of
smaller
retailers
begin
to
have
the same
look,”
Leslie
said.
“But
in these days of intense com-
petition, when much
of the merchan-
dise
formerly
sold
exclusively
by
smaller retailers
is available
in giant
supermarkets
and
large
variety
stores
in
shopping
plazas,
it
is
im-
portant
for
the
smaller
retailer
to
compete
aggressively,
and
the
com-
petition begins in the window.”
The
smaller
store,
the
survey
found,
has
one
advantage
over
its
bigger brothers:
It can often achieve
more
individuality,
character
and
charm. A
carefully
planned
window
display schedule, keeping in mind the
character
of
the
store,
type
of com-
munity,
and
kinds
of
merchandise
sold, can help the smaller store make
the most
of
its
sales
possibilities.
“Basically window
display
can
be
of two
types. One
is
the
closed-back
display,
which,
while
it
allows
the
display
of
a
large
amount
of
mer-
chandise,
cuts
off
the
view
into
the
store. A
more
practical
display
for
the
smaller
store
is
the
open-back,
which
is
less
formal
and
allows
passersby to look into the store, where
they may
be
attracted by
the
racks
of
colorful,
traffic-pulling records
in-
side. When
you’ve
decided
which
of
these
basic
types
to
use,
then
con-
sider
some
other
ideas.
1.
Seasonal—The
four
seasons
of
the
year
are
the
mainstay
of
your
year-round window
display
schedule.
They
often
offer
the
most
possibili-
ties
for
a
striking,
selling
display,
but
should
be
approached
with
ci’e-
|
ativity.
Try
to
avoid
the
cliche.
2.
Special Days—These
displays
can
be
alternated
with
seasonal
ones
at
Christmas,
Thanksgiving,
Easter,
I
Mothers’
Day,
etc.
If
there
is
little
Tour's End
Philip Skaff
(left), vice-
president
of
Liberty
Records,
recently
wel-
comed
the
Hollies
to
the firm’s west-coast of-
fices. The English group
had

“I

Seconds To

i
seasonal
climatic
change
in
your
area,
these
special
displays may
be
substituted.
3. Special Events—Some-
times
a
big
event
can
supply
the
theme for an attention-grabbing win-
dow display. This
is particularly true
when the title ties in with a play, TV
show
or motion
picture.
4.
Situation
—These
displays
set
a
stage,
using
realistic backgrounds and props, that
lure
the
customers
into
wanting
to
be part of the
scene. For instance,
a
beach
chair and
sand
could
be
used
for a summer promotion. While
situ-
ation
displays
allow
the
display
of
fewer
LP’s
and
can
be
expensive,
they provide
a hard
visual and emo-
tional impact.
“The
proper
use
of
color
in
your
window
can
be
a
powerful
selling
tool.
Follow
these
simple
rules
in
choosing your
display
color
scheme:
“Warm
colors
(such
as
reds
and
yellows)
can
produce many
striking
effects. They
do,
however,
cut down
apparent size of the display area, and
also
‘come
forward’.
They
are
gen-
erally
poor
choices
for backgrounds.
Also,
if you are displaying many
al-
bums,
steer

whelm
the

“Cooler

such

greens,
blues,
white-yellows,
and
neutrals
like
white
and
beige,
are
usually
more versatile. They are excellent for
backgrounds, and
have
the
effect
of
enlarging
your window.
“Other
useful
colors
are
a
white-
orange
of
grey-orange. When
white
or grey
is added to a red,
it becomes
pink
or
maroon.
Avoid
too
much
white,
which
can
give
a
stark
ap-
pearance, and
also shows
dirt
easily.
Black absorbs
light, and other
colors
are needed to avoid
a drab
look. Too
much
gray
can
make
your
window
look uninteresting.
“Regular and
enthusiastic window
planning
will
accomplish
several
goals.
First
you’ll
be
able
to
tie
in
on
schedule with national promotions
of major
events.
You’ll
also
be
able
to
achieve
a
better balance
of
prod-
uct, and
will have plenty
of time
to
1
assemble
all
of
the
necessary
stage
props
and
backgx-ound
materials.”

Charles Aznavour, Gianni Morandi and Ornella Vanoni were the “visitors of
the week” this time in Buenos Aires, setting a busy schedule for show business
fans and newsmen. Charles’
visit had been regarded with much
interest con-
sidering
the
success
of
his
recordings
released
here by
Disc
Jockey, whose
toppers moved fast to assure the maximum of promotion for this French artist.
The three
initial concerts
at the Opera Theater were complete
sell-outs, and
moved impresarios Lococo and Barujel to arrange two extra evenings, the May
6, and
7. TV
Channel
13
arranged
a
series
of
special
programs,
starring
Aznavour, and Rodriguez Luque’s label marketed coincidently his second LP in
Spanish, “Welcome.” It
is interesting to note that the audience at the theater
liked Aznavour’s original songs in French more than the Spanish versions he
had prepared. This point should be taken
in consideration by other top
inter-
national artists coming to this country. On the contrary, on TV the reception
of songs
in Spanish was better, as
it happened previously with the chanter’s
records. As a whole, this visit may be considered one of the main artistic events
of 1966, and was really a big success.
Italian teen chanter Gianni Morandi also came for several TV programs and
appearances. Gianni is well known through “Si Fa Sera,” “In Ginnocchio Da Te”
and several other good selling records, and his personality may be well accepted
by
this country’s
youth. RCA
released simultaneously
his
latest
single, “Mi
Vedrai Tornare” and arranged a radio promotional campaign covering not only
Buenos Aires but also several country
cities. Morandi will appear
in a group
of programs aired by Channel 9 as guest star; these segments were video-taped
at the end of the week.
Also well known
is Ornella Vanoni, a big surprise two years ago when she
arrived
in Buenos Aires to appear on stage with
Fabrizi’s
“Rugantion” and
turned into a top record star through the recordings marketed by CBS.
Since
then she has been
selling steadily and now her “Io Ti Daro Di Piu” appears
strongly in the sales charts. Ornella has also taped videos during her one-week
stay, complementing the promotional campaign held by her
label. CBS hosted
a dinner at one of the
city’s top restaurants honoring
this
visitor, inviting a
group of disk-jockeys and press people.
It is always interesting to have a chat with Ricardo Castelblanco, who works-
in many of the activities available in a record market: he’s a deejay, does also
special TV commercials
(e.g. Panagra), works with Edami (Southern Music)
Publishers as contact man with the
diskeries, and now has started
as record
producer,
believing
the
“guajira”
will
take
the
place
of
“cumbias”
in
the
audience’s taste. On the Italian
side Castelblanco has a strong bet: “Nessuno
Di Vooi,” recorded
originally by Milva
(here
released by Fermata)
for San
Remo, and now running
strongly
in
the version
of Richard Anthony.
Other
versions are Jose Antonio (Microfon), Victor Alfonso (Odeon Pops), Ricardo
Roda (CBS) and Gino Bonetti, also for Mocrofon.
After a
letup
of
several
years, Argentine
film
studios
are
steadily
going-
back to work, and several projects are being completed. Director Armando Bo
is shooting with the star Isabel Sarli a flick entitled “The Naked Temptation,”
and the
lait motiv
of
this
production
will
be
the
“guarania”
“Temptation,”
penned by Florentin Gimenez and Ben Molar. The rights to the tune are held
by Fermata, who
is
also working
on “Me
Sucedio,”
a
local
product
to
be
recorded by Ronnie
Loy
on Odeon
Pops,
and “Como
Esta
Noche
Nunca,”
Italian product cut by Ruben Carvalo for Music Hall.

There are new recording studios in Buenos Aires, built by a parallel society
to H y R Records, which will opperate independently. The name
is Guemes, and
technical equipment includes Ampex 351 tape
recorders, microfones Neuman
U-67 and a TR 51
mixer, along with complete mono &
stereo
facilities. The
studios’ aim
is to custom record for diskeries and TV, and the
official opening
will take place soon.

and show-biz people at tango night club “Cano

has also signed a contract with Odeon, who has released the album with these
tunes. “Cano 14”
is the swingiest tango night spot in Buenos Aires, with
big-
artists
like Anibal Trolio, Quinteto Real, Atilo Stampone, Eduardo Rovia and
Hector Stamponi performing permanently
Julio
Korn

continue

To Liberty A&R
HOLLYWOOD—Calvin Carter, veter-
an A&R man,
writer, has
joined
the
A&R staff of Liberty Records, accord-
ing
to Bob
Skaff,
vp. Carter
will
be
based at the
label’s west coast
offices
and
produce
sessions
for
all
of
the
label’s
divisions.
His
first

Liberty Buys All-Disc
LOS
ANGELES—Liberty
Records
has acquired All-Disc Records, a lead-
ing
eastern
pressing
plant.
Move
follows
last year’s
acquisition by
the
label of Research Craft, a west coast
pressing
plant,
and
the
recent
pur-
chase of TDC, a tape duplicating com-
pany
in
the
midwest.
According
to Al Bennett, president
of
Liberty,
an
agreement
has
been
signed
with
Ivan Amo
which
calls
for the business and substantially
all
of
the
assets
of
All-Disc
as
well
as
the services of Amo, who will operate
the company
as
general manager
of
the new
division.
Located
forty-five
minutes
from
Times Square in Roselle, New Jersey,
All-Disc
produces
records
for many
leading indie labels, including Disney-
land, Twentieth Century Fox and An-
somia.
Founded
in
1960
by Amo,
a
technical engineer, the company orig-
inally utilized four presses
in a 5,000
square feet plant.
It has
since grown
into
a
facility
which
encompasses
30,000
square
feet on two
acres and
houses 20
presses. Eighty people
are
employed by All-Disc for three
shifts
which operate twenty-four hours daily.

and games

en airport.
The

over the exhibition authorities who, in

(not to be played)

BLUE NOTE
43 W. 61st St, N.Y. 23, N.Y.
HONDELLS
“YOUNGER GIRL”
72563
FOCUS oiir jazz
illlllllllllllllUllllllllllllllllllllilllilllllllllllllllllllllll^
For years we have heard the
cry,
“Bring back the big bands!”. As far
as
live
performances
are
concerned,
there
is no indication that such a re-
turn is imminent. However, if we may
draw an inference from what the rec-
ord companies have been doing lately,
it might be safe
to say that on rec-
ords, at least, such a state of affairs
is not only imminent, but already upon
us.
Recently,
the
record
companies,
major and independent alike, have be-
gun to showcase their key jazz artists
in big band settings, much in the tra-
dition that has long been Duke Elling-
ton’s. This approach
is
not the
con-
ventional big band sound that we have
come
to know from regular working
bands of the past and present. In most
big bands the emphasis is always on a
smooth, cohesive ensemble sound, with
short, rather than extended, solo play-
ing by any particular performer. Ad-
mittedly, there have been exceptions,
but these have been rare; these were
usually characteristic to some special
work, written and performed for the
express
purpose
of
exhibiting
the
special talent of some deserving per-
former.
As
examples,
Benny
Good-
man’s
“Sing,
Sing,
Sing” for Harry
James
and
Gene
Krupa,
or
Artie
Shaw’s “Clarinet Concerto,” or Duke
Ellington’s “Concerto For Cootie” for
Cootie Williams. You might say that
what is happening now in the jazz re-
cording
field
is
an
extension
of
the
Ellington concept, which had been to
feature his solo artists, using the band
as a graceful attendant.
Big band album
production
neces-
sarily means an increase in cost, some-
times a prohibitive cost which makes
the break even point very
difficult to
attain. Why would the companies em-
bark on
a program which would
in-
crease the hazard
of breaking even?
Perhaps they feel that there has been
a saturation of small group jazz
re-
cordings.
Or
do
the
companies
feel
that the record buying public has be-
gun
to
feel
that
there
is
a
certain
anonymity
about much
of the
small
group recordings that have been pro-
duced with such abundance? Do
rec-
ord producers feel that big band jazz
is an easier introduction to the other-
wise non-jazz buying public? Maybe
the companies
feel that they have a
better chance of having their product
played on the
air
if
it has that BIG
sound which seems to please so many
program
directors
at
radio
stations.
With the fierce competition in the re-
cording
industry,
do
the
companies
sense
that
the
customer might
feel
that he is getting more for his money
when
he
buys
a
big
band
record ?
Whatever the reasons,
it becomes
in-
creasingly apparent that record pro-
ducers are leaning more and more to
the big sound in recorded jazz.
Among the recent releases that
il-
lustrate the big band
setting for an
artist known
primarily
as
a
small
group jazzman is guitarist Wes Mont-
gomery’s latest album, “Goin’ Out Of
My Head” (Verve
8642). On
this
al-
bum Montgomery is surrounded by an
array
of top jazzmen, with excellent
and
varied
arrangements
by
Oliver
Nelson. Montgomery, who burst upon
the jazz scene in the late fifties, after
having
been
a
long-time
legend
in
Indianapolis,
gained
his
reputation
making trio and quartet albums. Yet,
in his brief association with Verve, he
has already done two big band record-
ings. On
each album Wes
has
been
given
the
opportunity
to
show
his
lyrical
ballad
style,
as
well
as
his
ability
to
play
hard
swinging
jazz.
Oliver
Nelson’s
charts
afford
Mont-
gomery
full
freedom
to
exploit
his
Montgomery and Nelson forge from
“Chim Chim Cherie,” by way of Dis-
ney’s Mary Poppins. Wes’ solo playing
is immensely
exciting and
is
in no
way restricted by the larger setting.
“Jazz Dialogue”
(Atlantic 1449)
is
another recent
release
that
offers
a
small jazz group that rarely records
in
a
big band
context. The Modern
Jazz Quartet, considered by many to
be the essence of small group jazz, is
heard here with an
all-star band
of
twelve. The album
is aptly titled be-
cause, in effect, this is a jazz dialogue
between
The
Quartet
and
the
big
band. John Lewis, the musical
direc-
tor of The MJQ, did all seven arrange-
ments, and
it
is
interesting
to
note
that six of the seven vehicles recorded
on this album have been recorded pre-
viously by The Modern Jazz Quartet.
Thus, what we have is an opportunity
to
compare how
these
newly
struc-
tured
big band
sides
compare
with
what had been done originally by the
small
group.
“Jazz
Dialogue”
is
an-
other
strong
argument
for
the
re-
newed
interest
in
big band
jazz
re-
cording.
Stanley Turrentine, one of the most
original sounding and energetic of the
younger
tenor
sax
men,
has
been
working
for
the
past
several
years
with his wife, Shirley Scott, in a small
jazz group, usually a quartet. His re-
cordings, too, for the most part have
been
in
that same
small group
con-
text.
“Joyride”
(Blue Note
4201)
is
evidence
that
the
independent
jazz
label owners feel the necessity of pro-
ducing some big band jazz. Blue Note
could not have selected a more deserv-
ing artist for such exposure than Tur-
rentine. Once again the arrangements
have been written by
Oliver Nelson,
who conducts the
dates, as well. The
sixteen man
big band
reads
like
a
who’s who of jazz, including men like
Clark Terry, Jay Jay Johnson, Kenny
Burrell,
Herbie
Hancock,
and
Phil
Woods,
each
of whom
has
been
a
leader on his own recording dates. The
calibre of such sidemen
is an indica-
tion of the quality of this album, and
it
should
be
thus,
because
Stanley
Turrentine
outdoes
himself
on
this
“Joyride.”
The
final
album
for
discussion
is
Ahmad
Jamal’s
latest,
“Rhapsody”
(Cadet 764). This recording is a com-
bination
of
trio
sides
(five)
and
trio
accompanied by a fifteen piece orches-
tra of violins, violas, and
celli
(four).
The string tracks were arranged and
conducted by Joe Kennedy, himself an
accomplished
violinist, and
a
gentle-
man whose
star
as an arranger has
yet
to
ascend.
The
opportunity
to
listen alternately to just the trio and
then the
trio with the
string accom-
paniment points up how emphatic
is
the wedding
of the two
sounds. The
program
piaterial
on
this
album
is
especially
attractive,
too, comprising
seven
standards
and
two
originals.
Jamal
has
never
been
recorded
in
better form, and the ease with which
the
strings are blended with the trio
is
a
joy
to
the
ear. “Rhapsody” by
Ahmad Jamal is another strong argu-
ment for more such big band settings
for jazz artists.
Hopefully,
the
trend
toward
big
band recording by jazz luminaries will
continue.
This
direction
will
be em-
braced
by
the
buying
public
if
the
record
executives
will
recognize
the
latent
danger,
that
of
taking away
the
jazzman’s
identity
and
turning
him into a pop artist. If the jazz per-
former
is
allowed
to
maintain
his
identity,
the
stalwart
jazz
buying
public will continue to buy, and so will

ENTINA
Music Hall
is launching the Pye catalog this week
in Argentina, through
four albums recorded by some
of
the
top
artists belonging
to
this
British
label. Names
are
Sounds
Orchestral,
the
Searchers,
the Kinks and
Sandie
Shaw, and Luis Calvo, one of the diskery’s toppers, announced that there will
be a corresponding number of singles to reinforce promotion of these
artists.
MH’s prexy, Nestor Selasco,
is continuing his world wide
tour, and has
re-
ported
the arrangement
of new
contracts with
labels Ember,
Alegre,
Cox,
and Ce.
Each new release by Palito Ortega—currently in Europe—is news, and the
most recent RCA outing, “Convivir,” seems to be heading to big sales marks,
as have most of the artist’s previous efforts. As we commented before, Palito’s
album with the music of “Mi Primera Novia,”
his
latest
film,
will probably
appear among the top selling albums of 1966, thus continuing a success
last-
ing about five years, something exceptional for pop music in this country. Of
course, RCA
is devoting plenty of promotion to this record.
Lucio Milena’s Milrom organization reports that a promotion campaign
is
being held in behalf of “Lei Mi Aspetta,” Italian song originally cut by Gene
Pitney
(here released by CBS) and Nicola De Bari
(Fermata),^ and here by
Claudio and the same Lucio Milena (Disc Jockey), los Cinco Latinos (Quinto)
and Claudia (Odeon Pops).
Odeon
is releasing the well known Mexican
hit, “La Banda Borracha,”
in
two versions: by tropical music group
los Wawaned and by regional
artist
Canuto. Among the diskery’s best selling records appears the previous record-
ing by los Wawanco, “Quiero Un Sombrero,” along with several waxings by
the Beatles (Michelle), local artist Yaco Monti (“Siempre Te Recordare”) and
Claude Ciari’s instrumental, “La Plage.”
Public Relations man Roberto Quirno infos that Brazilian
artist Yuyu Da
Silva will stay during 1966
in Buenos
Aires, recording for Disc Jockey and
shooting a film
directed by Carlos Borsani under the
title
of “Panchito En
Buenos
Aires”. She has recorded two
of the
tunes, which
will appear as
a
single:
“La
Hormiguita”
and
“El
Chupetin”.
Another DJ
artist,
Rosamel
Araya, has been considered
“the most popular pop
artist”
after a research
made by one of the local public opinion organizations.
CBS reports the inking of teen actor and singer Sergio Mas, born in the
province of Cordoba, and the recording of his first singles for the
label. Mas
performs weekly on Channel
13, in the “Sabados Circulares” Saturday after-
noon spot, and will soon appear on the same Channel as actor. Melodic singer
Robetro Yanes will soon start a new tour. Next July he’ll jet to Bogota, Cara-
cas, Puerto Rico and Miami, returning to San Pablo, Rio and Buenos Aires after
three months
of
travelling. He’s currently performing on Channel 9 and
is
recording a new LP.
Phonogram
is releasing the
first album
of folk songstress Mercedes
Sosa,
one of the main names in the new stream of artists in this
field. The LP
in-
cludes
titles
like “Zamba Del Riego”, “Quena” and Chilean traditional tunes
“Tonadas De Manuel Rodriguez”. Other outings are a new LP by Edmundo
Rivero, “Espectacular”, and the second album hy Mina, “Studio Uno”.
H y R Records is outing an album by tango lark Mercedes Simone, featuring
several
standards
like “Motivo
Sentimental”, “Tu
Llegada”
and,
of

“La
Cumparsita”, Arrangements
and
the

in

artists

Zagarese, and Mario Lombardi.
From San Juan, Puerto Rico, we have received a postcard from the Mac Ke
Mac’s, reporting good success
in their appearances at the Caribe Hilton and
WAPA-TV. The contract will last a couple of weeks, and afterwards the group
will continue its tour.
Lagos Publishers informs us
that next month they
will print a
series
of
fifteen kiddie songs, written by Carlos Guastavino and Leon Benaros. Maria

is to renew the material currently available
for first-grade school, considered too old for practical use.
Trova continues its plan of strong jazz releases, with the labels
it represents
and several interesting local recordings. Some of the latest Contemporary re-

is an LP by tenor saxist Bud

LOVE LETTER TO THE EDITOR—It
is not our intention to polish any ap-
ples.
It’s neither necessary nor required basic training for editorial personnel
at Cash Box. But sitting here in our ivory Sunset-Vine Tower 2700 miles away
from 10th Avenue and 2699% miles from the CB
office on Broadway we read
an inspired few hundred words and we’d
like to
call your attention to them.
They’re on page 63 of the May 21st issue and if you haven’t read them as yet
.
i
(or hung them on your wall for all to see), please do. For here—in an editorial
succinctly titled “What’s New? Nothing Much”—is as basic as credo on what
^
was and
is happening with coin machines as anything we’ve ever read.
'
There’s no need to polish as we’ve already said. Because this
is as polished
a piece of editorial comment as we’ve ever seen in any publication. Do us and
yourselves a favor. Stop reading this
(for a moment only, please) and reach
for the May 21st issue. You might even read
it twice.
It’s that monumental.
WORLD TRAVELERS—Gilbert Chesterton, author and
critic,
once wrote
“It is a pity that people travel in foreign countries;
it narrows their minds so
much.” This, of course, has nothing to do with two of our “phonorow” friends
who have been and are involved in foreign
visits. Sammy Ricklin of Califor-
nia Music, just returned from his European jaunt, tells us he had a marvelous
'
*
time
(except for some ghastly weather, especially in England) and did man-
age to visit a few record shops even though
it was a pleasure trip. Circle In-
iw'
ternational’s Dean McMurdie should be in Hawaii as you read
this,
first stop
on a three week business voyage that should take him to Japan and possibly
the Philippines and Australia.
He’ll, of course, be
visiting his
offices
in both
Hawaii and Japan. Present plans are to spend four days with John Ditwiler,
^
office manager in Hawaii and about ten days with Jasuo Nakanishi in Japan.
He’ll be touring the islands as well—visiting with music and vending accounts. »
.
.
. Incidentally, we visited the Circle
office on S. Hill last week and tried out
;='
that new Shine ’Em Brite automatic shoe polisher which dusts, removes spots,
dries, waxes and polishes (with real shoe polish!)
all for a quarter of a dollar.
^
A great idea for railway stations, barber shops, super markets, hotels etc.

the organization are getting to work
in
their own backyards. Manager Jim
Wilkins
is spending weekends working
to improve
his property
in San
Cle-
mente and Paul Giannone, mechanic, is building a wishing well in his backyard.
Britt was packing for a three day Memorial weekend trip to Las Vegas with #-
hubby Len and their two daughters as we went to press. But took a moment
out to report their shipment of Bally single player Gold Rush is “going like
liol/ cr1c6S

NEW YORK—Rumors
indicating- the

of King- Records
to Liberty Re-
cords have been termed “baseless and
unfounded.’’

issued

ney
for
King.
“There
have
been
no
negotiations
and
no
agreement
even
contemplated for a

of King Re-
cords,
its

Dick Sherman To Head
WB-Reprise Sales In East
NEW YORK—Dick Sherman will join
Warner
Bros-Reprise
Records
later
this month
as eastern
sales
director.
He
will
headquarter
in New
York,
taking over a
position formerly
held
by
Sid
Schaefer, who
left
the
label
some months
ago
to
join Kapp
Re-
cords. Sherman,
expected
to
take up
his new
position
on June
17,
leaves
Mercury Records as product manager
of the recorded tape
division. Before
this post, he was associated with Mer-
cury’s jazz label, Limelight.
In other WB-Reprise appointments,
Don
Schmitzerle
has
been
appointed
to the WB home
office staff and Keith
Clark will replace Bob Lippert as or-
der service manager for Warner Bros.,
Reprise
and
Loma
at

labels’
production
facility
in
Terre
Haute,
Ind.
In
his new
position,
Clark
will
be responsible for taking phone orders
for all distributors who order through
Columbia
Custom.
Schmitzerle
will
join WB in mid-June and will function
in the promotion, merchandising, pub-
licity, and advertising areas.

As
the

of

number
of blockbuster soundtrack albums, the
films of which will be released under

ATV Buys Half Interest
In 2 Chappell Companies
LONDON—ATV,
the
giant
British
TV
producer-distributor,
has
pur-
chased a 50%
in two subsidiary com-
panies
of
Chappell
Music.
One
company, New World Music,
is a sub-
sidiary of Chappell
in England, while
the
second
firm,
Jubilee
Music,
is
a
subsidiary
of
the
international
pub-
lisher’s New York organization.
The
acquisition
of these two
inter-
ests
is important move
in ATV’s
di-
versification
policy.
The
move
will
also benefit the publishing complex in
the fact that Chappell
will now have
ATV’s
international
music
interests.
The directors of the joint publishing
venture
are
Louis
Dreyfus
and
Mr.
Ricketts
from
Chappell
and
Lew
Garde and Robin Gill of ATV.
ATV has been thinking for a num-
ber of years of diversifying
its inter-
ests. It already has a 50% in Pye Re-
cords,
and
has
recently
bought
the
Moss Empire
chain
of
theatres. The
firm
also
has
an
interest
in Muzak
and
in Ambassador Bowling.
The Chappel acquisition marks the
first time
that ATV has
entered the
music publishing
field. The publishing
additions give ATV over 300 standard
titles which
will in future be boosted
with the addition TV theme and series
music.
20th Fox Label
tures. These will include the spectacu-
lar,
“The
Bible,”
scheduled
for
re-
lease next
fall, and such future prop-
erties as “Dr. Doolittle,” a musical to
star
Rex
Harrison,
“Hello,
Dolly!,”
the
film
version
of
the
Broadwav
smash,
and
“The
Star,”
to
feature
Julie Andrews.
The ABC &
20th move
continues
the former
label’s concentrated
drive
on
acquiring,
through
outright
pur-
chase
or
distribution
arrangements,
tie-ins with important label catalogs.
The
most
recent
deal
concluded
by
ABC-Par
involved
the
purchase
of
Dunhill Records, a label that had been
previously distributed, but not owned
by ABC-Par.

Take Over Of New Deal
NEW YORK—A
deal
for
the ABC
label’s purchase of New Deal Records,
the rack-distrib-one-stop operation of
Long Island City, N.Y. has been com-
pleted,
according
to
information
re-
ceived
by
Cash

Garrett Starts Viva Records Thru Dot
HOLLYWOOD—Snuff
Garrett,

Re-

Dot

Productions,

Some
years
ago,
Bob
Crewe,
a
highly
talented
composer,
felt
that
in order to get ahead
in the strongly
competitive
music
and
recording
business,
it
would
be
a
great
ad-
vantage
for
a
writer to also produce
records.
And
so
Bob
Crewe
com-
bined
writing
with
arranging
and
producing.
He
achieved
great
suc-
cess,
and
now
both
Crewe
and
his
companies are known throughout the
world.
Russ
Miller,
profressional
man-
ager
of
Crewe's
publishing
firm,
Saturday
Music,
Inc.,
is
in complete
agreement
with
this
principle.
He
makes
it a
rule to select writers who
can
also be developed as producers.
This
policy
has
been
tremendously
effective
for
both
writer
and
pub-
lisher.
Russ
Miller, and Bob Coogan,
as-
sistant professional manager of Sat-
urday
Music,
are
always
on
the
lookout
for
writers,
and
since
it
is
known
that
they
are
genuinely
in-
terested, writers are eager to discuss
their songs with them. On
the other
hand, record producers from around-
the-globe
have
beaten
a
door
to
Saturday Music
in search of material
for
their
own
recording
sessions.
They
have
found
that
this
is
one
publishing
firm
that
really
has
its
finger
on
the
pulse
of
the
record
buying
public.
Outstanding
producers
who
have
found
that
they
can
always
count
on
Saturday
Music coming
up
with
the
right
song
for
them
include
Tom Wilson
of MGM, John Simon
of
Columbia,
Johnny
France
and
Lou
Reizner
of
Philips,
Dennis
Lampert
of Don
Ccsta
Productions.
Joe Rene
of
RCA
Victor,
Henry
Jerome
of
Coral, Joe Saraceno of Liberty, Luchi
De Jesus
of Mercury, Jerry Wexler of
Atlantic and Bob Keane
of Mustang.

Platters
The Platters have been on the mu-
sical scene since 1953 when the group
was
formed
by Herbert
Reed.
Since
their
first
hit, “Only You,” on Mer-
cury,
the
group
has
been
carrying
such
hits
as
“The
Great
Pretender”
and “Magic Touch”
(to name just
2)
to the ear of the music listening pub-
lic. The
Platters have
just completed
a college tour and are currently mak-
ing their way to Los Angeles via Bos-
ton, Baltimore, and Detroit. The group
is
scheduled
to
appear
in
Bermuda
and Japan before the end of Summer.
Herbert
Reed,
Sonny
Turner,
and
David Lynch are originally from L.A.
and
Sandra Dawn
and Nate
Nelson
are from New York. Sandra was with
the Shantells before joining the Plat-
ters
and
Nate was
lead
singer
for
the
Flamingoes.
Nate,
who
plays
drums on the
side,
also produces
re-
cords
and
writes
songs
like
“Hear,
Speak, See No Evil” which
is the flip
side of the
Platters’ Current Musicor
outing
“I
Love
You
1,000
Times”
(number 42 on
this week’s Top
100.)
Susan
Christie
Susan Christie has been singing for
most of her 23-years and somewhere
along the line developed a proficiency
on
the
Fender
bass.
The
pert
lass
teaches guitar as a sideline in Moores-
town,
N.J. John
Hill, who
is
Susan’s
husband, produced her Columbia
out-
ing
“I
Love
Onions”
while
engaged
in graduate studies in the music
field
at
Temple
University.
The
Onion
loving thrush was graduated from the
University of Penn, and in seemingly
almost
un-American
co-ed
fashion,
met her husband in high school rather
than in college.
Bratrice
(that’s the real name) has
often
been
featured
on
Philadelphia
television and
is presently
set for
a
Herman Spero TY’er. Long a regular
on
the
Philadelphia
entertainment
scene, Susan
Christie was
a member
of a folk group called the Highlanders
and in recent years she has been tour-
ing the U.S. with a pop group called
the Encores.

mentioned
