rock sound
of today. He has
scored sessions by Jay & the Ameri-
cans and
Patti Duke. In
addition, he
.is contracted writer at United Artists
Music.
Dave
Walker,
Don’s
son,
is
general manager of the company.
Original Cast LP’s
Walker,
currently
represented
on
Broadway with the scoring of “Fiddler
on the Roof”
(he also did Bock Har-
nick’s show
prior
to
“Fiddler,” “She
Loves
Me”),
feels
that
the
greatest
change
in
cast
recordings
over
the
past 10 or 15 years has been to bring
as much of a theatrical quality to the
cast LP
as
possible.
Thus,
he
says,
little
is done
in changing orchestra-
tions
for
cast
sessions
as
was
the
custom years ago. While he maintains
that most cast product comes off well,
he would have labels spend more time
in recording shows, instead
of cram-
ming in an entire score on a Sunday.
Also
advantageous,
he
feels,
would
be
a
uniform
arrangement
between
the
musician’s
union
and
Actor’s
Equity,
the
conflicting
interests
of
which
can
harm
a
cast
recording
session.

Int'l. Catalogs

Black Combo turns to a country music
repertory and comes up with a pack-
age titled “All Timers.”

of

business awaits only a sustained sales
effort. The

six-week summer

is

to

the

Promotional efforts on both the
in-
ternational and

Marks Catalog Featured
At Summer Music Festivals
NEW YORK — This summer’s music
festivals,
in
the
United
States
and
Europe,
will feature music from the
Marks catalog of serious music.
Roger Sessions’ “Psalm 140” will be
sung by Ann Elgar at the Tanglewood
Music
Festival on July
4th. The
Or-
chestra
will
be
conducted
by
Erich
Leinsdorf.
Also
at
Tanglewood,
on
August
6th,
Sessions’
Violin
Con-
certo”
will
be
performed
by
the
violinist Paul Zukofsky with Gunther
Schuller
conducting.
In
Bucharest,
Romania
on
June
10
and
11,
the
“Black
Maskers
Suite”
by
Sessions
will be played by Jassy,
the
leading
Romanian Symphony
Orchestra with
Peter
Paul
Fuchs
conducting.
Con-
ductor Ernest Ansermet will perform
the same work with the Orchestre de
la Suisse Romande at San Francisco’s
Stanford University on June 29 while
on
tour and
Sixten Ehrling and
the
Detroit Symphony Orchestra will per-
form
the
“Suite From
Montezuma,”
based on Sessions’ most recent opera,
on August
18.
Other Marks’ material to be played
this summer are Charles Jones’ “Five
Melodies
For
Orchestra”
(Aug.
14),
Darius Milhaud’s “Robin And Marion”
(Aug. 19, 20) and Jacques Offenbach’s
“The
Lantern
Marriage”
(Aug.
19,
20). These
three works
will be
per-
formed
at
Colorado’s
Aspen
Music
Festival.
Walker himself orchestrated at one
period about three shows a year. He
intends
to
limit
this
to
one show
a
year,
since shows today tend to stay
on the road for longer periods, coming
to New
York
only
to
hold
several
more weeks of “preview” shows. Both
the
road
and
“previews”
require
Walker’s presence for many possible
changes. He
figures he has
spent as
much as 24 weeks out of a year pre-
paring show orchestrations. His com-
pensation, however,
is
unique. While
most
orchestrators
receive
a
union
minimum
payment
and
a
weekly
royalty for the run of a show, he
is
paid a percentage of the nightly take
of a show. He
is
currently weighing
three properties due for presentation
next season. In addition, he will work
closely with new writers Lor Crane
(the ex-Columbia A&R producer) and
Nadine Lewis, who are writing a new
show. His firm will publish the
score.
The show
will
also open
a
theatrical
producing dept at Dacapo.
With the aforementioned shows
to
his
credit
plus
such
other
standouts
as
“Carousel,”
“Pajama
Game,”
“Damm
Yankees”
and
“Gentlemen
Prefer
Blondes,”
Walker
says
his
favorite
was
“Most
Happy
Fella.”
The reason:
it’s got everything, from
opera to Dixieland. He hopes to do a
Frank
Loesser
show
again.
Walker
could well become a sought after film
scorer, since he got an Oscar nomina-
tion this year for his arrangement of
the
music
for “A
1000
Clowns.”
It
was
his
first Hollywood
assignment.

NEW YORK—Since

The

Not

Nasatir reports that the branches are

During the past year, MGM/Verve
has been awarded RIAA gold records
for four albums. They are: “Introduc-

Herman’s

“Herman’s

“Wooly Bully” by Sam the Sham and
the Pharaohs, and “I’m Henry VIII,

Currently

are:
“Did You

by the Lovin’ Spoonful, “Don’t Bring
Me Down” by the Animals, “Twinkle
Toes” by Roy
Orbison and “He” by
the Righteous Brothers.
Coming down the home
stretch
of
the last quarter,
all of the company’s
labels,
MGM,
Verve,
Kama-Sutra,
Verve/Folkways, VSP, Leo
the Lion,
DGG
Metro
and
Helidor
show
tre-
mendous strides in
sales.
MGM
will
soon
reveal
its
plan
to
enter the tape cartridge
field.

Gift

ASCAP Symphonic Works
Up 70% Since 1959
NEW YORK—The symphonic
reper-
tory
cleared
through
ASCAP
has
increased 70%
since
1959,
according
to
the
society’s
second edition
of
its
symphonic
catalog.
In a foreword
to
the
new
catalog,
president
Stanley
Adams
notes
that
7000 new
works
bring
the
catalog’s
total
to
almost
17,000.
“The
enormous
increase
in
symphonic
repertory,” he points
out,
“in such a few years
is surely a result
not only of the
continuing prolifera-
tion
of symphony orchestras both
in
the
concert
halls
and
on
university
and college campuses throughout the
nation,
but
also
of
the
increasing
interest
in new works
of
all
styles.”
The new catalog
will be part of the
ASCAP
display
at
the
American
Symphony
Orchestra
Convention
in
St.
Louis, June
15-18.

Myers Exits Mercury; Mink Succeeds Him
CHICAGO—Following the resignation
of
Kenny
Myers
from
his
post
as
product
manager,
Mercury
Records
has named Alan Mink to succeed him.
Myers
leaves
the company
after a
15 year
association. According
to an
announcement, Myers
felt
“the
need
for
a
greater
challenge,
possibly
in
ALAN MINK
the record business
or
in some other
field,”
The
statement
said
he
was
leaving
to
explore
“objectively
a
number of business propositions.” He
joined Mercury in July, 1951, serving
as
ad
director,
merchandising man-
ager,
national
promotion
manager,
and, finally, a vp and product manager
(since
1959).
Mink
has
been
associated
with
Mercury for the
past
five
years. He
started as a local promo man in Cleve-
land, later joining Smash as midwest
regional manager. In 1964, he was ap-
pointed the
first national promo man-
ager
for Smash
Records,
a
post
he
held
until
he
was
recently
named
Mercury’s national promo
chief.
Ganim Is Promo Mgr.
Replacing Mink
as national promo
manager is Dennis Ganim, who previ-
ously was co-owner and general man-
ager
of
Claridge
Records
of New
York,
a company
he formed
a
year
ago with Frank Slay. Before that, he
was
alternately national promo
chief
and national
sales manager for Con-
gress,
a Kapp
subsid, and spent two
years
as
mid-west
regional
promo
manager for Kapp. He started in the
disk business with M.
S. Distributing
in Cleveland as a local promo man.

Columbia Promo, A&R Moves Shift Noonan, Weiss
NEW YORK—The Columbia label has
consolidated
its national promo
staff.
Move realizes two major exec
shifts:
Tommy Noonan becomes
director
of
national promo for the Columbia and
Date labels, and Gene Weiss has been
named A&R singles product manager.
Bill
Gallagher,
vice
president
of
Columbia,
said that the
“reorganiza-
tion was made in order
to cope with
the dynamics of a constantly changing
single
records
market,
to
further
strengthen
and
centralize
the
com-
pany’s
entire
promotional
effort and
to
speed and
refine communications”
between members
of the
label’s
field
promotion force and
its headquarters.
Noonan, who has been
elevated
to
an
area
of broadened
responsibility,
will report
to Joe Lyons,
director
of
Columbia
Records
Sales.
In
his new
capacity, Noonan
will
direct and
co-
ordinate the national promotion activi-
ties
of both
the Columbia and Date
labels,
insuring
that
such
activities
continually
reflect
changes
in
the
marketplace and tie in with merchan-
dising plans and programs.
Responsible directly to Noonan will
be
the
eight Columbia

field
promotion

strategically

throughout
the
country.
Harold
Komisar, manager

Noonan
will
continue
to
supervise
the
growth
of
the
Date
label,
and
Date’s four field promotion managers
will, as previously, report to him.
The reorganization
of the national
promotion
staff
is designed to enable
field
promotion
managers
to
keep
Columbia’s A&R staff apprised of new^
trends
in
all

They will continually be on the look-

indie

potential material for disti’ibution by

BLOWING MY MIND—Barry
Goldberg
Blues
Band—Epic BN-26199
The Barry Goldberg Blues Band does blow
its
mind
with
this
package
which
includes
such
outstanding tracks as “Whole Lotta Shakin’ Goin’
On,” “Big Boss Man,” “That’ll Be The Day,” and
the

chord, Maurice McKinley plays drums, “Memphis
Charlie”
Musselwhite
plays
harmonica,
and
Harvey Mandel plays guitar as does Roy Ruby.
Destined for quick movement in the pop, folk, and
blues bags.
The SOUND OF MUSIC—Mary Martin—Disney-
land ST 3936

ance
of
the songs and
story
of the

mainstemmer-film. A

JAZZ PICKS
I WANT TO HOLD YOUR HAND—Grant Green
—Blue Note 4202
Jazz
guitarist
Grant
Green
has
some
of
the
old and some of the new blended together to form
this

to

to
set. The

ney, and

“Corcovado” and

set for LP buyers.
AFTER THIS MESSAGE—Mitchell-Ruff Trio—
Atlantic 1458
Part of this group (then known as the Mitchell-
Ruff
Duo)
joined
the
Yale
Russian
Chorus
in
order to bring American jazz into Russia in 1959.
The
trio
is made up of Dwike Mitchell on piano,
Willie Ruff on bass and French horn, and Helcio
Milito on drums. “After This Message,”
“I Got
Rhythm,” and
“Solo For Unaccompanied
Bass”
are among
the
better
tracks. The
jazz market
will welcome this one.
I
JAZZ BEST BETS
MOSE ALLISON PLAYS FOR LOVERS—Pres-
tige/PR-7446
This package
is comprised of popular American
ballads. All love songs, but of different attitudes,
they have been
tied together by Mose
Allison’s
distinctive
combination
of
urban
sophistication
and rural wit.
“I Told Ya
I Loved Ya, Now Get
Out,” “You Belong To Me,” and “My Kinda Love”
are blue ribbon efforts. Not an overly sentimental
love
song
album,
this
one
is
likely
to
do
well.
THE JAZZ PIANO—Pittsburgh Jazz Festival—

recorded
in

Lenny Scheer Promoted To
MGM/VerYe's Marketing Head
NEW YORK—Record companies
are
failing
to recognize
singles
oldies
as
booming
sales
goodies.
This
is
the
contention
of Benny
Reminick, who
runs Town Hall One Stop in Brooklyn,
where, besides the regular line-up
of
current hits, dealers can obtain years-
back
singles going as far back as 20
years, the age of the one-stop
itself.
“We
sell more of some titles in the
oldie class than we do of many chart
items
that
reach
70
or
80
on
the
charts,”
Reminick
reports.
In
fact,
Reminick
points
out, somewhere
be-
tween 15%
to 20%
of his total busi-
ness
is
in “golden
oldies.” The
sales
of oldie singles
is “not a queer
little
quirk, but a national hobby
like
coin
or stamp collecting,” he explains. He
charges
the
regular
“competitive”
singles price for the oldies.
Town
Hall
has
between
15-20,000
different titles in stock, with a range
of 5 to 500 of each record. Reminick
notes
that
he became THE
place
to
come
for
oldies
virtually by
default.
Whenever
there
is
consistent
repeat
business on
a
single,
it
qualifies
for
Town
Hall’s
“back-file.”
This
policy,
Reminick
says,
is
the
opposite
of
other
one-stops
that
are
geared
to
deal only with newer product and do
not
want
to
apply
too
much
man-
power
and
time
to
oldie
inventory.
“As
our
oldie
line
grew,
dealers
stopped
making
inquiries
to
other
one-stops
for
years-back
hits
and
came
directly
to
us,” Reminick
says.
According
to
Reminick, LP
collec-
tions
of
oldie-goodie
sides
are
not
good
enough
for
the
oldie
hobbyist.
The market for
oldies, he notes, con-
sists
primarily
of
teenagers,
who
favor the 45 speed “They do not want
to be inconvenienced by album collec-
tions, which
often
contain
selections
they are not interested
in,” Reminick
explains.
Reminick feels that labels are losing
out on what can “key-off a new round
of profits, even a renewed chart stand
for
oldies.” Every
five
years,
there’s
a new market for old rock ’n roll hits,
bringing
in
audiences who were
too
young
to
purchase
them,
Reminick
adds.
Wants Label Stimulation
“Nothing
is
being
done by
record
companies,”
the
one-stopper
claims,
“to
stimulate
this
area,
perhaps
be-
cause they are unaware that it exists.”
Reminick feels that any area of music
that can bring 15% to 20% of a large
one-stop concern should interest labels
in promoting
it.
Dealers,
too,
Reminick
says,
are
reaping
the
financial rewards
of the
oldies trade, some of whom are paying
their
overhead
through
such
sales.
And, he adds, oldies sales are a bless-
ing when there are no real big hits on
the current singles scene.
What
establishes
a
single
as
a
“golden
oldie?” To
Reminick, steady
sales for a 2 to 3 year period follow-
ing
its
hit
status.
These
disks,
he
explains, have an “intangible appeal,”
and there are
“little epidemic indica-
( Continued on page

of

KRLA Uses Time Mag
Inspired Music Format
LOS
ANGELES—A
recent
Time
Magazine article labeling certain con-
temporary songs as salacious has had
an interesting effect on the program-
ming policies of KRLA-Los Angeles.
The outlet’s program director, Dick
Moreland,
decided
to
play
all
the
songs mentioned in the article and let
his
listeners
evaluate
the
tunes
for
themselves.
In
spite
of
the
obvious
controversy
of
the

MEL FUHRMAN & ED BARSKEY
Fuhrman, who had been
associated
with the parent company
in the east

transferred to Los Angeles, where he

ager. He entered

district manager.

will be
launched with
a
strong,
coordinated,
advertising, publicity and promotional
campaign that will include special in-
store sales aids and point-of-purchase
units. Co-op advertising funds will be
available.
Leslie commented that he does not
anticipate the present system
will be
the final form that tape will take. The
Pickwick
President
predicted
that
units will eventually be developed that
will have greater sound reproduction
fidelity and be more durable. “Despite
this system’s ease of handling, which
is
its greatest
asset,
it would not be
intellectually
honest
to
call
it
the
‘ultimate’.
Our
feeling
is
that
there
will be additional modification.”
Pickwick/8 and Pickwick/4, accord-
ing
to
Leslie,
will
be
distributed
in
Canada through the company’s wholly
owned
Pickwick
Records
of
Canada
Ltd. A study
is now
in
progress
to
determine
whether
or
not
the
lines
will
also
be
sold
in
England
and
Europe
through
Pickwick
Interna-
tional (Great Britain) Ltd.
The
35
tapes
that make up
Pick-
wick/8
include four
classics by Wil-
liam
Steinberg conducting the
Pitts-
burgh Symphony Orchestra;
19 pops
featuring such names as Jack Jones,
Ferrante &
Teicher, Gordon Jenkins,
Les Baxter, Jimmy Smith, Pete Foun-
tain,
The
Three
Suns
and
Harry
James; the complete scores of “Marne”
and “Sound Of Music” and five youth
oriented packages crammed with top
teen names. The balance of the single
unit
tapes
highlight
stellar C & W
performers
and
two
are
children’s
tapes.
The
six Twin
Packs,
that
bear
a
suggested
list price
of
$6.95,
include
a pair of complete shows
in each
of
two Twin
Packs
(South
Pacific
and
Oklahoma
in one and Porgy & Bess
and West
Side
Story
in
the
other).
The four remaining Twin Packs
are
“mood”
units,
three
by
the
Parris
Mitchell
Strings
and
one
with
the
Parris Mitchell Voices as well as the
Strings.

THE PROMISE

Trio & Paddie Bell—Elektra EKL-304/EKS-7304

Solid

here.

Lively sounds featuring the piano and vocal of

JAZZ BEST BETS
DREAM WEAVER—Charles Lloyd Quartet—At-
lantic S/SD-1459
A delightful jazz offering by the Charles Lloyd
Quartet,
this album was recorded
in the
U.S.A.
just
prior
to
the
group’s
debut European
tour.
Lloyd on tenor sax and flute,
is backed by Keith
Jarrett on piano, Cecil McBee on bass, and Jack
DeJohnette
on
drums.
The
title
song,
“Bird
Flight,” and “Love Ship” are
all blue ribbon
ef-
forts.
This
one
is
sure
to
find
favor with
jazz
buffs everywhere.
DIZZY GILLESPIE—RCA Victor LPV 530
This
is the latest addition to the growing RCA
Vintage Series catalog, a collection of repressings
of old folk, blues, and jazz recordings. The pack-
age
the
sides
Gillespie’s
big bands
cut
for
the
diskery between 1947 & 1949 and chronicles
the
decade when Dizzy emerged from the position of
a promising talent on the Philadelphia scene to a
position of national prominence. Sure to be sought
after by
those
interested
in
the
early
develop-
ments
in jazz.
OH BABY!—Big John Patton—Blue Note 4192
A jazz package featuring the Hammond Organ
as played by Big John Patton while being backed
up by Blue Mitchell on trumpet, Harold Vick on
tenor sax, Grant Green on guitar, and Ben Dixon
on drums.
This
is Big John’s
fourth album
for
Blue Note. “One To Twelve,” “Night Flight,” and
“Each Time” are outstanding tracks. A good one
for jazzophiles and pop fans.
THE WEARY TRAVELER—King Fleming Trio
—Cadet LP-4053
This
is an offering of
quiet,
lyrical jazz tunes
enhanced
by
King
Fleming’s
straight-forward
and
uncluttered
approach
to
the
piano.
King
Fleming
is backed up by Bugs Cochran on drums
and Melvin Jackson on
bass. “Taking A Chance
On
Love,”
“Green
Leaves
Of
Summer,”
“One
O’Clock Jump,” and the title song are outstanding
tracks. A must for the jazzophile.
CLASSICAL PICKS
BEETHOVEN/BRAHMS—Conrad Hansen, Hein-
rich Geuser, Arthur Troester—Mace M/MS-9038
This package features Conrad Hansen, Heinrich
Geuser, and Arthur Troester playing Beethoven’s
“Trio In B Flat Major Op. 11” and Brahms’ “Trio
In A-Minor Op. 114.” Both of these selections are
for piano, clarinet and violoncello. This one
is a
must for the
classical music
enthusiast.
SCHUBERT—SYMPHONY NO. 9 (‘THE GREAT
C MAJOR’)—Sir John Barbirolli—Angel S-36328
Sir

to be added
to

Phil Spector/Jeff Barry Pact
NEW YORK—Jeff Barry and Philles
Records’
topper
Phil
Spector
have
entered
into
an
agreement whereby
Barry
assumes
production
reins
for
that
firm,
which
enables
Spector
to
devote
all of his time
to the making
of motion
pictures. The
pact, which
is
non-exclusive,
permits
Barry
to
continue
as an independent producer
for other labels and artists.
Barry has
just completed
his
first
session with the Ronettes for Philles,
in New
York. The
sides,
which
are
scheduled
to
be
released
soon, were
written
by
him.
Barry
also
penned
“Hanky Panky.”

New Sheet Music Notation
Scheduled For Criterion
HOLLYWOOD—With
the
release
of
Nancy
Sinatra’s new
Reprise
record
of two
Lee
Hazelwood
songs,
“Fri-
day’s
Child’’
and
“Hutchinson
Jail,”
Mickey Goldsen’s Criterion Music will
incorporate into sheet music the “a-b-
cimplified system” of guitar notation.
This new style of copy will add letters
of each
note
of melody
so
that any
guitarist
can
read
it.
This
is
being
done
in
recognition
of
the
guitar’s
importance
in
today’s music
market.
Since
only
actual
notes
are
used
in
conjunction
with
their corresponding
letters, this system may be useful
in
guitar training.

Box—July

FOCUS ON jazz
This month marks the seventh an-
niversary of the passing of Billie Hol-
iday. Even though the
definition of a
jazz
singer remains
a very nebulous
thing,
Billie’s
acceptance
as
undis-
puted
champion
is
virtually
uncon-
tested. And
it
isn’t
as
though
this
legend
has
grown
since
her
death;
Billie was a legend in her own time.
Too
often we’re prone
to forget
the
great ones of the past, in deference to
the stars of the moment. Today, as a
token repayment for all the great mu-
sic
she
left us
as a legacy, we
shall
concern ourselves with Lady Day, as
Billie
Holiday came
to
be
known.
We’re fortunate
to have an abun-
dance of recorded works by Billie Hol-
iday, spanning an
era from
1933
to
1958. Admittedly, some
of what
she
recorded in the twilight of her career
left something
to be
desired, but
in
the light of comparison, even her less-
than-best
efforts
dwarfed
most
of
what
was
being
recorded
by
other
so-called jazz singers. She had an in-
defineable
quality
which
was
never
approached by any other female sing-
er; the fact that no other female sing-
er has had the temerity to try to imi-
tate
Billie Holiday
is
eloquent
testi-
mony to her uniqueness.
Always Recorded
with
the
Best
The
major
portion
of
Billie’s
re-
cordings can be found on three labels:
Columbia,
Decca, and Verve, and
in
that
chronological
order.
The
sides
she did for Columbia covered the pe-
riod from 1933
to 1942, and on these
recordings
she
surrounded
herself
with
such
jazz
notables
as
Benny
Goodman, Teddy Wilson, Ben Webster,
Bunny
Berigan,
Lester Young, Buck
Clayton,
Chu
Berry,
Roy
Eldridge,
and countless others of that high cali-
ber. One
thing was
for
sure:
Billie
Holiday never went into a recording
studio with anyone but the best! The
Holiday
sides on Columbia have, for
the most part, been consolidated into
two packages. The Golden Years, Vol.
1
and
Vol.
2.
Each
of
these
boxed
packages is made up of three albums,
and each box contains an
illustrated
brochure,
complete with many
valu-
able
photographs
and
all
the
perti-
nent data concerning each recording.
There
is
reason
to
believe
that
Co-
lumbia
still has a sufficiency of sides
to make up another volume.
From
the
mid-forties
to
the
very
early
fifties we have many
excellent
things
that
Lady
Day
did
for
the
Decca label. Most of these recordings
were done with large
orchestrations,
although there were some done
in
a
small
group
setting. The
Decca
re-
cordings included such legendary Hol-
iday
offerings
as “Lover Man,” “No
More,” “God Bless The Child,” “Crazy
He
Calls
Me,”
“You’re My
Thrill,”
and “Por^.” While she recorded for
Decca
Billie
did
some
wonderful
things with Louis Armstrong, a wed-
ding of talents that was so completely
right that
it defies description.
Billie Holiday’s last affiliation, with
the exception of two albums that she
did
for
Columbia
(her
last
two
al-
bums), was with Norman Granz and
his Clef
label, now Verve. There
are
those who feel that these are the best
she did, in spite of a lessening of that
pure sound that she
evidenced
early
in her singing career. In the absence
of that pure sound there was a much
more mature and emotional
delivery.
Again,
as
always.
Miss
Holiday
re-
corded only in the company of the top
jazz musicians of the moment. Some
of the Verve things were recorded in
concert, but for the most part Granz
recorded
Billie
in the studio. She re-
corded again many of the things with
which she was
identified, things
like
“Strange
Fruit,”
“Some
Other
Spring,” “My Man,” and she also per-
formed
many
formidable
standards
I
which lent themselves
so well
to the
I
Holiday approach.
j
Reprint of Eulogy
I
This
writer
had
the
privilege
of
j
writing the following for a program
!
of
the
1959
Randall’s
Island
Jazz
Festival:
DON’T EXPLAIN
Today
I
said, “Goodbye, Lady, and
Thank You.” As
I
sat
in the chapel
where
Billie
Holiday
lay
in
state,
I
observed
the
never-ending
lines
of
friends who came
to pay
their
last
respects
to Lady Day, who gave
so
much and
asked
so
little
in
return.
It was
obvious
that
these were
not
morbid
thrill
seekers who
came
to
see the Billie Holiday who was vilified
by
the
press,
even
as
she
lay
at
death’s
door.
Instead,
these
were
mourners
from
every
walk
of
life,
rich and poor, Negro and white, silent
and weeping, come
to repay
in some
small way the many gloriously
thril-
ling
moments
that
she.
Lady,
had
given
so
generously.
It has been said that Billie Holiday’s
voice was
like
a
piece
of
rare
silk,
with a tattered edge, and
so
it was,
filled with the emotion and the poig-
nancy
that
she
breathed
into
every
lyric. There was a tender and delicate
sincerity that made you feel that she
was
singing her
song,
ballad,
blues,
or
whatever,
just
for
you, and
you
alone.
It was
as though
she wanted
you to share her happy moments and
to
help
her
endure
her
sad
times.
Those
who
enjoyed
the
privilege
of watching the Lady work know the
magic she possessed; how, when it was
time for her
set, no matter how low
she felt, she became an articulate and
plaintive
teller of stories. There
is a
certain
indefinable
something
that
separates
the
great
from
the
near
great, and
this
quality,
call
it what
you will, was Billie Holiday’s heritage.
Much has been written about Billie
Holiday’s
life,
but
always
with
the
taint
of
sensationalism,
so
that
for
the
many,
her
very
existence
was
merely a source for tabloid exploita-
tion. This
I reject vehemently! What
about
Billie,
the
sincere,
Billie
the
warm, Billie the love kind of person?
Do you suppose
that she
could have
attained
that
pinnacle
of
greatness
that made her the peerless performer
without
all
these
qualities,
plus
the
inner
beauty
with
which
she
was
blessed?
Billie Holiday was a beauti-
ful person and a great artist, perhaps
the
greatest we
shall know
in
her
idiom;
I choose to respect and vener-
ate her memory for this, and for this
alone.
To sympathize
is not to condone, to
be
sure;
but
sympathy
and
under-
standing were owed
to
Billie;
unfor-
tunately, she received
little of either.
She
had
her
inadequacies
and
her
excesses, none will deny that, for she
was a mortal, even as you and
I, and
she
fell
prey
to
the
frailties
that
plague us
all. How many times, over
the
years, must she have asked
her-
self,
“What’s
the
use?” From
her
early childhood on, even as an estab-
lished
star,
the
indignities
heaped
upon
her must
have
taxed
her
re-
straint. Her experiences while travel-
ing
as
featured
vocalist
with name
bands,
both Negro
and
White,
have
been recounted so often as to be com-
monplace, as have her encounters with
the
law. However, one
incident
of
a
more recent vintage took
place
in a
large
Midwestern
city
where
Billie
was
performing,
and
this
incident
should
be
made
known.
While
she
was out having supper, her dressing
room
was
illegally
entered,
ran-
sacked,
and
her
expensive
wardrobe
slashed in fruitless search for damag-
ing evidence that would result in her
arrest.
This
hostile
attitude
was
Billie’s welcome wherever
she
went,
wherever she worked. Is it any wonder
she despaired, and asked, “What’s the
use?”
We should consider ourselves priv-
ileged
to have known
Billie Holiday,
the
singer,
from
her
performances,
both
live
and
recorded. We
should
consider
ourselves
even more
privi-
leged
to have known
Billie
Holiday,
the
Lady,
and
I,
for
one,
shall
be
eternally
grateful
for
her
legacy,
a
library of her recorded
efforts, which
I
shall
treasure
as
one
of my most
prized
possessions. Thank
you, Lady
Day, and
.
.
.
don’t
explain.

'Groove' Holmes
Richard
Arnold Holmes was

knowledge

Holmes can modify the instrument at

he is looking for. Named “Groove” by

as

philes through

5 LPs on the Pa-

Jazz
logo

is
currently

100 with his Pres-
tige
release

“Misty”
which
is
number 44 this week.

Capitol &
Pickwick
NEW YORK—Capitol Records’ entire
non-current album catalog will become
available
for
economy-priced
release
by Pickwick International, as a result
of
a
ten-year
agreement
announced
last week
(21)
by
Capitol
president
Alan W.
Livingston
and Cy
Leslie,
president of Pickwick.
Under
the
agreement,
which
be-
comes effective immediately, Pickwick
will
have
access
to
recordings
by
such pop
artists
as Nat King
Cole,
Dean Martin, Peggy Lee, A1 Martino,
Judy Garland, Tennessee Ernie Ford,
the
Louvin
Brothers, Ray
Anthony,
etc. The agreement
also
gives
Pick-
wick access to Capitol’s classical cata-
log,
including
artists
like
Leonard
Pennario,
Nathan
Milstein,
William
Steinberg, Carmen Dragon, the Roger
Wagner Chorale, the Hollywood Bowl
Symphony
and
others.
The
Capitol
recordings
will be
is-
sued on the Pickwick/33 and
Hilltop
labels, and album jackets will bear the
legend, “By arrangement with Capitol
Records.”
Commenting on the new agreement
Leslie
stated:
“The continuing addition of so much
fine material
to our Pickwick/33 and
Hilltop
lines
will
increase
our
sales
potential dramatically for the months
and
years
ahead.
Economy-price
rights to Capitol masters of such top-
name
artists
as Nat
Cole and Judy
Garland give Pickwick a broad mar-
keting
appeal
in
this
highly
com-
petitive field and insure that Pickwick
will
play
an
even
more
aggressive
In Ten-Year Pact
role
in
economy-price
marketing
throughout
the
United
States
and
Canada.”
Leslie
also
stated
that
Pickwick
licensing
agreements
now
in
effect
with many
other
record
companies
will
continue
and
will
be
enhanced
by the Capitol agreement.
Alan W. Livingston, Capitol’s presi-
dent, commented:
“Since
entering
into
our
first
licensing
agreement
with
Pickwick,
over a year ago, we have watched that
firm’s progress with
great
care
and
interest.
Our high
respect
for
Pick-
wick’s
merchandising
acumen
has
grown
rapidly
with
the
success
of
each Pickwick
release.
Thus, we
ap-
proach
our
new
relationship
with
Pickwick
in
a
spirit
of
great
confi-
dence and enthusiasm.”
Capitol
entered
into
a
limited
li-
censing agreement with
Pickwick
in
Mar.,
1965.
Since
that
time,
15 pop
and
15
classical
Capitol
recordings
have been issued on the Pickwick/33
label, and one Capitol C&W recording
has been issued on the
Hilltop
label.
Under
the
new
agreement,
Pick-
wick
is
issuing,
this month,

Capitol

on

pickwick/33

and

Artists
represented
in

Pickwick
releases
include
Nat King Cole, A1 Martino, Judy Gar-

HOLLYWOOD—The

of
well
fcoown

Bobby
Fuller
was found

night
(July
i8)

a

can

gasoline.”

Fought

is

Randy
(also a member of the Bobby
Fuller
Four.)

‘Showboat’: Sights & Sounds
Still A
Delight To Encounter
NEW YORK—“Showboat” refuses to
join
the
mothball
fleet
of
musical
shows of the
20’s. The
classic
sailed
smoothly
into
New
York’s
Lincoln
Center
last week with
all of Captain
Andy’s
hands
in
complete command
of
the
memorable
Jerome
Kern
&
Oscar Hammerstein
song and Ham-
merstein’s generally excellent libretto,
which
does, one has
to
admit,
falter
quite noticeably about midway in the
second
act.
The present production has the shiny
look of a full-scale Broadway musical
tr>nng to please
critics and audiences
the
first
time
around.
Performance-
wise,
the
score
couldn’t
be
in more
i
sympathetic
surroundings.
There’s
Barbara
Cook’s
Magnolia,
Stephen
Douglass’
Gaylord
Ravenal,
and
their singing
of “Make Believe”
(the
musical
theater’s
finest
love-at-
first-sight scene) and “You Are Love”
are among the production’s highlights.
Further
strong
points
in
song
are
William
Warfield’s
magnificient
“01
Man
River,”
still the
best American
protest song ever written, and lovely
Constance Tower’s
“Bill.”
As viewed at a preview, a charming
song,
“I
Might
Fall Back
on
You,”
seemed
a
victim
of
a
possible
post
11:30 curtain. Also, a fine addition to
the
score for the
1946
revival—“No-
body Else But Me”—also gets the ax.
“Showboat,” with a subplot involv-
ing
miscegenation
and
transition
music by Kern that contributes great-
ly
to the
overall drama of the show,
is
perhaps
the
pacesetting
musical
of
all-time. Add a score
of unfailing
melodic
wonderment,
it
seems
that
“Showboat’s”
outstanding
qualities
are
standards
that Broadway
should
continue to try to match. RCA Victor
was scheduled
to
cut the
cast album
last Sunday
(24).

RONNIE DOVE
NEW YORK—Although,
admittedly,
Ronnie Dove
is not without fault
as
a
‘live’
artist, the
overall impression
created by
his
opening
performance
at
the
Living Room
last week was
highly
favorable.
The
faults,
such
as a lack of the stage presence that
is
vital
in
such an
intimate
setting,
are greatly outweighed by the artist’s
ability in handling a song. There’s an
ease and
a compelling charm
in
his
style that certainly commands
atten-
tion.
Dove
is
not
merely
a
‘studio’
artist. He
is a performer who under-
stands a lyric and the feeling behind
it, and he delivers each different song
with that same understanding. He
is
one
of the few
talents on the
scene
who
can
captivate
an
audience' with
[ pop material
(e.g. “Kiss Away”) and
swing
right
into
a
country
ballad,
the
likes
of
“I
Can’t
Stop
Loving
You,” without
the
offensiveness
that
is so often generated by such a move,
j He
gives
each
tune
its
just
due,
whether it be pop or country. Musical-
ly his performance was faultless and
{
perfectly
entertaining,
which
is
the
prime goal of any
singer. The afore-
!
mentioned lack of stage presence can
be attributed to nervousness or inex-
I
perience
in
this type
of atmosphere,
!
both of which can surely be overcome.
I And when they are overcome, and the
diamond-in-the-rough
is
polished,
I
Ronnie
Dove
will
undoubtedly grow
to be an entertainer of the first order.

EDDIE FISHER
LOS
ANGELES — Eddie
Fisher’s
decision
to
follow
a
new
highway,
whistle a new song and “Open a New
Window”
for
his
fifth opening night
appearance
at the Grove was
a cun-
ning and, on the whole, winning con-
ception. Most of his repertoire, culled
from
the
Broadway
bag
( South
Pacific, Gypsy and
Sound
of Music)
also
included
three
tunes
gleaned
from 3 Beekman Place and the score
to Jerry Herman’s “Marne”. Later he
warmed
to
the
occasion with a
stii--
ring version
of the
title song
to the
I
show.
But
lost
us
again
as
he
re-
prised
the
tune
not
once
but
twice
more—practically
“maiming”
us
to
death.
On
the
plus
side
were
Fisher’s
warm
reading
of
“I
Will Wait
For
You”, the marvelous academy award
contender from “Umbrellas
of Cher-
bourg”,
a
delightful
challenge
duet
with
pianist-friend Eddy Samuels
to
“Do Re Mi” and a switch on his usual
Jolson medley as Fisher strolled thru
the audience directing one of the bal-
lads
to
a most
attractive
blonde
in
the
audience.
Another
series
of
switches were less successful as Fisher
attempted
to
update
his
standup
portion with some antiquated George
Jessel
lines
to
fit
the
marriage
of
Frankie and
Mia.
There were fewer
references
than
usual
to
his
own
marital
exploits
for which we were
grateful.
Fisher’s
voice
has
mellowed
with
the
years and
he’s
certainly
singing
with
a
greater
dedication than
ever
before. If he
is not yet “possessor of
one of the truly great singing voices
of our time”
(credited to him by an
overzealous press agent in the Grove
Playbill) he is definitely an improving
performer.
A huge
floral
replica
of the
Eiffel
Tower was presented by Carol Chan-
ning
at
the
conclusion
of the
show.
The
pointed
reproduction
arrived
from Paris and Maurice Chevalier
in
celebration
of
Fisher’s
opening
on
Bastille Day.

fied

ob-
jectives. In order that the

mine the winner,
all distributors will
participate equally on the basis

in

Epic Names Winners Of
'DeViile Run' Contest
LAS
VEGAS—A
Cadillac
DeVille
was
the
appropriate
first
prize
awarded
to Len
Silver
of Best Rec-
ords, the Buffalo distrib, in Epic Rec-
ords’
“DeVille
Run”
sales
incentive
program.
Announcement
of
contest
winners was made by Len Levy, vp
and general manager of the
label, at
Epic’s
national
sales
confab
in Las
Vegas
last week.
The
“DeVille
Run,”
launched
on
Jan.
1, was a “road race” in which a
distrib earned
points, translated
into
miles, based on his performance in the
sale of records during the race.
In
order that the
size
of an
indi-
vidual organization did not determine
the
winner,
all
distribs
participated
equally on the basis of a market-share
index compiled through electronic data
processing. The “DeVille Run” marked
the first time computers were used in
any record
label’s
sales program.
To maintain excitement throughout
the
“DeVille
Run”
program,
status
reports,
in
the form
of maps, were
mailed
to
distribs
every two
weeks.
These reports ended the last week of
June so that the winning distributor-
ships would be a surprise.
“DeVille Run”
saw
the
introduction
of computers
in
a
record company’s
sales program.
While
distribs
are
competing
for
points on a national level in the “Hot
100,” they
will
also be involved
in a
regional competition. The final results
of
this
competition
will mean more
valuable prize points for the winners.
The
country
has
been
divided
into
four
sales
regions.
Each
distributor
will be in competition with the other
distributors in his region only. At the
conclusion
of the “Hot
100,” the top
distrib
in
each
region
will
earn
a
large
prize-point
bonus.
The
second
distributor
in
each
region
will
also
earn an
additional
quantity
of prize
points.
In
addition,
each
total
region
will
be in competition with the other three
regions. In order
to maintain
a
fair
and
equitable
policy,
since
each
re-
gion does not have the same number
of markets, that region which exceeds
100%
of
its
dollar
quota
by
the
greatest percentage
will be
declared
the winner.

uct coordinator.
The
seven hours
of visual presen-

lumbia’s creative group. The 1966 con-
vention
presentation
is

three

a

September
product;
the
Cellomatic process, which creates ani-

still pho-

ROY DRUSKY IN A NEW DIMENSION—Mer-
cury MG 21083/SR 61083
Undoubtedly
a
leading’ name among
country
songsters, Roy Drusky
has
a
built-in
audience
for a good many of his single and album releases,
including this new Mercury package. The warm,
easy-going Drusky style
is set to a dozen charm-
ing tunes, including the songster’s former charter,
“Rainbows And Roses,” and his current hit, “The
World Is Round.” Other excellent grooves include
“You Don’t Know Me” and “Crying Time.”
KEEP YOUR HANDS OFF HER—Leadbelly—
Verve/Folkways FV/FVS 9021
An offering of the folksong artistry of the late
Huddle Leadbelly
(“The King Of The
12-String
Guitar”)
with
liner
notes
by Woody
Guthrie.
“There’s A Man Going Around Taking Names,”
“Stewball,” “Jean Harlow,” and “The Blood Done
Sign My Name” are among the better tracks of
this package. Leadbelly pounds out the rhythms
on his 12-String guitar and the album
is a must
for the folk enthusiast.
ALEXYS—Dot DLP 3713/25713
The
young
daughter
of
country
songstress
Bonnie Guitar, Alexys Guitar makes an exciting
debut on the recording scene with this Dot pack-
age. As both a writer and performer the young
lady displays a wide range of talent, running a
gamut from
jazz-
to
folk-
to
pop-oriented ma-
terial. An impressive amount of versatility comes
across as she
lets loose with
such items
as “A
Broken Piece Of Crystal” and “Kansas City,” as
well as “Miss Misfortune.”
WOMAN
TO WOMAN—Cleo
Laine—Fontana
MGF 27552/SRF 67552
After building a following for herself via her
British TV and night club appearances, Cleo Laine
can expect to bolster that following as she steps
into the American record market. Showcasing a
fascinating jazz-oriented vocal style, and a smoky
interpretation of lyric content, the lark gives out
with a golden helping of evergreens that should
attract plenty
of
spinners. Great grooves
in
“I
Cover The Waterfront” and “Bidin’ My Time.”

lUADAlAIARA KINGS!
RUBEN RODRIGUEZ & HIS GUADALAJARA
KINGS—Liberty LRP-3454 LST-7454
Ruben
Rodriguez and
his
Guadalajara
Kings
bring a sound that is all their own to this exciting
LP. The group’s bag lies somewhere between the
Mariachi
sound and
the
big band
effect, which
makes for a pleasant combination of both that is
not
really
either. Among
the
fine
cuts
offered
are
“Cu-Cu-Rru-Cu-Cu
Paloma,”
“Guadalajara”
and “The Shadow Of Your Smile.” Lots of listen
pleasure here for fans of different musical sounds.
VELVET IS THE BEAT—Conductor, John Ca-
cavas—Gallery 3201
This
collection
of
smooth,
easy
to
listen
to
tunes, performed by a lush, full bodied orchestra
conducted by John Cacavas,
is a
set that should
find
great favor
as
a mood
setter. Among
the
easily recognized tunes are “Try To Remember,”
“I
Concentrate On You”
and “The
Third Man
Theme.” Front
to back good music fans
should
dig this
offering.
JAZZ PICKS
OUT OF THIS WORLD—Three
Sounds—Blue
Note 4197
The
latest offering by the Three
Sounds,
this
one includes such blue ribbon tracks as “Girl Of
My Dreams,” “Sanctified Sue,”
“I’ll Be Around,”
and “You Make Me Feel So Young.” Piano, bass,
and drums played by Gene Harris, Andrew Simp-
kins, and
Bill Dowdy
respectively,
this package
is
good,
easy
listening
jazz
and
is
sure
to
be
sought after by the jazz buff.
A CHANGE IS GONNA COME—Brother Jack
McDuff—Atlantic 1463
On
this album
Brother Jack McDuff
reaches
way down into the blues bag, searching for the
roots
of
jazz.
This
is
McDuff’s
first album
for
Atlantic although he is well known to both Euro-
pean and American jazzophiles, having appeared
at “The Golden Circle” in Sweden and the Antibes
Jazz
Festival. “No Tears” and Minha Saudade”
are
outstanding
tracks. A
must
for
jazz
and
organ
fans.
JAZZ BEST BETS
DREAMS AND EXPLORATIONS—Don
Fried-
man Quartet with Attila Zoller—Riverside 485
This package features
Attila
Zoller on
guitar
backed
by
Don
Friedman,
piano;
Dick
Kniss,
bass; and Dick Berk, drums.
It
is an offering of
free moving, improvisational jazz as evidenced by
“Episodes” which has no written notes.
“Israel,”
“Exploration,”
and
“Blizzard”
are
blue
ribbon
efforts. As
its name
implies,
this album
delves
into
the
realm
of “Dreams And
Explorations”
and should be readily received by
jazzophiles.
AIN’T THAT A GROOVE I—Billy Larkin & Dele-
gates—World Pacific WP-1843
That special touch brought out by Billy Larkin
and the
Delegates, rhythmic and easy
to
listen
to,
is
especially
apparent
on
this
album
(the
^oup’s
third.)
“Don’t Mess With
Bill,” a high-
light of this album,
is a tune from the Motown
bag done recently by Martha and the Vandellas.
“Soul Sister,” “Where Did The Blues Go,” “Wil-
low Weep For Me,” and the title song are among
the other outstanding tracks.
Sure
to be a
fast
moving item.
CLASSICAL PICKS
BACH ON THE PEDAL HARPSICHORD—E.
Power Biggs—Columbia ML-6204/MS-6804
Well known organist, E. Power Biggs, playing
Bach
organ
music
on
a
harpsichord
equipped
with pedals (making
it a cross with an organ.)
This
is not “heretical,” as it may at first seem to
the Bach purist, because Bach, himself, had three
similar instruments
in his home, on which he
is
reputed to have practiced his organ music (rather
than
pay
someone
to pump
the
local
church
organ.)
Pleasant
listening for those who
enjoy
the harpsichord.
MOZART—SYMPHONIES NOS. 29 & 33—Klem-
perer—Angel S-36329
A delightful offering of two of the great Vien-
nese composer’s best works
as masterfully
con-
ducted by Otto Klemperer (guiding the New Phil-
harmonia Orchestra). The “Symphony No. 33 In
B Flat Major, K.319” is deserving of special note
in that
it
is one
of the few Mozart symphonies
to be
published before
his
death. This one
is a
sure
fire pleaser for Mozart enthusiasts and for
those who
are,
in general,
classically
inclined.

Music Hall’s topper Nestor Selasco has returned from a nearly three-month
tour of the
States,
Mexico,
several Latin American
countries, Honolulu and
Japan. During
his
tour, he arranged
several
important
representation
con-
tracts for his label. In the meantime, vice president Luis Cairo has been de-
voting many efforts to the establishment in this market of British label Pye,
whose representation was arranged a couple of months ago. Now, Calvo reports
the release of several Demon records, recorded
in
Chile by producer Camilo
Fernandez of that country.
RCA
is continuing its good tango music campaign, with an album recorded
by maestro Alfredo Gobbi. Last March RCA arranged a
special promo cam-
paign for
its tango music
catalog, with very good
results;
next September
the same thing will be done in behalf of
its folk music recordings, which are
also among the most important ones
existing
in Argentina.

NEW YORK—A1 Abrams
of Harold

in Minne-

hit
upon

to

of “Born Free.” He borrowed two lion

and

them
on
display
in

window
of

City Record

in downtown

as

from the “Born Free” cinema venture.

‘live’

boosted

consider-
ably.”
Kim Joins Monument As
Creative Director
HOLLYWOOD—Ken
Kim
has
been
retained
by
Monument
Records
as
Creative Director for all album covers
and allied areas effective immediately,
according
to an announcement made
by label prexy Fred Foster last week.
Kim
has
been
involved
in
the
re-
cording industry for the last 10 years,
having
done work
for
Capitol,
Dot,
Liberty, World Pacific, Dolton, Warner
Bros, and
Reprise. Kim has received
eight
L.A.
Art
Director’s
Club
awards for various album covers and
was nominated for a Grammy for his
cover of the Allen Sherman “My Son,
The Folk Singer” LP.

FILLING THE KITTY—C.
A.
Craig
II
(right)
veep
and
director
of
the
National Life and Accident Insurance Company, presents a $7,500 contribution
from the firm to the Country Music Hall
of Fame and Museum. Accepting
the

is
First
American
National
Bank
prexy
Andrew
Benedict,
chairman
of
the
association’s
fund-raising
campaign,
while
Decca
country
A&R chief Owen Bradley, a director of the CMA, looks on. The
gift, coupled
with

$10,000
contribution
by WSM,
Inc.,
the

Life
owned
and
operated radio-TV
outlet
in

BEVERLY HILLS—Officers
and
di-
rectors of the Country Music Associ-
ation held their third quarterly board
meeting at the Beverly Hilton Hotel
in Beverly Hills, Calif, on Jul. 14 and
15, covering a busy agenda.
Final plans were
discussed for the
Country
Music
Hall
of
Fame
and
Museum Building, which is under con-
struction
in
Nashville.
Completion
date on the building is expected to be
Oct.
1 of this year, with construction
running well ahead of schedule. Dur-
ing
the CMA
board meeting
it was
announced
that Liberty Records
will
make
a
$10,000
contribution
to
the
Hall of Fame, ABC Records will make
a $5,000 contribution to the Building
Fund
and
Dot
prexy
Randy Wood
increased his pledge
to total
$15,000.
The “Walkway
of the
Stars,” which
is
to
be
built
honoring
the
various
artists who have
contributed
to
the
building,
will be constructed
in mid-
August, with over ninety
artists
set
to be honored
in the walkway.
A “CMA
Country
Club” was
or-
ganized
by
the
board
to
honor
the
various
friends
of
country
music
around the world. Membership in the
newly-formed
honorary
club
will
be
restricted
to
those
individuals
who
have
made
significant
contributions
to the world of country music. Only
CMA organizational members, officers
of the CMA and directors on the board
will be allowed to present the special
memberships.
Hubert Long, chairman of the mem-
bership committee, announced country
music membership
has now
reached
an all-time high, with over 1,550 indi-
vidual
members
and
111
organiza-
tional members
in the CMA.
The
annual
C&W
broadcasters
meeting sponsored by the CMA has
been set for Oct.
19, just prior to the
annual
Country
Music
Festival
in
Nashville, with attendance at several
sessions limited this year to organiza-
tional members of the country music
association. The meeting will feature
industry
leaders
from
the
broad-
casting,
advertising
and
marketing
fields,
speaking
on
various
areas
of
country music.
The CMA
also
announced
a new
package
of programming
and
sales
aids
will be developed
for the C&W
broadcast members, including a series
of jingles for use by CMA broadcast
members. The package, which will be
developed
by
Bill
Hudson,
Jerry
Glaser, Dan McKinnon and Carl Bren-
ner,
is expected
to be ready for use
by organizational members
this
fall.
Dan McKinnon of KSON-San Diego,
reported on
his committee’s work
in
arranging a live country music presen-
tation before the motion
picture, TV
and
advertising
executives
of
Cali-
fornia this fall. The star-studded show
will be staged
at the
plush Coconut
Grove
in Los Angeles with over 900
key
executives
expected
to
attend.
Advertising
executives
from
San
Francisco
will be flown
in
to
attend
the show, along with top Hollywood
executives in Sept.
Frank Jones
of Columbia Records
reported on his committee’s work on
the annual CMA Banquet during the
Nashville
Festival
on
Oct.
21.
The
event which will be staged again this
year at the Municipal Auditorium will
feature a show, dinner and dance.
Jerry Glaser, chairman of the spe-
cial
projects
committee,
reported on
various projects aimed at both broad-
casters and advertisers, including par-
ticipation again
this year in the an-
nual
N.A.B.
convention
in
Chicago.
The
overwhelming
success
of
last
year’s participation by the CMA has
resulted
in
country
music
presenta-
tions before
several N.A.B. program-
ming seminars around the U.S. during
the past few weeks.

ule the “Masters

motion,”
the

of entertainers in

Shure Markets New
Mike/Instrument Mixer
EVANSTON,
ILL.—Shure
Brothers,
has
announced
a
significantly
new
microphone/musical instrument mixer
which according
to the manufacturer
makes
it
practical,
efficient and
eco-
nomical
for
musical
groups
to
use
up
to
five
electric
guitars,
basses,
consolette organs, or microphones, or
any
combination
of
five,
with
an
existing guitar or P.A. amplifier. The
new
device,
called
the
Shure
Model
PE68M,
has
a
standard phone
jack
output
for
connection
to any
guitar
amplifier;
a
Cannon
connector
for
high
or
low
impedance
microphone
inputs;
and
a
phono
jack
for
con-
nection
to
an
auxiliary
high
level
input on a P.A.
amplifier.
It
is fully
transistorized
and
portable.
Size
is
2-%" x 11-%"
x 5-%e", and
weight
is
only
4
pounds.
List
price
of
the
unit
is
$97.50.
Indicative
of
the
versatility
de-
signed
into
this
new
mixer
is
the
fact
that
if
more
than
five
inputs
are required, two or more mixers may
be
interconnected
to
accommodate
even
more
instruments
and
micro-
phones. Each input on the mixer has
a separate volume control. These sep-
arate
controls
allow
balancing
the
volume
between
instruments
or
be-
tween
instruments
and
vocalists.
There is also a master volume control
that simultaneously controls the gain
of
all
inputs.
Lenny Bruce Dead At 40
HOLLYWOOD—Lenny
Bruce, highly
controversial comedian, who recorded
for the Fantasy
label, and whose act
has lead him
to numerous
legal
dis-
putes over the years, was found dead
in his Hollywood home last Wed.
(3).
An
autopsy was
scheduled
to
deter-
mine the
cause
of
death.
Bruce was
reportedly preparing
to
move
in
federal
court
to
obtain
the
right
to appear
in New York again.
He
has
been
absent
from
the
city
since
being
convicted
of
giving
an
obscene performance
at the Cafe Au
Go Go
in
1964.
Bruce
is
survived
by
his
mother
and
11 year
old daughter Bonnie.

BMI Makes
Largest
Int'l.
Distribution
In
Its
History
NEW YORK—Robert B. Sour, presi-
dent
of
BMI,
announced
last
week
that
a
total
of
$1,175,000
has
been
paid out to writers and publishers by
the collection agency in the 19th semi-
annual distribution of monies received
from
foreign
performing
rights
so-
cieties
for
the
use
of
BMI
music
abroad. The sum
is
the
largest ever
distributed
by BMI
in
any
similar
period.
After deduction of a 10% adminis-
tration fee for handling of these reve-
nues, BMI
paid
$952,000
to
writers
and $223,000 to publishers. The lower
payment
to
publishers
is
due
to
the
fact that most
of them
are
paid
di-
rectly through their foreign
affiliates.
Writers are paid on the basis of per-
formances
tallied by
the
foreign
so-
cieties and reported to BMI.
BMI began
collection and adminis-
tration
of
foreign performance
pay-
ments
to
its
affiliates more than
10
years
ago.
Today,
it
has
reciprocal
agreements with 24 foreign
societies.
Bud Powell Dies
NEW
YORK—Pianist
Bud
Powell
died
(3)
in a Brooklyn hospital from
a
combination
of
malnutrition
and
tuberculosis.
The
41-year-old
artist’s
early
recordings
with
Charlie
Bird
Parker and Dizzy
Gillespie are
cred-
ited by many
with
having
been
re-
sponsible for the emergence of modern
day jazz from the swing era.

firms.
The pair was joined at the signing by
the pubberies owner, Claus Ogerman.
FOCUS ON JAZZ
A fairly recent development in the
field of recorded jazz is the increasing
number
of
releases
that
are
“Afro-
Latin”
oriented.
True,
it has always
been
possible
to
obtain
recordings
that featured
a wedding
of the two
sounds, jazz and
Latin rhythms, but
it would appear that of late there has
been
a
deliberate
endeavor
on
the
part of the record producers to make
a more overt attempt to romance that
particular segment of the record buy-
ing public.
Was
this
increased
interest
in
rhythmic
influenced
jazz precipitated
by the tremendous popularity
of
the
Bossa Nova movement several seasons
ago? Prior to the wholesale exposure
that Bossa Nova
enjoyed,
there was
always a small hard core of listeners
who
championed
the
Afro-Latin
sound, but the only air play that such
music
received was
on
specific
pro-
grams. Rarely,
if ever, was this type
of music played on the so-called popu-
lar music
stations. Came
the
Bossa
Nova and suddenly a whole new hori-
zon was opened;
consequently, a new
market was
created, and
the
efforts
of the record producers indicate that
their
current
product
is
geared
for
that new market.
Jazz that embodies
the Afro-Latin
rhythms
is
hot music
and,
as
such,
invites
participation
on
the
part
of
the
listener.
It
really
doesn’t matter
if the music
is being danced
to, per
se. There
is that basic pulsation that
invites one
to become involved, either
physically
or
spiritually.
Coupled
with
the
pronounced
rhythmic
im-
pulses,
there
is
also
usually
a
very
strong melodic content;
consequently,
there
is a greater inducement for the
listener
to become
involved, because,
in
essence,
this music
is more
basic
for
the average listener.
As
suggested,
isolated examples
of
the
Afro-Latin
jazz
sound
have
al-
ways
been
available.
Because
of
the
infrequency of this type of recording
it
was
considered
special
material.
There were some jazz
artists who in-
corporated the Latin rhythms in some
of
their
work.
Dizzy
Gillespie must
be considered an innovator because he
was one of the
first to popularize the
incorporation
of
Latin
rhythms
to
jazz.
Gillespie,
even
in
the
Forties,
blended
his
special
jazz
talent
with
the
Latin
influence,
using
authentic
Latin
percussionists
who
lent
their
native sound
to the wedding.
Charlie
Parker, another
of the
titans
of
the
jazz
world,
recorded
an
extended
Afro-Cuban
jazz
suite
with
Machito
in
the
Fifties.
George
Shearing
al-
ways
journeyed
into
the
Afro-Latin
sound
as
an
integral
part
of
his
program
material.
Johnny
Richards,
composer
and
arranged
par
excel-
lence, wrote, arranged, and conducted
his
own
suite,
“Cuban
Fire,”
which
Stan
Kenton
recorded
in
1955
with
an augmented
orchestra. Art Blakey,
whose
Jazz
Messengers have
always
been
in
the
vanguard
of
the
jazz
scene,
is another who has always
in-
vestigated the Afro rhythms with his
bands.
Cal
Tjader,
who
played
with
George
Shearing
in
the
mid-fifties,
has, probably, more consistently than
any
other
jazz
leader,
pursued
the
Latin
jazz
sound.
Tjader
didn’t
use
the
Latin
influence
as an
adjunct
to
his
regular
jazz
book.
On
the
con-
trary,
the
performance
of
a
vehicle
without
the
Latin
overtone was
the
departure from
the norm, instead
of
vice
versa.
During
his
association
with
the
Fantasy
label,
his
record-
ings
were
almost
exclusively
Latin
flavored,
and
because
there
was
a
dearth
of
that type
of
recording
at
that time, Tjader’s albums were pur-
chased in great volume. Actually, Cal
Tjader
might
have
been
considered
the
bulwark
of
the
Fantasy
cata-
logue, a testimony to his great popu-
larity
and
a
premature
indication
that there was a great market to be
sought
with
Afro-Latin
Jazz.
Since
his
affiliation
with
the
Verve
label,
Tjader’s
concept
has
remained
ba-
sically
the
same. We
say
basically,
because for a time the policy makers
at Verve made
an
abortive
attempt
to
take
Cal away from
the formula
which
had
made
him
so
successful
with Fantasy. However, we may
as-
sume
that Verve
has
taken
an
ac-
counting
because
his
last
three
al-
bums
have
proven
big
sellers
for
Tjader,
and
each
has
been
in
the
idiom that
first brought him to great
popularity, Afro-Latin jazz.
Mongo Santamaria, an alumnus
of
a Cal Tjader group
of the
late
Fif-
ties,
is a current favorite among jazz
afficianodos who
prefer
their
music
with
a
strong
rhythmic
impulse.
Mongo’s
music
is
less
subtle
than
Tjader’s
or
Shearing’s
because
he
uses more
conventional instrumenta-
tion, namely, reeds and brass. Mongo
Santamaria
emphasizes more
of
the
full sound, the urgent, almost relent-
less
sound
that
characterizes
good,
insistent, rhythmic music. Mongo has
been very consistent in his approach.
From his very first recordings on the
Battle label to his current recordings
on Columbia
his sound has been
al-
ways
the
same.
The
only
difference
that might
be
observed
is
that
his
current
recording
program
includes
many more
songs from
the
popular
field, where
in
his
early work most
of what he recorded was original ma-
terial from the members of his band.
This can only be construed as an
ef-
fort on the part of Columbia to make
Mongo
Santamaria’s
more
univer-
sally acceptable because of the famil-
iarity of the material being played.
Willie Bobo, another alumnus of a
Cal Tjader group,
is rapidly gaining
favor
as
another
leader
of
a
Latin
jazz group. Bobo, a great percussion-
ist, made
several
albums
as
leader
for
Roulette,
but
nothing
of impor-
tance seemed to happen for him. Re-
flecting
on
those
efforts,
they
were
more
jazz
than
Latin
and
because
they were they had no
specific
iden-
tification
for
that
audience
which
wants
its Latin LATIN. What Willie
Bobo and
his band
is now recording
for
Verve
is
readily
identified
as
Afro-Latin
jazz,
strong,
invigorating
music that makes you want
to do
it
to
it.
There are several other current re-
cordings
that
fall
into
the realm
of
Afro-Latin jazz which
are worthy
to
mention.
Montego
Joe,
a New York
based
percussionist
whose
talent
is
heard on many recordings
as
a
side-
man, has made two
excellent albums
for Prestige Records, ARRIBA CON
MONTEGO
JOE
and
his
latest,
WILD AND WARM. His
first album
for
Prestige was made up
of fewer
tracks
and
more
extensive
blowing
space
for
the
soloists.
Joe’s
latest
album
is made up
of
shorter
tracks
with
more
emphasis
placed
on
the
ensemble sound and
less on
the
solo-
ists.
Here
again, we must draw
the
inference that
this
is an overt
effort
on the part of the record company to
get some
play on
the popular music
stations,
who,
for
whatever
reason,
refuse
to
play
tracks
that run
over
three minutes. Long tracks
or
short,
these two albums by Montego Joe are
excellent
and
should
be
included
in
any library of Afro-Latin jazz.
Another
entry
into
the
field
of
Afro-Latin
jazz
is
the
Mira
al-
bum, INTRODUCING THE AFRO-
BLUES
QUINTET
PLUS
ONE.
This group
falls somewhere between
the
Tjader
sound
and
the
Mongo
Santamaria.
One
member
of
the
group,
Jack
Fulks,
doubles
on
alto
sax and flute; when he plays alto the
band takes on a much more muscular
sound,
a
harder
sound. When
Fulks
plays
flute, the sound
is very charac-
teristic
of the Tjader approach. The
material
on
this
album
is
excellent
and the pacing of the program makes
it completely enjoyable. One listening
convinces you that the group has been
working
together,
and
with
good
results.
There
is
every
reason
to
believe
that Afro-Latin
jazz has
only begun
to flourish in popularity. As a further
measuring
device
of
its
popularity,
one might
listen
closely
to
its
influ-
ence
on
the
groups
playing rhythm
and
blues,
or
if you bother
to
listen
to
commercials,
notice
how
often
these
rhythms
are
incorporated
into
the
background
music.
There
is
no
doubt
about
it,
Afro-Latin
jazz
is
here
to
stay.
WE’RE
TEUJW’
IT LIKE
ITUS!

Merger Of UA And
Food Co.
Is Called Off
NEW YORK — The
merger
of
the
United Artists Corp. into Consolidated
Foods
in
a
$153-million
deal
was
called
off
last week
just three weeks
after
it was
first proposed
publicly.
In
a statement issued by UA,
the
company noted that termination of the
agreement “was considered
advisable
in view of technical problems, market
conditions and
concern
expressed by
stockholders
in
each
company.”
The
statement quoted Robert S. Benjamin,
chairman and Arthur B. Krim, presi-
dent, as saying UA
“will continue
to
explore acquisitions or mergers.”
Joe Of Joe & Eddie Dead
LOS ANGELES—Joe Gilbert
(of the
blues/folk
duo
Joe
&
Eddie)
was
killed
early
Sat.
(6)
when
his
car
overturned and burned on
the
Santa
Ana Freeway. The
24-year-old
artist
was returning from an appearance at
the Cosmos Folk Club in Seal Beach.
Gilbert
is survived by his wife, Judy;
two
sons, two
brothers, and
five
sis-
ters.
Gilbert’s partner Eddie Brown was
in another car and was not involved
in the
accident.
Donovan's
Epic Bow
A 'Super' Top lO'er
NEW YORK—Donovan
has
debuted
on
Epic
in Top
10
fashion.
English
songster’s
first
date
for
the
label,
“Sunshine Superman” moves
into the
number 6 spot on this week’s Top 100,
after
a
swift
move
up
the
listing.
Epic
vp
Len
Levy
claims
that
the
five week sales total for the
effort
is
at
a
half-a-million.
The
single
was
backed by a comprehensive merchan-
dising & promo
campaign.
Donovan,
who
writes most
of
his
material,
is
the author
of “Sunshine
Superman,”
and the date was produced by Mickey
Most.
Barry White Named
A&R Dir. Of Stereo-Fi
HOLLYWOOD—Bob Keene, president
of Stereo-Fi, announced last week the
signing
of Barry White
as A&R
di-
rector on an
exclusive
basis
for
the
Mustang and Bronco labels.
White, who
is an arranger,
singer
and writer, as well as a producer, has
worked with such artists as the Olym-
pics, Bob and Earl, Jackie Lee, Jessie
Belvin, Johnny Wyatt, Bobby Day, the
Chantays,
Little Caesar and the Ro-
mans and others.
Alan White Named To
Paramount Artists Post
WASHINGTON,
D.C. — Alan White
has been appointed head of the college
division
and one
nighter
department
of Paramount Artists, according to an
announcement made by Mitch Corday,
vice
president
of
the
firm.
White,
a
former deejay and promoter,
is plan-
ning
a large expansion program and
has indicated that many new signings
will be announced
in the near future.

9110

Premier To Handle Jay Jay Catalog
NEW YORK—Premier
Albums
last
week
concluded a transaction giving
it exclusive world-wide manufacturing
and marketing rights of the Jay Jay
line. In a joint announcement,
Philip
Landwehr, president of Premier, and

E.
Jagiello, popularly known

Li’l Wally, disclosed that Premier
is taking

Jay
and Drum

viously produced the

Wally

to

for

proximately 200 albums in the polka

through
leading record distributors.

Inks

FOCUS ON MZZ
The constant growth of the recording
industry
imposes
ever-increasing
re-
sponsibilities
on
the
people who
are
I
in
a
position
to
influence the buying
I
habits
of
the
public.
That
area
of
influence
includes
buyers
for
retail
I
record
outlets,
critics,
disk
jockeys,
j
and
jazz
journalists. In the midst of
the growing number of new releases,
it becomes very easy
for
a
particu-
larly deserving album
to become
lost
in the
shuffle and go unnoticed. Such
would be highly inequitable, from the
points of view of the
artist, the pro-
ducer,
and
the
listener who
enjoys
knowing about the exceptional. So, in
an endeavor to preclude
this happen-
ing, periodically
it shall be a function
of
this
column
to
highlight
several
albums which
are worthy
of
special
comment. Necessarily, the selection of
these albums
will
reflect
the
opinion
of this writer and the high standards
of Cash Box.
AFTER
HIS
MESSAGE — THE
MITCHELL/RUFF
TRIO—ATLAN-
TIC
1458 Dwike
Mitchell and
Willie
Ruff have been
playing together for
about ten years and this new release
eloquently
testifies
to
the
fact
that
over the years they have really devel-
oped a tremendous empathy, the kind
of
communication
that
comes
only
from
working
together
for
a
long
period of time. Until 1961,
it was The
Mitchell /Ruff
Duo;
then
the
group
was expanded
to
include
a drummer,
which
is how we hear them
on
this
I
album. Actually,
it
is a trio, plus, be-
[
cause Willie Ruff plays both bass and
'
French
horn, and each one
expertly,
i
Mitchell’s piano is considered by many
j
to be the epitome of jazz on that in-
I
strument.
He
is
facile,
tender,
I
stormy, soulful; he
is a complete mu-
!
sician. The fact that these men don’t
record
too
often makes
the
issue
of
this album even more significant. The
program material
is tastefully chosen,
made up
of three
standards and
five
[
jazz
originals.
This
recent
Mitchell/
Ruff album is the embodiment of good
I
music
and
it
should
be
heard by
as
1 many
people
as
possible,
especially
people who
seek
the
best.
THE
DISSECTION AND
RECON-
!
5TRUCTION OF MUSIC FROM THE
PAST
AS
PERFORMED
BY
IN-
MATES OF LALO SCHIFRIN’S DE-
MENTED ENSEMBLE AS A TRIB-
UTE TO THE MEMORY OF THE
i MARQUIS DE SADE—LALO SCHI-
FRIN—VERVE
8654
Don’t
let
the
:ongue-in-cheek
title
of
this
album
fool
you!
This
is
substantial
music.
Last year Schifrin won a Grammy for
his
writing
of
“Jazz
Suite
On
The
Mass,” which was performed by Paul
Horn on Victor
This Verve album
is
his first effort since then. To describe
the flavor of the music
in
capsule,
it
is
a
modernization
of
the
baroque
music
of yesterday, always imagina-
tive,
always
swinging.
Lalo
and
his
music are portrayed in three different
settings: in a small group, in a string
setting,
and
in
a
brass
setting.
To
obtain
all
the
colorations
that
char-
acterize baroque
music,
Schifrin
has
used harp, harpsichord, and a
single
voice. Worthy
of
special
mention
is
rhe playing of Jerome Richardson on
flute. Gene
Bertoncini on
guitar, and
Richard Davis on bass. The main force
is
Lalo
Schifrin’s
writing
and
his
playing,
and
in
this
day
when
so
much begins to sound alike, this album
is a welcome departure into new pas-
tures. The Marquis de Sade certainly
would have dug
this album, and you
will,
too.
MACK THE KNIFE AND OTHER
BERLIN
THEATRE
SONGS
OF
KURT WEILI^THE SEXTET OF
ORCHESTRA U.S.A.—VICTOR
3498
This
small
band
from
within
The
Orchestra has gleaned from the
rich
library of Kurt Weill seven songs and
has endowed
each
with
a
rewarding
jazz treatment. The Sextet, under the
direction
of
Michael
Zwerin,
must
have enjoyed every moment spent
in
the recording studio at Victor, witness
the vitality that practically jumps out
of the grooves. Zwerin’s bass trumpet,
an instrument
that we hear
too
sel-
dom,
is featured, as
is the playing of
the late Eric Dolphy. This album also
affords
us
the
opportunity
to
hear
two
members
of
The
Modern
Jazz
Quartet, John Lewis and Connie Kay,
in
a new
setting.
Naturally, “Mack
The Knife”, “Bilbao Song”, and “Bar-
bara Song”
are
included
in
the
rep-
ertoire, but we also get the chance to
hear
some
of
Kurt
Weill’s
lesser
known works, “Alabama
Song”, “As
You Make Your Bed”, “Pirate Jenny”,
and “Havana Song”. One of the
out-
standing aspects of this album
is the
fact
that
it was
recorded
with
two
different groups, and
yet the
overall
feeling remains
completely
identical.
This must be considered as
a
tribute
to
the
solid
musicianship
of
all
the
performers.
RCA
Victor,
George
Avakian, Bob Prince, and the gentle-
men
of the ensemble
are
to
be
con-
gratulated
for
a
job
magnificently
done.
TIME WILL TELL—JOHN ANDER-
SON—TANGERINE
1506
One must
draw the inference that John Ander-
son
is
a
strict
disciplinarian,
other-
wise how could he have achieved such
a tight big-band sound from nineteen
men
who
obviously
don’t
work
to-
gether on a regular basis
Anderson,
a veteran
of the big band scene and
himself
an
accomplished
trumpeter,
although he
doesn’t play on
this
al-
bum, has put together what might be
the big band “sleeper” album
of
the
year. The
section work
bristles,
the
soloists are outstanding, and the ma-
terial is muscular whether it is at up,
medium, or down tempo. Of particular
interest
is the use of piccolo,
itself a
depai’ture from the normal instrumen-
tation, and an
instrument
which,
as
it
is used here, makes the altogether
sound even more
incisive.
Hopefully,
some
deejays
and program
directors
will
read
this
very
enthusiastic
cri-
tique and, as a consequence, will seek
out
this
John
Anderson
album
and
give
it some much deserved air play.
Music like this should be heard by the
many, not the few.
JUST ABOUT EVERYTHING—BOB
DOROUGH—FOCUS 336 In 1956 Bob
Dorough
recorded
a
vocal album
on
Bethlehem,
one
titled,
“Devil
May
Care.” By
now,
this album
has
be-
come
a
collectors’
item
In
spite
of
its scarcity and the fact that a decade
has elapsed, it continues to receive air
play from many discerning program-
mers.
Dorough’s
latest
album,
com-
prised
of
ten
vocals,
is
a
veritable
potpourri
of
good
music,
featuring
standards, ballads, jazz originals, and
a couple
of jazz
infected folk
songs.
By
some
standards.
Bob
Dorough
might
not
be
considered
to
have
a
good voice, at least not in the accepted
sense
of
the
word,
voice.
However,
let us hasten to add that Bob Dorough
is a great singer, one whose phrasing
is
completely
unique,
and
a
singer
whose understanding
of
a
lyric
is
a
joy to behold, especially
in the midst
of so many vocalists who
don’t seem
to
understand
the
meaning
of
the
words they sing. Dorough’s colleagues
on this recording are
all seasoned and
sympathetic
players:
A1
Schackman
on guitar, Percy Brice on drums, and
Ben Tucker on bass. It was with Ben
Tucker
that
Dorough
collaborated
several
seasons
ago
on
the
hit,
“Cornin’ Home, Baby”. On this Focus
album two more Dorough-Tucker
ef-
forts can be heard, each a jazz
orig-
inal by Tucker to which Bob Dorough
has
added
his
engaging
lyrics.
The
Dorough
piano
is very much
in
evi-
dence
throughout
the
album
and
it
fortifies the opinion, often expressed,
that no one can accompany a singer
better than
the
singer
himself.
This
Bob Dorough
vocal
album
signals
a
welcome return to the recording scene
for
one
of
music’s most
gifted
per-
formers,
a
singers’
singer,
a
musi-
cians’ singer, and, perhaps most impor-
tant
of
all, an
appreciative
listeners’
singer.

Milestone
Records
Bows
With
Emphasis On Jazz
NEW YORK—Milestone
Records,
a
new
label with
the announced
inten-
tion
of
concentrating
on
“quality
album product,” has just begun activ-
ity,
with
headquarters
in New York
City.
Milestone
plans
to move most
heavily
into
the
jazz
market,
and
has
stressed
this
point by
acquiring
the
services
of
jazz
producer
Orrin
Keepnews.
The
label’s
first group
of
releases
is
currently
being
shipped.
Included
are:
jazz
album,
“Mean What You
Say,”
by
the
Thad
Jones/Pepper
Adams
Quintet;
“Lead
Me,
Guide
Me”, by the
Duncanaires, a Chicago-
based
gospel
and
spirituals
group;
and “Classic Delta Blues”, by Missis-
sippi-born
blues
singer Big Joe Wil-
liams. The
first two
were newly
re-
corded
by
Keepnews,
with
the
Big
Joe
disc
being
produced
by
blues
man
Pete
Welding.
Subsequent
re-
leases, although emphasizing
current
jazz,
will
also
include
“important”
reissue
packages
as
well
as
further
material
in
the
blues
and
gospel
fields.
Distribution has been
set for most
key
territories,
and
organization
of
the
national
sales
picture
is now be-
ing completed, with
a
tape
cartridge
affiliation and overseas licensing deals
now also under discussion.
Keepnews,
vet
record
executive,
A&R
producer
and
jazz
voice
has
been retained to
supervise
all phases
of
initial
organization,
in
addition
to
serving
as
Milestone’s
recording
director. Keepnews
is best known for
his
long
association
with
Riverside
Records. One
of the founders of that
company,
he
was
instrumental
in
building
it
into
a
leading
jazz
label,
functioning as
its creative head until
1964. He has also been merchandising
manager
of Colpix
Records
and
has
most
recently
been
operating
as
an
independent producer.

TALENT ON STAGE
Sandler & Young
Vikki Carr
NEW YORK—If
you want an
eve-
ning’s pleasure, one way of being sure
to get
it
is to go
see Ralph Sandler
and Tony Young at the Persian Room.
The
continental,
multi-lingual
Tony
and the Bronxite Ralph are the per-
fect foils, one for the other. Whether
in
songs,
rhyme
or
patter
the
ex-
citement generated by their perfectly
coordinated
interplay
is
the
excite-
ment that arises out of the enjoyment
of pure talent.
The bulk of the
Capitol's
duo’s
act
is
contained
in
song
and
the
boys’
wonderful,
mellifulous
voices
blend
perfectly, no matter what the tempo
or mood of the song. Among the high-
light moments were an adaptation of
the
while
back
rock
hit
“Mr.
Bass
Man’’ that was milked for every pos-
sible
laugh
and
a
trip
around
the
world
with
a
popular
lady
named
Dolly, which earned
a
standing
ova-
tion from the packed
Persian Room.
The moods created with the French-
English
counterbalanced
version
of
“What Now My Love” (“Eh Mainte-
nant”)
and
the
pair’s
wonderful
knack
of
matching
English
and
French
tunes
in
simultaneous
and
harmonious
pairs
left
the
audience
stamping,
clapping and
shouting
for
more.
Ray Anthony
NEW YORK—Ray Anthony is taking
no
chances
as the master
of a
five-
man
instrumental crew and four gal
singers. He has something for every-
body:
sex,
sentimentality,
humor
(most of
it
blue)
and,
of course, an
agile trumpet of his own design.
This package,
called the “Bookend
Review,”
is
currently
on
display
at
the
Royal
Box
of
the
Americana
Hotel,
where
its
contents
were
un-
loaded with zest for the first time last
Monday
(15).
Instrumentally,
An-
thony and his boys are dishing out a
happy
sound,
covering
lots
of
pop
ground,
such
as
Dixie,
Swing
Era,
rock
’n
roll
and
the
sound
of
the
Tijuana
Brass
(this
is
a
“salute”
medley
and
a
darn
exciting
one).
The
girls,
all
striking and
always
garbed to the best physical advantage,
are
lively,
and,
one
of them,
Diane
Varga,
has
a
ken
comic
sense,
es-
pecially during a take-off on the songs
of the 20’s. The foursome, by the way,
can do a whacky teen
step with the
best
of
them,
with
an
“Everybody
Swim” format one of the uninhibited
joys
of
the
evening.
Anthony
and
drummer Tommy Melton are a
strik-
ing Swing Era
pair
on
“Sing
Sing
Sing” and “And The Angels Sing.”
Anthony’s
bassist,
Dave
Leonard,
also
fills
in as a comic, cracking one-
liners while Anthony is either playing
or saying something, and doing ade-
quate
impersonations
of
popular
singers and
actors. While Anthony’s
vaudeville-type approach has an
ele-
m.ent
of
sadness
in
that
it
under-
scores
the
end
of
Big Band
appeal
sans
hokum,
the
Capitol
Records
artist, blessed with a good personality,
is the emcee and fine artist in his own
right of an enjoyable break from the
summer’s heat.

Withbut You,” a rhythm treatment to

MEXICO
HOLLAND
The number one position on the Dutch hit-parade went early in August to
Karin Kent with her
lively rendition
of “Dans Je De Hele Nacht Met Mij”
(Dance All Night With Me) on the Decca label. The music for this song, edited
by U. A. Music-Altona in Amsterdam, was composed by Bert Baccarach and
could
be
heard
in
the
original
instrumental
version
in
the
U.
A.
picture
“What’s New
Pussycat”.
Via
a German
version
that
did
not
develop
into
greater popularity, Karin Kent picked out the song with Dutch lyrics by Willy
Rex for her repertoire to be sung at the recent Knokke Song Festival in Bel-
giurn, where the young lady from Amsterdam conquered
the
multi-linguistic
public. A
large
publicity campaign
in
close cooperation with
leading Dutch
daily paper “Het Vrije Volk” was the
second phase, and
also Belgium
took
over the release immediately with a great deal of success. “Dans Je De Hele
Nacht Met Mij”
is the fastest selling Dutch-sung single Phonogram has
re-
leased so far this summer.
Holland
is among the countries with
the best
classical LP
turn-over, Leo
Boudewijns of Phonogram told us, and among the most beloved classical com-
posers
in Holland
he mentioned
Vivaldi and Mozart
emphatically, and
also
Bach,
Beethoven
and
Haydn.
The
active
general
label-manager
was
quite
happy to announce the releases of a P. P.
I. production of new Vivaldi-inter-
pretations
by
I
Musici
(five
concertos)
and
a
Philips-album
featuring
the
brilliant Quartette Italiano with four of Joseph Haydn’s most popular string-
quartets.
Phonogram was proud to introduce the new French singer Georgette Lemaire
on the Dutch market. Otto Vriezenberg, label manager for Dutch Philips, told
us that the young woman
is considered in France as the sharpest competitor
in carrying
the
Edith
Piaf
torch.
Discovered
in
a
cafe where
“the
singing
lady”
(as she was called in her French village) used to sing along with juke-
box chansons. Georgette Lemaire won
the
first
prize
in
the
Tele Dimanche
contest, and was contracted by
S. P. P. in France. Released are her LP: “Mon
Premier 33 Tours” and her introductory^single “Et
Si
C’etait Vrai”. The LP
is already a big success in France.
The Sextet of the world-wide popular Dutch Swing College
(the line-up with
Oscar Klein and Dick Kaart,
brass,
leader
Peter
Schilperoort,
clarinet, and
rhythm-section Arie
Lighthart, Bob van Oven and drummer Lu
Sanet)
are
conquering the market with a highly commercial single taken from a previous
album,
the
Ellingtoned
“East
St.
Louis Toodle-Oo” and
the
bluesy “From
Monday On”. Rine Geveke, program-leader of Phonogram Hilversum, told us
that well-chosen
singles
of the
D.
S.
C. band, released
in
the proper
times,
keep up an unbroken chain of popularity-continuation in both the home-market
and abroad.
“The Best of Jim Reeves” by Faron Young
in his splendid Mercury-album
that was considered by the
official Dutch Jim Reeves Fan Club as one
of the
most
exciting and
fascinating C & W productions by
the Mercury
diskery.
Also released here was the Mercury-album by Clebanolf’s Ork with the amus-
ing
title: “Country Music For People Who Don’t Like Country Music”.
Julie Felix, the attractive and highly gifted American folk-singer, switched
from Decca to Fontana and consequently came on the Dutch market with her
first Fontana-single: “I Can’t Touch The Sun”. Manfred Mann’s first Fontana-
recording is a tremendous thing: “Just Like A Woman”, tipped for the top ten.
Other very interesting Fontana-releases by Phonogram are “A House In The
Country” by the Pretty Things, and a nice and hit-potential ear-catcher by the
Happenings: “See You In September”. Very popular Fontana-group the Troggs
have their first EP with accent on “Wild Thing” and the waiting
is for their
first LP.
In the jazz-field. Phonogram reported releases of a handful of solidly swing-
ing
albums
like
“Lester

Leaps

in Fontana’s Jazz Club

and

Les

Wilson
cooperation
“The
Wailers”
on
Fontana.
CBS Holland recently signed the Dutch group Les Cruches
(the Pitchers)
for recordings on the

during

in Holland

low countries and their records are considered hit-singles and continue to

Of

Current chart-items on the Dutch single-hitparade include the following CBS
