Until now Page One
product has been issued on Fontana who will in future distribute the new label
in the U.K. and the Orish Republic, Benelux, France, Japan, Scandinavia, Spam
and South Africa. Other release contracts are held by Ricordi for Italy, Hansa
for Germany, Austria and Switzerland. Individual agreements have been made
for

the
U.S.A. Apart from

British artistes for worldwide release Page One
is actively acquiring tapes
ot
disks by foreign artistes
for

Dot Seeks Indie Labels For Branches^
Now Known As World-Wide Records Dist,
HOLLYWOOD—Dot
distrib branches
across
the
U.S.
are
to
undergo
a
change
in name
to World-Wide Rec-
ords Distributing. Move, affecting the
company’s wholly-owned warehouses,
is understood to involve an attraction
to
indie labels for distrib representa-
tion. The
label runs nine warehouses
in seven areas plus two
sales
offices.
The warehouses are
in Los Angeles,
Chicago,
Nashville,
Newark,
Dallas,
Seattle
and Miami.
Sales
offices
are
located in Boston and San Francisco.
Fiscal '66 For Brit. Dacca Is Record Breaker
LONDON—Decca Limited of London,
Eng.
reached
record
profits
for
the
year ended March
1,
1966,
the com-
pany
reported
last
week.
On
gross
sales of |l01,640,000, the label showed
a
profit after taxes
of
$7,328,000, an
increase of $1,260,000 over the previ-
ous year. According to an annual
re-
port, the company’s
activities
in rec-
ords,
radio
and TV
accounted
for
57.4% in share of profits before taxa-
tion, compared to 66.7%
in 1965. Be-
sides
the
latter
consumer
functions,
the company also deals in electronics,
navigation,
radar,
etc.
British Decca
is the parent company of London Rec-
ords
of the
U.S. No breakdown was
made known for the U.S. operation.
UA Music Secures Rights To Kama Sutra
Copyrights In U.S., 'Round The World
NEW YORK— United
Artists
Music
has worked
out
a
deal
with Kama-
Sutra
for
rights
to
the
operation’s
entire
domestic
and
foreign
catalog
of Kama
Sutra
Music,
according
to
Murray Deutch, exec vp of UA’s pub-
lishing arm.
It was emphasized that the deal
is
not a purchase of K-S copyrights, but
one whereby UA will seek greater ex-
ploitation and exposure of K-S tunes.
On
the
international
level, UA
will
move along similar
lines and add an
interesting
feature:
it
will
act
as
a
sort
of an
agent
for
K-S’s
produc-
tion
division.
Foreign
labels

Chess To Market Its Own Cartridges
CHICAGO — Chess Producing Corp.
has
decided
to
run
its
own
tape
cartridge
business
after
turning
down
repeated
offers
for
exclusive
representation from almost every tape
company
in
the
industry.
The
an-
nouncement that the company would
have
22
four
and
eight
track
car-
tridges on the market by January
1
was
announced
by
Marshall
Chess,
who directed the label’s entry into the
cartridge
field, and Max Cooperstein,
national
sales manager
of
Chess.
Chess
will handle
its own distribu-
tion through
its own
distribs
as well
as
a
select number
of
tape
distribs.
Cash Box
also
learned
that Leonard
and

Chess
have
already
made
plans
to
construct
their
own
tape
duplicating equipment which
will
be
housed
in
their own new building
in
Chicago. Construction should be com-
pleted by
late February,
1967.
The
initial
tape
release,
out
this
week, includes 10 four track releases.
London To Start 20th Year In London
NEW YORK—London Records, about
to
open
its
20th
anniversary
year,
will
conduct
a
week-long
sales
con-
vention
in
London,
to
start
Jan.
15
to
be
hosted
there
by
Sir
Edward
Lewis,
Chairman
of
the
Board
of
London
Records’
parent,
Decca
Ltd.
Disclosure
of the
plans, now nearing
completion, was made by D. H. Toller-
Bond, president
of London Records.
The event
is expected
to draw the
heaviest participation
of independent
record
distributors
to
an
overseas
meeting in the history of the Ameri-
can
record
industry.
Every
London
and London Group distributor will be
represented
by
owners
or
operating
heads as well as by key
sales execu-
tives. Many wives are
also
expected
to
be
in
the
party.
With
acceptances
already
in from
points
as
distant
as
Honolulu
and
Hawaii,
6,000
miles from
the
locale
of
the meetings,
it
is
expected
that
nearly 150 will make the junket. Two
different
airlines, BOAC
and TWA,
will
share
in
carrying
the group
to
London
Airport.
London’s first-line executive echelon
will all be making the trip and will be
joined by
several
of the firm’s long-
est-standing
independent
producers,
who
will witness some
of their own
product being
presented
in
the new
release.
According
to
Toller-Bond,
many
special
functions have
been
planned
for
a
full
four
days,
some
for
all
members of the party and others for
the distaff side, while the distributors
assemble
for
business
sessions
and
the
major
product
presentation
on
Tuesday, January
17.
On
the
social
calendar, many
spe-
cial events are
in the
offering, high-
lighted by a banquet to be hosted by
Sir Edward and Lady
Lewis.
In ad-
dition, many of the stars of the Lon-
don talent roster are expected
to be
on hand to meet and perform for the
assemblage of visiting American rec-
ord men.
The London party will gather Sat-
urday evening, Jan.
14, for
cocktails
and dinner at the International Hotel,
adjacent
to John
F. Kennedy
Inter-
national
Airport,
New
York.
The
party
will
spend
Saturday
night
at
the
hotel
and
depart
early
Sunday
for London. The return trip
is slated
for
Sunday,
Jan.
22.
Recapping
the
gala
plans,
Toller-
Bond noted that “London has enjoyed
a long span of very successful years.
The
strong
indications
are
that
our
success will continue to expand as we
move
into
our
second
20
years. We
owe much
of our
success,
obviously,
to
the many
loyal
distributors who
belp us
sell our product. We believe
that by having them
join us in Lon-
don, we
can
express
our own
good
wishes to them and at the same tirne
infuse them with a great interest
in
a
quantity' of new
London
product,
which we know, with their help, will
set new
sales
records
for us
in
the
American mai’ket.”
Four more
will be issued by Nov.
1.
In November, the company will be-
gin issuing its first 8-track cartridges.
Price for 8 track will be the standard
$6.98. For four track,
$4.98.
Among the personalities to be fea-
tured
in the
first release are Ahmad
Jamal, Ramsey Lewis, Billy Stewart,
Chuck Berry, Bo Diddley and Moms
Mabley.

duced by General Recorded Tapes and

thru

Lipman Named Sales-Promo
Head At World Pacific
HOLLYWOOD—Dick
Bock,
general
manager
of
World
Pacific
Records,
has
named
Macey
Lipman
as
the
firm’s
national
sales
and
promotion
director,
filling
the
post vacated by
Bud Dain, who was recently upped to
general manager of Liberty Records.
Lipman
joined
Liberty,
the
parent
s^m'
LIPMAN & BOCK
company,
last March
as
east
coast
district
manager.
He’ll
relocate
to
Hollywood.
Raised in Philadelphia, Lipman en-
tered
the
record
industry
early
in
1954 with
the David Rosen
distribu-
torship as a shipping clerk. Later he
became
full-fiedged
salesman
and,
when the opportunity came about, he
broke
into promotion. By the end of
1959,
he
functioned
as
a
combined
sales-promotion
representative.
Kapp Records beckoned in 1960 and
he
joined
the company
as
southern
regional sales manager. A year later,
he moved to the eastern regional sales
manager
slot.
From
1962
through
1965
Lipman
covered
the
entire
United
States
as
a
field
representa-
tive.
During
the
latter
part
of
his
tenure with Kapp, he served as gen-
eral manager
of Congress and Four
Corner Records.

of an LP
dis-
count program and three new albums
were announced by Philips
last week.
The program, which
offers
discounts
on
the new
releases
as
well
as
the
entire
catalog,
a
10%
discount
on
SPM/SPS
series and a 20%
discount
on
all other classical albums became
effective
on
the
14th
and
will
run
indefinitely.
The three sets added to the Philips
catalog
include
Dusty
Springfield’s
“Golden
Hits
Of Dusty
Springfield,”
Brian
Hyland’s
“The
Joker
Went
Wild/Run,
Run, Look
and
See”
and
a
multi-record
package
of
Handel’s
“Messiah” interpreted by Colin Davis
conducting the London Symphony and
Choir.

LP's

JEANNIE SEELY
Most Promising New
C&W Female Vocalist
PHIL BAUGH
Most Promising New
C&W
Instrumentalist
Born in Pennsylvania, Jennie Seely
started
her
record
business
career
with Liberty Records—not as an art-
ist, but as secretary-girl Friday. How-
ever,
the
typewriter was
no
match
for
the
lure
of
the
pei-forming
bug,
and
Jeannie
struck
out
on
her own
to conquer the world of show business.
She met up with Hank Cochran, one
of
the
most
prolific
of C&W
song-
writers, who aimed her toward Music
City,
U.S.A.,
where
she
signed
a
lowed
his
advice,
Jeannie
signed
a
recording
pact
with
Challenge
Rec-
ords, but, unfoi'tunately stardom was
still
only
a
dream
after
her
first
several records.
It was back to the typewriter again,
but not for
long. This time
she was
“discovered” by Porter Wagoner, an-
other
judge
of
fine
talent.
Porter
booked her on his show to replace the
departing Norma
Jean,
and
the
re-
sponse was overwhelming. Back
into
the picture came Hank Cochran, who
brought her to the attention of Monu-
ment Records.
Soon Jeannie was no longer an un-
known,
but
the
most
exciting
new
personality to hit the business. When
“Don’t Touch Me” soared to the Num-
ber One
spot on the country
charts,
the typewriter was
laid away to
its
final resting place. Jeannie was a star.
Phil Baugh, who jumped
into
the
national
limelight
last year with
his
“Country Guitar” smash on the Long-
horn
label,
was
born
out
in
Long
Beach,
Calif, some 30 years ago. His
first
musical
expositions
came
in
church where
his
father would
play
the piano and
Phil would accompany
on
the
guitar and
banjo. After high
school he followed
his
father’s
trade
as
a
bricklayer, but remained
active
in
his
musical
interests,
playing-
before various groups and
clubs.
In
1954
he
cut
his
first
records,
“Bumble
Twist” and “Moon
Magic,”
for Crest Records, gathering a strong
following and healthy
sales.
His
big
break
came,
however, when
the
re-
lease of “Country Guitar,” which was
his first deck for Longhorn.
The lightning fast fingers and
au-
thentic guitar imitations of other
in-
struments are the keys to his success
and the basic reasons for
his
contin-
ued
acceptance
with
country
audi-
ences.
STATLER BROTHERS
Most Promising New
C&W Vocal Group
The Statler Brothers came together
in 1955 and gained a good amount of
recognition
as
a
gospel-oriented
group, playing in tent meetings, audi-
toriums,
arenas
and
all-night hymn
sings.
During
one
of
their
appear-
ances
on
a Roanoke TV
show,
they
were seen by Johnny Cash, who made
them a permanent part of his touring
show, where they
gained
even more
prominence.
A
recording
contract
with Columbia
Records followed and
the foursome
soon had
a
giant pop-
country
record
on
their
hands
in
“Flowers On The Wall.” Several other
hits followed and the boys had
built
up a strong following among deejays
and fans.
Of
the
four members, two
in
the
group are real life “brothers,” Harold
and Don Reid, while the remainder of
the ensemble
consists
of Lew Dewitt
and
Phil
Balsley.
Don
Reid,
who
writes and plays ukulele,
is the only
bachelor in the group. Brother Harold
sings bass, plays the banjo, and with
his
free
time,
manages
the
group.
Lew DeWit, who composed “Flowers
On The Wall,” sings first tenor, while
Phil
Balsley
handles
the
baritone
chores.
HARDEN TRIO
Most Promising New
C&W Vocal Group
The
Harden
Trio,
composed
of
brother Bobby and sisters Robbie and
Arleen,
were
fortunate
enough
to
meet very early
in
life
(being
in the
same
family),
which
gave them
the
opportunity
to
begin
their
collective
musical
career
as
wee
youngsters.
They became
so
proficient that
they
were
still youngsters when
they
got
their first radio show, on KVLC-Little
Rock.
As
they
grew
in
accomplish-
ment,
they
became
regular
visitors
before the “Ozark Jubilee” and “Lou-
isiana Hayride” audiences.
It
wasn’t
long
before
the
group
found
itself
recording
for
Columbia
Records, being groomed
for
national
attention. At
the
beginning
of
1966
they
released
a
record
called “Tippy
Toeing,”
which was
preceeded
by
a
minimum
of
hullabaloo.
The
record
turned out to be a “sleeper,” the name
given to a record that lays around for
a
while
then
suddenly
breaks
-wide
open.
And
when
it
broke,
it
shot
straight to the top of the C&W charts
(not
to
mention
the
excellent
pop
chart
action
it
received). A
short
time
later,
Columbia
released
the
group’s
first LP, which
also became
a healthy
chart
item. From
then
on
in, the Harden Trio was on the way.

Adair Advises Ops:
Two
for a Quarter
Play
is Only Way
to Offset Costs
WILLIAM
f. ADAIR
CHICAGO—When
William
F.
Adair,
president
of
the
Seeburg
Sales
Cor-
poration,
recently
sounded
the
key-
note urging the burgeoning need
for
“a
gradual
increase
in
the
price
of
plays
to
two-for-a-quarter” he
noted
that
this
vital increase must
be con-
sidered
by
operators
everywhere
if
they are to keep their present business
on
a
profitable
basis.
Adair
further
noted that operators, as a group, have
always been reluctant to increase the
cost of the entertainment they provide,
but
that
their
rising
costs
of
doing
business make an increase
“vital and
necessary.”
Buttressing
this stand by Adair
in
the
huge
Seeburg
organization
are
vice
president
Bill
Prutting,
national
sales manager Edward F. Clalfey; and
Frank Luppino, advertising and
sales
promotion manager. Luppino submit-
ted some
information
to
supplement
and
substantiate
Adair’s
stand
gar-
nered from the United States Dept, of
Labor, Bureau of Labor Statistics.
He
said:
“If the coin machine ope-
rator
will
just
reflect on merely
the
cost of operating his vehicles over the
time
since he inaugurated dime play,
and then check some
of
his pay
rec-
ords on increased costs of service and
and route personnel, he will certainly
see the advisability of inaugurating a
two-for-a-quarter
policy
right
away
with many of his locations.”
Luppino, as did Adair, cited numer-
ous cases where the feasibility of
in-
creasing
to
two-for-a-quarter
play
pricing should be considered
at
least
in
part.
They
feel
that
operators
should
at
least
condition
themselves
to this necessary coming trend due to
the overall higher cost to do business.
Claffey
explained
that
there
have
been skyrocketing costs in such neces-
sities as copyright costs, taxes
in
all
areas,
interest
rates,
bookkeeping
costs, and
vastly higher
salaries for
personnel
in
all departments.
“Whenever we go out into the
field
to
call on our customers we are con-
stantly
bombarded
with
facts
and
figures of these
ever mounting
costs
to do business,” Claffey
asserted.
“When you
consider
the
fact
that
many of our operator friends literally
work
out of
their
‘hip
pockets’
it
is
no wonder that
it
is virtually impos-
sible for them to keep a sound record
of their overall costs to operate.”
Adair
stressed
the
need
for
a
thorough
‘soul-searching’
attitude
among
operators.
He
said:
“If
an
operator
can
find
a
capable
service
man today, he has to pay him two or
three times the salary paid just a few
short years ago. If an operator figures
up
the
current
cost
of
his
vehicles,
his cost of operation and maintenance
and
his
cost
of insurance,
the
astro-
nomical
rise over the costs of just a
year or two ago are nothing short of
amazing.
“If an operator looks at the rise in
the cost of living
since the
last time
phonograph
play
was
increased
in
1954,
he
will
soon
wonder why
he
didn’t think of increasing the cost of
play
a
long time
ago,” Adair
noted.

NEW YORK—Within

Originally

in

the
treaty became effective in 1952 and to
date
50
nations
have become
signa-
tories.
Music publishers have been among
the
groups which
have
for
a
dozen
years
urged
that
the
United
States
become a party to the treaty. Leonard
Feist, then president of MPA and now
executive
secretary
of NMPA,
has
been
a
participant
in
the
activity
since
its beginning.
The
United
States
Senate
ratified
the
treaty
in
1960,
but
it was
nec-
essary
to
implement
this
action
by
changes in our tariff laws.
Between
1960
and
1965
no
steps
were taken
to introduce
this
legisla-
tion, but after
its introduction at the

PETULA
NEW YORK—The rhythm of the day
is
being
splashed
about
with

common

at

Copaca-
bana, where England’s Pet Clark has
started her second engagement at the
nitery. With an entourage of Warner

offered her disk
hits plus nitery
spe-
cialties with an abundance
of energy

sounds
often
seemed
like
recording
takes,
especially
those
coming
from
the
augmented
Copa

Or
perhaps
it’s just that this lass has the

achieved
thi'ough

re-

“Typi-

stacks

the
teen-beat's

answer
to
Julie
Andrews.
command
of

and

band

Vic,
his
caddy)
Joe Parnello along with drummer Sid
'
Bulkin,

and
bassist Cris Clark. The arrangements
^
were
crisp
and
artful
adding
up
to
an almost
perfect
score
and
impres-
sive round.

lililiiiiiiiiniiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiiilii
NEW YORK—Jimmy Reed, vet blues
singer,
has
inked
an
exclusive
with
ABC
Records,
according
to
label
president Larry Newton.
Newton, who flew to Chicago to ne-
gotiate
the
long-term
pact
with
Reed’s manager, A1 Smith, and attor-
ney, W. Yale Matheson, also said that
Smith
will be
exclusive producer
for
Reed sessions.
In
the
sixteen
years
since
he
left
his job in a Gary, Indiana, iron foun-
dry to make his way as a blues singer,
Jimmy Reed has become one of the top
artists
in
his
field.
Not
only
is
he
known
as
a
blues
artist, he
crossed
the
field into pop music with “Honest
I Do” and other hit recordings. Many
of
his
hits
including
“Good
Lover”
and
“Bright
Lights And
Big
City”
have
been
written
by
his
wife,
and
Reed
himself
has made
a
mark
as
songwriter.
He plays guitar and harmonica and
in
addition
to
single
recordings,
he
has cut about a dozen albums, mostly
for
the now defunct VeeJay
label.
The
first ABC
session
with
Reed
will
be
held within
a week, with
re-
lease
scheduled
shortly
after.
Plans
are
also
in
the works
for an
album
on ABC’s jazz label. Impulse.

pur-

Becaud
In U.S. For B'way;
Liberty Rushing Deck
NEW YORK—Internationally known
vocalist-composer
Gilbert
Becaud
is
in the United States to star in a one-
man
Broadway
show,
opening
Oct.
31, for a 2-week run at the Longacre
Theatre under the auspices of Norman
Twain.
The chanter
will make
his Ameri-
can
network
television
debut
on
“Hollywood
Palace,”
beaming
on
ABC-TV Nov.
5. While on
the West
Coast, Becaud
also taped an appear-
ance on “The Danny Kaye Show,”
in
which he
sings two of
his own com-
positions, “What Now My Love” and
his
current
single,
“Sand And
Sea”.
During the run of Becaud’s Broad-
way
show,
he
will
take
a
two
day
leave in order to appear in London at
the
invitation
of
the
Queen,
for
a
Command Performance on November
14th.
Becaud
recently
signed
a
dual
contract with Liberty Records, which
feted
him
at
a
party
in
N.Y.
In
addition
to
the
exclusive
release
of
all of his products in the U.S., Metric
Music
Company,
a
Liberty
division,
exclusively
represents
Becaud’s
pub-
lishing
firm,
Editions
Le
Rideau
Rouge,
in
this
country
and
Great
Britain. The Becaud catalog contains
some
eighty
songs,
including
hereto-
fore
unpublished
material.
Future
copyrights
will
also
be
geared
to
Metric.
Previously, Becaud permitted
only a few songs to be sub-published,
among them, “What Now My Love,”
which has been recorded by countless
artists.
Becaud debuted on Liberty recently
with
a
French
language
album
re-
corded entirely at the Olympia Theatre
in France, titled “His Newest Songs”.
Becaud’s first single, “Sand And Sea”,
sung
in
English,
is
receiving
strong
reaction
everywhere. A
new
single
has been scheduled for a rush release,
“Mon
Amour”
coupled
with
“The
Other
Three”.
These
sides
are
also
performed
in
English.

stances and would probably work with
him on future projects.

CHICAGO—Philips
Records,
for
the
first
time
in
its
history,
is
setting
aside an
entire month
of marketing
endeavor
in
tribute
to
the
contribu-
tion made
to
the
label
by
one
act.
Lou
Simon,
product
manager
of
Philips, has designated Nov., 1966 as
official
4 Seasons month.
Heralded
as
“November
is
the
4
Seasons’ Month,” the 31-day period
is
in
tribute
to
the
five
years
of
con-
sistent singles and album hit flow by
the New Jersey quartet. Historically,
the
Seasons’
hit
single,
“Sherry,”
reached
its sales peak on VeeJay ex-
actly
five years ago.
Throughout
this
period
the
group
has
remained
constant with
the
ex-
ception
of
Joe
Long.
Long
joined
Bob Gaudio, Frankie Valli and Tommy
de
Vito
as
replacement
for
Nick
Massi following
his
retirement from
the group and an interim period dur-
ing
which
arranger
Charlie
Callelo
filled
in.
Highlighting the
4 Seasons month,
product-wise,
Philips
is
releasing
three new
albums by
the
foursome.
“The 2nd Vault
of Golden
Hits”
in-
cludes
all
of
their previous
big
sin-
gles, not
yet
released
in
Philips
al-
bums,
ranging
from
the
original
“Sherry”
to
their
currently
charted
item, “I’ve Got You Under My Skin”;
“Lookin’ Back” which
spotlights
the
Seasons
in a dozen performances
of
outstanding
hits
made
famous
by
other names;
while
the
third album
is “The 4 Seasons Christmas album.”
Nine
new
Double-Hit
series
singles
are being released. Eight are by The
4
Seasons
while
the
ninth
is
their
“Wonder Who?”
pairing.
The
Sea-
sons catalog on Philips now includes
ten
albums
and
eleven
Double-Hit
singles.
Point-of-purchase
material
to
ex-
cite
in-store
interest
includes
a
di-
mensional,
day-glo,
die-cut
browser
box
card.
Printed
on
both
sides
to
afford maximum browser area
atten-
tion,
the
three-color
card’s
front
carries
the
added
eye-traction
of
a
molded
styrene
number,
4,
spot-
mounted
on
the
card.
The
versatile
display may
be
utilized
as
a
wall
mount,
counter
display
or
elongated
browser
card. Die-cut jackets on the
three new albums and special catalog
order
sheets
carrying
the
complete
4
Seasons album and
single
catalog
are available.
To
stimulate
consumer
interest
a
major campaign of sixty-second spots
is
being
conducted
on
major
radio
stations
in
metropolitan
markets.
In
addition,
Philips
distributors
are
equipped
with
advertising
kits
en-
abling them
to
do
co-op
advertising
with
eligible
accounts
in
local
and
regional printed media.
Over
one
thousand
radio
stations
are
being
mailed
kits
containing
4
Seasons five year tribute radio scripts
together with copies of the three new
albums.
In
addition,
Philips
promo
managers
will
service
local
stations
personally
from
bulk
mailings
of
these same materials.
To
insure maximum
coverage
on
juke boxes, kits containing the new 4
Seasons Double-Hit
Singles, together
with
fifty
cards
of
title
strips
for
each
are
being
mailed
to
over
one
hundred major one-stop record buyers.
Complete
publicity
kits
containing
pictures and
story
material
covering
the
five years
of
the
success
of
the
group have been sent to over six hun-
dred
editors,
free
lance
writers
and
TV
talent
coordinators.
In
addition,
individual
features
and
picture
lay-
outs
are being sent out
highlighting
the month. First such published
trib-
ute
appears
in
the
December
issue
of
the
Charlton
Publication,
Song
Hits, which
carries
a
cover and
in-
side
spread feature.
In keeping with
the momentum
of
the
4
Seasons
Philips program,
per-
sonal manager, Fred Weintraub
and
the
Seasons’
booking
office,
Ashley-
Famous, report that November, 1966
is
solidly
booked, marking
the most
active period
of appearances and
en-
gagements
in
the
group’s
lengthy
career.

Atlantic Wins Temporary
Injunction Re: Rascals LP
NEW YORK—Atlantic
Records
and
the Young
Rascals
have
obtained
a
temporary
injunction
against
Pick-
wick
International,
Design
Records
and
the
Keel
Manufacturing
Corp.,
prohibiting
Pickwick,
et.
_ al.
from
manufacturing, selling or distributing
the
album
“The
Young
Rascals
The
Isley
Brothers.” The temporary
injunction was secured
in New York
State Supreme Court.
Atlantic
and
the
Young
Rascals
brought
suit against Pickwick claim-
ing that the performances on the
al-
bum
designated
as
by
The
Young
Rascals, were not by the Young Ras-
cals,
and
asked
that
the
album
be
taken
off
the
market.
Judge
Nathaniel
T.
Helman, who
issued
the temporary
injunction,
en-
joined
Pickwick
and
the
other
two
defendants
from
“stating,
claiming,
implying
or inferring ...
in
adver-
tisements
or
advertising
materials
.
.
. that the performances reproduced
on Design Records DLP 253
entitled
“The Young Rascals-The Isley Broth-
ers”
were
by
the
plaintiffs.”
_ (The
Young
Rascals).
He
also
enjoined
Pickwick
from
offering
for
sale
to
wholesalers,
record
dealers
or
the
public
any
copies
or
jackets
of
the
LP, or offering the tapes from which
it was made
to anyone
else,
or
ad-
vertising the album, or from
distrib-
uting,
circulating
or using the name
or
any
photograph
of
the
Young
Rascals in connection with the album.
Atlantic was asked
to post a bond
in
the amount
of
$1,000.
_
The temporary
injunction
remains
in
effect until the case goes
to
trial.

A History of the Jukebox Royalty Debates, 1945-1966
(Continued from preceding page)
ity.
The
board
of
directors
therefore
became the governing body
of MOA.
It was something
like
a
South Am-
erican
revolution
where,
after
the
smoke
blows
away,
a
committee
an-
nounces sweeping
revisions and then
narrows
its
members
down
to
one
man
for
leadership.
The
jukebox
junta,
after
accepting
the
resigna-
tions
of
Miller
and
Ratajack, prom-
ised sweeping reforms
in the associa-
tion’s
by-laws,
a
national
member-
ship
campaign
and
a
new
business
manager,
someone
“who
(has)
had
no
previous
affiliation
with
the
in-
dustry.”
The
Celler
Bill,
H.R.
70,
had
not
gotten
out
of
committee
that
year,
but MOA counsel Nick Allen warned
the audience at the copyright seminar
that
another would
be
introduced
in
the spring of 1963. He told them that
a general revision of the entire copy-
right
law
was
coming—something
which
almost
saw
a
similar
Celler
Bill on the floor of the House in 1966.
Ratajack, in one of his
last
official
speeches,
attacked
the
societies’
‘feeding’
of newspapers with
reports
of
“powerful
jukebox
lobbies”
in
Washington. “Look
at
this
powerful
jukebox
lobby!”,
he
cried,
pointing
to
Allen, Miller and himself. “George
hasn’t been paid for
awhile, Allen
is
paid weekly, very weakly, and
I have
been asked by George
if my paycheck
could
be
held up from time
to
time,
in
order
that
the
Cellar
Bill
be
fought.”
As of Wednesday, May 9, the MOA
had
to
contend
with
two
disasters:
its
own,
which
had
appeared,
and
Celler’s, which was
promised
to
ap-
pear.
The
board
of
directors,
with
Clinton
S.
Pierce,
chairman,
Lou
Casola,
vice-president
and
J.
Harry
Snodgrass,
secretary-treasurer,
were
now
the
governing
body
and
were
most
anxious
to
find
someone
who
,
could take over the duties as manag-
ing director. They needed a man with
some public
relations and
association
j
experience, and a man who could
de-
vote
all
his time
to the
job. He was
to be given
loose
reins and asked
to
make

Bantam Books Forms Label
NEW
YORK—Bantam
Books
has
formed
a
record
division,
Bantam
Records. The new company’s first sin-
gle, “A Wilderness Of Monkeys,” was
released Nov.
1. The song is based on
the novel
of the same
title by Paige
Mitchell. The book was also
released
on Nov.
1.
The
precedent-setting
theme
song
for a book was written by Raymond
Allen
to
which
the
novelist
affixed
lyrics.
Miss
Allen
also
penned
the
flipside, “Once
I Had A
Spring,”
a
ballad. The writer’s appearance on the
scene was a major factor
in prompt-
ing Bantam to form the new division.
The
disk, performed by a new rock
n’
roll group, the Restless Natives,
is
being sales-tested in
Dallas.

For ‘61 Music Plans
NEW YORK—Big 3 Music
(Robbins-

7-15

1967

Big
3
vice-
president and general manager Arnold
Maxin and professional manager Jay

Hy

and

have
arrived
to
huddle
with
New
York
staffers Ed
Slattery, Murray
Baker,
Hy Ross, Dick
Milfred, A1 Kohn and
A1 Rickey.
The Big
3 agenda
includes

plans for extending the organization’s
build-up
on
the
contemporary
pop
j
scene
and
is
also
covering
current

of music from new mo-
tion
picture
scores
“The Sand
Peb-
bles,”
“The

Memorandum,”
“Grand

“The

Dozen,”
and “The Blow-Up.”
Malek Joins UA Art Dept.
NEW YORK—Jordan Malek, a youth-
ful
veteran
of
nearly
15
years
in
magazine
editorial work,
has
joined
the art department of United Artists
Records and will assume his new post
immediately.
Malek will function
as assistant to
)
UA
Records
art
director,
Frank
Gauna, and will administer final prep-
aration
to
all album mechanicals and
art work prior
to actual printing. In
J
addition, an
integral park of Malek’s
duties
will
be
in
assisting
as
staff
photographer
at
all
label
recording
sessions and organizational functions.
In the latter capacity, Malek will co-
ordinate
his
activities with
those
of
j
UA’s Creative Services Department in
an
effort
toward maximum
publicity
and promotion
of both UA’s product
and
roster of
artists.
Previous to joining the label, Malek
was
art
director
of
Popular
Movie
Magazine
and
Fab
Teen
Magazine
and has also served in the art depart-
ments
of numerous men’s
periodicals
in New York.
In
his new
position, Malek
will be
based
at
the
label’s
main
offices
in
New York.

first in a series
of
Capitol
8-track
stereo

cart-
ridge
variety twin-packs
will
be
re-
leased by the label

The

“pro-

reference

All

Each

will

to

(and program)
with

Pairings on

3);

FOCUS ON MZZ
Instead
of
concerning
ourselves
with one particular subject, today we
will
do
a
little
wool-gathering from
the many faceted world of jazz.
JATP Coming Back
Word has reached us that Norman
Granz
is about to resume his pi’esen-
tation
of Jazz At The
Philharmonic
throughout the United States. Granz,
long
in
a
state
of
semi-retirement,
has
announced
from
his
villa
in
Europe
that he has made
firm com-
mitments for an extended tour of his
traveling
jazz
troupe.
Like
the Jazz
At
The
Philharmonic
tours
of
the
past,
this new
presentation
will
fol-
low
the format
of
the
past,
featur-
ing regular working jazz groups, jam
sessions by a host of prominent jazz
soloists,
singers,
a
ballad
set, and
a
gi'and
finale
including
the
talents
of
all
the performers.
There are
those, we are
sure, who
will
say
that
this
re-activation
of
JATP
is
setting jazz back ten years.
However,
if generating excitement
in
an audience and making that audience
feel
like
a
vital,
living part
of what
is happening onstage
is
setting
jazz
back, we
are very much
in favor
of
the
regression.
It
has
been
all
too
long since audiences have been made
to
feel that the music performed on-
stage
is for them
as well
as for the
musicians who
are performing
it.
It
should be observed that for some time
the communication between
the
jazz
performer and the
jazz audience has
left a
lot to be desired. True, there
is
that
cult
of
jazz
appreciator
who
thrives on the
cerebral,
over-intellec-
tualized form
of jazz that has found
favor, but certainly these cultists are
in
the
minority. To
substantiate
this
point
of view,
refiect on
the number
of
jazz
albums
that
are
sold
which
feature the exploratory form of jazz.
The
continual
search
for
something
new, even
if not original, has
intimi-
dated many
of
the
new
jazz
affici-
anados; too often, these new affiliates
to jazz are afraid to decline from the
revolutionary,
for
fear
of
being
branded “unhip.” The legend of Bebop
and the many who
didn’t
dig
it has
left
its mark on the wary ones of the
mid-sixties.
Granz Is Accurate Forecaster
Congratulations
to Norman
Granz
for his vision! He, perhaps more than
any
other
producer
of
jazz,
has
a
winning
batting
average
when
it
comes to feeling the pulse of the jazz
listening
public. Apparently he
feels
that now
is
the
time
to
bring
jazz
back to the many instead of the few.
If
re-activating
Jazz
At
The
Phil-
harmonic
is
a
step
in
that
direction,
we say “STRAIGHT AHEAD!”
Thoughts On
Release
And Distribution
It
is
difficult to recall exactly when
it started, but the practice of multiple
album
releases
is
firmly
entrenched
as
a
part
of
the
album
distribution
scene.
Previously,
recording
com-
panies
followed
the
practice
of
re-
leasing
several
albums
each
month,
perhaps
one,
two
or
three.
As we
think about
it, the company that re-
leased three albums at one time was
considered
to be glutting the market.
What jazz fan had the time
to
fully
digest
three
albums
in
one month?
Perhaps even more to the point, what
jazz
fan
could
afford
to
buy
three
long
playing albums
in
one month?
If
the
albums
were
worth
owning,
and
at
that
time
they
generally
all
were, how
could
one
keep
abreast?
As we
look
back,
it makes
today’s
scene almost ludicrous.
Today,
the
practice
of
recording
companies
is
to
release
anywhere
from six to twelve albums at a time,
jazz albums, that
is. We must assume
that
there
are
economic
benefits
to
be enjoyed from
such
a program
of
distribution. When the promotion man
for
the
record company embarks
on
his campaign
it
is easier for him
to
cover the entire gamut in one swoop,
than to make his territory in bits and
pieces.
Then,
too,
the
cost
of
distri-
bution
is
lessened
when
bulk
ship-
ments can
be
employed. The promo-
tional
material
that
is dispatched
to
disc jockeys, librarians, retailers, and
trade
publications
is much
easier
to
coordinate
when
it
is
done
in
one
large
dose
instead
of
several
small
mailings. The
benefits
to
the
record
companies
that
follow
this
multiple
(Continued on page
46)

Sinatra Tops British Poll
NEW YORK—When asking an Eng-

bore

to the currently popu-

ert

Longhairs weren’t

out

also

a
classical

which
was topped by Joan
Sutherland,
fol-
lowed

and

tyne

niscent of the while-back “Moon River

Jimmy

Jimmy
Smith

in

Pa.,
a
suburb
of

He
once
said in a “Downbeat” interview, “No-
body needed
to interview or influence
me.
I
was
always
a
jazz
musician,
even when
I
didn’t know
it.
I was
like
a
horse who
didn’t know where
to
run.
The
world
was
a
little
too
slow
in
recognizing what
I was, and
I was too young
to understand what
I
had.
But my
parents
knew,
and
they
encouraged my
playing.
I
was
nine years old before the world began
to take
notice of me, but
I was born
a jazz musician.” As is often the case
among
jazz
artists, Jimmy Smith
is
represented
by
recorded
product
on
more than one
label. He
is currently
affiliated with the Verve
label and
is
currently represented on the Top
100
Albums by
his “Bucket” LP
on
the
Blue Note
label. “Bucket”
is number
68 this week.

The Electrogenic sounds of Eric Siday
are
being
aired
daily
over WMCA-
New York. The outlet is using Siday’s
“Identitones”
subliminally
through-
out
the
day
on
its
public
service
features. The weather and
traffic
re-
ports as
well
as
the time
signatures
are
enhanced by an
undercurrent
of
electronic
sound
especially
designed
to
invoke
the mood
or
ambiance
of
the
particular
report.
In
discussing
the
addition
of
“Identitones”
to
its
programming,
Ruth
Meyer,
the
out-
let’s pd
said;
“With
the
tremendous
amount
of
creativity
that went
into
the
conception
and
execution
of
a
package
like
Eric
Siday’s
“Identi-
tones,”
it’s
natural
to
suppose
that
the
overall
effect
on
the
air
would
be a violent change
in
station
sound.
That
just
isn’t
true,
this package
is
designed
to
create
an
environment
which
will surround
in a
subtle way,
the
actual program
material we
use
with
it.
It
enhances
rather
than
in-
trudes.” WMCA has
exclusive
rights
to
“Identitones”
in
the
New
York
Area
(50-mile radius) for a four-year
period.
Perhaps
one
of
the
better
known
examples
of
Siday’s
electro-
genic sounds
is the American Express
commercial
with
all
the
staccato
“beeps”
in the background.

FM Sales In Sept. Up 27%;
Phono Business 'Healthy'
WASHINGTON, D.C.—FM
radio
dis-
trib sales of 428,876 units
in Septem-
ber were
28.1 per cent over the
334,-
762
moved
in
September
1965,

Association’s

services

has
reported.
Home radios
(including table, clock
and portable models)
also passed out
of
distributors’

healthy
clip,

1,747,711
units
reported
moved
in
September,
21.5
per

1,438,605
sets
moved

distributed

ner

JUMP INTO
“PARADISE”
Where The Beat
Is Brassy!
RECOROED BY
JOE SHERMAN AND THE ARENA BRASS
EPIC RECORDS
Conn
Unveils Amplifier
For Wind
Instruments
NEW YORK—Since
the
dawn
of
rock
’n
roll, when
the
spotlight was
claimed
by
sideburns
and
swiveling
hips
instead
of
the
current longhair
fruggers, the amplifier has been pro-
bably the most essential piece of any
combo’s
artillery.
As
the
big
beat
became
a
stronger and
stronger
in-
fluence
among
terpsichoreans,
the
amplifier
was
the
thing
that
gave
the
extra
twang
to
the
guitar
and
made
the
big
beat
even
bigger.
Although the guitar was perhaps the
first rock instrument to be
amplified,
in later years amplifiers were develo-
ped
for
the
organ,
bass,
electric
piano and hordes of other instruments
indigenous
to
rock
or
dance
bands.
Recently amplification was added in
a brand new area—wind instruments,
according
to
the
Conn
Csrp.
of
Elkhart,
Ind., which
claims
a
“first”
with
the
innovation.
According
to
Conn,
which
also
claims
to
be
the
nation’s largest manufacturer of band
instruments,
the
firm
has
developed
a
small
device
called
the
R-B
elec-
tronic
pickup, which can
be used
to
amplify
any
wind
instrument.
The
device
sells for less than
$50.
Up
until
now
soloists
on
wind
instruments
had
to
use
a
standard
microphone to add volume, a practice
which invited distortion and
distract-
ing
surface
noises. The new
pickup,
however,
will
eliminate
such
flaws
because
it
will
be
activated
by
air
inside
the
insti'ument.
The
wiring
setup
will allow
all instruments
in a
single combo
to hook
into
the same
amplifier,
or
separate
amplifiers,
whenever desirable.
Accordind to the firm, “a musician’s
special
effects
will
be
limited
only
by
the
amplifier
itself. Reverbration,
echo and vibration can
all be induced
by the amplifier. Conn estimates that
the
electronic
pickup
to
be
most
widely
used
by
combos
and
dance
bands,
more
so
than
marching
or
concert
bands,
although
it
foresees
the day when a soloist with a concert
band
doing
an
outdoor performance
might
use
the
device
to
enforce
its
sound.

HOLLAND
A very popular singer in Holland and Belgium
is Boudewijn de Groot
(22),
comparable, in a way, to Bob Dylan and Donovan. His intriguing troubadour-
like songs were labelled as “protest” in his beginning period two years ago as
a
result
of
his
hit-recording
“Sleep
Well,
Mr.
President”
(a' free
Dutch
adaption of Boris Vian’s “Le Deserteur”). Later, Decca
artist de Groot found
a large response with folk-type ballads and songs of excellent poetical value,
written for the great part by a young Dutch student of law, Lennaert Nijgh.
The cooperation
de Groot-Nijgh
resulted
in
a
fascinating new
Decca album
entitled “For The Survived.” A first-class Dutch publisher, Gert Lubberhuizen
(owner of publishing cy. De Bezige Bij) was so impressed by the lyrics of the
songs that he decided to
edit a book devoted
to Boudewijn de Groot singing
Lennaert Nijgb’s poetiy.
The American
Walker
Brothers,
recording
in
England
for
Philips,
have
made a magnificent new LP recording:
“Portrait.” Orchestras were conducted
by Reg Guest and Ivor Raymonde. The album
contains, no
doubt,
their best
repertoire and their best performances. Phonogram Amsterdam has used two
strongly hit-potential tracks for a
single-release:
“Living Above Your Head”
and “Young Man
Cried.”
Bobby
Hebb’s
second
single-release “A
Satisfied
Mind” (Philips) has been received very well in Holland. The popular singer, on
tour
through
England,
is
contracted
by
his
Dutch
representing
company
Phonogram for a TV-performance here.
Jumping to the top
of the Dutch
hit-lists
is
the song “Sammy” by multi-
faceted showman Ramses Shaffy. This fascinating personality
(actor, excellent
pianist, composer, singer and humorous entertainer)
is
of Russian, Egyptian
and Dutch-Jewish
orgin. For
Philips,
Shaffy recorded
his “Shaffy Chantant”
Cabaret with the famous Liesbeth
List, an LP that surpassed
all expectations
in sales. From the English and American sides, much interest has already been
shown for the internationally-oriented Dutchman.
Dutch Vocalist Willeke Alberti flew to Paris to meet and congratulate popular
French singer Michael Polnareff who was honored with a party and a press-
conference
there regarding
his
recent
hit-successes.
One
of them
has
been
adapted
in
a Dutch version under the
title “Rozen, Tien Rozen”
(Roses, Ten
Roses)
on
Philips. This song
is coupled with a Dutch
rendition
of “Born A
Woman.”
The biggest event
in the domain
of
jazz that ever took
place
in
Holland
was
last
Sunday, Monday
and
Tuesday
(Nov.
6-7-8). A
large
number
of
famous jazz musicians performed in the brand new huge
(and every evening
full-house) concert hall of “De Doelen” at Rotterdam under the title “Newport
Jazz
Festival
in Europe
1966.” Amongst the performing groups and
artists
during this 3-day Festival were Dave Brubeck Quartet, the Stan Getz Quartet,
Astrud
Gilberto,
Sonny
Rollins,
the Max
Roach
Quintet,
the
Albert
Ayler
Quintet and many
others. The “Newport Jazz
Festival
in Europe 1966” was
presented
in
the Netherlands by “De Doelen”
at Rotterdam
in
co-operation
with
Festival
Productions,
Inc., New York
(George
Wein,
president),
Alan
Bates, London, and the Theaterbureau, Paul Acket, The Hague. On Saturday
last Norman Granz’ “Jazz At The Philharmonic” appeared at The Hague and
Amsterdam, with
such names
as
Dizzy
Gillespie, Coleman
Hawkins, Benny
Carter, Teddy Wilson, Clark Terry, Louis
Bellson, Zoot
Sims, James Moody,
Bob Cranshaw and T-Bone Walker.
Artone’s Funckler exec Pete Felleman reports that the Tamla-Motown sound
has come back strongly on the Dutch scene. During the past weeks two singles
have appeared in the leading local Top 40 chart, to wit “Blowin’ In The Wind”
by Stevie Wonder and “You Can’t Hurry Love” by the Supremes. Currently
riding the local Top Ten
is the exciting Four Tops reading of “Reach Out,
I’ll
Be There.” New LP album product released on the
label
in the Benelux
this
week includes Stevie Wonder’s “Blowin’ In The Wind” and the Supremes’ “A
Go Go.”
Having been on the charts for five consecutive weeks, Donovan’s initial Epic
etching “Sunshine Superman” continues to sell very well on single as well as on
LP. The Donovan disc is the hottest thing on Epic since the label was launched
in The
Netherlands. Another
highly promising
platter
out
of
the
Funckler
stable, Billy Stewart’s “Summertime” on Chess, has hit the charts.
Platter
is
being followed-up by “Secret Love,” released this week. Both discs are getting
tremendous radio and jukebox play. Also new on the Chess label
is the Ramsey
Lewis Trio plus orchestra-version
of “Uptight.” The Pete Felleman-compiled
Album Series “I Love Jazz On Chess,” released last month, has proved
to be
very successful saleswise so far. Series consists of one album each by such Jazz
greats as harpist Dorothy Ashby, drummer Art Blakey, guitarist Kenny Burrell,
multi-instrumentalist
Roland
Kirk,
reedman
Yusef
Lateef,
pianist
Ramsey
Lewis and Big Band boss Oliver Nelson. All seven LP’s are in Stereo and fea-
ture one
of Holland’s top models on
the
full
color
sleeves.
Artone’s
locally-
produced
classical
line has seen an important further spreading
this month.
Among the newly-recorded
issues are
pianist Gerard Hengeveld’s
interpreta-
tions
of Mendelssohn’s “Songs Without Words,”
organist
Albert
de
Klerk’s
performances of Ceasar Franck organ works and Haydn organ concertos and
the Amsterdam
Chamber
Orchestra
playing
Mozart’s
29th
Symphony
and
C.P.E. Bach’s Symphonies
Nos.
15 &
18 under
the
direction
of Andre
Rieu.
Four more albums are slated for release in this series later this month.
One of the most important releases in the single
field
is the brand new hit-
single by the famous Simon & Garfunkel “A Hazy Shade Of Winter” c/w “For
Emily, Whenever
I May Find Her.” These singers are currently very popular-
in the low countries. In the very near future, CBS

to

ances.

Serkin's Annual Carnegie
Recital Set For Dec. 7
NEW YORK—Columbia Masterworks’
virtuoso
pianist
Rudolf
Serkin
will
give his annual Carnegie Hall recital
on Wednesday, Dec.
7.
Repertoire for the performance
in-
cludes Schubert’s Sonata
in A Major,
Op.
120, and
Four Impromptus,
Op.
142,
as
well
as
Beethoven’s
Sonata
in B-Flat Major, Op.
106, “Hammer-
klavier.”
Serkin
is one of Columbia Master-
works’ most successful and respected
artists.
The
repertoire
on
his many
albums
ranges
from
Baroque
to
Twentieth Century and contains works
by composers from Bach to Prokofiev.
His
recordings
are
produced
by
Thomas
Frost,
executive
producer,
Columbia
Masterworks
Artists
and
Repertoire.
This year also marks the 30th anni-
versary of Serkin’s American concert
debut.
Since
that
perforaiance
with
the New York
Philharmonic,
Serkin
has come
to
be
regarded
as
one
of
the
most
persistently
admired
and
influential musicians in the world. He
has
received
critical
praise
for
his
performances with the world’s great-
est
orchestras,
his
solo
recitals, and
his participation
in outstanding sum-
mer
music
festivals.
One
of
the
founders of the Marlboro Music Fes-
tival
in
Marlboro,
Vermont,
Serkin
also serves
as
the
Festival’s
Artistic
Director.

SEARCH FOR THE NEW LAND
LEE MORGAN

BUCKET
JIMMY SMITH
BLP 4235/BST 84235
I
FOCUS OJir JAZZ
Among
the new
jazz
releases
this
week
is an album by
Illinois Jacquet
on the Cadet
label. GO POWER! The
advent of this album opens a horizon
of jazz that
is much worth exploring,
for
it
concerns
itself
not
only
with
Illinois
Jacquet,
but
with
so
many
other players
of
his time and
of
his
talent.
Ruth of Jazz
Jacquet’s name
is
as
analagous
to
jazz as Babe Ruth’s
is to baseball, or
Red Grange’s
is to football. When you
mention
Illinois Jacquet you can only
think about
jazz,
as we have
for
at
least a quarter of a century. Yet,
Illi-
nois
is
uncommonly
young
to
have
been a star for so many years. At the
time of this writing, Jacquet has just
celebrated his forty-fifth birthday, and
his
energy,
verve,
and
constant
searching for new ways to please
his
audiences belie even that age.
Illinois
Jacquet fans the world over will testi-
fy to that fact. Less than a year ago
he shook the jazz world up by playing
jazz on a bassoon, no small
task. Be-
fore
he
made
his
debut
on
bassoon
before
the
public,
Illinois
had
been
practicing
several
hours
a
day
for
over
a year and
a
half. When asked
why he waited so long to play in pub-
lic on bassoon,
he
said, “This
instru-
ment
is very
difficult
to master, and
I wanted to be sure that
I had every-
thing
together
before
I
played
it
in
front of a paying audience.
I don’t be-
lieve
in
doing my
practicing
on
a
bandstand.
I practice on my time, and
I
perform
on
the
customer’s
time.’’
This
point
of view
is
quite
a
depar-
ture from the attitude of so many of
our younger jazz musicians who some-
times evidence almost disdain for the
feelings of the audience. And,
it might
be
added,
Jacquet’s
concern
for
the
welfare
of
his audience
is character-
istic of the musicians of his era. They
come
to
play, not only for their own
enjoyment
but
for
the
enjoyment
of
the audience,
too.
Greater E.xposure
Everyone
will
acknowledge
that
there has been a population explosion
in jazz. This state of affairs has been
brought
about
by
a
combination
of
events:
first of
all, the opportunity to
be heard
is far greater today than
it
was
years
ago. The recording
indus-
try has made
this
possible.
In
years
gone by, when a player first came on
the scene,
it was almost standard pro-
cedure for him to serve a tour of duty
on a big band that traveled, always as
a
section man, with
only
limited
op-
portunity
to
be
heard
as
a
soloist.
Today,
with
the
accent
on
small
groups,
a young jazz musician has a
far greater opportunity to stretch out,
and
if he
is particularly
talented, he
can
attain
recognition
in
a
much
shorter time. Once
the young player
has made his mark, some record com-
pany rushes to record him, often pre-
maturely. Another
substantial
factor
in the population explosion
in jazz
is
the
undeniable
fact
that
today’s
young musicians are
infinitely better
equipped to pursue their craft. It has
become commonplace to hear a young
man
of
seventeen
or
eighteen
play
jazz
so well that
it defies belief. Sev-
eral such young players who come to
mind
immediately
are
Gary
Burton,
Anthony Williams, Bobby
Scott, each
in
his own time a phenomenon.
With the increased number
of jazz
performers and the decreased number
of clubs featuring jazz we are faced
with
a perplexing
inversion. What
is
to become
of
the many
jazz
perfor-
mers who never attain headliner
sta-
tus ? Where
are
they
to
play ? How
are
they
to
sustain
themselves
eco-
nomically?
It
becomes
particularly
acute among so many
of the veteran
jazz performers who have known only
one
pursuit
since
first
they
began
working.
To
return
to
Illinois
Jacquet,
his
new album on Cadet was recorded live
at Lennie’s On The Turnpike in West
Peabody, a suburb
of Boston, Massa-
chusetts. Lennie’s
is one of many such
clubs around
the country which
con-
tinue to feature name jazz musicians,
and
it
is
clubs
like
this
that, almost
exclusively,
afford
the
veteran
jazz
musicians gainful employment. Along
these
lines,
it
has
been
pointed
out
that Buck Clayton, a titan among jazz
trumpet
players,
gets
more
jobs
in
Canada and
Europe
than
he
does
in
the United
States. A
pitiful
state
of
affairs, but true, nevertheless. Roy El-
dridge,
recently
departed
from
the
Count
Basie
band,
is another
of
the
younger
jazz
veterans
who
has
to
venture
far
afield
for
steady
work.
Jazz
players
like
Illinois
Jacquet,
Buck
Clayton, Roy
Eldridge, and
so
many more of that
ilk, have so much
to offer an appreciative audience that
it
seems
untoward
that
more
club
owners in the metropolitan areas don’t
sense that
it would be to their advan-
tage to book these men.
‘Elder Statesmen’ Noted
Credit
should
be
given
to
George
Wein who produces most of the major
jazz
festivals
in
the
United
States,
and who
is very
active
in packaging
jazz
troupes
for
overseas. Wein
has
never
lost sight of the importance
of
the “elder statesmen” of jazz, and sel-
dom,
if ever, does one
of his presen-
tations
exclude
a
set
by
some
of
young
“oldtimers”. From
a
personal
observation,
it
can
be
reported
that
Wein’s
awareness
in
this
regard
is
very much appreciated. Very often the
most
stimulating
portion
of
a Wein
presentation
is the
set played by the
veteran jazzmen.
It
is
hoped
that
the
era
of
“hot
jazz”
will
return
to
popularity. May
we
assume
that
the
extraordinary
popularity
of
Herb
Alpert
and
The
Tijuana
Brass
is
an
indication
that
the public
is ready for a return to the
music that
lets you participate ? The
hard-nose
jazz
buff
might
say
that
Herb
Alpert’s
music
isn’t
jazz,
but
let
it be
stated
that
it
is more
jazz-
inflected than any commercial music
has been for too long a time.

Illinois
Jacquet, Buck
Clayton,

dy
Wilson,

McGhee,

Braff, Bud Freeman, Red
Allen,

Dickenson,
Sweets
Edison,

Hackett,

Hall,

Hines,
Budd
Johnson,
Ray
Nance,
Stuff
Smith, Pee Wee
Russell, Slam Stew-
ai't. Buddy Tate, Ben Webster, Mary
Lou Williams we
say, “PLAY ON!!”.

Kate Smith Single
Airs For U.S. Troops
Kate
Smith’s RCA
Victor
Christ-
mas
single,
“Christmas
Eve
In My
Home Town,” written by two ex-GI’s,
Stan Zabka and Don Upton,
is being
released this week with “Happy Birth-
day, Dear Christ Child.” The “Christ-
mas Eve”
side
has been
selected by
the
Armed
Forces
Information
and
Education Department
of Defense
to
be
the
first track
of
a
specially
pre-
pared
album
for
use by
the Armed
Forces
Radio
and
Television
Service
for Christmas programming.
In
appreciation.
Miss
Smith
has
taped for
the American
Forces Net-
work
over
40
individual
Christmas
greetings
to
be
aired
by
the AFN
during the holiday
season, from Viet
Nam,
to
Pago
Pago.
The
greetings
will
also be
aired
over
the
Voice
of
America
and
Radio
Free
Europe.
Special taped greetings have also been
made for
Pacific, Atlantic, and Medi-
terranean
aircraft
carriers.
The
story
behind
“Christmas
Eve
In My Home
Town”
dates
back
to
1951
when
Zabka
and
Upton
were
both pages
at
a
television
studio
in
New York. A year
later, both young
men found themselves
in uniform
at
the
American
Forces
Network
in
Frankfurt, Germany. At that time the
song was heard and recorded by an-
other GI, PFC Eddie Fisher with the
Lutz
Dietmar’s
German
Orchestra,
especially
pressed
by
the
Armed
Forces
Radio
Service.
It
made
its
debut on the AFN in December, 1952.
Until
recently
presented
to
Miss
Smith, “Christmas Eve
In My Home
Town” had never before been recorded
commercialy.
Kate
Smith
is
scheduled
to
sing
“Christmas Eve
In My Home Town,”
on ABC-TV’s Hollywood
Palace,
De-
cember 24.
The
single was produced by Andy
Wiswell.
Pitney Scores
in Europe
NEW YORK—Gene Pitney, who came
off in top form
(14 in his appearance
at the 1966 Royal Command Perform-
ance
at The London
Palladium,
left
immediately
for
a
television engage-
ment
in Rome.
Pitney was accompa-
nied at the Palladium by his American
arranger, Gary Sherman.
In Rome,
Pitney was
scheduled
to
make his latest appearance on a tele-
vision program which
incorporates
a
continuing elimination tournament
to
determine an eventual winning artist.
This was Pitney’s third apearance on
the show.
At
the same
time, the chanter an-
nounced that he will again appear at
the
annual
San Remo Song
Festival
in January
of
1967.
His
appearance
this past year resulted in his finishing
in second
place,
the highest ever for
an American performer.

Back from

to America,
Leslie

to

that

start
Dusty Springfield
is now playing
to packed houses
in her cabaret season
at
Basin Street East. Gould
is delighted with the continued popularity of Philips
artists not only in America but throughout the world. British
artists are ap-
pearing with regularity in the charts of Japan, Scandinavia, France, Germany
as well as Canada and America. Whilst in the States Gould negotiated to bring
American artists Bobby Hebb, Brian Hyland and Keith to Britain early in the
new year.
A new company, Mann Music
Publishers
Ltd.,
is being
set up
jointly by
Manfred Mann and Bron Music
to
publish
compositions by members
of the
group and acquire copyrights penned by
local British writers. Plans are
also
in hand to form a company in association with Gene Pitney for whom Gerry
Bron acts as manager in Great Britain. The new deal will enable the company
to activate
th extensive amount
of material already owned by Pitney
in
the
United

and agency
side
of the business
and,

Pitney, negotiations are almost complete
to

folk

to

four weeks
in Britain during which he undertook a nationwide ballroom tour
and had the satisfaction of seeing his Stateside release “Holy Cow” (published

that plans are underway
for Dorsey
to

in-
creased gigantically, especially among college students.

of

CAPITOL’S CAPITOL DAY;
Put
a
famous Senator with
a famous voice
on
commercial
records
for
the
first
time, and you’ve got quite a drawing-
card. The Senator
is Everett Dirksen,
whose voice
is heard on a new Capitol
album,
“Gallant Men,” which
is
also
the
title
of
a
narration-with-music
single
featuring
the
Senator.
This
development was
the
occasion
for
a
cocktail
party
in
the
Senate
Confer-
ence
Room
last
Wed.
(30),
which
drew the attendance of major report-
ers and networks, with the result that
the event received extensive coverage.
Senator Dirksen was intent on
listen-
ing
to
the
complete
album
at
the
party
(he
said he had never heard
it
with
musical
background,
composed
by John Cacavas, director of publica-
tions
for
Chappell
Music),
and
is
shown
doing
so
in
the
right
hand
photo
on
the
far
right. On
the
left,
the Senator
displays
the LP’s jacket
to the press. “Gallant Men,” designed
to
instill a sense of pride in the tradi-
tions of the
U.S., will be followed by
another album by the Senator with a
religious
theme.
Alan
Livingston,
president of Capitol Records,
also at-
tended
the
affair.

Schiessinger
Narrates
New Kennedy Disk
NEW YORK—Arthur Schlesinger, Jr.
has just written and nari’ated a com-
pletely new LP on President Kennedy
and the Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962.
The
album
is
scheduled
for
release
this week.
In
a
45-minute
assessment
of
the
crisis, Schlesinger recalls the delivery
of Russian nuclear warheads to Cuba,
the U-2
flights, the decision to quar-
antine, and the startling correspond-
ence between Kennedy and Khrushev.
And he relates the outcome to today’s
world power struggle.
The contents of the disk are as fol-
lows:
Side
1—Tuesday morning
.
.
.
Oct.
16,
1962,
The
Russian
Plan,
American
Intelligence.
Side
2—“The
moment
of
truth."
Sunday
morning
.
.
. Oct. 28, 1962, Aftermath.
The Kennedy album
is the first in a
new
sei’ies of record albums to be re-
leased by Citation Records. Each LP
aims
to present accounts
of turning
points in the lives of men and women
who have shaped the world
in which
we
live. Among the
first Citation al-
bums
will
be
“General
MacArthur:
Korea And Red China,” narrated by
Barry
Goldwater
and
“Senator
Mc-
Carthy And ‘McCarthyism’,’’ narrated
by Eric Goldman, former Special As-
sistant to President Johnson.
Citation records will be
sold
in
se-
lected
record
and
book
stores
and
through
the
new
Citation
Record
Club. The Club will be introduced this
week
in the Book Review sections of
the New York World Journal Tribune,
the Washington Post and the Chicago
Sun-Times. Albums will also be made
available to schools and
libraries.

KRLA-Los
Angeles
has
signed
satirist
Stan
Freberg
to
create
a
continuing
series
of
on-air
promo
campaigns,
the
first
of which began
last month. Having launched
satirical
attacks
on TV
commercials,
trading
stamps
and
consumer
games
used
by
mass-merchandisers, KRLA
has
created
a mythical
oil company, run
commercials
for
the
fictitious
firm,
and
answered
listener
demand
by
issuing
more
than
60,000
unusable
credit cards for the “Gasoline
of the
Gods.” Taking advantage
of KRLA’s
belief
in
self-satire,
Freberg,
in
his
debut drive for the outlet, has created
a
mythical
station
manager,
“Mr.
Hardrock,”
and
his
secretary,
“Miss
Groove.” The two, in order to improve
the outlet’s public image, and to lend
it an aura of social
significance, have
revamped the 30-foot Sonny Bono wig
atop
the
outlet’s
studios
(in
fond
dedication
to
Sonny
and
Cher),
and
up-dated
it into a Bob Dylan wig.
Hoping
to
project
the
image
of
Oregon
as
a
great
waterfowl
state
nationally, KEX-Portland, Oregon has
sent Brian Davis
of Clatskanie,
Ore-
gon,
to
the
World
Duck-Calling
Championship at Stuttgart, Arkansas.
Davis,
the
defending
champion
of
Oregon,
is unusual in the field in that
he
uses
only
his
throat
for
calling,
while most of the competitors and the
past champions use
artificial
devices.
The contestant is a commercial fisher-
man
and
waterfowl
specialist
who
learned
the
art
by
spending many
hours simply watching ducks,
listen-
ing to their various
calls, and observ-
ing their flying and feeding habits. At
Stuttgart,
where
the
World
Cham-
pionship has been held since the mid-
thirties,
each
competitor
is
allowed
only one-minute-and-one-half to show
the judges what he can do.

“The Young Sound,” music for the
“neglected”
generation,
(those
be-
tween 20 and 35 years
old), can now
be
heard
weekdays
between
6
p.m.
and midnight and weekends between
6
a.m.
and
midnight
on KNX-FM-
Hollywood. “The Young Sound”
is a
brand
new
syndicated
specialized
music programming developed by the
CBS-FM
Broadcasting
Department,
headed by W'illiam D. Greene, for the
seven
owned
and
operated CBS-FM
outlets.
The
generation
of
young
adults between 20 and 35 have grown
up with a different sort of music than
that aimed at teenagers and the over-
35 group, states CBS-FM. They enjoy
the
modern
rhythm,
instrumentals,
and
vocal arrangement
of
the music
of
the
’50’s
and
’60’s.
These
sounds
will be heard on KNX-FM. Producer
John DeWitt, a graduate
of the
Juil-
liard
School
of
Music,
describes
the
programming structure
as “a maga-
zine
of
music”
or
an
audio
docu-
mentary of modern music of the past
ten years. Each selection must have a
modern beat and complement the pre-
ceding and following
selections.

As

as
“psychedelic” sound. This
is their bag
and they play
it to the virtual exclu-
sion
of
everything
else.
The
group
was
primarily
for
the
“underground
rock” movement at
its beginning but
has

a
teen following
as
well. The
five Blues Magoos
are:

Ronnie,

left of the original group);
(leoff, and

nitery.)
About 90%

used

of “concert rock group”; a group that
must be

as opposed

dancers’ rock group. They

ing for what they
call
“total impact

is number 82 on this week’s Top

Laura
Nyro
Laura Nyro was born Oct. 18, 1947.
Some time after this date, she attend-
ed New York’s High School of Music
and
Art.
The
Verve/Folkways
lark
considers
her
favorite
artists
to
be
Nancy Wilson, Sarah Vaughn, and the
Vibrations.
Her
favorite
colors
are
black
and
brown.
Laura’s
choice
of
song material
fluctuates between the
opposite poles of joy and sorrow. She
seems to be as much at home with a
“soul-searching”
blues
or
some
vi-
brantly
aware
song
of
warning. A
certain tenderness pervades her mu-
sic
as
she
tries
to
create a
sort
of
spectrum
of emotion. Laura Nyro
is
currently
represented
on
record
by
her Verve/Folkways outing of “Wed-
ding Bell
Blues.” She
likes
to watch
“in person” performances by the
Vi-
brations.

Spk D&ii^ Well In C&W, Pop, & R&B
NEW YORK—Epic Records
is enjoy-
ing a “holiday
sales surge” with LP
and singles product doing well in sev-
eral musical areas.
“Mellow Yellow” by the British vo-
calist,
Donovan,
is
currently
in
the
No.
3
spot
on
the
Top
100,
eight
weeks
after
its
release.
The
record
shows signs of following sales pattern
established
by
the
young
artist’s
“Sunshine Superman”
single and LP.
The LP is currently listed on the Top
100 Albums.
Vocalist Bobby
Vinton
has
scored
again
with
his
latest
Epic
single,
“Coming Home
Soldier.”
“The Eggplant That Ate Chicago,”
a single by Dr. West’s Medicine Show
and Junk Band
(released on the new
Epic-distributed Go Go label) has been
making noise, and
is now making
its
way up the chart. Response has been
such toward
this recording, that Epic
is rushing the group’s debut LP, “The
Eggplant That Ate Chicago” into
re-
lease.
One
of
Epic’s
hottest vocal-instru-
mental groups. The Dave Clark Five,
is currently represented on the charts
with
two
LP’s,
“The
Dave
Clark
Five’s
Greatest
Hits,
and
“More
Greatest
Hits.”
Another
popular
British group, the Yardbirds,
is mak-
ing a strong showing with their single
“Happenings Ten Years Time Ago.”
In addition, the group
is listed on the
LP
best-selling
charts
with
“Over
Under
Sideways
Down.”
A
single
entitled
“Shapes
In
My
Mind”
by
Yardbirds member Keith Relf
is
also
showing some
action.
David Houston has
recently ridden
high
on
the
Pop
as
well
as C&W
charts
with
his
hit
album,
“Almost
Persuaded.”
In
addition,
his
latest
single, “Where
Could
I Go
(But
to
Her)”
is
already
listed
high
on
the
C&W
chart,
and
Epic
now
reports
that the
flip
side, “Loser’s Cathedral”
is also beginning to make an impres-
sive
showing. A new
single
“Apart-
ment #9” by songstress Tammy Wyn-
ette
gives an
indication
of becoming
another strong for Epic
in the coun-
try fleld.
Vocalist Damita Jo
is also enjoying
outstanding
success
with
her
latest
Epic single, “If You Go Away,” which
marks
a
radical
departure from
her
traditional
style
repertoire.
Two new Okeh
singles, “Command-
ments of Love” by Little Richard and
“Ain’t No Soul” by Major Lance are
enjoying
widespread
sales
success,
and
look
to be strong contenders for
the top spot on the
best-selling R&B
charts.

Single On Soul City
LOS ANGELES—To
bolster
the
re-
lease
of a new single by the 5th Di-
mension, on Soul City Records, Macey
Lipman,
national
sales
manager
of
World Paciflc, distributor of Soul City
product, has planned an
all-out cam-
paign on the
disk, which
will include
extensive trade advertising.
According
to
Lipman,
Soul
City’s
Marc
Gordon
puts
the
platter
in
a
“mod bag,” that
is
a combination
of
pop, R&B and psychedelic sounds. The
new
single
was
penned
by
Johnny
Phillips, notable for
his success as
a
tunesmith
for
the
Mamas
and
the
Papas.
Johnny Rivers, owner of Soul City
product, and general manager Gordon,
concocted
the
name,
5th
Dimension,
for the vocal quintet (three boys, two
girls)
formerly known as the Versa-
tiles,
when
they
toured
with
Ray
Charles
for
six months
last
year.

'A Joyful Noise'
HOLLYWOOD —

Records
j

i

\
A1 Bennett, label president, person-

administrative director Dick Peirce to
research the project.
The new musical
is being produced
by Edward Padula and
Slade Brown
in association with Sid Bernstein. Di-
rected by Dore Schary and written by
j
Padula,
it stars musical veteran John
|
Raitt. Oscar Brand and Paul Nassau
1
wrote the music and lyrics with Rene
Wiegert billed as musical director.
Based on Borden Deal’s ‘The Inno-
;
cent Breed,” the production also stars
'
Swen
Swenson
and
features
George
Matthews, Leland
Palmer, Art Wal-
!
lace. The
Motley

Mor-
!
row,

Rusid Productions
On Busy Schedule
NEW YORK —
Rusid
Productions,
headed
by
Russ
Miller,
Sid
Ascher,
and Tony
Camillo,
is now preparing
a TV game show for network presen-
tation next season, scheduling a mo-
tion
picture
for
filming
in
Mexico
next summer, and producing
records
which
are
being
placed
with
major
labels.
The
organization’s
operation
includes
music
publishing,
and
per-
sonal management.
Russ
Miller
is
a
veteran
of
the
music
and
record
production
fields,
and
most
recently
was
professional
manager
for
Saturday
Music.
Tony
Camillo, head of the music department
at
Alma
White
College,
Princeton,
N.J.,
is
a
noted
composer-arranger-
conductor-producer.
Sid
Ascher
is
known
for
his
work
in
public
rela-
tions,
promotion, and
personal man-
agement. He has been responsible for
national
buildups
of many
stars
in-
cluding
Tony
Bennett,
Vic
Damone,
and Lisa Kirk.

Mamas And Papas Album
Hits Million Dollar Mark
. NEW YORK—ABC
Records’ Dunhill
label
continues
to
enjoy
good
sales
with
its
highly
popular
group,
the
Mamas
and
the
Papas.
The
Record
Industry
Association
of America
re-
;
cently
officially
certified
the
group’s
second
album,
called
“The
Mamas
And The Papas,” as qualifying for the
gold record award.
The
quartet
appeared
on
The Ed
Sullivan
Show
on
Sunday,
Dec.
11,
singing their latest single, “Words Of
Love.”
Cowen Laffs Up
Gilbert & Sullivan
NEW YORK—Roy Cowen, lyric writer,
has
written
a
series
of
take-offs
on
Gilbert &
Sullivan.
Based
on
their
operetta team’s works, the efforts are
to
be known
as “The Best
of
Gold-
berg &
Solomon.” G&S’
“Pirates
of
Penzance”
is now “The Tale
of Poz-
nance.” Ian Kerr produced the
series.
Cowen
is now
in
England
to
study
further projects.
PLANNING FOR ’67—Songwriting team Eddie Snyder and Larry Kusik (2nd
and
3rd from
left)
meet
with
professional manager Jay Lowy
(left)
and
Arnold Maxin, head of Big
3 Music to
set plans for new Snyder-Kusik songs
for 1967. The recently formed pair had a great measure of success with “Games
That Lovers Play.”
Illllllillllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllllillillllllllll^
TALENT ON STAGE
llllllllllllllllllllllllliillllllilillilllllillllllilllllllllll^
THE KNACK AND
LEE MALLORY
HOLLYWOOD—Places
like
the
Vil-
lage
Gate
in New
Yoi'k
have
long
been known for discovering new
art-
ists. This town seems
to have found
the answer
to these New York clubs
with
the
Ice House, which
is
located
in, of
all places, Glendale. They were
the
first
to
present Tim Morgan
to
west
coast
audiences,
most
recently
it was the Association. This time they
out
did themselves, as
if finding one
talent
wouldn’t
be
good
enough
but
they have two, and both on the same
bill! The dynamic duo consists of one
part Knack
and
the
other
part
Lee
Mallory
which
equal
one
fantastic
night of entertainment, complete with
fire
crackers
(literally).
The Knack have
all
the earmarks
of
being
just
about
ready
for
the
big
time
circuit.
Except
for
some
sharp
impersonations,
they
stick
al-
most
entirely
to
their own
material.
The impersonations include such well
known
artists
as
the
Rolling
Stones,
Elvis
Presley,
Sonny
and
Cher
(we
weren’t
sure which was
supposed
to
be
Cher)
and
Gerry
and
the
Pace-
makers.
Lead
singer,
Mike
Chain,
quipped,
“I
really
admire
a
guy
(Gerry)
that can
smile
all
the
time,
especially when his hair
is thinning.”
For
good
measure
they
even threw
in
their
unique
version
of
Connie
Frances. Their top notch arrangement
of a song called “The
Spell” saved
it
from being what otherwise might have
been
rather
bland. They
did
a bang
up
job
on
such
solid
rock numbers
as “Time Waits For No
One,” “My
Heart Says Yes But My
Pride
Says
No” and the song that
is soon
to be
released on Capitol, “I’m Aware.” For
a
change
of
pace
they
showed
that
they knew how to handle a soft ballad
such
as “Sunshine And Rain” and
a
particularly beautiful song “Girl With
The
Dark
Brown
Eyes.”
For
their
closing number they did “Smokestack
And Lightning,” which happens to be
just
about
the
hardest
rock number
that we
have
ever
come
across.
It
shook the Ice House to the very roots
(that
is where the
firecrackers came
in)
and
showcased
Pug
Baker,
one
of the most electrifying young drum-
mers to come along since Gene Krupa.
Lead guitarist. Dink Kaplan and bass
player, Larry
Gould, both
fine musi-
cians in their own right, accompanied
Pug for a few minutes and then
left
him alone to beat the skins for a good
ten minutes to close out the set.
Lee
Mallory has
the
soul and
the
talent, and he knows what to do with
them,
it’s
as
simple
as
that.
Right
now he seemed a
little restrained and
nervous
on
stage but
that
soon
will
pass.
His
version
of
“Hey
Joe”
is
just about the best one that we have
heard to date. He has a way of mak-
ing a song like that grow with inten-
sity,
while
building
to
the
climax,
without actually singing much louder.
From there he goes into an old Irish
love song “Will You Go
Lassie, Go.”
He displays another facet of his char-
acter and
style with
a number
dedi-
cated
to
Cass
Elliot
(of
the Mamas
&
Papas)
entitled “Fat
Angel.”
It’s
very
reminiscent
of
a Donovan
type
of
song.
Through-out
the
show
Lee
was backed by three superb musicians.
Butch
Parker
on
bass
guitar,
Ben
Benet on lead guitar and Toxie Sewell
on
drums.
His
standout number
for
the show would
have
to
be
a
song
that he recorded for Valiant Records
“That’s
The Way
It
Has
To
Be.”
After hearing that song,
it seems sad
but
true,
a
hit record can most
cer-
tainly
get
lost.

Elvis Presley—RCA Victor
Every
era has
its
national phenomena—Babe
Ruth,
Marilyn
Monroe,
Charles
Lindberg,
Shirley Temple
and
a
few
select
others.
Elvis
Presley
is
one
of
those rare phenomena.
His fantastic acceptance and
unbelievable sales success throughout the world are
unmatched
by
any
other
single
recording
artist
popular
for the same
short period
of time as
Elvis.
He
is
truly an
artist
in
a
class
all by
himelf.
Elvis
Aaron
Presley was born January
8, 1935
in Tupelo,
Miss.,
to Vernon
Presley,
a
paint
factory employee
and the
late Gladys
Presley.
Elvis
is
the survivor of
identical
twins.
There
were
no
other
children
in
the family. He graduated from Hume High School
in
Memphis.
It was
pure chance
that brought him
to
Elvis
Presley—Con’t.
a professional career and overnight fame.
Elvis was
going
to school
during the day and studying nights
to
be an
electrician when
he decided
to make an
amateur recording as a gift for his mother. He went
to the Sun Record Company,
in Memphis, and
cut a
record
titled
“That’s
All
Right Mama." Sam
Phil-
lips,
Sun’s
president,
heard
the youngster sing and
saw
possibilities
in
his unique
style. He asked
El-
vis
to
leave
his name
for a
possible audition
at a
later
date.
Presley
heard
no more
from
Phillips
for
a
year
and a half and meantime had
taken up
truck
driv-
ing,
It being a more
lucrative
job ($35.00 a week)
than ushering
at the theatre ($14.00 a week). Then
Phillips
called
and
before
Elvis
knew
what
had
happened,
he was rushed
into a
recording
session,
a
contract
was
signed,
and
“That’s
All
Right
Mama"
with
“Blue Moon
Of
Kentucky"
on
the
other
side, was
released.
The
night
the
record was
played
over Memphis
station WHBQ, 14 telegrams and 47 phone calls
hit
the
station
during
the
three
hour
broadcast
and
disk
jockey Dewey
Phillips
had
to
play
the
same
record
seven
times.
During
the week
that followed
seven
thousand
of
Presley’s
first
records were
sold
in Memphis
alone.
Soon
RCA
Victor
heard
the
reverberations
from
the South,
and bought
Presley’s contract from
Sun,
along
with
his
original
recordings
and
four
addi-
tional
discs.
“Mystery Train," backed by
“I
Forgot
To Remember
To
Forget"
was
one
of
the
Sun
re-
cordings
released
under
the RCA
Victor
label
and
was
soon
a
runaway
hit.
This was
followed
by
Victor's
“Heartbreak
Hotel,”
backed
by
“I
Was
The
One.”
From
then
on,
Elvis’
records were
the
sensation
of
the
music
world.
He
has
twenty-eight
gold
records
and
even
held
his
leadership
in
his
field
while he was
in
the Army. He has an endless
list
of
top
hits.
Personal
appearances,
always
accompanied
by
the
screams
of a
sudden
legion
of teen-age wor-
shippers,
and
nationwide
TV
Guest
Appearances
(frequently
stirring
up
controversy
because
of
his
eloquent
hip
movements
and
gestures
which
ac-
company
his
singing)
had
been
the
inevitable
re-
sult
of
his fame, and
in
1956
Elvis
signed
a
pic-
ture
deal
with
Hollywood
producer
Hal
Wallis,
and
the
deal
to make
his
film debut for
the
20th-
Fox
in
“Love Me Tender."
Elvis
followed
this
with
“Loving
You,"
“Jail-
house Rock" and “King Creole,"
all of which were
enormously

For example,

Fox
estimated
that

Tender”

in

Most entertainers end up

ing

He made one

“special"
for

reported

for a

He

for

Highlighting

were

“Blue
Hawaii,"
Girls
Girls
Girls,”

big
soundtrack
sellers
for
Victor. One

to Sender."
His

Ray

More

.
.
. many

(“City

The

!n),
5 ’

have,
once
again,
been
named
the
most
programmed
band
in
a
poll
conducted among
the
plotter
spin-
ners
of
country
music.
Also,
the
outfit continues
to
be booked
solid around
the
country,
playing many
spots
that
are
usually
dominated
by
pop
artists.
The Thompson
story began back
in Waco,
Texas,
on
Sept.
3,
1925,
the
year
Henry
William was
born.
After
mastering
the
harmonica
Hank
turned
to
the
guitar—which
so
impressed
officials
of
a
flour company, when
they
heard
him
over WACO,
that
he was
sponsored
on
an
early morning show
as “Hank The
Hired Hand.” A
’43
to
’46
hitch
in
the Navy
followed. He then auditioned
as a
singer
on
KWTX-Waco,
and
won
a
noon-time
slot.
His
activities
broadened
when
he
put
together
the
Brazos Valley
Boys and
played
dances and shows
throughout
Central
Texas.
Label-mate
Tex
Ritter
became
a
fan
and
introduced
him
to
Capitol
of-
ficials.
This
year,
after
his
long
association
with
Capi-
tol,
he
switched
to
Warner
Bros.,
where
his
first
single
and
his
first
album,
both
titled
“Where
Is
The
Circus,”
lost no
time
in becoming
chart
items.
Johnny Tillotson—MGM
Though
only
26,
the MGM
disk
star boasts
of
an
unusually
intensive
training
program
in
show
biz.
Born
in Jacksonville,
Fla.,
April 20,
1939, he moved
to
Palatka,
Fla.,
at age
8
(he
still
calls
it home)
and
there
developed
his
early
musical
interest
country
music.
By
the
time he
entered
high
school
he
had
earned
a
local
reputation
as
a
fine
per-
former.
Then came
a
3-year
contract
as
a
regular
on
a
TV
variety
show,
“The Tom Dowdy Show.”
Lee
Rosenberg
of
Southern
Belle
Music
heard
him
and
arranged
an
audition
with
Archie
Bleyer,
Ca-
dance
Records
prexy.
Bleyer
inked
Tillotson
im-
mediately
and
then
followed
“Dreamy
Eyes,”
(which
became
a
hit
reissue)
“True,
True
Happi-
ness,”
“Jimmys
Girl’,”
“Without
You,”
and
“Poetry
In
Motion.”
When
Cadence
closed
its
doors,
Tillotson
signed
with MGM
where
he
has
continued
in
his
chart-
Johnny Tillotson—Con’t.
winning
ways.
1964
saw
the
chanter
go
great
guns
with
such
hot-selling
items
as
“Talk
Back
Trembling
Lips"
and
“She
Understands
Me."
The Ventures—Dolton
The Ventures are four young men
in
their twenties,
who
have
succeeded
in
capturing
that
indefinable
teen age
flavor
that means
success on
singles and
LP’s.
Paraphrasing
their
first
hit,
it
is
a
matter
of
“Run,
Don’t
Walk”
up
the
stairway
to
stardom.
Beginnings
for
the
group
go
back
several
years
when
Don
Wilson
and
Bob
Bogle
had
a
local
guitar
act
but
decided
to
expand.
They
added
guitarist Nokie Edwards and drummer Howie John-
son
and
soon
after
recorded
“Walk,
Don’t
Run.”
The
disk
was
released
first
on
the
Blue
Horizon
label
in
their
local
Tacoma,
Wash,
area,
but
Liberty Records
sensing
a
hit, picked up the master
and
signed
the
group
to
a
wax
pact.
The
boys
now
spend
most
of
their
time
promoting
their
records
with
personal
appearances.
The
group
has always had
consistent
success
in
the
LP
field.
“Secret
Agent Man”
was
a
chart
item
for
the
Ventures
in
1966.
Bobby Vinton—Epic
Vinton organized
his
first band
in high school play-
ing
proms
and
parties
for
students
at
Duquesne
University
which was
near
his hometown
of Can-
onsburg,
Pa.
Later
Vinton
formed
a
second
group
which
was
soon
a
favorite
at
teen
dances
in
Pittsburgh.
The
youngster began
singing a few
of
the numbers with
the orchestra and
his vocals soon
became
the band’s most
popular
feature.
Bobby’s
career
went
into
high
gear
in
1960
when Guy Lombardo discovered him
at a hop
out-
side
Pittsburgh. Some TV
dates followed and soon
Vinton was on
his way
to
stardom.
In
November
of
1960
Bobby’s
crew
was
fea-
tured as
the band
of the month on NBC's Saturday
Prom
and
played
with
a
succession
of
stars
in-
cluding Bobby Vee and the late Same Cooke. Bobby
continued
his
fast pace
in 1961, making a nation-
wide
tour
with
Tony
Orlando.
More
club
dates
followed—the
rest
is
history.
Bobby
likes
sports,
particularly
baseball,
which
he
plays
almost as
expertly
as he
does
the
saxo-
phone.
The
multi-talented
performer
is
currently
studying acting and reading plays.
As a
vocalist,
his
hits
include “Roses Are Red,”
his
first
smash,
“Rain,
Rain Go Away,”
“Trouble
Is
My
Middle
Name,”
“Blue
On
Blue,”
“Blue
Velvet,”
“There!
I’ve
Said
It
Again,”
“Mr.

Tokens
have
been
signed as independent producers
for the Warner
Bros,

Recordings
for
the
label
will
be
produced
through

being prepared and are expected
to be

in

(left
to right)

(Tokens), Seymour Barash
(manager, Tokens),
J.

(seated)

of Warner

Records,

kens), having just signed an exclusive independent production
contract with

BURBANK, CALIF.—Marvin

Portable/Table Phono
Sales Zoomed In Oct.
WASHINGTON, D.C.—There
will
be
a lot of portable or table phonographs
under
the
nation’s
Christmas
trees
this year, according to the figures re-
leased
by
the
Electronic
Industries
Association.
October distributor
sales
of phonos
and color TV’s registered the highest
gains of
all consumer electronic prod-
ucts, EIA
said.
Phono
makers
are
doing
a
brisk
business
in
the
portable/table
cate-
gory,
which
showed
a
36.5
per
cent
distributor
sales
jump
in
October
618,157
units
vs.
452,779
in
the
1965
month.
Christmas
purchases
are
be-
lieved
to
account
for
the
rise,
since
the
year-to-year
growth
is
a
more
modest 4.7 per cent, from 2,840,257 in
1965
to 2,973,001
so far
in
1966. Con-
sole phonographs, on
the other hand,
while
registering
a
healthy
gain
for
the
year
(1,400,411
for
the
year
to
date, up 11.8 per cent over the
1,252,-
881
sets
in
the comparable
1965
pe-
riod),
don’t appear
to
be
as high on
the
Christmas
gift
list.
Distributor
sales of consoles dipped to 154,349 in
October, down 12 per cent from
175,-
381
in the same month
a year ago.
The total phonograph picture, how-
ever,
is
rosy,
showing
a
rise
of
23
per
cent
in
