Shuman & Carr & Chappell
Partners In New Pubbery
NEW YORK—Earl Shuman and Leon
Carr entered
into an agreement with
Chappell &
Co.
for
the formation
of
Earleon
Music,
a
firm
to
be
jointly
owned
by
Chappell
and
the
two
writers.
The
first major Carr-Shuman work
whose score will be published by Ear-
leon
is
the
new
musical
version
of
“The
Last
Holiday,”
which
first
ap-
peared as
a
J.
B.
Priestly screenplay
in
1949
starring
Alec
Guiness.
The
new
production,
to
be
produced
by
Edgar Lansbury, has a Broadway tar-
get date for the
fall of
1967.
Also
to
be
included
in
Earleon
is
the
team’s
title
song
for “The
Sub-
ject Was
Roses,”
the
movie
version
of
which
goes
before
the
cameras
next
summer.
Lansbury
is
also
the
producer
of the
film.
Currently, they have recordings on
the market or about to be released by
Barbra
Streisand,
Perry Como, Mike
Douglas, Vic Damone, Johnny Mathis,
and Steve Lawrence. In addition, they
are
the
composers
of
“Confidence,”
originally
from
the
“Walter
Mitty”
score and now
the
official CBS
foot-
ball song used
in connection with the
telecasts
of
all
National
Football
League games.
The movie credits of Carr and Shu-
man
include
“Monica
(Love
Theme
From ‘The Carpetbaggers’) ,” and
the
title
themes
from
“Judith,”
“Barab-
bus,”
“Robinson
Crusoe
On
Mars,”
“The
Disorderly Orderly,” and
“Situ-
ation Hopeless But Not Serious.” Vic
Damone
has
just
cut
“Love
Me
Longer,”
from
the
motion
picture
“Arrivederci Baby.” This song by the
team
is
published
by Famous
Music
in the United States and by Chappell
in
all other territories.
Under
the
new
agreement
with
Chappell, Carr and Shuman are on
a
non-exclusive basis which allows them
to continue writing under assignment
from
certain
other
entities.
It
is em-
phasized, however,
that
all
the work
turned
out by
the
pair which
is
not
otherwise tied up will go into Earleon.
A
sustained
effort
will
be
made
to
build
the
firm,
with
the
possibility
that
other
writers
will
be
brought
into the fold at some later time.
Shuman,
who
started
his
cleffing
career when
he won
a
first
place
in
the
erstwhile
“Songs
For
Sale” TV
series,
said that there
is now consid-
erable
interest
in
re-staging
their
“Secret
Life Of Walter
Mitty,” done
tw-o seasons ago, as a regular Broad-
way
production.
It was
originally an
off-B’way
show.
The
interest
stems
from at least two separate but equal-
ly solid sources, posing the possibility
that
the
composers
could
be
repre-
sented
on Broadway
with two musi-
cals next season at this time.
Shuman,
a
Yale
graduate
and
a
former captain
in the Marine
Corps,
is the
lyricist on such
hits as “Seven
Lonely Days,”
“Caterina,” “Close To
Cathy,” “Hey There Lonely Boy,” and
“Clinging Vine.” He has
also written
lyrics
for
a
number
of
film
tunes.
Carr,
an
arranger-composer,
gradu-
ated
from
Penn
State
and
studied
composition
under
the
Schillinger
System
at New York
University. He
composed
the
melody
for
the famed
“See The U.S.A. In Your Chevrolet,”
as
well
as
such
hits
as
“Gina,”
“There’s No Tomorrow,” “Hotel Hap-
piness,”
and
‘Most
People
Get Mar-
ried.”

PHILADELPHIA — Joe Tarsia, for-

to

post.
Tarsia,

facili-

left
his
post
with

in

to work

such
accounts
as
Basin

studios, which

avail-
able

bookings,

operation
and

and

systems.

NEW YORK—Musicor

several months

set

floor.

is Musicor’s own

on

is

plete mastering and editing

in

han-
dling
Musicor’s own

oper-
ations.

The Building Of Monument
' World Over
HOLLYWOOD—The
global
distribu-
tion
network
of Monument
Records
will be launched soon with the Holly-
- ood-Nashville
diskery
being
identi-
fied
for
the
first
time
with
its own
Monument
trademark
in
22
major
world markets and more than
33
as-
sociated trading areas
as
a result
of
these 22
direct licensing agreements,
it was announced today
(19) by Fred
Foster, president of the
label.
Under the guidance of Bobby Weiss,
vice
president
and
director
of
the
international
division
for Monument,
the global marketing concept for the
Foster
waxery
was
changed
when
Weiss
joined
the
firm
in
Nov.,
1965.
As
a
result
of
the
world
contract
Monument
had
with
English
Decca
at that time, Weiss conducted a world-
wide marketing survey for Foster and
Monument
to
determine
the
best
course of action
to take
in order for
Monument to begin to garner a better
share
of
the
foreign
market.
Weiss
trekked
to
more
than
24
different
countries
during
the
course
of
18
globe-girdling weeks in order to finally
outline the present
international
net-
work
of
having
the
strongest
inde-
pendent
companies
representing
the
expanding Monument catalogue. As a
result, Monument did not renew with
English Decca via their London
label,
when the contract finally expired last
Oct.
Now, Monument
artists, plus those
on
the
associated
Sound
Stage
7
and LTD International
labels, will
all
appear on the Monument label hence-
forth
internationally
and
initial
re-
leases
will
spotlight singles and LP’s
by
Boots
Randolph,
Fran
Jeffries,
Jeannie
Seely,
Billy
Walker,
Don
Cherry, the Hangmen, Joe Simon, and
Roscoe Shelton, plus the original mo-
tion picture score
to MGM’s “Around
The World
Under
The
Sea,”
as
the
film is just beginning opening dates on

in

pointing

has

from

of

Wright. Leaves NARA For Minit Post,
Del Shields Is Acting President
NEW
\ ORK—Ed Wright

deeja.v
asociation

to

7. Minit
is operated by

Meanwhile

Shields
has been named acting president, with
elections
to
be
held
at NARA’s
an-
nual convention next Aug.
(Louisville,
Ky.)
to

As an ex-president, Wright pointed
out, he automatically becomes a mem-
ber
of NARA’s

board, and
intends
to remain

or-
ganization. A
14-year veteran
of

of music, Wright has

NARA post for 16 months.
Shields indicated that NARA would
continue
to

programs
set
in
motion
under

of

the

is

ment’s

drive
involving

NARA-prepared

of
buttons

Negroes,
whose rate of dropout from school
is
higher
than
the
rest
of
the
popula-
tion.
Buttons
sport
such
slogans
as
“I’m a Standout Not a Dropout” and
“I’m No Fool
School
is Cool.”
If the
Government fails to act, Shields hopes
the
record
industry
will
undertake
the
manufacturing
function,
with
NARA making the
distribution to
its
members.

Vinton Wins Gold
Record
For Album
NEW YORK—Bobby
Vinton,
one
of
Epic
Records’ most
consistently
sell-
ing
artists, has achieved a Gold Rec-
ord
for
his
best-selling
LP,
“Bobby
Vinton’s
Greatest
Hits.”
The
award
signifies sales
in excess of one million
dollars
as
certified
by
the
Record
Industry
Association
of
America
(RIAA).
This
is the second time that Vinton
has been honored with a Gold Record.
He
received
his
first one for
his mil-
lion-seller
single,
“Roses
Are
Red.”
He
is
currently
riding
high
on
the
best-selling
charts
with
his
latest
Epic
single, “Coming Home
Soldier.”
This
summer,
Epic
launched
an
advertising
and
merchandising
cam-
paign to promote Vinton’s entire cata-
log
of
LP’s.
In
addition
to being a
top
record-
ing
artist,
Bobby
Vinton
is
a
busy
nightclub performer. He has appeared
in nearly every major nightclub in the
United
States
and
in
many
of
the
prime
night
spots
in
Europe.

NEW YORK—Audio Fidelity and
its
affiliated labels showed strong domes-
tic and foreign
sales
for
1966, Her-
man
Gimbel,
president, has
reported
to
his

Interim

Co.,

pany,

in-

over

comparable

for
1965 and
a 36%
gain
in
sales by Audio Fidelity Records’ for-
eign
licensees. The Canadian
opera-
tion reflected an increase of 22% over
last year. The labels include Karate,
Little
Darlin,’
Audio
Rarities
and
Kinor.
Since
Gimbel
assumed
control
of
Audio Fidelity, the company has been
undergoing a vigorous expansion pio-
gram. Auffio Fidelity entered the pop
market with
its Karate
label
which,
within a short period of time, enjoyed
its first hit single, “Juanita Banana”;
this
was
soon
followed
by
the
“Juanita Banana”
album.
Since
its
inception
in
the
middle
of
1966,
the
Little
Darlin’
label
singles
and LP
releases have appeared on the country
and western charts
consistently. The
Audio
Fidelity
label
itself
added

NEW YORK — Ken Luttman Enter-
prises,
an
indie
promo
service,
has

in sales and promo, said he would ap-
proach this area with a limited num-
ber
of
accounts
in

to
give
a
maximum
of
effort
in
obtaining
air-
play and sales. He will contact major
radio
stations
and
one-stops
in

New
York,
Philadelphia,
Hartford
and Boston markets. He was national
promo
manager
for
United
Artists
Records and, for the past
five years,
district
singles
promo
manager
for
Capitol Records. His firm operates out
of
20
Balmoral
Crescent
in

Plains, New York.

BRITAIN
Sales of grammaphone records in September, the first month of the Autumn
releases, totalled £2,168,000, 2% less than the same month of 1965. Home sales
fell by 10%
but export sales
(which accounted for about 21%
of
the
total)
shot up b:^ 52%. Despite the drop in singles sales during the year, taking the
fii-st nine months as a whole, total sales increased by 2% compared with the
corresponding period
of
1965.
Export
sales,
representing 16%
of
the
total,
were up by 11% but home
sales, alas, increased by
less than 1%. Total
pro-
duction
for the
first
nine months
of the year was 4%%
lower than
in
the
same period
last year. Eleven per cent fewer 45
r.p.m.
disks were produced
but LP production rose by 9%.
Britain’s entry
for the Eurovision Song Contest
to
be
held
in Vienna
on
April 8th will be chosen from five songs selected by a committee of the Music
Publishers Association from 122
entries,
all
of which were submitted anony-
mously. Sandie Shaw
will
sing the numbers
in
five programs
of “The
Rolf
Harris Show” commencing Jan.
21st. As
in previous years, viewers
will vote
by post card for the winning song. The songs are:
“Ask Any Woman” by Jimmy
Stewart and Gerry
Langley
(published by
Mills); “Pll Cry Myself To Sleep” by Roger Webb (published by Jemb Music);
“Tell The Boys” by Mitch Murray and Peter Callander (published by Shapiro
Bernstein); “Puppet On A String” by
Bill Martin and Phil Coulter
(published
by DPM Music); “Had A Dream Last Night” by Chris Andrews
(published
by Fortissimo MUsic).
Tamla Motown star Jimmy
Ruffin, accompanied by
label boss Barney
Ales,
flew into London
recently and were guests of honor
at
a
reception given by
E.M.I. Records to celebrate Ruffin’s first entry into the British hit parade with
“What Becomes
Of The
Broken
Hearted.”
During
his
week’s
stay,
Ruffin
appeared on BBCTV’s “Top Of The Pops” and filmed an insert for his follow-
up disk “I’ve Passed This Way Before” just issued
in the
States.
Geoffrey
Bridge, managing
director
of EMI
Records, accompanied by Rex
Oldfield,
general manager Licensed
Repertoii-e
Division,
recently
visited
the
United States where they extended for three years
their
licensing deal with
the Amy Mala label. Bridge and Oldfield also had discussions with A1 Bennett,
president of Liberty Records, regarding future releases of their product.
Australian pop
star Normie Rowe, with
his
first
British
single
“It’s Not
Easy” released on Polydor, flew home for Christmas
in
the
sun. By the time
he returns
early
in
1967,
his Australian backing group
the Playboys
will be
in Britain to accompany him on future recordings and
to appear as an
inde-
pendent group.
Top recording star Georgie Fame has
left the Columbia
label and signed a
five-year recording contract with CBS. The company plan
to put him
in
the
studio
early
in
1967
to
cut
his
first

are
reported
to have
paid
handsomely
for

of Fame whose
past
hits
include
“Yeh
Yeh,”
“Get Away” and “Sunny.” CBS also may have a new single by Sandy Posey
“Single Girl.” Her previous single “Born A Woman”—although failing to get
into the Top Twenty—registered good sales. Willie Bobo has waxed his version
of “Sunshine Superman” for CBS.

CBS' Boutet- Visits London
PARIS—Philip Boutet of April Music
and CBS
Records
in
Paris
flew
to
London recently where
his copyright,
“Le Soleil Blanc” by Tshuka, issued in
France by CBS, has been covered
in
Britain by
Valerie
Masters
on
Poly-
dor.
Barbara
Hayes
of
April
Music
London
has
the
new
Los
Bravos
single
on
Decca
“Going
Nowhere”
Wilson
Pickett’s “Mustang
Sally” on
Atlantic and “Cry
Like A Baby” by
Aretha Franklin on CBS.
Germany and the music business are
still
in
a
state
of semi-war
with
the
radio stations here, and a reduced number of platters are crossing the
radio
turntables. Most of the stations have increased their record programming
as
of the 1st of January, but the fight is
still not settled. Everyone
is hoping that
the disagreement will reach a final settlement early in the year and that things
will return to normal, especially in the popularity and sales of German singles
productions. One thing
is
certain. When a German language
disk
“clicks”,
it
outsells considerably
its foreign counterpart. The trade paper “Music” with its
analysis of their charts for 1966 showed 18 of the 20 top hits of the year to be
foreign
recoi-ds, but the top
2 were “Ganz In Weiss”
(All
In White) by Roy
Black from Polydor
(published by August
Seith) and “Hundert Mann & Ein
Befehl”
(Ballad
of the Green
Berets)
by Freddy Quinn from Polydor
(pub-
lished by Francis, Day and Hunter).
Top artists chartwise here were the Beatles, Roy Black, Chris Andrews, the
Rolling Stones, the Beach Boys, Dave Dee, Dozy Beaky, Mick & Tich, Freddy
Quinn, Draft Deutscher, the Troggs and Nini Rosso.
The record companies racking up the highest positions were in order: Teldec
with 46 songs
in the charts and 4969
points, Electrola with 31 songs making
the
listings and 4359 chart points, Polydor with 41 songs
in the coveted
list
and 3963 points followed by CBS with 48 songs and 3694 points.
Philips with
32
songs and
3679
points,
Deutsche Vogue
with
22
songs and
2158
points,
Ariola with 22 songs and 2158 points, and Metronome with 23 songs and 877
points.
Deutsche Grammophon takes over the
Sonet-Storyville Scandinavian
lables
as of Jan.
1st.
Ralph Siegel, Jr., is swinging with
his Newbeats stateside disc “My Yester-
day Love” which he wrote. The son of Ralph Maria Siegel
is also making his
mark locally with a new Dorthe recording which looks like
it’s chartbound. In
the meanwhile
the
publishing
firm
is
swinging
with
“Distant Drums”
in
a
German recording by Fred Bertelmann.
.A1 Martino’s
first
visit to Germany seems
to have paid
off
“in spades” for
the artist’s I’ecordings for Electrola here. After appearing on a top TV broad-
cast
with
“Spanish
Eyes”
and
“Auf
Wiedersehn”—both
written
by
Bert
Kaempfert—the songs
started moving
like mad
salewise. Although “Spanish
Eyes” made the charts here
in Summer, the show started such a run on sales
that immediate repressing of the record was necessary to keep up with orders.
A1 made such a great impression on the German public that he now has offers
for virtually every top TV show
hei’e and
will be back
in May
to
fulfill TV
and other shows. The question
is only when he
will start with German record-
ings.

Chi Expansion For
USA, Destination
CHICAGO—Climaxing a
rise
in
rec-
ord
producing
which
started
three
years ago with a national hit tagged
“California
Sun,” Jim
Golden,
presi-
dent of USA Records and Destination
Records has announced this past week
that he has moved his companies into
“considerably” larger quarters at 2131
South Michigan Avenue, in the heart
of record row in Windy City.
Other
subsidiary
companies
under
the same
roof
include
M.G.
Produc-
tions
and
Independent
Productions.
The
companies
produced
such
single
hits as “Sugar ’N Spice” and “I Want
To Meet You” by The Cryan Shames.
Also,
“Can’t You
See That
I
Really
Love Her” by The Flock.
The
combined
companies
under
Golden’s direction are celebrating with
a new smash single titled “Kind Of A
Drag”
by
The
Buckinghams,
which
has hit the Cash Box Top 100.
The firm now has its own recording
studio on the premises. This new fa-
cility
will
enable
Golden and Robert
Monaco, national sales and promotion
manager, to experiment with new re-
cording techniques and to develop new
ideas coming out of the Chicago area.
TAP Moves To New HQ
HOLLYWOOD—Don
Blocker, former
general manager
of Liberty Records
and currently head of his own Holly-
wood
based
record
promotion
firm,
TAP, has moved to larger
offices.
Although TAP has only been
in
existence since September
’66, Block-
er reports that because
of the
firms
success in the record promotions field,
expanding interest
in other activities
connected with the recording industry,
and an enlarged
staff, T A P’s previ-
ous
office facilities were not adequate
to accommodate the firm’s expansion.
New quarters are located in the form-
er
Reprise
Records
offices
at
1347
Cahuenga Boulevard in Hollywood.

Warner Bros. And
Anro In Prod. Pact
BURBANK—Negotiations have
been
completed between Warner Bros. Rec-
ords and Anro Productions for an ex-
clusive independent production pact.
The principals of Anro Productions,
Anita Kerr and Rod McKuen, will be
responsible for producing the San Se-
bastian Strings. An album containing
their interpretation
of European hits
of the
last year
is being readied for
an early Spring release.
In
another

involving

Kerr,
the

Brothers

part
of
the
show. The show is expected to be aired
in Feb.
'67 Music Show To
Stress Hard Sell
CHICAGO — “Hard
Sell
in
a
Soft
Economy” will be the keynote theme
of the 66th annual Music Show.
“Anticipating
future
sales
is,
of
course, a
critical phase of marketing.
With many economic indicators point-
ing to an easing off of business levels,
it would seem quite prudent and pre-
cautionary for the music industry not
only
to
size up
future
business
but
also
to
set a
strategy for tomorrow
to assure that
it will continue to cap-
ture
a major
segment
of
America’s
leisure-time and educational income,”
noted William R. Gard, executive vice
president of the National Association
of
Music
Merchants,
sponsor
of
the
big
industry
event which
is
set for
Chicago’s
Conrad
Hilton
Hotel
July
25 to
29.
The
1967
Music Show
will
stress
sales saturation of the music market
through
every
conceivable
channel
from schools and studios to every type
of retail outlet in the nation.
“Despite slipping business indices,”
said Gard, the industry can and must
continue
to
grow
in
excess
of
the
averages for other businesses and
it
is the purpose of the Music Show
to
set the direction for such growth. The
theme
of the 1967 show will be hard
selling
to
compensate
for
any
gen-
eral
economic
declines. “We
are
on
the
threshold
of becoming
a
billion-
dollar
annual
business,”
declared
Gard.
“There
is
no
reason why
the
musical
instrument
industry
cannot
pass that mark in annual retail sales
very soon
if we but continue the kind
of aggressive, alert selling which has
marked the past decade when we en-
joyed a bountiful boom economy.”
“Hard Sell in a Soft Economy” can
assure that there will be no slowdown
in the music industry because the po-
tential market will exist regardless of
any
general
business
decline,
the
NAMM executive vice president
stat-
ed. The 1967 Music Show will aim to
focus
on
the
best marketing
tactics
to
capitalize
on that
sales
potential,
Gard concluded.

Kama Sutra On The Move
NEW YORK—Hy Mizrahi, president
of Kama Sutra, is currently in Holly-
wood
opening
the
west
coast
offices
of
the
firm. Bob
Krasnow, has been
hired to run the
office. Mizrahi is look-
ing for talent, producers, writers and
artists.
The
office
is
located
at 7122
Sunset
Blvd., Hollywood. Area
Code
213-469-1101.
While in Hollywood, Mizrahi
is also
contacting independent film producers
and
indie
television production
com-
panies. He plans to offer the services
of
Kama
Sutra
Productions
and
Kama
Sutra Music to
film
television
production
companies.
The
KS
production
corporation,
with
its
president
Artie
Ripp,
em-
ploys thirteen writers active publish-
ing
firms
and many
producers.
It
originates TV
and
Radio
commer-
cials, songs for K.S. artists and songs
for
artists on other labels.
Mizrahi,
has
also
appointed
Eddie
Levine
director
of
national
promo-
tion
for
all
Kama
Sutra
product.
These
include
records,
productions
and music.
Levine
is
currently on
a
national
tour
contacting
distributors
of Kama
Sutra
product,
promotion
men, and radio station personnel.
The
company’s
future
plans
also
call
for the
imminent
release
of
a
“Best
Of The
Lovin’
Spoonful” LP
and a country and western EP by the
same group.
Silverman Appointed
Bruno-New York Veep
NEW YORK —
Bruno-New
York,
local RCA distributor, has announced
the appointment of Phil Silverman as
vice
president,
RCA
Victor
record
and tape division.
Silverman has been associated with
Bruno-New York for
over 43
years,
beginning his career there as a record
sales specialist in 1923. For ten years
prior to that period he worked in the
record retail
circles of Great Britain
and Europe as well as in America.

Victor Ups Hendrickson,
Mulligan To New Posts
NEW YORK—J.
W.
Hendrickson
and W.
A. Mulligan have been
pro-
moted
to new positions in the custom
records
marketing
organization
of
RCA Victor Records.
R.
C. Williams, manager of custom
records marketing,
said
the
appoint-
ments are effective immediately.
Hendrickson, formerly manager of
personnel
in New York, assumes the
position of manager of marketing ad-
ministration and planning; Mulligan,
formerly
manager
of
custom
sales
planning
and
service, becomes man-
ager
of special
custom
projects.
BILL MULLIGAN
JOHN HENDRICKSON
“In
anticipation
of
continued
growth
of
the
Custom
Records
market, we
have
created
these
two
new positions to assure RCA Victor’s
position in this important
field,” Wil-
liams said.
Hendrickson will be responsible for
administration
activities,
for
short
and
long-range marketing plans and
programs and for liaison with record-
ing studios and manufacturing facili-
ties regarding customer service,
sales
commitments
and
production
sched-
ules.
He
also
will
work
with
sales
managers
in
development
of
special
programs and campaigns.
Hendrickson
joined
RCA
in
the
Radiomarine Division
in 1941
as
as-
sistant personnel manager. Following
service in World War II during which
he became
a
Sergeant Major
in
the
Army
and
was
decorated
with
a
Bronze Star for meritorious action
at
Anzio Beachhead, he returned to that
position. In 1951, he was transferred
to the RCA exec offices as a personnel
administrator.
In
1955,
he
became
manager of personnel, New York, for
the label.
Mulligan, who will manage
special
custom
recording
projects,
joined
RCA Victor in Indianapolis in 1949 as
an
order
analyst. The next
year, he
was
promoted
to
leader
of
order
service
group,
and
in
1953 became
manager of production planning and
scheduling,
and
thereafter was
ele-
vated
to manager
of production
con-
trol and manager, Indianapolis plant
production
and
material
control.
In
1961,
he
was
transferred
to
New
York as manager, custom sales, plan-
ning
and
service
in
the
Custom
Record organization.

NEW

Bolsom Exits Cash Box;
Joins Goldstein Setup
NEW YORK—Cash
Box
editorial
staffer Rick Bolsom has resigned his
position here this week
(3)
to under-
take duties with the New York-based
publicity firm of Michael F. Goldstein,
Inc. Bolsom joined Cash Box
in
1965.
In
his
new
role,
he
will
head
up
Goldstein’s
pop
music
department,
concentrating on the office’s promotion
of two popular groups from East and
West
respectively,
the
Rascals
and
the Mothers of Invention.
In
addition
to Bolsom, the
firm
is
expanding with
two
other
publicity
and public relations
specialists, Ruth
Cage, formerly of Howard Atlee As-
sociates,
and
Joseph
Viggiano,
for-
merly
of Ashley-Famous.
Miss Cage
will
be
associated with
Goldstein
staff member
Robert
Gan-
shaw in
the
“legit”
department, and
is
the
account
executive
for
Act
I,
Stouffer’s theatrical restaurant in the
Allied
Chemical
Tower. Ganshaw
is
charged with promotion of Evergreen
Records,
singer
Chad
Mitchell
and
Budd Friedman’s Improvisation Cafe.
Viggiano
is
account
executive
for
Cheetah, New York, as well
as sister
Cheetah
operations
in
Chicago
and
Union, N.J., the latter to be unveiled
Jan.
13.
Other
recent
staff
additions to
the
two-year-old firm are Marti Holladay
and Pamela Schad, who are primarily
involved
as
associates
to
long-time
Goldstein
staffer Paula Weinstein
in
women’s features and fashion promo-
tions for
the
Cheetah
boutiques.

Magic
City Releases 2
Victor Cops
14 RIAA
Gold
Records
In 1966
NEW YORK—In
1966 RCA
Victor
had
14
gold
records
certified by
the
Record Industry Association of Amer-
ica—more
than
any
other
company
in the industry.
These
included
eleven
albums
and
three singles on several of the labels
in the RCA Victor catalog.
Four
of
these
gold
record awards
came from
simultaneous
certification
of
a
single
and album by
the same
artists, and one was
the
first album
ever
to win
certification on an
econ-
omy line label.
To qualify for certification, a single
must have sold one million copies, an
album must have accumulated a mini-
mum
of
$1
million
in
sales
at
the
manufacturer
level, and an economy
line album must have done both.
Barry Sadler and the Monkees were
the artists who had single records and
albums
certified
simultaneously.
Sad-
ler’s
“Ballad”
and
“Ballads
of
the
Green Berets”
constituted the indus-
try’s
first big hit of the year.
“Last Train to Clarksville” was the
single
and
“The
Monkees” was
the
album
which
were
certified
simul-
taneously late
in
1966. These record-
ings, on the new Colgems
label, were
followed by a
second Monkee
single,
“I’m a Believer,” which was
certified
the week
it was
released and which
had
sold over two
million
copies
be-
fore
the
end
of
the
year.
The
first
Monkee
album
had
sold
more
than
3,000,000
copies by
the beginning
of
1967.
Champion among
all RCA
Victor
artists once again was
Elvis
Presley
who had three more albums
certified
during the year.
Perry Como, who has had numerous
gold records on the RCA Victor label,
became the first artist ever to have an
album
certified on an economy
label
when
his “Perry Como
Sings Merry
Christmas Music” was certified on the
Camden
label.
Other RCA Victor
artists who had
product
certified
during the year
in-
cluded
A1
Hirt’s
“The
Best
of
A1
Hirt,”
Eddy
Arnold’s
“My
World,”
the late Jim Reeves’ “The Best of Jim
Reeves,”
the
original
cast album
of
“Oliver” and an album from the past
which proved the lasting populai’ity of
stars
from
another
era,
“Jeanette
MacDonald and
Nelson Eddy
Favor-
ites.”

NEW
YORK—Bobby
Hebb,
whose
self-composed song and record there-
of, "Sunny,” on the Philips’ label was
a
confirmed
1,000,000-unit
seller
in
1966,
married
Constance
P.
Vail,
a
registered
nurse,
here
on
Dec.
31,
1966. The newlyweds will reside in an
apartment on the upper east
side.

7
NEW YORK—Philips

ter. The

Don Ho
Rides
High
In
Hawaii
HONOLULU—Don
Ho
last
week
agreed
to
add
three
shows
to
his
nightly performances
at Duke Kaha-
namoku’s. The
nightery, which holds
650
patrons,
had
already
scheduled
two shows for the Hawaiian songster.
Since
it
is
estimated that Ho
will
perform before at least 2,000 patrons
each
evening,
bleachers,
seats,
and
loud speakers have been
set up
out-
side Duke Kahanamoku’s to accommo-
date customers who are unable to get
inside.
Ho,
recently
selected by
a conven-
tion
of
travel
agencies
as
Hawaii’s
No.
1
tourist
attraction,
began
his
engagements on the mainland this fall
at the Cocoanut Grove in Los Angeles
and the Royal Box at the Americana
Hotel
in New
York. He
returned
to
Duke Kahanamoku’s three weeks ago
and will stay there until late January,
when he
will go
to the mainland for
his first engagement at Harrah’s Club
in Reno.
Needham Twins Bow On
World Wide Label
ATLANTA—Two new recording
art-
ists, the Needham Twins, made
their
debut
disk
last week with “Drunken
Sailor
(The
Airborne
Song)”.
The
song,
a modem
version
of
the
sea
chanty “What Shall We Do With The
Drunken Sailor?”, was released on the
Atlanta-based World Wide label with
new
lyrics which the twins wrote
as
a tribute to the army’s airborne units.
Int'l Sub. Band Inks
Contract With Columbia
NEW YORK—“Columbia Records has
signed
The
International
Submarine
Band
to an
exclusive
recording
con-
tract,”
announced
William
P.
Galla-
gher,
vice
president, Columbia
label.
The
Band’s
first
single,
“Sum
Up
Broke” c/w “One Day Week,” was re-
leased by Columbia a short time ago
and
has
been
enthusiastically
re-
ceived
by
Top-40
radio
stations
in
Nashville and Los Angeles.
Recordings
by
the
Band,
whose
members include Gram Parsons, rhy-
thm
guitar
and
electric
clavichord;
John Heuse, lead guitar; Ian Dunlop,
bass; and Mickey Gauvin, drums, are
produced
for Columbia by K-L
Pro-
ductions. Monte Kay and Jack Lewis,
partners
in
K-L,
also
manage
the
Band.
The
International Submarine Band
was
organized
a
year
ago
in Cam-
bridge,
Massachusetts.
Recently,
the
quartet
has
played
some
of
New
York’s top
discotheques.
DETROIT—Magic
City
Records,
the
new Detroit based firm will launch its
1967 season with two releases by two
new
artists.
The first release slated for Jan. will
be “Why
Weren’t You
There”
b/w
“You Are Not Prepared To Love Me”
by
Thelma
Lindsey.
The
artist who
hails from Saginaw, Michigan recent-
ly inked a long term pact with Magic
City.
Also slated for Jan. release is “With
a Broken Heart” b/w “Rolling” by the
Versatones. Ernest Burt, president of
the
label says that plans
call for the
release
of
approximately
16
records
by new artists between Jan. and May
of 1967.
The diskery made its bow in
Oct. with the release of “My Mechani-
cal Man” by Leah Dawson. Currently
new
distributors
are being
signed
to
handle
the
products
nationally.
Boston To Host
U.S.
Fest. Of Music
'67
BOSTON—The
Boston
Herald-Trav-
eler
Corporation
will
present
a new
program
in the
arts, the
first Ameri-
can
Festival
of Music
’67,
scheduled
for four days, April 20 through April
23.
Completely
underwritten
by
the
Herald-Traveler,
it
is conceived
as a
cultural
enrichment
program
for
young people and adults.
The Festival plans
to trace
in cap-
sule form the
origins and growth
of
our
American
musical
heritage
in
popular music from the earliest fron-
tier songs to the latest modern music.
Major performers in each of the vari-
ous forms are being invited to partici-
pate.
George
Papadopoulo,
noted
Boston
impresario
of popular music through
his Unicorn Coffee House Productions,
is the producer of this Festival.

How To Succeed' Album
NEW YORK—The

motion
picture

album
from

musical “How To Succeed In Business
Without
Really
Trying”
will

leased
shortly by United Artists Re-
cords.

Prize winning
Broadw'ay
production,

Atlantic
Releases
'Shingaling
'67'
NEW YORK—The
first recording
of
the new dance craze, The Shingaling,
has been released by Atlantic Records.
It
is called “Shingaling
’67,” sung by
Don Covay. The Shingaling, the new
dance that
is now
starting
to sweep
the country via the nation’s teenagers,
is the follow-up
to The
Skate, which
succeeded The
Boogaloo
as
the
teen
dance fad a few months ago.
Don Covay, who wrote “Shingaling
’67,” had a noise-maker a while back
with “Seesaw,” and he followed
it up
with
“Sookie
Sookie,” another dance
hit.

Leontyne
Price Talk
Being
Aired On NET
NEW
YORK—The
noted
soprano
Leontyne
Price
discusses opera with
author-musicologist George R. Marek,
vice
president
of RCA
in a TV pro-
gram
produced
for
National
Educa-
tional TV which are being shown on
NET-affiliated
outlets throughout the
nation.
The show was televised in the sing-
er’s
New
York
home.
The
prima
donna and Marek
discuss
opera
and
various aspects of singing as a career
in
an
informal
conversation.
Recalling
her
childhood
in
Laurel,
Mississippi,
the
soprano
tells
of her
early interests
in singing as a gram-
mar
school
student,
reflects
on how
she began
serious
voice
study when
awarded
a
scholarship
at
Juilliard,
and
talks
of some
of her more
per-
sonally
rewarding
professional
per-
formances including her frequent ap-
pearances at the Metropolitan Opera.
The
program
is
scheduled
to
be
telecast
the week
of
Jan.
8
in New
York, Chicago, San Francisco, Boston,
Durham, N.H., Lewiston, Me., Orono,
Me.,
Presque
Isle,
Me.,
Calais,
Me.,
Pittsburgh, Washington, D.C., Seattle,
Yakima, Wash.,
Milwaukee, Houston
and Los Angeles.
During the week
of January
29,
it
will
be
shown
in
Philadelphia,
St.
Louis,
Sacramento,
Redding,
Calif.,
East Lansing, Mich., Columbus, Ohio,
Newark,
Ohio,

Louis
C.
Singer
Dies
NEW YORK—Louis C. (Lou)
Singer,
composer-arranger,
died
suddenly on
Dec.
30,
1966
at
his
home,
110-45
Queens
Boulevard
in
Forest
Hills,
New7 York.
Born in New York City on Feb. 26,
1912,
Mr.
Singer
was
educated
at
Juilliard
School
of
Music,
Columbia
University, New York University, and
studied music with Alexander Lipsky,
Bernard Wagenaar
and
Wallingford
Riegger.
Staff
arranger
with CBS
for two
years, Mr.
Singer was arranger and
editor-in-chief
in various music pub-
lishing houses including Chappell and
Schirmer.
In
1941
Mr.
Singer
joined
the
American
Society of Composers. Au-
thors
and
Publishers
(ASCAP).
Among
his songs
are: “Sleepy
Sere-
nade”
which
won
the
Film
Critics
award;
“One Meat
Ball”;
“Song Of
The Army Nurse
Corps”,
official
an-
them
of the USANC; “Woman
Is A
Five
Letter
Word.”
He
also
wrote
such works
as
Little
Songs On
Big
Subjects: Little Songs About The UN,
commissioned
by
that
organization;
and Ballads For The Age Of Science.
His
larger
musical
works
include
a
ballet,
Soliloouy
At
Midnight;
and
two works commissioned by the U-
S.
Government, Patrick Henry And The
Frigate’s Keel
(folk Opera) and The
Grpat
Assembly
Line:
as
well
as
T
Spoke
To
Jefferson
At
Gnadalcanal
and Israel’s Freedom Ballad.
Singer
is
survived
by
his
widow,
Rosalie;
two
daughters,
Ranny
and
Barbara; and by two brothers, A1 and
David.
"King" Cole
Benefit
Staged At Philharmonic
The
second
annual
“Festival
of
Stars”
show,
presented by the Con-
ference
of
Personal
Managers
East
for the benefit of the Nat “King” Cole
Cancer Foundation, was held at Phil-
harmonic
Hall
on Sunday, Jan.
8
at
8:30 p.m.
Among
the many
star performers
who entertained at the two-hour show
were Eddy Arnold, Tony Bennett, Dia-
hann
Carroll, the Four Seasons, Con-
nie
Francis,
Jack
E.
Leonard,
Jerry
Stiller
and
Anne
Meara,
and
Flip
Wilson.
Ed
McMahon
hosted
the
event, the net proceeds of which went
to the Nat “King” Cole Cancer Foun-
dation,
which
raises
funds
for
the
establishment
of
professorships
for
qualified cancer researchers in
select-
ed medical schools.

Doc Severinsen Renews
Contract With Command
NEW
YORK—Loren
Becker,
vice
president
and
general
manager
of
Command Records, has announced the
re-sig’ning
of
Doc
Severinsen
to
a
long-term contract.
The Command
catalogue
currently
features seven albums by Doc. All of
his albums have been highly
success-
ful
and
the
latest
release
“Doc
Severinsen-Command
Performances”
is riding the chart best
seller
list
at
present.
Becker announced
his
intention
of
issuing more
single
releases by Doc
Severinsen in the coming year as well
as
a minimum
of two new
albums.
“All of us at Command are convinced
that Doc
Severinsen
will
emerge
as
one of America’s Top recording artists
in
1967. We
are
planning
to
go
in
several exciting new directions in
re-
cording Doc and plan an all-out radio
promotion/display/advertising plan on
his forthcoming albums.”
The sextet is booked into
a number
of
top
locations
including
the
Fla-
mingo
in Las Vegas
in mid-January,
and
a
number
of
prime
time TV
starring spots
are now being
set. In
addition, Doc makes over one-hundred
special concert appearances yearly
all
over
the
United
States
to
audiences
averaging
in
the
thousands.
Becker ended the announcement by
saying “Command
intends
to
make
1967 Doc Severinsen’s year.”
Doc Severinsen
(l.)
is shown
here
re-signing a long-term
contract with
Command
Records.
At
right
is
the
label’s
vice
president
and
general
manager, Loren Becker.

HOLLYWOOD—Continuing

ex-
pansion plans established one year ago
in offering a wider variety of artists
and repertoire on the Monument label,
president Fred Foster has announced
that the Hollywood-Nashville waxery
just
signed
an
exclusive
recording
contract with international screen star
Robert Mitchum.
The
initial Mitchum waxings,
will
begin in Nashville today
(9) and will
finish
in
Hollywood
next
week.

weekend
(7)
for
final meetings with
Foster
prior
to
the
initial
session,
accompanied by George “Bullets” Dur-
gom
who
agented
the
deal
for
Mitchum
in
behalf
of
the
Ashley
Famous Agency.
Mitchum’s
deal
with Monument
is
for three years, calling for singles as
well as longplay material to be issued.
Bobby
Weiss, Monument
vice
presi-
dent and
director
of
label’s
interna-
tional division who directs the Holly-
wood
office
for
Foster, negotiated
in
behalf of Foster and Monument with
Mitchum and Durgom.

FOCUS ON JAZZ
With
1967
at
its very
beginning,
most people will be forecasting about
what
will happen
in the next twelve
months.
However,
since we
concern
ourselves
with
jazz,
and
jazz
being
the
unpredictable medium
that
it
is,
let’s pause to reflect about some of the
things
that
have
happened
in
1966,
and from what has already happened,
perhaps we can draw an inference
ox-
two about what
is
about
to
happen.
Instead of reviewing 1966 in any kind
of chronological order, let’s just muse,
at random, and see what we come up
with.
Hot Lou Rawls
One of the most significant develop-
ments
in 1966 was the emergence
of
Lou Rawls
as
a hot property.
Lou’s
singing
is,
for
the most part,
blues-
oriented and
because
blues
are
such
an
integral
part
of
jazz, Lou Rawls
is
a worthy
subject for our observa-
tion.
To
many, Lou
might
seem
to
have made
it
overnight
because
he
skyrocketed
to
the
top
so
quickly.
But,
like most of the top performers
who have preceded him, he has been
out there paying
his dues. He
really
got
off
the
ground with
his
“Live!”
album on Capitol, but that album was
Lou’s
sixth
for
Capitol. What about
the
five
that
he
did
before
he
con-
nected? Why didn’t they take
off the
way the “Live!” album did?
Prior to
the
hit
album,
Rawls
cut
two
with
Onzy
Matthews,
one
with
Les
Mc-
Cann,
one
with
Benny
Carter,
and
one
with
strings. With each
succes-
sive album
it became
apparent
that
those who were guiding his destinies
were searching for that magic, ever-
elusive formula which would catapult
Lou way out in front, where the
stai--
dust
is. Right now Lou has two
al-
bums on the charts, and a brand new
release,
“Carryin’
On,” which
prom-
ises
to
take
its
place
alongside
the
other
two.
Lou
Rawls
has
had
his
share of working the joints, his share
of
dry
spells
when
gigs
were
as
scarce as they are
plentiful now, his
share of wondering when and if it was
ever going to happen for him. All of
this
was
only
part
of
his
“gettin’
ready.”
Lou
is
plenty
ready
now,
and
we
must
assume
that
he
will
gradually depart from
his blues bag
and
introduce
mox
-e
of
sophisticated
material into his act. This assumption
is drawn from the fact that on each
of
his
best-selling albums
there
ai-e
at least a couple of selections that are
in
the
pop
or
standard
idiom.
Ulti-
mately,
Lou
should
be
appearing
in
the
better rooms where the working
hours
are
shorter and
the money
is
longer. As a pattern for this develop-
ment, we
offer
the
career
of Nancy
Wilson,
with whom
Lou
has
a
lot
in common, particularly the ability to
communicate with an
audience. And,
if you have
to use
a
pattern, Nancy
Wilson’s
is not a bad choice.
“The New Thing”
1966
saw
a
modest
affirmation
of
“The New
Thing,”
as
the
msuic
of
the
avant
garde
has
come
to
be
known. The record
sales
of
this new
music indicate, undeniably, that there
is
a
solid,
devoted
audience
for
the
music of Ornette Coleman, John Cole-
trane.
Sonny
Rollins,
John
Handy,
and the many other jazz players who
have dedicated themselves to the pur-
suit of this musical philosophy. Inves-
tigation shows
us
that
the
principal
followers
of
this
music
are
the
younger
jazz
fans,
which
is
as
it
should be. This new jazz, a product of
the restlessness that
is characteristic
to
each new
generation, would seem
to
have
an
affinity
for
the
world’s
young
people
who
are
constantly
striving
to
find
their own
identifica-
tion,
their
own
expression.
Surely,
there
will be a further
distillation of
this concept of jazz, but in the mean-
time,
“outside”
jazz
has
made
its
presence
very much
felt among
the
many
interests
which
comprise
the
jazz
community.
1967
should
be
a
critical
year
for
the
purveyors
of
“The New Thing,” proving or disprov-
ing whether or not
it is here to stay,
or whether
it
is
only
a
transitional
development, of which only the efforts
of the
giants
will be remembered
to
serve
as an
influence. The
increased
number of free jazz albums produced
last year by
the many
record
com-
panies would lead us
to
believe
that
1967
should
be
a
banner
year
for
those
musicians
invested
with
the
urge
to
exploi-e
and
emote
through
their manner
of jazz expression.
Fine Re-Issues
As
the
companies
increased
their
l-eleases
of
new
jazz
musicians
in
1966,
so
did
they
increase
their
re-
leases
of many
fine albums that had
been previously issued. Several major
labels
actively engaged
in
a
re-issue
program, which made available again
many
excellent
albums
which,
for
whatever reason, had become unavail-
able
to
the
average
l-ecord
buyer.
This activity on older recordings adds
a very pleasant balance
to
the
spec-
trum
of
jazz,
and
it
is
hoped
that
other
record
companies
will
follow
suit in 1967, and unloose much of the
precious
material
that
is
gathering
dust
in
the
vaults.
To
support
the
belief
that
thei’e
is
a
formidable
market
for
not
only
re-issues,
but
also new recordings by many
of the
elder statesmen
of jazz, we
offer the
resurgence
of
popularity
of
Earl
“Fatha”
Hines.
Hines
made
several
excellent albums in 1966, and also led
a
State
Department
sponsored
tour
of Europe, including
visits
to Russia
and
the
Iron
Curtain
countries,
al-
ways
evoking
accolades
for
himself
and
his band.
Another
noteworthy
development
in 1966 was the
incorporation
of
In-
dian rhythmic conception
in pop mu-
sic,
and
in
some
instances,
this
in-
fluence could be heard
in the playing
of
our jazzmen,
as
well.
The music
of Ravi Shankar and Ali Akbar Kahn,
two of India’s premier exponents, has
always
attracted
a
small,
inside
co-
terie of followers; today, the number
of
music
appreciators
who
suppoi-t
this music
is growing by
leaps and
bounds.
One
would
have
to
be
less
than clairvoyant to
anticipate an
ex-
pansion
of
this concept by
jazz mu-
sicians in 1967.
It should be interest-
ing to see if this occurs in the coming
year.
Limited
space
precludes
an
in-
depth
recapitulation of
all that hap-
pened in the jazz world in 1966. As in
all matters, the minuses were
repre-
sented by the passing of many stellar
jazzmen; the pluses were represented
by
the
discovery
of manv new
and
talented players. Jazz in 1966, like the
adolescent
it
is,
suffei’ed
growing
pains, and from those growing pains
will come
the
evolutions
and
resolu-
tions that have kept it the vital, crea-
tive music
that
it has proved
itself,
in
its brief
history,
to
be.

‘I

AGAC
Cites Renewal
Rights Of Writers
Harry Fox
Sees Need
For Copyr't
Experts
Blue Note
Inks
Ornette Coleman
Columbia Joins DGG To
Sponsor Concert
Series
NEW YORK—Thousands of songs by
more than 700 songwriters, including
Richard
Rodgers,
Harold
Adamson,
Jimmy McHugh, Jimmy Van Heusen,
are
involved
in
a
campaign
by
the
American
Guild
of Authors & Com-
posers
to
remind
publishers
that
writers have renewal
rights
of
their
songs
even
though
the
writers may
have
originally
signed
contracts
giving
these
renewal
rights
to
the
publishers.
AGAC Cites Clause
In a memo to music publishers who
were
signatories
to
the
1939
Basic
Agreement, when AGAC was known
as
the
Songwriters
Protective
Asso-
ciation, AGAC pointed out that under
the
Basic
Agreement, “Compositions
acquired
by
you from
a member
of
SPA on
or
after June
1,
1937, were
deemed
to have been acquired pursu-
ant to said Basic Agreement.” AGAC
goes on to say that
if “any terms of
any contract entered into between you
and such member on or after June
1,
1937, were less favorable to the writer
than those contained in the Standard
Uniform Popular Songwriters Agree-
ment of
1939, the terms
of the 1939
Uniform
Contract apply.”
This means
that
the
writers,
not
the publishers, have these songs back
for
the
28
year
copyright
renewal
term.
Burton
Lane,
president
of
the
American Guild of Authors and Com-
posers,
informed
music
publishers
that
.
.
all songs acquired by you
from SPA members between June
1,
1937 and January
1,
1947
(the
date
when the 1939
Basic Agreement was
superseded by the 1947 Basic Agree-
ment)
revert
to
the
writers
for
the
U.S. at the end of their original copy-
right
term,
and
at
that
time
your
U.S. rights in these songs ends. (This
is
true
even
as
to
songs where
the
first
contracts
gave
you
renewal
rights.) The writers are then free to
make
other
disposition
of
the
songs
for
the
renewal
terms,
except
in
cases
where
you
negotiate
renewal
contracts with
these
writers
for
the
songs.”

NEW YORK—The music industry
is
now
in
a
period
of
great
need
for
additional
expertise
in
the
highly
specialized field of copyright law. This
is the view of Harry Fox, publisher’s
agent
and
trustee,
who
made
the
statement
in
officially
endorsing
the
forthcoming dinner dance being staged
next
21
March
at
the
Americana
Hotel
by The
Friends
of
Robert
J.
Burton.
The
Burton
committee
has
set
a
goal of $100,000 to be realized out of
the proceeds of the dinner dance. The
annual interest from the fund will be
used
to
establish
a
fellowship
at
Columbia
University
for
a
worthy
student
specializing
in
research
in
copyright or related areas of law.
Fox
said
that
with
impending
changes in the provisions of copyright
law,
the
day-to-day
job
of
working
with the law will become increasingly
complex for
all
entities
of the music
business. “There are excellent men in
the
field now,” Fox
said.
“It’s not a
matter
of
quality.
We’ve
got
that.
What we
will need
in
the future
is
quantity.
More
copyright
specialists
are needed, not only
to interpret the
new
facets
of the law but simply
to
handle the routine copyright work in-
volved
in
a
rapidly
expanding
in-
dustry.”
The
fellowship
will
honor
the
memory
of
the
late Judge Robert
J.
Burton, a longtime expert in the copy-
right
field.
Although
Burton
was
identified for a number of years with
a
specific
organization
within
the
industry, Burton committee chairman
Morris Levy
last week
stressed
that
the
dinner
function
itself
will
be
associated
with
no
specific
industry
groups.
“Our
working
committee,”
Levy
said,
“is composed
of representatives
of
all
elements
of
the
music
and
record
business, and
includes
talent-
agency personnel
as
well. We expect
the dinner to reflect that same broad,
all-industry participation.
“There
will
be
room
for
2,000
people
at
the
dinner, which
will
be
held in the Imperial Ballroom
of the
Americana
Hotel,”
Levy
continued.
“The
subscription
charge
is
$50
per
plate. A
sell-out
will
assure
us
the
$100,000 we need to set up the fellow-
ship. Early indications are very good;
and as the pace of the campaign now
moves into high
gear, we expect the
picture to become even brighter in the
next few weeks.”

in sponsoring future concerts of The

the announcement at a press confer-

6,

City, L.I.
Deutsche
Grammophon
Records
(DGG),

Gerdes
of

West
Germany,

of

of Columbia Rec-

emphasized

is unique

are the only record companies in the

in

Bonfa
Inks With
Para
NEW
YORK—Paramount
Pictures
Corporation has signed guitarist and
composer Luiz Bonfa
to
a long-term
agreement encompassing motion
pic-
tures,
television, recording and
sheet
music.
The
pact
covers
Bonfa’s
services
not
only
for
Paramount’s
motion
pictures
but
also
for
the
company’s
key music
subsidiaries,
Dot
Records
and Famous-Paramount Music.
A composer of over 1,000 songs and
one of the
figures
in the Bosa Nova
movement
that has been
popular
in
recent
years,
Bonfa
will
compose,
arrange and conduct the
score
for a
forthcoming
Paramount
motion
pic-
ture, with Paramount holding options
for two
additional
pictures.
At the same time, Bonfa has signed
an
exclusive
recording
contract with
Dot
Records
for
both
singles
and
albums. This deal includes the sound-
track
recordings
of
Bonfa’s
scores
for the Paramount films and will also
involve
original
recordings featuring
Bonfa.
Famous-Paramount Music will also
acquire
all rights to the music Bonfa
composes and
aranges
for
his
Para-
mount films.
Bonfa is known for his award-win-
ning
score
for
“Black
Orpheus,”
filmed
in
his
native
Brazil. He
also
composed
the
scores
for
the
“The
Hours
of
Love”
and
“The
Gentle
Rain.” His songs include “Samba
de
Orpheo,”
“Mahia
de
Carnaval,” “A
Day in the Life of a Fool,” and “Dia
das Rosas.”
The
guitarist
has
recorded
ten
albums
for
such
labels
as
Verve,
Phillips,
Capitol,
Epic
and
Atlantic.
Among them
are
“Jazz Samba
En-
core,”
with
Stan
Getz,
and
“Bra-
ziliana,” with his wife, singer-lyricist
Maria Toledo.
Bonfa
has
had
his
own
one-man
TV shows in Stuttgart, Berlin, Rome
and Amsterdam, and has been a guest
on many TV programs in the United
States.

Stan Marshall To Capitol
As Eastern Premium Head
HOLLYWOOD — Stan
Marshall
has
been appointed creative products east
coast
sales manager
at
Capitol Rec-
ords Distributing Corp. The announce-
ment
was made
by
Harry
Mynatt,
CRDC’s national manager of creative
products.
In
his new
position,
Mar-
shall will be responsible for premium
sales
and
special
merchandising
of
premium tapes, LP’s and related prod-
ucts on the East Coast He will head-
quarter
in
Capitol’s New York exec-
utive
offices and report to Mynatt.
Marshall comes to CRDC after sev-
en years in the record, premium prod-
ucts
and
custom
recording
business.
A native of New’ York, he began his
career
in
the
record
industry
seven
years ago as
sales manager for
Cri-
teria
Recording
Studios
in
Miami.
Three
years
later,
he moved
to
Co-
lumbia Records Productions where he
first
served
as an
account
executive
in the custom manufacturing division
and then as auravision product
sales
manager
for
Columbia.
In
1966,
he
joined
Kapp
Records
as
operations
and
international
sales
manager,
a
position
he
held
until
his
present
CRDC appointment.

Watts: Author/Cartoonist
NEW YORK—The
Rolling
Stones’
Charlie Watts, has a new career which
will
be
introduced
to American fans
for
the
first
time
with
the
Stones’
new
album.
The
LP,
whose
release
is to be announced officially at London
Records’ January
sales convention
in
London,
contains
backliner
cartoon
illustrations
and
captions by
Watts.
This
latest
project adds a new
di-
mension
to
Watts’
literary
career,
which
began
in
England
with
the
publication
of two
books
written by
him. One
of these,
titled “Ode To A
Highflying Bird,”
is a treatise on the
late Charlie “Bird” Parker. Picturing
the
“Bird”
as
a
real
cartoon
bird
bursting forth from an egg in a nest,
the story traces the career of Charles
Christopher “Yardbird” “Bird” Parker
from the moment he cracked his egg
in Kansas City to his unhappy demise
in New York City.
Another
Wattsian
effort
is
titled
“The Zoo Of Flags.” The 48-page book
consists of color drawings of animals
from countries all over the world, with
rhyming
couplets
for
each.
Every
animal—from Orang-Outang to Kan-
garoo—carries
the
colors
of the
flag
of
its native
land.

label’s
slogan, “Look To Liberty
For ’67,” Liberty Records
is releasing
eight albums in Jan. The new release
as well as the entire Liberty, Liberty
Premier Series and Dolton back cata-
log
figure
in
the
program,
effective
immediately through Feb.
28.
In
the
teen-oriented
category,
the
new
LP’s
include
the
Ventures’
“Freakout” and Gary Lewis and the
Playboys’
“Paint
Me
A
Picture.”
Lush music
is
also

via
the
Fifty
Guitars
of Tommy
Garrett
in
“In A
Brazilian
Mood,”
the
Sunset
Strings’ “Film Music,
Italian
Style,”
and Julie London’s “Nice
Girls Don’t
Stay For Breakfast.” Gilbert Becaud,
who
recently appeared
in
a one-man
Broadway show, gains another Liber-
ty
entry,
done
entirely
in
English,
“Mon Amour.” Trombones Unlimited
showcase their sound with “Big Boss
Bones,” while another Guitar Phonics
instructional
LP
introduces
C&W
music lovers to the instrument by way
of “Play Guitar With Chet Atkins.”
Numerous merchandising sales-aids
will
be
provided by
Liberty
distrib-
utors.
A
multi-purpose
Lewis/Ven-
tures
display
which
can
be
used
over
and
over
has
been
created
in
addition
to
“Look
To”
streamers,
color-keyed for complete unit display.
Miscellaneous materials are
available
on Gilbert Becaud and the other new
LP’s. A
special
catalog counter sup-
plement on Gary Lewis, the Ventures,
50
Guitars
and
Guitar
Phonics
and
advertising aid sheets are
also being

Cyrkle Rounds Off;
Losekamp Joins Group
NEW YORK—Columbia Records’ The

has
added

joined
the

a

ago.
The
Cyrkle is currently represented on the
Top 100 with the single “I Wish You
Could Be Here.”
Mike, formerly a
resident
of Day-
ton, Ohio,
is a friend of Cyrkle mem-
bers Tom Dawes, Don Dannemann and
Marty
Fried. A
musician
composer,
Mike plays piano and harpsichord as
well as organ and has been studying
music
since
the
age
of
eight.
His
interest
in
music,
said
Mike,
was
fostered by his father, a former band-
leader.
Mike is 20 years old, has brown hair
and eyes, stands
5' 9" tall and weighs
130
pounds. A
graduate
of
Beaver
Creek High School in Xenia, Ohio, he
also attended Wright State University
in Dayton.
Co-managed by Brian Epstein and
Nathan
Weiss, New York
attorney,
the Cyrkle has had a number of chart
singles
and
a
chart
album.
The
Cyrkle’s
recordings
are

John Simon, producer, Columbia Rec-
ords
popular
artists
and
repertoire.

75% Sales Increase
NEW YORK—Gene
Simmons,

eral manager of Original Sound Rec-
ords,
has
announced
that
Original

is up 75% over the

quarters’

He

Music Machine and their single, “Talk,
Talk,” which
is

32
on
the
Top
100.
The
Music
Machine’s
album, “Turn On The Music Machine,”
is
No.
107
on
the Top
100
Albums.
Adding
to
the upsurge
in business
is
the
purchase
of
a
master
from
Phoenix,
“Funky
Broadway
Part
I
And
Part
II,”
by
Dyke
and
the
Blazers.
This
single
is
seeing
sales
action
in
Cleveland,
San
Francisco,
Los Angeles, Chicago, and Detroit.
When
Simmons
joined
Original
Sound
in August,
his
first move was
to jump on the cartridge tape band-
wagon. This has proven so successful
that the
Original Sound
“Oldies But
Goodies”
LP
product
will

available
not
only
in
the
original
4
track tapes but

will also be available in both 4 and 8
track tapes. By producing specialized
“oldies” picked by program

KHJ,
KFRC
and
pertaining
only
to

has

New releases are scheduled for the
Music
Machine
and
Dyke
and
the
Blazers,
and

Simmons is now on a multi-state sales
and

tour
which
began
Jan. 15.

Radio, Phono Sales Help
Electronics Industry
Reach New Highs In '66
WASHINGTON — Radio and phono
sales played key
roles
in the banner
year just past for the consumer elec-
tronics
industry,
reports
the
Elec-
tronic Industry Association.
Total consumer
electronic
sales
to
dealers in 1966 amounted to approxi-
mately
$4
billion
last
year, up from
$3.3 billion in 1965, according to pre-
liminary
year-end
estimates
of
the
marketing services department of the
EIA.
In the last 10 years radio has grown
spectacularly
despite
television.
The
total U.S. market is estimated to have
grown from
sales of 15 million units
in 1956 to 44 million in 1966, including
imports, a large percentage of which
are produced abroad for U.S. manu-
facturers.
FM has added another dimension to
the radio renaissance. FM or AM/FM
sales to dealers in 1956 were a negli-
gible quantity. In 1966 estimates are
that FM
or AM/FM
factory
sales
amounted
to
11.7
million
units,
ap-
proximately
27 per cent of the
total
U.S. radio market.
The growth
in FM has
paralleled
the increase in FM stations from 530
in 1956 to over 1,500 in 1966.
Total sales of phonographs (exclud-
ing TV-phonograph
combinations)
in
1966 were
6.1
million
units,
50
per
cent obove the 4 million units sold
in
1956.
Stereo
sound,
both
in
records
and
radio,
has been
the
chief
factor
of
growth, literally adding a new dimen-
sion to reproduced sound.
The real gainers
in the phono
field
were
radio-phonograph
combinations.
450.000
such
units came out
of
U.S.
factories
in 1956
(11 per cent of the
total that year)
. In 1966 sales had in-
ci-eased fourfold
to
1.8
million
units,
and
this
represented
30
per
cent
of
the year’s total phonograph sales.
Portable and table phonograph sales
increased
from
3.3
million
units
in
1956 to 4.3 million units in 1966.
The U.S. tape recorder market has
increased
to
an
estimated
5
million
units in
1966. up from approximately
200.000 in 1956.
The
advent
of
cartridge
systems,
for auto and home, will give continued
impetus
to
this
as
yet undetermined
market, the EIA
said. Magnetic tape
equipment could become the most out-
standing growth area
in an industry
that has been setting records in near-
ly every product line for the past 10
years.

In New Hartford

Decca Names Sloman
Its Man
In Europe
NEW YORK—In
a
continuing
drive
to expand the company’s operation on
all
levels,
Leonard
W.
Schneider,
executive vice president of Decca Rec-
ords,
has appointed Mike
Sloman
to
the newly
created
post
of European
representative
for
the
U.
S.
label
Sloman’s duties will encompass liaison
between
the
U.
S.
Decca
label
and
European producers in the acquisition
of masters, talent and projects for re-
lease on
the Decca and
Coral
labels
throughout the world.
Sloman
joined
English
Decca
in
1959 as the manager of their
Italian
Division,
branching
out,
soon
after,
into promotional duties covering Eng-
land,
Germany,
Italy
and
Luxem-
bourg.
In
June
of
1962
he
came
to
the
United States to join Liberty Records
as their assistant to the International
sales
director. He
served
in
this
ca-
pacity
until September of 1964 when
he was transferred by Liberty back to
England
to
take
charge
of
their
European
operation,
a
post
he
held
until resigning
to accept
his
present
position with U.
S. Decca. During his
European
tenure
with
Liberty,
Slo-
man
is
credited with
bringing many
top names
to
the
indie
U.
S.
label.
Among these are the Hollies, Billy J.
Kramer,
the
Swinging
Blue
Jeans,
Frank
Purcell and Adamo.
Sloman
will
headquarter
in
Lon-
don
at
the
offices
of MCA
Artists
Ltd.,
139
Piccadilly, making
periodic
trips
to
the
Continent
in
pursuit
of
his
over-all Decca
duties.

Sheppard To Direct
King's A&R, Promotion
MIAMI BEACH, FLA.—Syd Nathan,
president of King Records, announced
last
week
at
his
winter
offices
in
Miami, the
exclusive signing of Wil-
liam
“Bunky”
Sheppard
to
a
long-
term
contract
as A&R
director
and
promotion
chief
for
King
and
its
subsidiary
labels.
Nathan
also
an-
nounced the subsequent release of the
first two
records
produced by
Shep-
pard
under
the
new
arrangement,
“Why, Why, Why” b/w “Right Now”
by
Mill Evans and “Why Am
I Cry-
ing”
b/w
“That’s
How
Long
I’m
Gonna Love You” by Shirley Wahls.
A veteran of more than ten years in
the record business, Sheppard owned
and operated his own company Apex
Records
during
the
late
1950’s
and
produced the
label’s only
hit, “Island
of Love” by the Sheppards.
In
1961, Sheppard produced a
ses-
sion by a then unknown
artist, Gene
Chandler,
and
leased
the
sides
to
Ewart Abner
at Vee-Jay. From that
session
came
the
smash,
“Duke
of
Earl,” which
earned
for
Sheppard
a
key
position
on
the
Vee-Jay R&B
staff. Abner
also
utilized
Sheppard’s
strong
established
relationships
with
the
country’s
leading
R&B
disk-
jockeys
by
appointing
him
national
director of R&B promotion.
Sheppard
left
Vee-Jay
in
1963,
along with Abner, to form Constella-
tion
Records.
At
the new
label,
he
was much
the same
as
at
Vee-Jay.
During the years at Constellation, he
produced the following hits with Gene
Chandler:
“Just Be True”; “Nothing
Can Stop Me”; “Rainbow ’65” and the
album
“Gene
Chandler — Live
On
Stage.”
Sheppard will for the time being be
operating from
his home
in
Chicago.
Any
artists,
songwriters,
etc.,
wish-
ing to contact him can do so at 7750
S.
Calumet,
Chicago.

HOLLYWOOD:
If such grand cordons were

little catalog
in the world”

into

winter. And with

ac-

of the

a
total

18
in

album catalog. It would be a safe bet

Dr. Albert Sirmay Dies
NEW YORK — Dr.
Albert
Sirmay,
music
editor
for many
of America’s
top
songwriters and
a composer
(as
well as conductor)
in
his own
right,
died last week (15) in New York Mid-
town Hospital at the age of 85.
A longtime friend
of the
late Max
Dreyfus,
founder
of
the
music
pub-
lishing
firm
of Chappell &
Co.,
Inc.,
Dr. Sirmay
joined
that
organization
in 1927 and became
chief music
edi-
tor. He w-as a close friend, as well as
the
music
editor,
of
such
famous
composers
as
Richard
Rodgers,
Cole
Porter,
George
Gershwin,
Jerome
Kern,
Jule
Styne
and
almost
every
writer who composed for this firm. As
a
composer, himself,
Dr. Sirmay be-
came a writer member
of the Amer-
ican
Society
of
Composers,
Authors
and Publishers (ASCAP)
in 1933.
Born in Budapest, Hungary on July
2,
1882
Dr. Sirmay was
educated
at
the Royal Academy of Music in Buda-
pest
and
received
his
Doctorate
of
Music from
the
University
of Buda-
pest.
He
composed
the
scores
fox-
eleven
musicals
in
Budapest
and
Vienna
including
Dancing
Hussars,
Alexandra,
The
Gingerbread
Heart,
etc. His London stage scores included
Bamboula and Lady Mai-y; as well as
Girl on the Film and Px-incess Charm-
ing
which
wei-e
also
produced
on
Broadway. His score, Ripples, wx-itten
with Oscar Levant, was
px-oduced on
Broadway in
1930.
In addition to his music editing and
composing,
he
edited
many
song
books for the Chanpell firm including
A Treasury
of
Gilbert and
Sullivan,
Songs
of
the
Rivers
of America, A
Treasury of Grand
Opei-a, Rodgers &
Hai*t
Song
Book,
Rodgei-s & Ham-
merstein
Song
Book,
Cole
Porter
Song
Book,
George &
Ira
Gershwin
Song Book, Jerome
Kei-n Song Book
and Lerner & Loewe
Song- Book.
ASCAP
President
Stanley Adams,
upon learning of Dr. Sirmay’s death,
said:
“All
of
us
in
the
music
field
mourn the loss of Dr. Albert Sirmay,
a
gentle,
talented music man. Many
of
our
outstanding
American
com-
posei’s
relied upon
his judgment and
good taste
in music matters. In addi-
tion to his own compositions, he was
always
ready
to
be
helpful
to
his
fellow comnosers in the oi'oduction of
their
works.
We
shall
miss
him
greatlv.”
Dr. Sirmay is survived by two nieces
and
grandnieces.
Services were
held
at
Campbell’s
in
New
York
last
Thursday
(19) at 11 AM.

The LP should move well with devotees
of folk
music everywhere.
THE IMMORTAL MA RAINEY—Ma Rainey—
Milestone MLP-2001
This album
spotlights
the famed
1920’s
blues
singer Ma Rainey in a dozen of her most popular
numbers. Included in the set are “Jealous Hearted

Honry
Scat,” and “Slow Driving Moan.”

be big with fans of “old time” blues sounds.
AFRO-JAZZIAC—Herbie Mann—Roulette R/SR-
52122

flautist

offers
a

selection
of self-composed numbers
on

swings
through

Mancini Pens 2 Scores
NEW YORK—Composer Henry Man-
cini has finished the score for one and
is working on the score for another of
Hollywood’s film projects. Both movies
are
scheduled
for
release
next sum-
mer, and RCA Victor will release an
album of music from the score of each
coincidental with the film’s opening.
Mancini has completed the score for
the
Stanley Donen
production, “Two
For The Road,” starring Audrey Hep-
burn and Albert Finney, and
is cur-
rently putting the finishing touches to
the score of a feature length theatri-
cal
film, “Peter Gunn,” based on
the
TV series of the same name.
The music
for that
series won for
Mancini
his
first
gold album award
from
the
R.I.A.A.
The
film
“Peter
Gunn” was produced and directed by
Blake Edwards and stars the original
TV Peter Gunn, Craig Stevens. Also
starring is Laura Devon.
As
is
the
case
with
all
of Man-
cini’s RCA
Victor albums, these two
will not be soundtracks but perform-
ances of music from the
scores with
Mancini conducting a
full symphony
orchestra.
Mancini
said
that
he
will
deliver
the finished “Peter Gunn” score to the
film’s
producer
in
February.
The
score
will
retain the familiar “Peter
Gunn”
and
“Dreamsville”
themes
from the original series, but
all other
material will be new.
Okeh Lets
Out 'Fat Cat'
NEW YORK—As part of its new ex-
pansion program, Okeh Records
has
purchased
the
master
single
“Fat
Cat” by Washington Smith, and is re-
leasing
it
nationally
on
the
Okeh
label.
“Fat
Cat”
was
originally
re-
leased
in
Detroit
on
the
Rainbow
label.
The record was jointly produced by
Joey Brooks and Barry Kornfeld.
Lloyd To Appear
At Bergen Festival
NEW YORK—Atlantic
jazz
artist

the Bergen

7. He

ever
booked

For the next two weekends Lloyd is

It’s
an
unusual
booking
for
Lloyd
since
the

Auditorium
is
usually
devoted to rock and roll shows.
Geartner Exits CP
NEW YORK—Clark

sales
manager
of
Wyncote
Records,
re-

last week
that
he has

ture plans at a later date.

aspects

Stan
Soifer Marries
NEW YORK—Stan
Soifer,
account
exec
at
Cash
Box, was
married
to
Carol Leichman
on
Dec.
29.
Couple
has just returned from a honeymoon
in Acapulco, Mexico. Pair
will make
their home in New York.
It looks like the original Five Spot,
maybe about two and a half times as
large, and the layout
is much better
for seeing the musicians, but basically
it’s
very much
the
same.
The New
Five
Spot, which really
isn’t new
in
the
strict
sense
of
the
word,
is
the
third jazz club in New York City that
has been owned and operated by the
brothers, Termini, Joe and Iggie.
Every jazz soon has a certain flavor
about
it, and
usually
a
colorful
his-
tory. If there
is a room in New York
City that
is
the
exemplification
of a
jazz
club, none has worthier
creden-
tials than The New Five Spot Cafe.
If
there
are
jazz
club
owners who
have been good friends to jazz musi-
cians and
audiences,
again none
are
more worthy of recognition than the
Termini
brothers.
Sure,
there
have
been, and
still
are,
others who have
fought the
fight for
survival
in
this
hazardous
business, and have fought
it
well,
without
exploiting
the
jazz
musician.
There
are men
like Max
Gordon, long-time operator of the re-
nowned
Village
Vanguard,
the
Can-
terino
brothers,
Mike
and
Sonny,
whose Half Note has earned the
re-
spect
and
admiration
of
performers
and audiences, and Art D’Lugoff, who
operates The Village Gate, which has
been the home for many performers,
jazz
and
non-jazz,
alike.
But
today
we pay homage to Joe and Iggie Ter-
mini and their New Five
Spot
Cafe,
within
whose
walls
they
spend
the
major
part
of
their
waking
hours.
They’re both ordinary guys, but
in a
very extraordinary way.
Up From the Bowery
Their
indoctrination
to
jazz
came
late in 1955 in the original Five Snot
Cafe, when they first tried presenting
live entertainment, mostly piano duos,
or
solo
piano.
Until
then, The
Five
Spot
had
been
just
a
neighborhood
bar,
located
on
Cooner
Square,
the
uptown periphery of The Bowery. The
Termini family,
Joe,
Iggie and
their'
father before them, had been serving
a
neighborhood
trade,
and
the
geo-
graphy
dictated
that
it was
several
notches below what might
be
called
an average neighborhood. Long after
the jazz policy was instituted,
it was
not uncommon to see an ill-clad dere-
lict wander into The Five Spot during
a
set by Thelonius Monk
or Ornette
Coleman,
pause
for
a moment,
then
retreat
to
his more
familiar
haunt,
the
streets
of the Bowery, where,
in
his low state, he had much more com-
pany.
So, from
this
inauspicious
be-
ginning
The
Five
Spot
Cafe
came
into
existence
as
a
jazz
emporium,
and one which was to gain much re-
spect from the entire jazz world.
Stature With Monk
Little by little The Five Spot, under
the
naive guidance
of Joe and
Iggie
Termini, began
to
stretch
its wings.
Soon they were booking quartets, then
quintets,
then
large
groups.
Some-
times they would feature two groups,
so
that
the
music
was
continuous,
with very little time out between sets.
Being
a
small room,
it was not
un-
common to see patrons lined up on the
sidewalk, waiting
to
gain
admission.
One of the most attractive aspects of
The Five Spot operation was the in-
formality that prevailed. A large seg-
ment
of
the
artist
colony took The
Five Spot to its bosom, and it became
the place
to meet, the place
to com-
mune.
After
about
two
years
of
operation as a jazz Club, a most
sig-
nificant booking was
affected:
Thelo-
nius Monk was contracted
to appear
for
the
Terminis.
Immediately
this
gave The Five Spot stature as a jazz
Club.
Joe
and
Iggie
had
scored
a
coup.
It was hard
to
recall
the
last
time Monk had played in a New York
Club.
The
Mystique
about
Monk,
coupled
with
his
rare
appearances
made “standing room only” common-
place night after night for weeks at a
time. With
this kind of business The
Five Spot was firmly established as a
major jazz room in New York.
The
Terminis
prospered,
but even
in
the
light
of
this
prosperity,
the
climate
of
The
Five
Spot
did
not
change. Prices weren’t jacked up, as
is
so
often
the
case
when
a
room
catches on and the number of
custo-
mers exceeds the room’s capacity. The
trappings
of The
Five
Spot
weren’t
changed,
nor were
the
waiters
and
their casual attire. The only difference
you
could
detect was
that
the
place
was always crowded.
Suddenly, many
record
companies
did
“location”
re-
cordings at The Five
Spot. This was
the place where things were happen-
ing. Where
else
in New York
City
could
you
hear Monk ?
Where
else
could
you
hear
Mingus
in
a
loose,
relaxed setting?
Then, in 1962, Joe and Iggie booked
Ornette
Coleman
for
his
first New
York appearance. Word of Coleman’s
exploits
on
the West
Coast had
fil-
tered East, and these rumblings plus
two recordings that Ornette had done
on Contemporary, were enough to con-
vince the brothers that
it would be a
good engagement. The rest is history,
because
since
Ornette
Coleman
ap-
peared
at
The
Five
Spot
the
jazz
world
hasn’t
been
the
same.
Once
again
the
Termini
brothers had
up-
staged
their
more
experienced
col-
leagues in the jazz club business.
The Jazz Gallery
Now, looking for new horizons, Joe
and
Iggie
opened The
Jazz
Gallery,
which was located in the same general
area
of
Manhattan,
four
blocks
farther uptown and
one
block
East.
Unfortunately,
this turned out to be
an ill-advised move. The Gallery was
a much bigger and much more elabor-
ate operation than what they had been
accustomed
to.
Lighting
engineers,
designers, big name bookings all con-
tributed
to
the
decline.
The
Jazz
Gallery was operated concurrent with
The Five Spot Cafe and whatever was
being accomplished and earned at the
smaller room was being poured
into
the
new
venture
to
keen
it
going.
Ultimately, The Jazz
Gallery had
to
be foresaken as an unwise undertak-
ing. That meant
all hands went back
to
the mother room, The Five
Spot.
But now Joe and Iggie were informed
that
condemnation was
in
store
for
the
site of The Five Spot, as part of
a
face-lifting
for Lower Manhattan
All of which leads us to where they
are now, The New
Five
Spot
Cafe,
just four blocks North of the original
location, and
just one block West
of
the ill-fated Jazz Gallery and for the
benefit of those not familiar with New
York
City,
on
the
corner
of
Third
Avenue and
St. Marks
Place.
The New Five Spot
In
The New
Five
Spot,
Joe
and
Iggie have tried just about everything
they know to make it a going proposi-
tion. They have staged Monday night
specials, featuring painters who
also
play jazz. They have always been most
co-operative in offering their premises
in
conjunction with worthy
benefits,
they continue to strive to give engage-
ments
to
deserving
musicians,
often
to
their
economic
detriment.
In
essence,
they
remain
nice
gentle
people
in
a
business
where
these
characteristics
are
suicidal.
Joe
and
Iggie
Termini
are
stickouts
in
The
New York jazz scene, dwarfing most
of their colleagues when
it comes
to
consideration,
appreciation
and
con-
sternation regarding the plight of the
jazz musician in New York City. The
men who play jazz should rally round
Joe
and
Iggie
and
lend them
their
every assistance, the better that they,
the
brothers,
may
resist
the
final
erosion which
will
drive them from
the
jazz
world
into
something com-
pletely unrelated. The New York jazz
Community will be much poorer with-
out them.

Ed Lawson confirms
all the
action reports on
soul sounds
in Montreal. He
tells C.B. that not only the Ben E. King
record, but also the
Billy Graham,
Atlantic
side, “Oop-Poo-Pa-Doo”
is soaring into the top ten on CFCF
in the
big town.
John Pozer’s organization in Ottawa has debuted a new teen-oriented label,
"Sir John A” records. He can be reached at Box 1015 Station B, Ottawa. Norm
Greene handles promotion for the fledgling
label. They have two great sides
for their first releases: “Low Man” by Don Norman and the other four, will be
a winner with anybody programming R&B. Second Pozer release
is “You Gotta
Try” by the Deuces.
“Summerwine” by Nancy Sinatra with Lee Hazlewood,
flip
side of “Sugar
Town,” continues to come on
like a new
release.
It’s prolonging the “Sugar
Town” action by weeks in several important markets.
Bob Burns reports that the Guess Who’s great single, “His
Girl,”
is really
off on a chart ride in England. All three “pirates” Caroline, London, and 270
have charted the
record,
as high
as #21 on
the Radio London
list for
this
week. The group
will shortly
visit the British
Isles and Europe. As a result
of heavy
airplay on the song through
the
Guess Who’s
version
of Johnny
Cowell’s good song, the side by A1 Hirt
is getting almost as much air play
if not more—than what was supposed to be the big
side
of the Hirt outing
“Music To Watch
Girls By.” Guess Who’s out
in the U.S. on Bell
Jan.
20th.
SWEDISH NEW YEAR—Manfred Mann and group are shown here soon after
their arrival in Sweden for the New Year’s holiday. A press conference was
hosted by Philips-Sonora for the group. As a frostbite preventitive, the boys
were given warm Swedish ear-muffs.

Phil Steinberg will represent Kama
Sutra
Corporation
at

at Cannes, January

Mr. Steinberg
is president of Kama
Sutra International. He will meet in-
ternational music
publishers and
re-
cording
artists and film producers
in

in

Little LPs This Month
In Release For January:
As
part
of
their
continuing
coop-
erative program with
various
record
companies,
Seeburg
has
released
six
Little LPs
this month covering
vari-
ous
music
fields. The
reviews below
are
given
on
the
basis
of
probable
jukebox market potentiality, but loca-
tion
preferences
should
be
kept
in
mind. Operators should consult
their
local
one-stops
or
local
record com-
pany distributing offices for the avail-
ability
of
these
or any
other
Little
LPs
desired.
JIMMY SMITH
“Hoochie
Coochie Man” Verve SLV-
8667
* Seeburg Part No. 1094
Considered
to
be
the
top-ranking
jazz organist, Jimmy Smith had some
national chart success with “Hoochie
Coochie Man” and this Verve little LP
features
the
complete
five
minute
track. The
tune
is from
the
prolific
pen of blues writer Willie Dixon, and
was originally a hit by Muddy Waters.
Smith
takes
the
vocal
in
his
rough,
gravel-like
tones
at
a
blues
tempo,
then turns confidently to the organ to
bat out
several
choruses. “One Mint
Julep” scored by
Oliver Nelson
in
a
tribute
to
the
Ray
Charles
instru-
mental, features Smith pulling pranks
in
Part
I
and
getting down
to
the
nitty-gritty
in
Part
II.
John
Lee
Hooker’s “Boom Boom”
is
more
or
less an organ solo with orchestra
fill-
ins, Smith mumbling a
la Earl Hines
as he explores
his instrument. These
sides are examples of the turning of
jazz
musicians
to
rock
and
blues
numbers, and although they may
call
it
“soul
music”
it
is
simply
Roots
with
a few new
Leaves
grafted
on.
Not to take away from Smith and his
comrade
Nelson, however
These
are
good sides and should
sell
like crazy
in any R & B
location
in any
large
city. Ops should pick up.
HANK WILLIAMS
“The
Legend
Lives
Anew”: MGM
SLM4377
* Seeburg Part No.
1091
Since
Williams’
death
in
1953
the
masters he left behind for MGM have
been repackaged time and time again.
Perhaps this
little LP represents the
ultimate
in
repackaging—Williams’
vocal
tracks from the
original
1940s
and
1950s
masters
with
strings and
bump-bump rhythm
added
on.
It
is
not
so much
an
attempt
to
update
Williams, as the work he
did
is con-
sidered
immortal
by
country
musi-
cians and fans—but an
effort
to
up-
date
his
backing,
or
simply
another
way
to
sell
a
product
that’s
been
around
for
a
long
time.
The
same
technique was
applied
to Caruso
re-
,
cordings in the 1930s. Almost anything
by Williams is immediately soaked up
by
country
fans
and
with
country
music
rapidly
crossing
or
happily
straddling
the
border
between
itself
and
cosmopolitan
“pop,”
this
little
LP
should
go
on
any
jukebox
in
a
country location, or any location that
has
country
fans.
Selections
include
“I’m So Lonesome
I Could Cry,” “You
Win
Again,”
“Lovesick
Blues”
and
three
others. Sure programming.
ERNEST TUBS
“Sings Country
Hits Old and New”:
Decca DL 74772
* Seeburg Part No.
1100
Mr. Tubb takes
it easy through
six
vocals
while
the
Texas
Troubadors
play
the
usual
country
background.
Tubb has been a consistant seller over
the
years
and
receives
happy
yells
whenever
he
appears on
stage.
Safe
programming
for
country
locations.
Songs: “Memphis,” “Waitin’ In Your
Welfare
Line,”
“I’m Gonna
Tie One
On Tonight” and three more.
CONNIE FRANCIS
“Movie
Greats
of
the
60’s”: MGM
SLM
4382
*
Seeburg
Part
No.
1090
Gone
to the brass and
lush
violins
is
Connie
Francis,
taking
six
tunes
from last decade’s movies. “Strangers
In
The
Night,”
“Forget
Domani,”
“Second Time Around,”
“I
Will Wait
For
You,”
“Call
and
“Somewhere
Me
Irresponsible”
My
Love.”
Miss
Francis takes “Second Time Around”
a
la Mae West. Interesting. Program
where desired.
SAMMY KAYE
“Let’s
Face The Music
and
Dance”:
Decca 74823
* Seeburg Part No. 1097
A
well-drilled band
blares
out
six
danceable numbers, or music to listen
to
highballs
with.
Title
tune,
plus,
“The
More
I
See
You,”
“Marne,”
“Smile,” “In The Arms Of Love,” “If
Ever
I Would Leave You.” Program
for cocktail lounges.
CARLA THOMAS
“Carla
Thomas”
Stax/Atlantic
SD
70709
* Seeburg Part No. 1088
The debut album from one
of
the
newest
blues
birds
from
the
famed
Atlantic
factory. No
other company
in modern
times
have
so
effectively
tied up the R & B market or produced
such
a
list
of
selling
singers
and
groups. Miss Thomas’ “B-A-B-Y” was
high on the national charts not long
ago and is a well-produced and played
side.
She
can
sing. A
nice
job
on
Jimmy Reed’s “Baby, What You Want
Me To Do” and standard
stuff on the
four
remaining
tracks
“For
Your
Love,”
“Let Me
Be
Good
To
You,”
“What Have You Got To
Offer Me”
and “I Got You, Boy.” Safe program-
ming for R & B locations.
