Dana Valery To Be Subject-
Of Strong Columbia Promo
NEW YORK—Columbia
Records has
released
a
single by new female
vo-
calist
Dana
Valery,
signaling
the
start
of an
all-out promotion by
the
label
on
the
artist.
The
record
fea-
tures
the
song
“You
Don’t
Know
Where
Your
Interest
Lies,”
written
by
Paul
Simon
of
Simon
and
Gar-
funkel and recorded for a Top-40 au-
dience. Deck
is backed with “Having
You
Around.”
The
label
is
investing
extra
effort
on the debut
single not only because
of
its
hit
potential,
but
because
of
the
company’s
belief
in
the
artist’s
star-level
capabilities.
Miss
Valery
was
born
in
Milan,
Italy,
spent
some
time
in
South
Africa, and then moved to England to
pursue a career in entertainment. She
came
to New
York
with
a
starring
j
role
in
the
hit
musical
“Wait
A
Minim,”
now
enjoying
a
successful
run
on
Broadway.
Since
her
arrival
here, she has had numerous
offers of
starring roles
in upcoming Broadway
musical
productions.
Under
direct
contract
to Columbia
now,
Miss
Valery
formerly
recorded
for CBS Records in South Africa and
in England. Her recordings are super-
vised
by pop A&R
producer
Charlie
Calello.
VICTOR
INKS
COMIC — Young
stand-up comedian George Carlin has
been
signed
to
a long-term
exclusive
pact by RCA Victor Records.
Carlin,
a former
deejay who
bases most
of
his
material
on
the
communications
media, has already cut his first Victor
album
“live”
at
the
Rooster
Tail
in
Detroit.
Produced
by Tom
Berman,
the LP
is
titled
“Take-offs And
Put-
ons,” and
will
be
released
in
March.
A
single, “Wonderful Wino
(Top
40
Disc
Jockey)”
b/w
“A1
Sleet,
The
Hippy-dippy
Weatherman,”
will
be
xeleased shortly. A frequent guest on
the “Tonight Show,” Carlin
is sched-
uled
to make
his
debut
on
the “Ed
Sullivan
Show”
Jan.
29.
Other TV
commitments include “Hollywood Pal-
ace” on Feb.
25, a return to the “Ed
Sullivan Show” on Mar.
19, the “Per-
ry Como Show” on Apr.
15, and
ap-
pearances on the “Tonight Show” and
“The Mike Douglas
Show.” On
Feb.
6,
Carlin
will open
at the
Latin
Ca-
sino in Camden, N.J., and on Mar. 11
he will play the Cellar Door in Wash-
ington, D.C.
ASCAP Infringement Suit
Upheld By Appeals Court
NEW
T YORK—A decision in favor of
ASCAP members
over an
infringing
Washington
State
broadcaster, KIXI,
Seattle, has been upheld by the Unit-
ed
States
Coui't
of
Appeals
for
the
9th
Circuit.
In
a
unanimous
decision,
Judges
Barnes, Koelsch and Duniway upheld
a 1964 decision by Judge Gus
J.
Sol-
omon, awarding damages of $250 for
each infringement and enjoining fur-
ther
infi-ingements.
KIXI’s
defenses
were alleged violations by ASCAP of
iederal
and
Washington
State
anti-
trust laws.
The court held that ASCAP’s activ-
ities
do not
violate
either
federal
or
state
law.
Said Judge
Barnes,
writ-
ing for the
Coui't:
“We agree with the trial court that
the
activities
of ASCAP do
not
con-
stitute
a combination
in
restraint
of
trade or a monopoly within the mean-
ing
of
the Sherman
Act. ASCAP
is
certainly
a
combination, but
not
ev-
ery
combination
is
a
combination
in
restraint
of
trade
or
a
monopoly.
ASCAP
cannot
be
accused
of
fixing
prices
because
every
applicant
to
ASCAP has a right under the consent
!
decree
to invoke the authority
of the
United
States
District
Coui't for the
Southern
Distinct of New York to
fix
a reasonable
fee whenever the
appli-
cant
believes that the
price proposed
by
ASCAP
is
unreasonable,
and
ASCAP
has
the
burden
of
proving
the
price
reasonable.
In other words,
so long as ASCAP complies with the
decree,
it
is
not
the
price-fixing
au-
thority.”
Pointing out that of the five options
available
to
defendant
it
chose
an
“unconscionable”
one,
Judge
Bai'nes
said.
“As
appellees
point
out,
appellant
had
five
options open
to
it. Four
of
them were:
“(1) Appellant could have obtained
a blanket license and along with it the
right
to
play
as much
or
as
little,
as
frequently
or
as
rarely
as
it
de-
sired, any of the compositions
in the
ASCAP i-epertory.
“(2)
Appellant could have obtained
a
per program
license which would
have required
it to pay a license fee
only for those programs in which ap-
pellant
broadcast
music
from
the
ASCAP
x’epertory.
“(3)
It
could
have
undertaken
to
deal with ASCAP members directly.
“(4)
Appellant
could
have
re-
frained from
giving
public
perform-
ances
for
profit
of
music
in
the
ASCAP
repei'tory.
“Instead,
appellant
chose
the
fifth
option. Appellant never obtained any
license.
It never sought
to
deal with
anyone.
It
continued
its
unconscion-
able conduct
in unlawfully appropri-
ating
appellees’
pi-operty
without
cause and
without
justification.”
The Court found that ASCAP had
complied with
the
filing x'equirements
of
the Washington
statute
and
that
the plaintiffs (ASCAP members) had
acted
propei-ly
in suing a broadcaster
who could have obtained
a
license
at
a fee judicially found reasonable, but
who
chose
instead
to
infi'inge.
“We find
(1)
all filing requirements
of the State of Washington have been
met;
(2)
no ‘extortionate means’ nor
‘terrorizing
practices’
are
found
in
the
bi'inging
of lawsuits
against
in-
fringing
broadcasters;
(3)
R.C.W.
I
§19.24.020 prohibiting blanket licenses

POP BEST BETS
CRY—Ronnie Dove—Diamond D/SD 5007
Ronnie Dove, whose single “Cry” was a recent
item on the Top 100, stands a good chance of in-
creasing
his
popularity with
this album
of
the
same
name.
Besides
the
title
song,
the
set
in-
cludes such numbers as “Walkin’ My Baby Back
Home,” “Wheel Of
Fortune,”
“Tell The Lady
I
Said
Goodbye,” and
“I
Won’t Cry Any
More.”
Dove
could
really
fry high with
this
one.
THE THIRTEENTH FLOOR ELEVATORS—In-
ternational Artists 1A-LP-1
A
“psychedelic,”
experimental
sound
is
pre-
sented
by
the
Thirteenth
Floor
Elevators.
In-
cluded on the LP
are “You’re Gonna Miss Me,”
“Don’t
Fall
Down,”
and “Monkey
Island.” The
effects produced are interesting and the set might
well be
in widespread demand before long.

The 30’s weren’t short on talent or fine material,
as
this salute
to femme
stars
of the decade can
attest
to.
It’s
a 2-LP
affair, which
is plenty
of
room for displaying the big ones of the day, 20

It
all sounds campy but
there were real giants in those days!
THE
VELVET
TOUCH—Cesana
Orchestra-
Audio Fidelity AFSD 6167
A package of orchestral selections which serve
as mood music. Included on the LP are “Yester-
day’s
Love,” “When
Will
It End?”
and
“Once
Over
Brightly.”
The
melodies,
played
by
a
75

and imaginative. The tunes are richly orchestrated
and

executed. The
disk, marked by
a high
degree of professionalism, is likely to prove quite
popular.

Son Remo Song Fast Pulls Largest Turnout Ever
San Remo,
Italy
The biggest turnout ever packed the Italian city of San Remo for this year’s big song festival. Hotel accommodations were almost impossible
to book
if you were a late comer. Word around town was that a pair of tickets to the three nights of the song festival were worth as much as $200 to $300.

King Carol Adds
Mezzanine With
Accent On Tapes
NEW YORK—With an opening
full-

last week
(2), King Carol opened
its
enlarged
disk &
tape
dealership,
in-
cluding
a
new
mezzanine
fioor,
on
42nd
St.,
this
city.
The
Times
ad,
to
be
followed
in
the

weeks
with
other
an-
nouncements
covering
various New
York newspapers, gave the refurbish-
ing an
official
send-off, although
the
job was completed
three weeks
ago.
One
of
the
chief
reasons
for
the
enlargement of the store, according to
Ben
Carol,
is
the
growth
of
the
dealership’s
tape
sales,
which
now
account for 20%
of King
Carol’s
in-
come. A separate tape section has been
installed
on
the
mezzanine.
“Tape
needs its own department and people,”
says
Carol.
While
reel-to-reel
tape
material outsells tape cartridges 5 to
1, Carol notes, he
is optimistic about
the future of tape cartridges.
Six
of
the
outlet’s
30
employees man
the
tape
section.
King Carol, which claims the larg-
est
selection
of
records
and
tapes,
is,
as the ad
says, “open every day
of the year
’til 11 P.M.”
Looking
to
the
future,
the
label
already has
its next singles
releases
recorded
and
scheduled
and
several
album projects are
in the works.
On
the
foreign
end,
a number
of
companies have already made known
their interest to Kapp and a complete
foreign distribution set-up will shortly
be
finalized.

'K-K-K-Katy' Writer Dies
ST. PETERSBURG, FLA.—Geoffrey
O’Hara,
writer
of
the World War
I
novelty
hit,
“K-K-K-Katy,”
and
a
founding member of ASCAP, died last
week
(Jan.
31)
in
St.
Petersburg
at
the age of 84. O’Hara, who had writ-
ten songs performed by Enrico Caruso
and A1 Jolson, tried a lower-pitch re-
write of “The Star Spangled Banner”
in 1929, acting on the belief that the
original key was too high for Ameri-
can
voices.
O’Hara,
a
native
New
Yorker,
is
survived by
his widow,
a
son
and
daughter
and
one
grand-
daughter.

Schwartz’ Publishing Firms
Consolidate Under Day, Maresca
NEW YOEK — The Bob and Gene
Schwartz
publishing
interests
have
been consolidated under the direction
of Joey
Day,
professional
manager,
and Ernest Maresca, creative consult-
ant,
according
to
the
Schwartz’ and
Elliot Greenberg, secretary of the op-
eration. Also, Regina Reiss
will han-
dle
the
copyright
dept,
as
adminis-
trative
assistant.
The
consolidation
has
evolved,
it was
said, because
of
the
firms’ activity and growth
in
re-
cent
months,
including
two
top
ten
hits, “See You In September” by the
Happenings on the B. T. Puppy label
and “Sweet Talkin’ Guy” by the Chif-
fons on Laurie Records.
In addition to the standard respon-
sibilities of professional manager, Day
will
consult
record
company A&R
men to determine their specific needs
and then furnish them with material
designed
especially
to
satisfy
their
requirements. He
will
further
assist
the diskeries by providing strong LP
suggestions arranged around a central
theme. For example, Day
is including
“See You In September” in an
origi-
nal
list
of
suggested
ideas
for
a
“September” album.
Twenty-seven-year-old
Ernie
Ma-
resca,
already
one
of
the
industry’s
most
successful
contemporary
song-
writers,
will
fill
the
newly-instituted
post of creative consultant by work-
ing with new composers, guiding and
refining their creative ability to maxi-
DAY,
REISS, MARESCA
mize the quality of their musical out-
put. He
is
the
author
of
such
hits
as
“Runaround
Sue,”
“No
One
Knows,” “Lovers Who Wander,” “The
Wanderer,” and
“Donna,
the
Prima-
donna”
all by
Dion;
“Shout,
Shout,
Knock
Yourself
Out,”
which
he
re-
corded
himself
for London
Records;
“Whenever A Teenager Cries” by Re-
parta
and
the
Deirons;
“Come

Little Angel” by
the
Belmonts;
and
“Run

by

on

has
also

signed to the pubbery as an exclusive
writer.

Opens S.
F. Branch

Tom Sawyer Promotions, 1680 North
Vine,
Hollywood,
California
has
an-
nounced the
first major expansion of
his firm since
it was formed one year
ago.
Sawyer
will open
a branch
of
his
office
this month
in
San
Francisco.
The company offers record promotion
and
distributor
sales throughout
the
eleven
western
states.
The
opening
of the Bay Area
office
will allow for
more
concentrated
sales
and promo-
tion service in the north-western area
of the country.
Sawyer’s promotion firm now
rep-
resents Momentum
Records,
Trident
Records,
Vandan-Caprice
Records,
Rojac
Records
and
Parade
Records
which
is the new company formed by
Billy Vaughn and
distributed by Dot
Records.
Sawyer
has
also
announced
the
forming of
his own record company,
Sierra Recerds which
will release
its
first two records this month. The first

Eduardo Davidson To UA
NEW YORK—United
Artists
presi-
dent
Mike
Stewart
has
just
an-
nounced the signing of Cuban singer/
composer Eduardo Davidson to an ex-
clusive
long-term
contract
with
the
label.
Davidson has composed fifty Latin-
American
songs
and
a
number
of
ballets
and
musical
productions. He
has
also
acted and danced in movies
and written poems, short stories, film
ci’iticism, and TV and radio shows.
Initial
singles
and
albums
from
Davidson will be l’eleased in the near
future. Among
his
fii’st UA
efforts
will be “Le Frissen,” a new vocal and
dance number which combines
go-go
rhythms with Latin-American tempos.
Eduardo Davidson
(seated) makes
his
new
exclusive
contract
with
United
Artists
Records
official with
the traditional pact-signing formality
at the UA
offices in New York. Label
President,

left,
and

of Morro Music, David-
son’s music publisher, happily super-
vise proceedings.
Fabien Sevitsky Dies
NEW YORK—Fabien
Sevitzky,
con-
ductor of the Greater Miami Philhar-
monic
Orchestra,
died of a heart
at-
tack Feb. 2 in Athens while on tour.
He was
73. He was to have appeared
on
Feb.
6
as guest conductor
of the
Athens State Orchestra.
He was
noted
as
a
champion
of
American composers and attempted to
introduce new pieces by writers in his
adopted country in every program he
conducted.
This
often
led
to
critical
displeasure,
especially
of
the
Hitler
regime, when he insisted on perform-
ing American works in Germany. He
was at one time a double bassist with
the Philadelphia Orchestra.
The Russian-born conductor fled the
USSR
in
1922,
migrating
to
Poland
and then to the U.S., where he became
a naturalized citizen in 1928. He was
conductor
of
the
Indianapolis
Sym-
phony and led the Lewisohn Stadium,
N.Y., concerts
several
times. He
left
Indianapolis
in
1955
to
form
the
Miami Orchestra.
He was a nephew of Serge Kousse-
vitzky, conductor of the Boston Sym-
phony,
but
shortened
his
name
to
avoid confusion with his uncle.
He
was
manned
to
the
foi’mer
Maria Dormont, from whom
he was
divorced
in
1956. He
is
survived by
his widow, Mary Spalding, hai’pist.

Pittsburgh Bow

M.
Records
and

in

involved

the

business, but

love, the record business. He formerly

a
one-stop
rack
service.
He
worked in promotion for ABC Para-
mount
and
Bill
Lawrence
for
five
years.
McGrath
feels
that
with
the
tre-
mendous possibilities and challenge the
Pittsburgh market offers, the new dis-
tributor and promotion service should
be an extremely successful venture.

Harold Rand
Opens New Div.
NEW YORK—A
new
division,
de-
signed
to
fulfill
the
signal
needs
of
clients
in
the
music
and
recording
fields, has been formed by the public
relations
firm
of
Harold
Rand
&
Company,
it has
been announced by
president Harold Rand.
Eddie Kalish, most recently public-
ity
and
advertising
director
for
Greengrass/Talan Management Asso-
ciates and GLG Productions, has been
named to head the new operation.
At
Greengrass/Talan,
Kalish was
responsible for the creation and exe-
cution of
all promotional and related
activities, including personal appear-
ance
tours, for such
artists as Steve
Lawrence,
Eydie
Gorme,
Diahann
Carroll
and
Florence
Henderson.
In
that capacity, he worked closely with
record
company
and
network
TV
executives,
theatrical
management
and the consumer and trade press.
Prior to joining Greengrass/Talan,
Kalish was a member of the publicity
department
of
Paramount
Pictures.
He went to Paramount following six
years
as
a
reporter-reviewer
for
Variety, writing
first
for
the music,
then the film desk.
Assisting
Kalish
in
his new
post
will be Martin Goldblatt, veteran pub-
licist and present member of the Rand
agency who was
formerly
executive
assistant
to Don
Kirshner, president
of Columbia-Screen Gems Music Divi-
sion and Colgem Records.
CBC
Cites
Big
Sales Figures
NEW YORK—Ron Terry, 23-year-old
pi’esident
of
Capitol
Booking
Corp.,
which started with a limited
capital-
ization in April, 1966, claims that the
agency’s
billings
for
its
initial
six
months
of operation were
$1,500,000
and
that
the
company
projects
its
first
year
of
billings
as
reaching
$4,000,000.
The roster of clients under the CBC
banner,
according
to
Terry,
has
grown
enormously.
There
are
now
some 60 acts signed to the agency and
another 65 with which
it has booking
commitments.
“Capitol
Booking’s
intention
from
the
beginning,”
says
Terry,
“is
to
build
the most
perfect
personal
ap-
pearance-type agency and when that
is fully established, our plans call for
expansion
into TV
packaging,
legit-
imate theatre and film production.
CBC
plans
to
continue
developing
those
artists
who
project
perform-
ancewise
in
all
areas
of show
busi-
ness.
Others
will
be
channeled
into
different
areas such as concerts, col-
leges
and
lounges
when
they
are
ready
for
such
activity.
“Our' aim,”
notes
Terry,
“is
to
sign
established
artists as well as ones we can develop
and diversify.”
To the latter end, CBC has opened
a West Coast office and is in the proc-
ess of establishing a Chicago base of
operations. Among recent acquisitions
to the agency roster are such acts as
Tom
Jones,
Joe
Cuba,
Chris Montez
and Eileen Fulton.
Signing
A1
Rosenthal,
president
of Cameo/Parkway, looks
on
from
the
left
as
Yvonne
Baker
(former
lead
with
the
Sensa-
tions) and Kae Williams
(standing,
right)
sign
with the
label. Williams
will
produce
the
lark’s
C/P sessions.

Liberty Opens Tape Dup Plant In Omaha
OMAHA, NEBRASKA — With
con-
struction
completed
on
the
spacious,
$500,000 three
level building housing
LTD
(Liberty
Tape
Duplicating),
a
division of Liberty Records, label and
plant last week hosted a preview here
for friends in the trade. Out of town
guests, numbering about
50, included
reps from record manufacturers, tape,
electronics,
packaging,
printing
and
plastics firms along with trade press
and
city
officials who
viewed
what
Ronald Bledsoe, who co-ordinated the
project,
termed,
“undoubtedly
the
most modern, best equipped and most
efficient plant
in
the business.”
Specifically For Tape
New structure, heralded as the first
to be built specifically for tape dupli-
cating,
encompasses
17,500
square
feet with ample
office and plant area
in addition to space for research and
development. More than
37,000
cubic
feet is available for inventory storage
and shipping with an additional mez-
zanine
level
scheduled
to
be
added
in the near future.
Liberty’s
60 employees
utilize
spe-
cially designed high speed equipment,
including
five master playback
units
and
fifty
4 and
8
track
duplicators,
automatic
label and shrink wrap ma-
chinery as well as a modern conveyor
system
which,
in
effect, produces an
image
of
a
continuous
cartridge
be-
ginning
at
the upper
level and
con-
cluding
with
finished
product
pack-
aged and ready for shipment at street
level, just across from Omaha’s main
post
office.
Thirty machines
dispense
8 track cartridges while 20 produce 4
track and
reel
to
reel. Firm
is
also
running
and
testing
cassette
which,
according
to
general
manager
Leo
Colvin, can now be “produced with a
half hour’s
notice.” Colvin and
chief
engineer
Stan
Nick,
who
initially
founded the
firm under the name
of
TDC Electronics some
five years ago
at
another
location,
retained
their
positions when the company was
ac-
quired
in
April,
’66.
Outside Accounts
In
addition
to
the
production
of
Liberty
product, LTD
custom
(and
Colvin emphasizes the last word)
du-
plicates for several other record firms
—reel to reel for Warners-Reprise and
Dot, with cartridges and reel
to
reel
for
Music
Tapes,
Stereo
Tape
Inc.,
Stereo Devices, Word, Nivico
(a Jap-
anese label) and Double Shot Records.
Bledsoe estimates that about $500,-
000 has already been invested in the
new facility, adding that this is a con-
servative
figure.
“We’re
stressing
quality—every tape
tested before
la-
beling
and
checked
after
shrink
wrapping. And, although we’re
pres-
ently
equipped
to
duplicate between
18
and
20
thousand
units
a
day,
we’re not making any grandiose state-
ments
about
producing
enough
re-
corded tape to go three times around
the
globe.”
Plant
is presently work-
ing
two
shifts,
duplicating
between
10
to
12
thousand
units
daily. And
offering
a
complete
package—from
Ampex and Magna-Tech mastering to
labeling,
wrapping,
shipping
and,
if
requested, inventory
control.
Colvin suggests that
there’s going
to be enough demand to go around for
all systems—existing tracks, cassette
etc. Tape
should not be confused
or
equated with record speeds. The con-
sumer
is, more and
more,
tape
ori-
ented.
One
of
the
reasons,
for
ex-
ample, why
reel
to
reel
sales
have
improved.
“We’re
fortunate
to
have
the
best
engineer
in
the
country
(Stan Nick) and we’re flexible. We’re
ready and able to convert to any ex-
isting or projected duplicating meth-
od. You name
it—we’ll tape
it.”
Ampex Sees Big Tape Sales For ’67
NEW YORK—Sales
of
stereo
tapes
for home and auto listening will
rise
from
approximately
$45,000,000
in
1966
to
more
than
$100,000,000
in
1967,
according
to
Donald
V.
Hall,
general
manager
of Ampex
Stereo
Tapes,
largest
producer
of
recorded
tapes.
Hall
said
the
most
dramatic
in-
creases
will
be
made
by
cartridge
tapes primarily for auto
use. At the
same time, traditional open-reel tapes
for high
quality home
listening
will
also enjoy substantial gains.
Sparked
by
auto
industry
promo-
tion, popular new cartridge tapes will
account for approximately 65 percent
of
1967
industry
sales,
according
to
the Ampex exec.
“Automobile
stereo
systems
have
contributed greatly to increased gen-
eral interest in tapes,” Hall said. “In-
dustry
sources
estimate
that
from
300,000 to 400,000 of the automobiles
sold
in
1967
will
include
eight-track
stereo
tape
playback
units.
Auto
stereo systems added
after purchase
will add another 650,000 four-track or
eight-track playback units.
“Cartridge tapes
will
also
find
in-
creasing use in the home,” the Ampex
executive
said. “A number
of manu-
facturers are offering home cartridge
units compatible with
auto
playback
systems. While
sound
quality
is
not
equal
to
that
of
open-reel
tapes,
cartridge tapes are
entirely satisfac-
tory on the road and for casual home
listening.”
Ampex
Stereo
Tapes
offers
more
than 1,600 selections of all types from
47 recording
labels. The new Ampex
cartridge tape catalog, begun in mid-
1966, already has more than 200 selec-
tions
from
such
labels
as
London,
MGM, Verve, A & M and Vanguard.
Substantial
additions
will
be
made
during
1967.
The Ampex Stereo Tapes duplicat-
ing
center
is
located
in
Elk
Grove
Village, Illinois.

Most Australians
are, of course, very interested to see that American star
Bobby Hebb is now out with his version of “Ooh La La” which has been such
a fantastic smash here for Normie Rowe, presently in England.

in turn is part of the publishing house of J. Albert & Son Pty, Ltd.), had re-
cently returned to London to assist
in the production

Phil Skaff Sets-Up New Label
PHIL SKAFF
NEW YORK—Phil
Skaff, former vp
and board member of Liberty Records,
has
organized
his
own
label.
Inde-
pendence Records, based out of Hol-
lywood.
Skaff told Cash Box that he
is
al-
ready negotiating with more than one
indie producer and
artist and should
have
further announcements regard-
ing talent roster within the next ten
days.
Label
will
“not
discriminate
in
terms
of good
product—^whatever
is
current.
Is
it and can
it
sell? Those
are the fundamentals in this and any
other industry.”
According to Skaff, the label’s name
Independence expresses
his emphasis
for
utilizing “the best sources
avail-
able
in
independent
production
of
product,
as
well
as
other
areas
of
manufacturing and distribution.”
Distributor appointments have
not
been made, he said, due to early inter-
est of other record companies to
dis-

NARM To Honor
Monty, Marek
NEW YORK—Mantovani and George
Marek will receive special Presidential
Awards
at the NARM
(rack-jobber)
Awards Banquet during the
associa-
tion’s upcoming confab in Los Angeles
(Mar. 5-10). The award to Marek, vp
of RCA and former vp and
general
manager
of
RCA
Victor
Records,
marks the
first time a disk exec has
received this recognition.
NARM
makes
the
Presidential
MANTOVANI
GEORGE MAREK
Award on
the
basis
of
“unique
and
outstanding contributions to the
field
of
recorded
music.”
Mantovani
is
being specifically honored for his 20th
anniversary year as an artist on Lon-
don Records. He and
his wife, Wini-
fred,
will
fly
directly
from
London
and
participate
in
entire
convention
program.
In
previous
years,
Frank
Sinatra and Mitch
Miller have
been
similarly honored by NARM.
John
Billinis,
president
of NARM,
will make the presentations to Manto-
vani and Marek on Thursday evening,
March
9,
at which time NARM
will
also make
its
annual
“best
selling”
artist and
label
awards
in
23
cate-
gories.
Marek keynoted the NARM conven-
tions of 1962 and 1964.
AH CBS Disk Units Contributed
To Record Soies Yeor In 1966
NEW YORK—1966 was the best sales
year
in the history
of CBS Records
Clive Davis, vp and general manager,
reported an increase of 22%
in
sales
over 1965. He said that all units under
the CBS Records banner “contributed
significantly”
to
the
year-end
tally.
These include Columbia Records, CBS
Legacy Collection, Epic Records, Date
Records
and
Columbia
Masterworks
Audio Products.
While looking forward to a “broad-
ening and strengthening” of the label’s
catalog and a “concentrated
effort
in
the
development
of new
artists”
in
1967,
Davis
cautions
that what “we
must
especially
do
in
1967
is make
sure
that
the growth we
experience
does not become a profitless prosper-
ity.”
“It
is
this
problem
and
chal-
lenge,” he says, “that everyone in the
industry must
iDe prepared to meet
if
1967
is
to achieve
its
full potential.”

Records
maintained
a
leading

in

with a stream

and albums by leading artists includ-

Paul
Revere
and
The
Raiders,
Simon and Garfunkel, The Byrds and
The
Cyrkle. Columbia
also

in

Robert

Two

Columbia

John

and
Jim

scored
heavily
in
the
competitive
Popular

Both
Davidson
and

with
their
Columbia
LPs.

Sherman Heads WB Sales
NEW YORK—Dick Sherman has been
named
national
sales
manager
of
Warner
Bros.
Records,
reports Mike
Maitland, president. Sherman has been
upped from the post of eastern district
sales
manager,
working
out
of
the
label’s offices in New York. While the
appointment
is
effective immediately,
he does not report
to the west coast
until mid-March. His successor in the
east was not named. Sherman
fills a
post vacated by Gene Block six months
ago. The
10-year music
business vet
formerly held posts in a sales capacity
with
the
Columbia
and
Mercury
labels. In his new post, he will direct
the
sales
activities
of WB,
Reprise
and Loma, and will be responsible for
liasion
with
the
company’s
distribs
and district sales managers.
DICK SHERMAN

Kapp Re-Elected RIAA Prexy, Slate Returned
TOP HITS OF 1967
NEW YORK—Dave Kapp,
president
of Kapp
Records,
Inc.
has been
re-
elected president of the Record Indus-
try
Association
of
America
for
a
second one-year term. The entire slate
of officers who served during 1966 was
also re-elected.
Members of RIAA, who account for
better than 90 per cent of the records
made and
sold
in the United
States,
also voted into office all but one of the
directors who
served
last
year. The
new director
is Norman Racusin,
re-
cently named the new vice president
and general manager of RCA Victor
Records. He succeeds George Marek,
previous head of RCA Records.
The other directors are: Clive Davis,
vice
president and
general manager,
CBS Records; Herman
Glass,
assist-
ant
vice president and general man-
ager,
Ansonia
Records;

B.

of

land Records; Alan Livingston, presi-

one-year
term
include:

Capitol
Forms
Real
Estate
Dept.
HOLLYWOOD—Robert E. Carp, vice
president
and
general
counsel
of
Capitol
Records,
has
announced
the
establishment
of
a
corporate
real
estate department to handle the real
estate needs of all corporations in the
Capitol family, including construction
of buildings and related
facilities.
At
the
same
time,
Carp
also
re-
ported
that
Philip
Koenig
will
join
Capitol in the newly-created position
of
director
of
corporate
real
estate.
Koenig
holds
a
B.S.
in
architecture
from the University of Illinois and a
Masters
Degree
from
the
Harvard
Graduate
School
of
Design. He was
formerly
vice
president
of
National
Properties
of
Beverly
Hills. Among
his projects with the
latter company
were
the
complex
comprising
the
Palm Springs Spa Hotel and Mineral
Baths,
and
the
Rox
San
Medical
Building in Beverly Hills. Koenig will
headquarter in Hollywood and report
directly to Carp.
Tom Springfield
In N.Y.
NEW YORK—Tom Springfield, writer
of the smash hit “Georgy Girl” by the
Seekers, was
in town
last week be-
fore returning to
his native England
on the
17th. The busy tunesmith was
here to search for new Seekers mate-
rial and to lobby “Georgy Girl,” which
has been nominated for an Academy
Award. When asked about the song’s
chances for winning, Springfield said,
“Well,
I
hope we win ...
I
don’t
know
.
.
.
it’s
nice
to be nominated
anyway, but it would be even nicer to
win.”
While in Gotham, Springfield made
the rounds of the trades, and
filled a
week-long schedule
of press and TV
interviews. High points of the week’s
activities
were
appearances
on
the
Clay Cole and Joe Franklin TV’ers.
Springfield
is
arranger,
producer
and musical advisor to the Seekers.

during
an RCA
Victor
recording
session
in
Manhattan’s Webster
Hall
are Nick
Palmer and Joe Rene. This
is Nick’s
first RCA Victor album and contains
his current “Worlds Of Time” single.
The album was
supervised by Ernie
Altschuler and produced by Joe Rene.

(Continued from page
12)
JOHN
NICE
OF
BURLINGTON
MUSIC (BRITAIN)
I
have
nothing
but
praise
for
MIDEM. During the week
I acquired
from Igloo Music
(France)
rights to
"Manchester Liverpool” for
all Eng-
lish speaking countries including The
U.S.A. and Clanada. Marcell Stellman
was
commissioned
to
write
English
lyrics and already one British and one
American record has been
set.
I be-
gan
negotiations
for
the
acquisition
of an American catalogue which
is to
be
finalised
in
London
immediately.
The highlight of the week for me was
the discussions which took place with
Spanish
and
South
American
pub-
lishers with a view to setting up
of-
fices in those territories. Next year
I
would
like
to
see more
independent
producers and A & R men present and
Burlington Music will be there with a
much better presented stand than we
had
this year.
BRIGITTE BERTHOLIER OF
BA-
GATELLE (FRANCE)
Our
participation
at MIDEM
has
been worth while. We have signed a
deal
for
exclusive
representation
of
all Joe Dassin material and signed a
contract with Teldec for France Gall
and a recording in German is set for
next month. We
have
arranged
for
the
release
of
The
London
Dance
Orchestre
recorded
independently
in
London by AIR Productions to be
is-
sued
in Spain, Canada and Germany.
We
also
completed
several
separate
deals for songs.
ALBERTO MARUANI
OF
PERU-
DISCOS SA (PERU)
I went to San Remo and found that
everyone was going to Cannes. I came
and have completed several deals
in-
cluding a catalo^e deal with Palette
Records of Belgium and am also
set-
ting up
a
publishing
deal for
Peru.
MIDEM has enabled me
to meet
all
the European record company repre-
sentatives and music publishers which
would
have
taken
me
months
of
travelling to accomplish.
BOB KINGSTON
OF SOUTHERN
MUSIC (BRITAIN)
MIDEM provided
a wonderful
op-
portunity to meet all our representa-
tives under one
roof. Those
present
were
Ralph Marbot
(Germany),
Al-
bert Carish
(Italy), Han Dunk
(Hol-
land), Mr. Brunner (Switzerland) and
Felix
Faeq
(Belgium).
It
has
been
wonderfully
organised
and
it
has
made me
realise
that
record
com-
panies, who are more used to taking
in
such
conventions,
knew how
to
make their stands attractive whereas
music
publishers
were way
behind.
We have learned a lot from the
first
MIDEM
and
will
certainly
be
back
next year with
a much
better
pre-
sentation.
JOAQUIN
MERINO
OF
ZAFIRO
(SPAIN)
I played the
tajoes of Los Brincos
which were made in England to sev-
eral people at MIDEM and have had
many
offers
for
international
repre-
sentation,
as
well
as
other
Zafiro
artistes
Massiel,
Los
Relquampalos
and
Mariso.
I
spend many
months
travelling
around
the
world
and
MIDEM
has
enabled
me
to
meet
many people
I would not meet nor-
mally because of shortage of time.
FRANCIS DREYFUS OF LABRA-
DOR (FRANCE)
MIDEM
is an excellent idea and
is
the only way in which to meet people
from all countries at one time. I have
had talks with A1 Gallico and United
Artistes
for
representation
of my
original French copyrights but
I am
disappointed not to
see more Ameri-
cans
present.
I have
also
negotiated
deals
for
soundtrack
recordings
in
various countries. I shall certainly be
at
MIDEM
next
year
and
hope
America
will
be
better
represented
too.
MR. GURTLER OF SAAR
A
most
successful

In

I have met

Next

As also President of Chambre Syn-
dicale
Des
Editeurs
De
Music
Leguere France
I have nothing but

It is very efficient and has done

industry.
I have
found
it
has
been
the
unexpected
which has been such an asset for in-
stance the success of the artistes tak-
ing part in the galas who have been

the

composers

in-
cluding Hubert Giraud who made

FELIX FAECQ OF WORLD MUSIC
(BELGIUM)
MIDEM
is
something
which
has
been lacking from the profession and
it
is
our
good
fortune
that
it
has
happened now. The

that music
publishers and record companies can
get together under one roof can only
be
good
for
the
industry.
Since
be-
ing
at MIDEM
I
have
negotiated
deals with
12
different
countries
in-
cluding those behind the iron curtain.
This is good business completed in the
shortest possible time.

100% Booked For
’68
From these observations
is can be
clearly seen that MIDEM has proved
to be an unqualified success resulting
in a vast volume of business.
It was
not without
its mishaps however. On
Wednesday morning—^the third day of
the
exhibition—due to a
strike there
was
no
electricity.
Telephone
com-
munication was impossible, turntables
were
silent
and
many
exhibitors
called
it a day whilst
others
carried
on by candlelight. Happily, however,
the
current was
switched on
during
the afternoon.

Muggsy Spanier
Dies
SAUSALITO, CAL.—Muggsy Spanier,
Dixieland
jazz
cornetist,
died
in
his
home
on
Feb.
12,
apparently
of
a
heart attack.
Spanier grew up in Chicago just as
the
first generation of jazz musicians
began streaming
into the
city. As
a
teenager he played with Louis Arm-
strong, Joe
(King)
Oliver, Jelly Roll
Morton, and Sidney Bechet.
The
cornetist was born
in Chicago
on Nov.
9,
1906, according
to Who’s
Who
in America. However,
his
step-
son, Tom
Cries, a
film
director,
said
Spanier was 64.
During
the
nineteen-twenties,
the
artist
played
with
Elmer
Schoebel,
Sig Meyers, Charlie Straight, and Ray
Miller. He
recorded
with
the
Buck-
town
Five
and
toured
with
the Ted
Lewis band from 1929 to 1936. In 1941
he formed a big band to play his own
“up-from-New Orleans” music. During
World War
II
he
returned
to
small
bands.
Besides
his
widow,
Ruth,
and
his
stepson,
Spanier
is
survived
by
another
stepson.
Buddy
Charles,
a
musician in Chicago.

ai'tist’s

100,000
shortly
before

Of

and

tory problems.

On
the
back
of
a new
Victor
re-
lease,
“The
Caribbean
Suite,”
pro-
ducer
Brad
McCuen
takes
special
pains
to mention the
invaluable help
he

from
Fred
Norsworthy,
our
subject
for
this
column.
In
all
fields
there
are
always
the
unsung
and
often unappreciated
people who,
in spite of a lack of recognition, con-
tinue to serve the cause in which they
believe.
Such
a man
is
Fred
Nors-
worthy!
If what
is written here
will
serve to bring him to the attention of
the many instead of the few, the time
and effort will be well spent.
Down From Canada
A Londoner by birth, Fred migrated
to Canada in 1954, whence he came to
the States
in 1961. Since then he has
been living in New York City, where
he has continued to be a vital part of
the
jazz
scene,
albeit
in
a
less than
sensational manner. For the past sev-
eral years Norsworthy has been doing
independent promotion for Dick Bock
and his Pacific Jazz label. And he has
been
doing
it
the way
it
should
be
done,
by
personal
contact
with
the
deejays and the retailers in the area,
the people who make things happen.
All
of
this
is done
in
his
free
time,
his regular job being one of the better
informed
salesmen
with
the
Sam
Goody
record
stores
in New
York
City.
Fred’s
first
interest
in
jazz began
with
a
love
for
swing
music
a
la
Goodman, Dorsey, and Shaw. “I heard
my first bop record, a 78 on Dial, and
from then on
I bought every modern
jazz 78
I could get my hands on. That
first record was Bird’s Nest by Char-
lie
Parker,”
Norsworthy
related.
“LP’s from the States were available
only by mail,” he continued, “and they
were really a luxury so
I bought only
English LP’s and
78’s.
Hell, the
78’s
even cost twelve and
six, that’s about
two and a half bucks.”
Tutored On Alto
It seemed a natural question to ask
if his love of jazz was a result of his
playing an instrument. “I studied alto
for
five
years
with
a
professional
tutor, from age thirteen to eighteen,”
he answered. “Then
I did my military
service, two years in the army. No,
I
couldn’t play
in the military because
it would have meant signing up for a
regular
tour,
ten
years minimum.
I
had no eyes for that,” he hastened to
assure me.
In
1954, when he was twenty two,
Norsworthy moved to Toronto, where
he had a
sister living
there. By -day
he
did
office
work,
clerking,
filing,
etc., and
at night he worked
at pro-
moting live jazz presentations. In 1958
he
initiated a
jazz
policy
at
a
place
called
Jazz
City
in
Toronto.
After
that he branched out to present jazz
at
Le
Cor
Door,
.also
in
Toronto,
where he presented for the local gen-
trv
such
jazz
lurhinaries
as
Donald
Byrd, Art Blakey, Zoots Sims, Lennie
Tristano, Johnny
Griffen,
and
Dizzy
Reece.
Formed Jazzline
Later in 1958 Fred Norsworthy em-
barked on
his most ambitious under-
taking,
the
institution
of
a
jazz
re-
cording label. Jazzline. In partnership
with
three
other men,
one
of whom
was his friend Dave Bailey, the
well
known
drummer,
he
produced
seven
12" albums. Jazz
collectors who own
these albums will attest to their high
quality,
as
will
I.
The
dates
were
done
in New York City and the
dis-
tribution was set up to emanate from
Canada.
Jazzline had
thirty-six
dis-
tributors
throughout
the
United
States
and
practically
all
of
their
business was conducted by phone and
mail. The net result was that he
lost
about $10,000 in two years, and it cer-
tainly wasn’t because
the
recordings
weren’t of top
flight quality. The
al-
bums
featured
Dave
Bailey,
Rocky
Boyd,
the
late Frank Haynes, Duke
Pearson,
and
Walter
Bishop,
Jr.
These
five
were
released
and
two
others, one bv
Willie Wilson, an
ex-
traordinary
trombonist,
and
a Duke
Pearson
trio
date,
remained
in
the
can and were
never
released
on
the
label.
In
spite
of
the
negative
re-
sponse
to his
efforts to produce good
things
and
further
the
cause,
Nors-
worthy
never
went
sour
on
jazz.
Maybe
he was
a
little
bugged
with
the
people
in
the
record community
who
led him down
the
not
so
rosey
nath
to insolvency, but he never
lost
his
faith
in
good
jazz.
Ultimately,
t'ne
Jazzline
masters
were
sold
to
Britisher
Alan
Bates,
and
I
might
add
for
a
pitifully
small amount
of
money.
McCuen Hears Graham
In
December
of
1964
Norsworthy
approached
Brad
McCuen
at
Victor
and played
for him
the
original
10"
Esquire album of the Kenny Graham
Afro

on

At

voiced the opinion that such a project
could be done

that

would be highly musical and still have
a
gx-eat
commei’cial
appeal. McCuen
agreed and said that he was interested
in the project. He commissioned Nors-
woi-thy to set things in motion by ap-
proaching
the
musicians
whom
he
thought could get it done in the man-
ner in which they had discussed. After
many abortive attempts, all time con-
suming because these matters have a
way of eating up weeks, months, and
sometimes

Fred
finally
con-
nected with Harold Vick who was most
enthusiastic. Vick threw himself into
project
and
spent two
solid months
re-ari-anging the
entire

ing
the
hai-monies which were
done

in
1953. The net
result
is
an excellent album which I recommend
most highly!
No

This

the
intei'est
of

is

His experiences have
foi’tified his

I
solve and

When

Club

You have

which ends up sounding

I hear evei’y new jazz i-elease, at least

in terms of jazz, fx-om my owm stand-

of course. Ninety
pex’cent

tx’ades and while putting

Both

I’m

thex-e

Fred

Mr. Machijiri, president of King Records here, presented a Golden Record
to Joan Baez on Jan. 28 at Tokyo Hilton Hotel in honor of the sales of 150,000
of the LP “Joan Baez Golden Album.” The
artist
left Japan
Feb.
2
after a
successful tour throughout the main
cities of Japan.
The Grand Prix Award, which
is given to the best local record of the year,
was awarded
to “Muhyo”
on
Nippon
Victor,
written
by
Tetsuo Miyagawa,
composed by Ichiro Tone and sung by Yukio Hashi, the top artist of Nippon
Victor. This
is the 4th time that Nippon Victor has received the award
in the
8 years of
its
existence.
Relating to the other local awards of 1966, Composers Award was given to
Kuranosuke Hamaguchi for “Baraga Saita” and “Star Flamenco,” and Lyric
Award was given to Tokiko Iwatani for “Kimito Itsumademo” and “Aitakute,
Aitakute.” The Arrangement Award went
to Kenichiro Morioka
for “Kimito
Itsumademo.”
Nippon Columbia came out with an extraordinary release of “Blue Comets
Recital” which was the real recording of the very popular
recital show held
in Nov. last year at Tokyo Kyoritsu Kodo Hall. The LP includes recent smash
hit tune “Blue Eyes” and 11 others.
U.
S. Capitol Records
is reportedly releasing “Stereo March LP Spectacle”
in March with the Japanese Self-Guard Army Central Music Band. The LP
includes “Do Re Mi,” “Saint Louis Blues” and others.
Teichiku Records came out with “Countess From Hong Kong,” sound track
of the Charles Chaplin film, scheduled to be released the middle of March.
Teichi Records released LP “Folk Album” by very popular pianist Hachidai
Nakamura and
his New Sons which
included “Donna
Donna,”
“500
Miles,”
“Greensleeves” and 9 others. Hachidai Nakamura
is also well-known as a lead-
ing composer here in Japan.
Nippon
Victor
released
11 LPs on
Feb.
15 under
the
series
title
“Victor
Grand Prix Series” which was the re-formation (or re-release)
of masterpieces
on RCA records. Among the 11 LPs are artists such as Belafonte, Glenn Miller,
Perry Como, Chet Atkins and Art Blakey.

This

and

Dassin
pro-
vided a spectacular

to MIDEM
1967.
For the
first time
since the
estab-
lishment of the iron curtain, MIDEM
gave the chance of assessing properly
what
is going on with
the exchange
of pop
music, between
Western and
Eastern
countries.
Czechoslovakia,
Yugoslavia,
Hun-
gary and Poland were in fact officially
represented at MIDEM. Moreover Mr.
Chmelev,
the commercial
representa-
tive
of
Soviet music
in
France, was
at MIDEM as an observer.
It
wasn’t
difficult
to
find
out
at
MIDEM that
all the countries behind
the curtain are today very much after
Western
pop
music.
Eastern
public
require
it and
even
unwillingly—be-
cause
it means
a
loss
of
hard
cur-
rency for a kind of goods considered
not
essential—the
various
Govern-
ments cannot deny
it. Eastern
coun-
tries are therefore buying pop music
from West and through MIDEM they
found
a
good
opportunity
of
selling
also
their music
to
West.
Obviously
the
aim
of
Eastern
countries
is
to
balance the exchange of incoming and
outgoing music;
but notwithstanding
their
efforts,
the
balance
is
still
lai’gely favourable
to West.
The
most
active
country
of
the
Eastern
group,
in
commercial
deal-
ings for pop music with the West,
is
still
Yugoslavia.
But
Czechoslovakia
is
quickly
catching
up
with
Poland
and Hungary
following.
Mr.
Chmelev,
from
the
U.S.S.R.,
has declared that next year his coun-
try
will
be
commercially
present
at
MIDEM,
providing
they
can
display
their
classical
music
catalogue
as
well.
Another
important
aspect
of
MIDEM
for
Eastern
countries
was
the
opportunity they were
given
for
booking
Western
artists
for
their
Festivals of pop music. Good dealings
apparently
have
been made
for
the
Festivals of Bratislava and Budapest.

Cash Box—March
4,
1967

===== PAGE 10 =====
1
1967: Revival Year For Keat-Modern
TOP HiTS OF M967
HOLLYWOOD—Kent-Modern, a
dor-
mant and virtual outcast in the R&B
field
a
year
ago,
is
bouncing
back
onto
the
national
charts. And
with
renewed vigor. “We’re definitely back
in the business,” says president Saul
Bahari,
“and
starting
to
make
our
share of the noise around.”
Firms,
which
include
the
Crown
pressing plant
(averaging between
2
and 3 million gross each year) should
“realistically” add another million and
a half in
’67 as a result of regenera-
tion
in
the
R&B
market.
“We’ve
been in the blues business for over 20
years,”
says
Bahari,
“and
in
the
early days we were one
of the more
prominent
labels. We
expect
to
be
up
there
again—and
perhaps
before
the year
is out.”
Formed
In
’44
Modern, which started
in
’44
(with
RPM joining
in
’49) were both basi-
cally R&B
labels
and featured
such
artists
as
Hadda
Brooks,
Johnny
Moore and the Blazers with
Charles
Brown, Gene Phillips, Jimmy Wither-
spoon, Lightning
Hopkins, John Lee
Hooker, the Teen Queens, Etta James,
Jesse
Belvin,
the
Jacks,
the
Cadets
and B. B. King. In
’61 the Kent label
was added, primarily for B. B. King
who
was,
until
recently,
Kent-Mod-
ern’s
only
artist. Though he has not
been on
the
label for
the
past four
years
(King
is now an ABC
talent),
Kent has enough King
sides
to
con-
tinue releasing his singles for several
more years. Newest is “Jungle,” a six
year
old master
overdubbed
to
offer
a more
current
sound.
According
to
Bahari, King continues to sell a mini-
mum of 75,000 with each release and,
occasionally,
will blossom
forth with
a “giant”—“Rock Me Baby,” released
just a couple of years back, sold well
over 400,000.
Just about
six months
ago,
partly
as a result of continued requests from
distributors, Kent
and Modern were
reactivated.
First
single was
Lowell
Fulsom’s “The Tramp”
(produced by
Jules Bahari), an R&B smash which
also
climbed
onto
the
pop
charts.
“Between
’57
and
’66 we
had
been
sitting on the fence,” says
Saul,
“in-
volved
with
the
Cadet
(budget
priced)
LP’s. And doing well enough.
But
the
Fulsom
single
provided
the
incentive and enthusiasm for the
re-
formation.”
(New
single
by
Fulsom
is
“Make A
Little
Love.”)
Current
roster
includes
Fulsom,
Mary
Love,
Z.
Z.
Hill, Vernon Garrett and Willie
Garland, a “down home blues”
artist
whose
initial
single
is “Black Widow
Spider.”
Saul
Bahari
has
just come
off
a
promotion tour which covered Chicago,
Detroit, N.Y., Philadelphia, Baltimore
and
Washington,
with
brother
Joe
Bahari
covering
the
south. And
re-
cently
appointed
A&R
chief
Mike
Akopoff
(former
producer
for
Ray
Charles’
Tangerine
label)
in
Pitts-
burgh, Cleveland, Oklahoma and N.Y.
where
he
also
contacted music
pub-
lishers,
searching
for new
material.
George Panos is general manager and
sales manager in charge of developing
new product. Current LP catalog
in-
cludes about 18 titles but “it’s not just
a
question
of
turning
out
product.
We’ve had a lot of experience with the
LP business and we know you have to
have something there to sell. We think
we
have
the
product. We know the
bag—it’s R&B—and

Stevie Wonder To Star
At Cornell
Concert
DETROIT—To culminate a
series
of
programs
scheduled by
Cornell
Uni-
versity on behalf of “Negro Heritage
Week,”
Detroit’s
Stevie Wonder has
been invited to headline a special con-
cert
in the
University’s
Field House,
Friday evening, March
3, which
will
feature Motown recording talent.
According to Samuel Berger, presi-
dent of Cornell’s interfraternity coun-
cil, the 16-year-old artist was invited
to
participate
as a
representative
of
the Negro
teenagers
because
of
his
extraordinary
talents
as
a
singer,
composer, and musician.
Wonder, who was recently selected
as a NARAS Grammy Awards
final-
ist for 1966 for the best R&B record-
ing and the best R&B solo vocal per-
formance,
will
sing
“Uptight,”
the
song for which he was nominated, in
addition to his other Tamla recording
hit, “A
Place
In The
Sun” and
his
latest release, “Travelin’ Man.”
Others on the program will include
Motown’s Tammi Terrell, Jimmy Ruf-
fin, Gladys Knight and the Pips.
SAC Inks Nine Jazzmen;
Stephens Heads Jazz Dept.
NEW YORK—Personal manager John
Levy and Don
Soviero,
president
of
SAC
(Shaw
Artists
Corp.)
have
jointly announced the signing of nine
jazz performers. At the same time,
it
was revealed that Levy’s
aide, War-
ren Stephens, will leave the manage-
ment firm
to become head
of SAC’s
jazz department.
The
nine
jazz
artists
(with
their
record
affiliations)
who
will now be
represented
exclusively by SAC,
are
Ray Bryant
(Cadet), Kenny
Burrell
(Verve), Lou Donaldson (Blue Note),
Shirley Horn
(ABC), Ahmad Jamal
(Cadet),
Yusef
Lateef
impulse),
Herbie Mann
(Atlantic), Wes Mont-
gomery
(Verve)
and
Lovelace Wat-
kins. Mike
St. Shaw & the Prophets,
an R & B act that records for Capitol,
was also signed to SAC at the same
time.
The
jazz
booking
agency
already
has such
artists on
its roster as Ro-
land Kirk, Les McCann, Jack McDuff,
Jimmy McGriff, Rufus Harley, Sonny
Rollins and Sonny
Stitt.
Warren
Stephens, who
is
leaving
John
Levy’s
personal
management
office
to take up
the reins
of SAC’s
augmented jazz department,
is a for-
mer professional guitarist who headed
his own booking agency in Columbus,
Ohio for five years prior to spending
three years with Levy’s firm as asso-
ciate.
In
his
new
position,
he
will
supervise
all
activities
in every area
of the entertainment
field for SAC’s
jazz
talent with
particular emphasis
on packaging.

Following the introduction of the Stax label in Britain, the “Hit The Road
Stax” package tour hits town on March 17th thru April
9th featuring
Otis
Reading, Percy
Sledge, Booker
T. and the M.G.s, Eddie Floyd and Sam and
Dave. The three-hour show
is set for a nation-wide tour and Polydor will be
issuing many
Stax

including

well as

Manchurian-born group the Beegees get their first release on Polydor with
“Spicks and Specks” which has
also been recorded by O’Hara’s Playboys on
Fontana) and the
first non-American artist to be signed by Atlantic Records
Sharnon Tandy makes his debut with “Toe Hold.” Polydor also report healthy

of
their “Good Times”
film
scheduled

in April when Polydor will issue the soundtrack album.
Writers Ken Howard and Alan Blaikley and publisher Harold Geller of Lynn
Music
delighted with the success of “Save Me” by Dave
Dee, Dozy, Beaky,
Mick and Tich in Germany where it is heading the charts. On March 3rd they
fly to Germany to collect their Radio Luxembourg Silver Lion award—the first
time that a group has been so honored. Their latest single “Touch Me Touch
Me”
is again
a Howard-Blaikley composition published by Lynn and issued
on Fontana.
Dick James has formed a new record company to be known as This Record

will be
issued by

in no way
aifects or alters James’ participation with Larry Page in the Page One label,

POLAND—Plans are in hand for the
7th International Song Festival, which
will take place in Sopot, Poland from
August
17
to
20.
The
festival
will
be
divided
into
four
parts
“Inter-
national Day”
during
which
singers
from
all
over
the
world
will
sing
songs

by

native
com-
posers;
“Polish
Day” when
singers
perform
songs by
Polish
composers;
“No

Song” when
singers will perform songs from their
repertoire in an optional language and
“Records Day” when singers will rep-
resent record companies and sing the
I
top songs of that company. The Festi-
I
val
will
take
place
in

Forest
j

MEXICO
AUSTRALIA
Since the Australian Record Cempany boys
decided
to work on “Summer
Wine”
(the reverse of “Sugar Town”) by Nancy Sinatra, they find they now
have a terrific hit on their hands. “Summer Wine” is catching all kinds of air-
play and is making a bold bid for top ten ratings.
Local
girl Bev Harrell continues to make
strong headway with her HMV
release of “What Am I Doing Here With You.” It
is now showing well in
all
States and assured of national acceptance.
Local
releases
of
late through EMI
include Buddy England with “Movin’
Man” (We note that a
version has
just been
issued
in America by Dion).
Dinah Lee
is
out with
her
version
of
“98.6.”
Cheryl Gray has “The
Real
Thing” and “Move On”; Jade Hurley is on HMV with “True Love Begins” and
“It’s Too Cold”; Des Ellis has an instrumental release with “Mr. Chihuahua”
c/w “Sidewalk Cafe.” The Twilights, an Australian group, are heard with two
sides they recorded during their recent visit to England: “What’s Wrong With
The Way I Live” and “9.50.”
RCA
are plugging away
at
the new
Elvis
Presley
single
“Indescribably
Blue” and “Fools Fall In Love.” There
is also a heavy campaign behind both
the mono
and
stereo
albums
featuring
the
soundtrack
material from
the
Presley
film, “California Holiday.” On the
local scene with RCA, they have
Gino
Ginetti
on two
singles,
the
English and
Italian
versions
of
“Doesn’t
Anybody Understand” and “II Mondo”; whilst Ernie Sigley has “A Boy With-
out A Girl” and “True Love,” written by Frankie Davidson.
It now appears that the newie by the Beatles, “Strawberry Field Forever”
and “Penny Lane”
will be
released here by EMI
during
the
first week
in
March
.
.
. copyright in both titles is held in this territory by Northern Songs
through the Leeds Music
Organization.
Local artist Sandy Scott has his new single out on the ATA label, distributed
nationally by Festival;
titles are “In The Arms Of Love” and “Such A_ Lovely
Night.” The topside of the
latest issue
is composed by Henry
Mancini, Jay
Livingston and Ray Evans, and
is from the film “What Did You Do In The
War Daddy?” Copyright
in the song
is owned by Chappell &
Co. who have
also issued the sheet music.
Local group the Id are having their best result to date on
disc_ with their
rendition
of “Big Time
Operator.” The
release
is
on
the
receiving end
of
some solid disc-jockey attention and could well become a national success for
the group.

ash Box RECORD REVIEWS

Pick of the Week
CRY TO ME (3:09)
[Mellin and Progressive BMI—Berns]
NO ONE COULD EVER LOVE YOU
(3:29)
[Web IV and Rittenhouse BMI—Berns, Ragavoy]
FREDDIE SCOTT (Shout 211)
Stock as much of this one as you can get, Freddie Scott should rocket
to the top of the charts with this smooth, shuffling, soulful, tear-stained,
pulsating, Blues-romancer called “Cry To Me.” On the reverse, “No One
Could Ever Love You” holds more of the same.
YOUNGER GENERATION BLUES
(2:49)
[Dialogue BMI—Ian]
I’LL GIVE YOU A STONE IF YOU’LL THROW IT
(3:45) [Dialogue BMI—Ian]
JANIS IAN (Verve Folkways 5041)
Young writer/songstress Janis Ian, riding close on the ground broken
by her “Society’s Child” deck, offers a strong, driving, rocking, poignant,
social comment venture that should get plenty of spins and thus expand
her already wide following. “I’ll Give You A Stone
If You’ll Throw It”
offers more from the same bag.
MAKE LOVE TO ME (2:18)
[Melrose ASCAP—Norvas, Copeland,
Roppolo, Mares, Pollack, Brunies, Stitzel, Melrose]
TEACH ME TONIGHT (2:21) [MCA ASCAP—Cahn, DePaul]
JOHNNY THUNDER & RUBY WINTERS (Diamond 218)
A strong, thumping, wailing,
soulful R&B workout, “Make Love To
Me” should carry Johnny Thunder and Ruby Winters to the top of the
charts and get plenty of spins. Over on the other
side, “Teach Me To-
night” is a medium-paced, bluesy reworking of this
oldie.
BEND IT (2:25)
[Spectorius, BMI—Blaikley]
I WOULDN’T BE A FOOL
(2:13)
[Kita, BMI—Redd, Torok]
BARBARA EDEN (Dot 16999)
Newcomer lass Barbara Eden could
rise
like a puff of smoke (from
a bottle)
to the top of the charts with this steady, building, thumping,
driving workout entitled “Bend It.” The reverse of the sleeve holds in-
structions for the “Bend It” dance. On the
flip, “I Wouldn’t Be A Fool”
is a smooth, melodic outing
SHE’S GOT THE TIME (SHE’S GOT THE CHANGES)
(1:50)
[Good Sam, BMI—Shipley]
POOR
(York 402)
Might be the right time for the Poor to ride to the top of the record
S
ile with
“She’s Got The Time
(She’s Got The Changes.)”
Side
is a
lumping, medium-paced, rhythmic, pounding rock workout that should
prove a pleaser.
No information available on the flip side at this time.
THIRD MAN THEME (2:37) [Chappel & Co. ASCAP—Karas]
WILDWOOD FLOWER
(2:55)
[Shelby Singleton BMI—Singleton, Venneri, Carl]
TENNESSEE GUITARS
(Bell 665)
Already starting to kick up a fuss, this revamping of the well-known
“Third Man Theme” could make national names for the Tennessee Gui-
tars. Tune’s built-in sales potential gets an added boost with a flavorful
rock treatment.
Flip
is a folksy version
of the
traditional “Wildwood
Flower.”
LISTEN BOY
(2:15)
[Jaypaul SESAC—Brynner]
BOBBY ARVON (MTA 1,19)
MTA makes its first strong bid for honors with Top 40 music lovers
as a result of “Listen Boy.” Bobby Arvon does an attractive job on this
potent, swinging ballad. Flip information
is not available
at this
time.
TOUCH ME, HOLD ME, KISS ME
(2:30)
[Jobette, BMI—Redd, McCoy,
Crosby]
WHAT AM I GONNA DO WITH YOU, HEY BABY (2:38)
[Screen Gems-Columbia, BMI—Goffin, Teittleman]
INSPIRATIONS
(Black Pearl 100)
Both the newly-formed Black Pearl label and the Inspirations may well
come into the limelight via “Touch Me, Hold Me, Kiss Me.” The
girls
have an appealing sound, pointed up nicely on this pounding R&B-slanted
ode. “What Am
I Gonna Do With You, Hey Baby”
is a more subdued
stanza.

SHING-A-LING TIME
(2:35)
[Andros, BMI—DeCoteaux]

[DeCoteaux, Barkan]

The Liberty Belles ring out with a goodie that could break wide open.
Dubbed
“Shing-A-Ling,”
this
one
is
a
wild,

terpsichorean

with a pleasant sound.
GO GO RADIO MOSCOW (3:25)
THE SPOILER
(2:25)
[Last Resort, BMI—Labunski]
NIKITA THE K (Warner Bros. 7005)
Top 40 radio gets the “comrade-ly” treatment in this winning spoof. A
highly commercial item, the lid should definitely be in for heavy airplay
and top-notch sales. Flip is an instrumental version of the TV commercial
theme, done by the Friends of Ed Labunski.
THE WEATHER MAN (1:46) [Canada Ltd., BMI—Emmerson]
HALF PAST MIDNIGHT (2:13) [Canada Ltd., BMI—Emmerson]
STACCATOS (Tower 322)
The Staccatos offer a session here, titled “Weather Man,” that could
well launch the Staccatos into the ionosphere. This one is a soft, chamber
music
stanza, well handled by
the
group.
“Half Past Midnight”
is
a
swinging soft-rocker which also has lots of appeal.

last

4-Track Offers Rejected
We,
too, have
received
substantial
monetary
offers from those who seek
to
license
the
manufacture
of
our
catalog
in
the
4-track
format. We
have
rejected
these
offers
on
several
grounds. As a leader in this industry,
we cannot justify to ourselves the en-
couragement
of
dealers
to
invest
in
product in which we would not invest
ourselves.
Furthermore,
we
do
not
deem
it proper to encourage the con-
sumer
to
invest
in
product
bearing
our name for which we are not pre-
pared
to
assume
full
responsibility
with respect
to
quality and
satisfac-
tion.
Inasmuch
as we believe
in the
su-
periority
and
long
range
growth
of
Stereo
8, we
can
see
nothing
at
this
point
to
justify burdening
our-
selves,
our
distributors
and
our
re-
tailers
with
costly
and
unnecessary
duplication of our catalog in another
cartridge
format.
Concern Over Bootlegging
We
are
seriously
concerned
with
unauthorized, illegal dubbing of RCA
catalog
material
on
4-track
car-
tridges. RCA Victor
already has
de-
manded of the most flagrant violators
that
they
cease
such
practices
im-
mediately. We intend to institute legal
action
under
appropriate
circum-
stances
for
the
enforcement
of
our
rights
against unauthorized dubbing.
Furthermore, RCA Victor shall on
its
own
behalf—and
in
conjunction
with the Record Industry Association
of
America—redouble
its
efforts
to
secure in the Congress of the United
States remedial legislation which will
afford
uniform
protection
to
sound
recordings in
all jurisdictions.
This, we believe,
is the path of
re-
sponsibility.

RCA Cuts Coleman's
Classical
Jazz Work
NEW YORK—RCA
Victor
has
re-
corded a live performance which took
place Friday
night
(17)
the
Village
Theater
at
which
a
new
serious
classical
composition
for
woodwind
quintet by the famed jazz
innovator
Ornette
Coleman
received
its
world
premiere.
Title of the composition
is “Forms
In Sounds,” which was perfoi-med by
the
Philadelphia Woodwind
Quintet,
comprising members
of the Philadel-
phia Orchestra.
RCA Victor will soon studio record
two
other
new
classical
pieces
by
Coleman and the Philadelphia Cham-
ber Symphony quartet to complete the
album. These are “Space Flight” and
“Saints And
Soldiers.”
During the Friday night program,
works by Villa Lobos and Chambers
were
performed by
the
Quintet and
Coleman’s
trio.
The album of Coleman compositions
will
be
released on
the RCA
Victor
Red
Seal
label. Howard
Scott,
Red
Seal A&R producer, was in charge of
the live session in the theater and will
direct the
studio sessions.
Fall
release
of the album
is plan-
ned.
BluesWay Inks Roy Brown
NEW
YORK—ABC
Records’
new
BluesWay
label
has
signed
singer-
composer Roy Brown.
Since
his
last
single
in
1957, “Let The Four Winds
Blow,” the artist has been inactive in
the music business.
After
a
false
start
as
a
boxer.
Brown won an amateur contest with
his impressions of Bing Crosby. That
was
the
start
of
his show
business
career and his first job lasted for six-
teen months in Shreveport, La.
The trends
in music began
to
dis-
courage Brown
and he
slowly
with-
drew form the music business, cutting
short
his
career ten
years
ago. Lee
Magid, who manages
such
artists
as
Della
Reese
and
Ruth
Olay,
met
Brown recently and encouraged him to
make a comeback based on increased
enthusiasm
for the
blues
and
blues-
oriented recordings. The result
is the
singer’s first single release for Blues-
Way and the
first single on the new
label,
“New
Orleans
Woman”
and
“Standin’ On Broadway,” both com-
posed by Brown and marking his first
recording
in ten years.
The
single
will be followed by an
album on BluesWay for release
at a
later date, consisting entirely of Roy
Brown compositions.

FOCUS ON jazz
MORT FEGA illillill|||||lilllllllllllii ^
Several
months
ago,
concurrent
with the
first news release, we made
mention of the reincarnation of Jazz
At The Philharmonic. At the time we
did not go into depth, mentioning only
that once JATP would
be- under the
aegis of Norman Granz, whose brain
child
it was originally. From an
edi-
torial point of view
it was suggested
that coming
at
this
particular
time,
JATP should have a very salutory ef-
fect upon
the
current
state
of
jazz.
Nationwide Tour In Store
Now,
with
the
kick-off
date
less
than a week away, Easter Sunday in
New
York, we
should
contemplate,
even
speculate
about
the
projected
twenty five city tour, a tour that em-
braces two visits to Canada in April,
one
at Massey
Hall
in Toronto and
the other at Place Des Arts
in Mon-
treal. In essence, the structure of the
’67 tour will be similar to the original
presentations, last seen and tour will
be
similar
to
the
original
presenta-
tions,
last
seen
and
heard
in
1957.
The
principal
difference
is
the
pres-
ence of The Duke Ellington Orchestra
and
Ella
Fitzgerald.
In
years
past
JATP,
by
virtue
of
its
personnel,
probably
had
a more
free
wheeling
attitude
about
it.
Also,
the
history
making
appearances
of
the
original
tours were sans vocalist, always with
the emphasis on the instrumentalists.
Who
is to say which type of program
is
better?
The
audiences
that come
out to hear this new JATP
will give
us the answer.
The element of speculation centers
around
the
thinking
of
Norman
Granz.
_ Granz, perhaps more than any
other jazz presenter, has always en-
joyed a fantastic batting average
in
evaluating
the
tempo
of
the
times.
When he
elected
to
discontinue Jazz
At The Philharmonic in 1957 we must
assume that he felt the blush was
off
the
rose,
that
too many
other
pro-
moters had jumped on his bandwagon
and had,
in
their
avarice,
killed
the
proverbial goose that laid the golden
egg.
Even
if
this was
not
Granz’s
thinking, retrospect shows us that in
the
late
Fifties
there was a glut of
concert hall jazz. Too often, I’m sorry
to
say,
these
presentations
were
staged in such a tasteless manner that
they were
a
disservice
to
both
the
audience and the performer. As a con-
sequence, the public seemed to become
disenchanted
and
the
box
office
re-
flected
it. In the past couple of years,
at
least
in New York, which
is my
habitat,
there
has
been
a
dearth
of
jazz promotions. Oh, there have been
some
things
done,
but
not with
the
regular
frequency
of
the
halcyon
days, when you had to book Carnegie
or Town Hall six or eight months
in
advance
in order
to be sure of a
lo-
cation. We all agree that things have
a
curious way
of coming
full
cycle,
^
and we may assume that Granz feels
that since the rookie promoters have
burned their fingers and have
retired
^
from the business of promoting jazz,
the time
is ripe for him to return to
^
the arena and do
it the way
it should
|
be done, on a professional level with
taste
and
consideration.
Mind
you,
I’ve
never
discussed
this
with
him,
nor have
I ever read a quote by him
i
on
this
subject,
but my
intuition,
coupled
with my knowledge
of how
\
strongly he feels about the jazz artist,
,
fortifies my point of view.
Will Recordings Be
Available From Tour?
Along with The Ellington Orchestra
and Ella Fitzgerald, the JATP roster
'
of performers will include The Oscar
Peterson Trio, The Jimmy Jones Trio
i
and jazz instrumentalists Benny Car-
ter,
Coleman
Hawkins,
Zoot
Sims,
(
and
Clark
Terry.
It
is
to
be hoped
that
whatever
contractual
obstacles
might
present
themselves
can
be
worked out with the recording compa-
nies so that these concerts can be re-
corded. The recent Ella and Duke
al-
bum on Verve is a wonderful example
.
of
what we
can
expect
from
this
troupe,
particularly
after they have
-
had
the
opportunity
of working
to-
gether
night
after
night.
Certeinly
one
of the more
significant
series of
recorded
jazz
is
the
original
set
of
JATP albums on Verve, which is
still,
^
in spite of the passage of time, some
of the most often requested.
I think
j
it

if negotiations

Granz

^
vinced that Granz has done as much

The
basic concept
of Jazz At The
,
Philharmonic has always been to pro-
vide top talent in a professional man-
ner for the enjoyment of the many in-
stead of the few. Now we are about
to witness the re-birth of a presenta-
tion that has,
over the
years, given
untold pleasure to hundreds of thou-
sands
of
listeners, both here
in The
United States and abroad.
I urge you
to keep
alert for the time and place
when JATP is within your area. Once
you
have
witnessed
a
performance
you might better understand the Jazz
At
The
Philharmonic
philosophy,
“Jazz
Is For Everyone.”

Kangaroo Jumps Into Scene;
Kenny Young Prod. Co. Bows
NEW YORK—Kenny Young has just
formed Kangaroo Music, a publishing
firm, and Kenny Young Productions.
He
also
signed
a
deal
with
Mickie
Most
for
the
overseas
publishing
rights. Young will be writing and ac-
quiring material for Most’s
artists.
In
its
first two weeks
in existence,
the
production company and Kanga-
roo
Music
have
had
three
releases:
the Seagulls, “Twiggs” on Date which
is already making
noise;
the
Squir-
rels’, “Who’s The Bird?” and a nov-
elty number by
Jose
Cool
on Amy
Records
called
“Don’t
Worry
’Bout
Me.”
Releases of Kangaroo Music sched-
uled for near future release are
Bill
Dana’s
(Jose Jimenez), “Bongo Boy”
on A&M
Records
and
“Just Let
It
Happen,” by Eddie Rambeau.
Kenny Young
will be
scoring and
writing the theme song for the
flick,
“The Chasid,” which will begin shoot-
ing
in the summer. The theme song
will be published by Kangaroo Music.
Young
is
presently
the
singing
voice of the Beagles cartoon show on
CBS. Most
recently he
has
had
his
songs recorded by Herman’s Hermits,
Gene Pitney and Connie Francis. He
is now
looking
for material
for
his
artists and songs for the pubbery.

TALENT ON STAGE
ORNETTE COLEMAN TRIO
PHILADELPHIA WOODWIND QUINTET
NEW YORK— On
Friday
evening,
March
17, the Ornette Coleman Trio
and the Philadelphia Woodwind Quin-
tet gave a joint concert at the Village
Theater. The Trio came on
first and
performed
two
wild,
polytonal
jazz
works,
“The
Little
Symphony,”
and
“Just For You.” Coleman played alto
sax on the
first piece and trumpet on
the second.
Providing a strong contrast to Cole-
man’s freaky sounds, the Philadelphia
Woodwind Quintet offered a spare and
angular
(but
well
formed)
classical
composition
entitled “En
Forme
De
Chores,” by Heitor Villa-Lobos. Cole-
man
then
returned
to
the
stage,
picked up a violin, and played another
groovy
jazz
piece, “A
Cappella For
Three Wise Men.”
During the second half of the con-
cert, two classical works, “Titles,” by
S.
A.
Chambers,
and
“Forms
And
Sounds,”
received
their premier
per-
formances. The
latter
piece,
written
and played by Coleman
(on trumpet,
with
the
Quintet), was
recorded by
RCA Victor Records and
will be
in-
cluded
in
a
forthcoming
LP,
along
with two other classical compositions,
also by Coleman, “Space Flight,” and
“Saints And
Soldiers.” The album
is
scheduled for release
in the
fall.
BLUES PROJECT
NEW YORK—The
Blues
Project
is
currently
holding
forth
at
Sleeker
St.’s
Cafe Au-Go-Go,
that basement
nitery from which they first emerged
some year-or-more-ago. They changed
a lot since then and are currently on
the verge of far-reaching fame
.
.
. the
international kind. They’re in a posi-
tion right now that could lead them all
the way to the top. Musically they are
particularly good and they put on
a
good stage show.
They compose much
of
their own
material
and
are
a
very
inventive
group;
to wit, having placed an elec-
trified
flute
in
the middle
of a rock
group, they retain complete control of
its sound by means of a bank of foot
pedals
that
create
such
effects
as
echo
and
reverb.
In
short,
they
are
not dependent on the recording studio
to
create
and
maintain
their
own
sound. And that ...
is a joy.
They are completely at home with
tunes
by Muddy
Waters,
old Chuck
Berry
efforts, and
their own modern
compositions,
to name only a few of
the bags from which they draw ma-
terial. Perhaps foremost among their
tunes
is a venture
called “The Flute
Thing.” Much of the material in their
current show
is taken from the latest
Blues Project album, “Projections” on
Verve/Folkways.
BUFFY
ST. MARIE
NEW YORK — Vanguard
recording
artist Buffy St. Marie made her major
concert debut
(as
a
solo performer)
at Philharmonic Hall on Mar. 17th;
it
was a triumph. She walked on stage
to
a
surge
of
applause
that
nearly
turned
into
an
ovation
and
finished
the
concert
in much
the
same way
with
two-encores,
repeated
curtain
calls,
a
large bouquet
of
roses,
and
the
enthusiastic
cheers
of
a
very-
much-pleased audience.
Accompanying herself on guitar or
mouth-bow
(a
magnificently
primi-
tive droning instrument,) Buffy went
through a repertoire of songs that at
least equalled that of any other folk
singer as far as scope, intensity, and
authenticity are concerned. “Until It’s
Time To
(io,” “Cripple Creek,” “The
Universal Soldier,” and a Jacques Brel
type
of tune
called “Montreal,” were
among the highlights of the evening
for this reviewer. She seems to draw
heavily on the jazz bag for her music,
filling
her
concert
with
modernistic
chords on the guitar and Blues/Jazz
phrasings on many of the vocals.
Throughout
the
concert,
the
lark
dwelled
frequently
and
at
varying
length
about
the
double-standard
so
often applied to the American Indian
throughout the United States. Notable
examples are: the usurping of Indian
lands
without
“adequate
compensa-
tion,” Indians not being allowed
full
franchise,
etc.
Discussions
of
the
plight of the American Indian are
a
definite and expected part of a Buffy
St. Marie concert. She
is particularly
well
qualified
and
informed
on
the
subject as
she
is
a Cree Indian her-
self.

Columbia’s ‘Theater Express’
Rolls This Week
NEW YORK—Columbia Records will
underwrite the operating expenses of
a special theatre bus service starting
this Monday (27). The new service, to
be known
as
the “Columbia Records
Broadway Theatre Express,” will offer
four
buses
running down
Fifth
and
Lexington Avenues beginning at 7:40
P.M.
and
returning
after-theatre
up
Madison and Third Avenues at a cost
per passenger of only 30^ each way.
The buses will run nightly except Sun-
day.
The
service
was
conceived
by
Mayor
Lindsay,
in
conjunction
with
the New York City Transit Authority
and
the
League
of
New
York
Theatres.
In
a
statement
regarding
the
re-
cording firm’s sponsorship of the serv-
ice, Clive
J. Davis, vice president and
Cardini
Heads A&R
Of Jingle Co.

spin-off

Films,

shorts & commer-
cials
film

is
oper-
ating out

704,
this

general manager of CBS Records, said
that
the

provided
by

frustrating conditions that discourage
many New Yorkers from attempting
to
enter
the Broadway
area
during
the rush hours preceding curtain time.

con-
tribute to this service, which will sure-

encourage
more

ance.”
Columbia
Records
has
recorded

way’s
current

“Marne,”
“Cab-
aret,” “The Apple Tree” and “Sweet
Charity.”

at 7:15 P.M. The pas-

a
fan
letter,
maybe not the conventional
style fan
letter because
I know him pretty well
on a personal level. But a letter telling
him what a great privilege it has been
to know him from
his music, and an
even
greater
privilege
to know him
as a friend, and that
I feel
infinitely
richer in my
lifetime for having had
this
privilege. As we
all
know,
the
road
to
hell
is paved with
good
in-
tentions, and up until now I’ve never
gotten around to writing him.
I would
have told him personally, but knowing
Woody,
it
would
have
embarrassed
him, I’m
sure. Perhaps doing
it
this
way,
as
a
sort
of
open
fan
letter,
might be better. True, it’s not as per-
sonal,
but,
inversely,
it should make
more people aware
of
his greatness.
And please bear
in mind that this
is
being written by someone who
holds
the word “great”
in high veneration,
and by one who
is quick to recognize
the proverbial feet of
clay.
It would be
like “carrying coals
to
Newcastle” to recount Woody’s many
accomplishments
as
a
bandleader,
a
career that has spanned some twenty-
eight years, even longer
if you want
to count his time as leader of a group
of
Isham
Jones
alumni
after
the
Jones band broke
up.
If we were
to
chronicle the players who have worked
with and for Woody Herman
during
this
era
it would
read
like
a
who’s
who in jazz. From that list of Herman
graduates
it would be
difficult to find
one who has anything but good to say
about Woody. Naturally,
I’ve not had
the
opportunity
to
speak
to
all
of
them,
but
those
to
whom
I
have
spoken always
refer
to him
in much
the same way, with a warm, respectful
devotion. You know
the
old
saying,
“If you really want to know about a
guy,
ask
someone
who
has
worked
for him.”
Woody’s Great
Inspiration
As
Bandleader
With
a
track
record
like Woody’s,
it
is apparent that he
is an outstand-
ing
musician,
using
the
term
in
its
broadest
possible
sense.
Perhaps
equally important to his uninterrupted
successes
is
his
stature
as
a human
being. Even if you aren’t familiar with
the
big
band
business,
you
must
realize that
it takes a special kind of
leader to make things hang together.
When you deal with that many differ-
ent personalities and their respective
problems,
it
takes
a unique man
to
maintain
the
captain’s
role.
Unlike
conventional business organizations, a
band of musicians is much more com-
plex,
and
The
Herman
Herds
that
have prevailed through the years are
eloquent
testimony
to
the
fact
that
Woody has had to be father, mother,
teacher,
psychologist,
disciplinarian,
boss,
friend,
and
whatever
else
it
takes to endure and conquer as he has.
If
I were asked what impresses me
the
most
about
Woody
Herman,
I
would
answer,
unhesitatingly,
the
fact that he
is always
a
gentleman.
This impression comes not only from
my
personal
acquaintance
with
him,
but
also from
watching him
behave
with
others.
I’ve
been
witness
to
several
instances
when,
at
the
con-
clusion
of
the
last
set
and
in
the
small
hours
of
the
morning, Woody
was tired and anxious to get back to
the hotel and to sleep. On the way out
of the club, he would be stopped by a
fan, more than half drunk with booze
and
nostalgia, and he would, be
sub-
jected
to
interminable
questions and
feeble
attempts
at conversation, and
never
for
a
moment
would
he
be
abrupt
with
this
early
morning
reveler. We must assume that Woody
is
ever
mindful
of
his
debt
to
the
people who have kept him up
front
for
so many
years.
Still,
there
are
many
performers
in
the
limelight
who don’t practice this courtesy, and
who
are
not
only
abrupt
but
often
rude to their fans. I guess that differ-
ence
is
really what makes me
dig
Woody Herman as much as I do. He’s
ever
unassuming,
even
shy,
and
he
has
the
stamp
of
gentility
all
over
him,
in a word, CLASS!
Played One For Johnny
Hodges

Everyone
asks
the
same
question,
“How
does Woody
keep
coming up

so many good young players?”
Well,
the
big
band
business
is
a
fairly small fraternity in which news
travels
fast,
and
if
he
weren’t
the
kind
of guy he
is, you
can be
sure
that
getting musicians for
the band
would be much more
difficult than
it
has
been.
And
let’s
not
overlook
Woody’s
playing.

night
in The
Metropole
in New York, where
the
band plays from atop the bar, Johnny
