GERMANY
The “Grand Prix” which will be held for
all of Europe on April 8th of this
year in Vienna
is a festival steeped in a very young but woi'thy tradition. One
star who was launched on a European career through the festival was certainly
Udo Jurgens. Udo, who had “been around” for years and
years, never quite
found
his
style through
other song writers and producers, but when he was
able to turn to his own song writing talent for hits, the result was high places
in the festival two years running and a first place last year. Since then, Udo has
drawn top dollar all over the continent for his personal appearances and is most
probably Germany’s highest paid artist at present. On June
1st, his new record
tie
will be
the young firm Ariola-Eurodisc, which
has signed up top
talents
such as Peter Alexander, Rex Gildo and Rudolf Schock among others. The con-
tract may be history making. The famous German journalist “Hunter” wrote
in his nationwide column that the guarantee sum is set for 450,000 DM per year
which
is about $112,000. This sum
is only for the German language areas of
Germany, Austria and Switzerland. The only contract which can compare with
this
is that of Caterina Valente who did a world-wide deal with Teldec for a
%
million
($125,000) DM guarantee
several years
ago. Although no
official
confirmation
of
the guarantee sum
is
present, Udo’s manager-producer-pub-
lisher Hans R. Beierlein remarked “Pm content with the new contract.”
Export manager George Ehmke of Ariola writes us that the firm has 3 songs
set for this year’s “Grand Prix” including entries from Germany, Austria and
Italy. Early in March Ariola partners CUPOL from Sweden, Metronome from
Denmark and Nor-Disc from Norway met at Ariola
in Guetersloh
to
discuss
new release and publicity plans.
One of Germany’s top promotion men-publishers Jack Martin who left Poly-
dor where he headed the radio promotion department for years to take on the
task at the newly-formed Hansa Productions of Peter Meisel has reported that
he will leave Hansa to go to another new outfit. The Rhenus organization under
industrial boss Karl Heinz Muenchow which already has
built new recording
studios and pressing plants
outside
of Cologne and
will enter the
field with
new productions
in the next few weeks. Rumors have
it that the break from
Hansa goes together with the fact that Peter Meisel has had several offers to
sell
his Hansa
operation and
Intro
publishing
house.
Interested
buyers
are
listed as RCA Victor, United Artists and Ariola. No decision has been made as
of this writing, but
if the
fii'm
is
sold
it will be
of tremendous impact to the
industry here. The young Hansa label and productions have turned out an un-
precedented series of hits over the past few years and have not only developed
their own artists but also, have distribution deals for such powerhouse groups
as the Hollies and the Troggs.
The Rolling Stones who packed houses during their tour here recently
also
picked up a “Golden” record from Teldec for the
sale of more than 3 million
records
in Germany.
Charles Aznavour has started his 2nd tour of Germany and will visit Berlin,
Cologne,
Essen,
Stuttgart, Hamburg,
Frankfurt
and
finish
in
Munich.
The
French star who
is represented here by Metronome records, can expect com-
plete sell-outs in every city just as he had for his last tour.
On the beat side, the Easybeats and the Who are also
set for tours late this
month and early in April. Both groups are represented by Polydor here.
Peter Kirsten has reorganized his publishing and production interests under
the banner “Global Music” which
will house Minor Music
Production, Altus
Music, Fanfare Music and Furioso Music. The firm
is now swinging with the
Austrian entry in the Grand Prix Eurovision which he produces and publishes.
He also now sub-publishes “Here Comes My Baby,” the smash
hit from the
Tremelows on CBS from England. On the export side of the picture, the new
Horst Jankowski single “Big Big River”
is getting a new release as the
title
song for a TV series called “Journey in Germany.” The song has also been re-
named to
fit the TV picture. The new Horst Jankowski LP for Mercury has 3
tunes published by Peter in
it and the present LP “So What’s New” contains
5 Globus Music tunes. That’s
it for this week in Germany.

Epic Names Two
For
West Coast
Office
NEW YORK—Epic Records has made
two new appointments
to
the
label’s
|
West Coast operation.
Julio Aiello has been named Epic’s
|
manager
of Western
regional
sales.
He will be responsible to Nick Alba-
rano,
Epic’s
national
sales manager,
JULIO AIELLO
for the sale of Epic, Okeh, Crossroads
and Go Go product on the West Coast.
Based
in
Los
Angeles,
he
will
also
cover
San
Francisco,
Seattle,
Den-
ver and
Honolulu.
Aiello’s
sales
ex-
perience
is extensive. During the four
years
prior
to
joining
Epic
he was
branch manager of Liberty Records in
Los Angeles.
Rick
Larence,
formerly
promotion
manager
for MGM
Records
in
Los
Angeles,
joins
Epic
as
Western
re-
gional promotion manager. He will be
responsible to Fred Frank, Epic’s na-
tional
promotion
manager,
and
his
territory will be the same as Aiello’s.

C-P Inks Ed McMahon;
Promo On 2 Groups
NEW
YORK—TV
announcer
Ed
McMahon
has
moved
into
the
disk
field as an exclusive, long-term artist
on Cameo-Parkway
Records,
accord-
ing to A1 Rosenthal, president.
Part
of
the
NBC-TV
“Tonight
Show’’ roster, McMahon also appears
on NBC radio’s “Monitor’’ and NBC-
TV’s
daytime
quizzer,
“Snap
Judg-
ment.’’ He will sing for his supper on
C-P,
his
first
release
a
single
called
“Beautiful
Girl.”
In
other
C-P
activity,
the
label
plans
a
strong push
for
the
British
Walkers and Bob Segar and the Last
Heard. The British Walkers, out with
a
side
called “Shake,”
will
visit
Co-
lumbus, Baltimore, Washington, Dal-
las, Houston and Miami. C-P promo
manager Marty Thau will accompany
Bob Segar and the Last Heard, who
have
cut “Vagrant
Winter,”
for
the
label,
on
a
cross-country
trek from
April 15-May
16. The BW
are
pro-
duced by Bobby Poe and Mitch
Cor-
day, while the Segar crew
is
cut by
Hideout Productions.
New Cleveland Distrib
C-P has
also named a new
distrib
in Cleveland, New Seaway, to handle
the
line
in
Ohio.
David
Glew
will
handle
sales
and
Mike
Drages
will
direct promo at the distrib level, Neil
Bogart, C-P
national
sales manager,
announced.

NEW YORK—MGM

MGM

Mischa Elman
Dies
NEW
YORK—Mischa
Elman,
the
violinist, died last week (5) of a heart
attack
in
his
apartment
on
Central
Park West. He was 76 years old.
Mischa Elman’s
professional debut
at
the
age
of
12
in
Berlin was
in-
stantly
successful. He
was
born
in
Talnoye,
in the Ukraine, on Jan.
20,
1891.
His
grandfather was
a
noted
violinist, and music was an early part
of his
life.
Elman
performed
in
London
in
Queen’s Hall in 1905 with the London
Symphony
Orchestra
under
Charles
Williams.
He
made
his New
York
debut on Dec.
10, 1908, with the Rus-
sian Symphony Orchestra, playing the
Tchaikovsky concerto.
In the following years, Elman, who
had
an
unusually
large
repertory,
made
annual
tours
of
the
United
States and Europe. He became famous
for
what
many
critics
called
the
"‘Elman
tone,” which was
described
as “warm,
sensuous,
opulent—as
vi-
brant as a living thing.”
Elman
is survived by his wife, Mrs.
Helen Katten Elman,
a
son,
Joseph,
and a daughter, Mrs. Nadia Mack. He
also
leaves
two
sisters,
the
Misses
Liza
and
Esther
Elman,
who
are
music
teachers
in
Philadelphia,
and
three grandchildren.

Roulette
Line

NEW YORK—Beta

lo-
cated at 599
10th Ave.,
will move to
larger
quarters,
reports Johnny Ha-
lonka, owner.

The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band consists
of Bruce “Spider Bones” Kunkel, gui-
tar,
kazoo
and
washtub
bass;
Jeff
“Spanky
Duff”
Hanna,
washboard,
sandblocks, guitar, comb, kazoo, and a
new instrument called the “phinius;”
Jimmy “Starch Harpo” Fadden, har-
monica, washtub bass, phinius, kazoo
and
cigarette;
“Raucous”
Ralphy
Barr,
kazoo, washtub
bass and bub-
bles; Les “Totally” Thompson, mando-
lin, kazoo, washtub bass, and phinius;
and
John
“King
of
the
Banjo”
McEuen,
banjo
and
washtub
bass.
The
Nitty
Gritty Dirt Band evolved
from Saturday night hoots at a Long
Beach,
Cal.,
coffee
house
at
which
the
boys
performed
spontaneously.
Kunkel
and Hanna
organized
their
“bang band”
into a group
called the
Illegitimate Jug Band, since they had
no jug. After a bit more organizing
and a
lot more
rehearsing,
they
be-
came the Nitty Gritty Dirt Band. The
group
is managed by John’s brother,
William E. McEuen. The band’s Liber-
ty single, “Buy For Me The Rain,” is
number
67
on the
charts
this week.
Blues Project
The
Blues
Project
is composed
of
Danny Kalb, lead guitar; A1 Kooper,
electric
organ
;
Roy
Blumenfeld,
drums; Andy
Kulberg,
electric
bass
and
flute
;
and
Steve
Katz,
rhythm
guitar and harmonica. The band grew
out of a group called the Danny Kalb
Quartette,
which was
formed when
Kalb became
interested
in
the
elec-
tronic
instrument
scene.
The
Blues
Project
displays
great
versatility;
Kooper,
for
instance,
does many
of
the
quintet’s
arrangements,
and
he
has written many of the numbers in
the
group’s
repertoire.
He
penned
“This
Diamond
Ring,”
the
recent
chart item which was performed by
Gary Lewis & the Playboys. Blumen-
feld, who
is
very
serious
about
his
music, studied with Art Blakey of the
Jazz
Messengers.
Kulberg
composes
both pop and classical music, and Katz
has written most
of the
sweet, slow
folk-rock ballads in the Blues Project’s
repertoire.
The
multi-talented group
is currently represented on the charts
with
its Verve /Folkways
single, “No
Time Like The Right Time,” which is
number
71
on
the
charts
this week.

CHICAGO—It’s
“Smothers
Brothers
Month”
at
Mercury
Records
from
April 1-May
10, a move prompted by
the comedy duo’s strong stand on TV
and the additional spark
it’s given to
their LP catalog.
The month long promo features ac-
tivity keyed
to
include
radio
station
personnel,
editors,
distribs, and
deal-
ers.
The
month
culminates May
10
with
a 24 hour radio
station satura-
tion campaign.
Since
July,
1961 when
their
first
LP,
“The
Smothers
Brothers
at
the
Purpole
Onion”
was
released,
the
Smothers Brothers have accumulated
total sales of over ten million dollars
wholesale.
Mercury
claims.
Two
of
their
albums
have
been
certified
as
million dollar sellers at the manufac-
turer’s
level by the Record Industry
Association
of
America.
They
were
“Think Ethnic” and The Two Sides of
the Smothers Brothers.
Their Sunday night CBS-TV Show
showed up at number 23 in the rating
originally when the show began two
months
ago.
Since
that
time,
the
brothers
comedy
show
has
vaulted
into the top ten among approximately
ninety video entries.
“Their
far
reaching
impact
in
so
many
different
phases
of
entertain-
ment
is what specifically caused us to
plan
this
special
observance,”
ex-
plained Alan
Mink,
national
product
manager for Mercury.
The Smothers Brothers themselves
Month At Mercury
are
actively
participating
in
the
month’s activities. They will plug the
month via their TV show. They have
prepared
special
open-end
interview
records and
spots
to
be
supplied
to
radio
stations. They are writing per-
sonal letters to key dealers and mass
merchandisers.
Special brochures are being mailed
to radio stations asking them to par-
ticipate
in
the
special
“Smothers
Brothers Day” May
10.
All
partici-
pating radio personnel become eligible
for a sweepstakes drawing, winner of
which will receive an all expense paid
trip
to
Los
Angeles
to
visit
the
Smothers
Brothers
and
personally
witness the production of their weekly
TV
show.
A
special
commemorative
record
containing
highlights
of
their
best
selling albums
is being prepared.
In
addition to radio coverage, the record
will be

to hundreds
of TV and

Extensive

vertising
at

will

Special

A

CashJiQX
GERMANY
New German
General Manager
Siggy
Loch
and European Manager
lion
Kass from Liberty records dropped by the
office for a long talk about their
new interesting operation. Liberty will be the only major U.S.
firm
to form
an
operation
here
with
their
own
production,
publicity
and
exploitation
but with
distribution handled by
a major
local
fiim.
All
risk
will
be taken
by
Liberty
as
to
pressing,
covers,
etc.,
and
only
the
actual
sales
will
be
undertaken by the distributor much
like
it is done by indie
distribs
stateside.
According
to Mr. Kass, Germany
is
the
only major market
left which
is
>
underexploited.
Italy,
for
example,
has
about
40
different
firms
whereas
Germany has 8 major firms doing all of the business being done. The German
record business
is growing, but
in which
direction?
Singles
sales—especially
on German language
product—have been
dropping
at an alarming
rate for
several years now and, with the exception of a very few major
artists such
;
as
Ariola’s Peter Alexander &
Polydor’s Freddy and Roy
Black, fewer and
fewer local names seem
to appear on the
charts.
Company A&R men seem also to have lost their lucky hand in the last few
years. Most
all
of the
productions being
done
which make
the
charts
are
being handled by independent A&R
firms doing contractual
or leasing
jobs
j
on
their
product
but producing
for more
than
one
label. Of
course,
there
’
are
glaring
exceptions which
only seem
to
strengthen
the
rule.
Even
the
most conservative firms have lowered their barriers to available indie masters
produced
locally and
foreign
product
continues
to
gobble up
a tremendous
piece
of the
total
sales
here.
On the other hand, LP sales continue
to zoom up making the record
busi-
ness a much more “business-like” but somewhat less exciting business. Firms
like Deutsche Vogue, which has
its
basic home
in France, Metronome which
i
is partly owned from Scandinavia & the swinging CBS operation have made
heavy inroads into the sales picture
in the past few years, and local produc-
tion and label operations like the Coronet operation of top producer-executive
team Gunter Ilgner & Heinz Gietz and the Hansa
operation of Peter Meisel
are growing in importance every day. Karl-Heinz Munchow has gone
so far
;
as
to
build
his own
factoi'y
for production and
pressing
to
really kick
off
t
his
“Mondial”
label
and
companies
are
overrun
with
offers
of productions
from
indie sources.
The German market seems
to be
in
a very uncertain
position
today, but
new blood on the singles picture and a concentration of LP sales by the major
labels seems to be the trend that the record business here
is headed for. The
near future will probably see more and more foreign countries looking for a
j
piece of the pie
in Germany, and even opening their own distribution setups
to push for
it. Promotion will be heavily increased by
all firms to be able
to
compete in this over-saturated market, and
all firms will be in the market for
1
young up and coming A&R
talents
to produce
acceptable
material
for
the
[
teens who always want the newest. It looks like highly competitive confusion
in the months ahead in Germany, but the results
will probably be a stronger
i
more
solid market for
all concerned.

INELCO
released the LP “More Of The Monkees” here
in
Belgium. The
television series with the Monkees will start on B.R.T. (Flemish television) on
May 29th.
The firm also released a single by the Chackachas (RCA) which
is climbing
fast on the Flemish Top 20. Titles are “Love Is Like A Violin” and “El Char-
latan.”
Inelco
is
also
releasing two
music
casettes
of
5
records
each
featuring
Arturo Toscanini’s most known works. The promotion
price
is
BFr.l99,-per

($4).
Inelco’s jazz albums
in the Vintage
series reach high
sales
figures. In
this
series old recordings are brought of a.o. Fats Waller, Benny Goodman, Lionel
Hampton, Earl Hines, Count Basie and Duke Ellington.
Barclay signed popular Flemish songster Anneke Soetaert. Her
first record-
ing on the Barclay label
is: “Ik Verlang Naar Jou”
(I’m Longing For You)
c/w “Ciao, Bye Bye, Adieu.”
Gramophone Belgian songster Lize Marke brought the Flemish version of
“This Is My Song” and “Lara’s Theme.” This record
is one of the firm’s latest
blockbusters, as well as Gilbert Becaud’s “L’Important C’Est La Rose”
(The
Most Important Is The Rose).
Ardmore & Beechwood obtained the publishing rights for George Chelon’s
“Est-Ce Que Tu Resteras?” (Will You Stay?), “II N’a Suffi Que D’Un Sourire”
(A Smile Was Enough) /cw “Peut-Etre” (Perhaps That Perhaps) and “Eve-
lyne.” Also for German Udo Jurgens song “Geh Worbei” (Pass By).
Humo, a popular Flemish radio & television magazine
is organizing a great
talent-hunt. Every month a contest takes place in a different town where pre-
liminary selected singers and groups may compete. A jury of
10 prominent
radio, television and press people elect the best participants who will partake
at the finals on July 8th.

Liberty Sets Nat'l
Nitty Gritty Tour
LOS
ANGELES—Liberty
Records
has planned a national promotion tour
for the Nitty
Gritty
Dirt Band. Ac-
companied

manager
Bill
McEuen and Liberty
ai’tists relations
manager Harvey Goldstein, the group
jets

(17)

^en

“Nitty
Gritty” chartered bus, decorated with

Nitty
Grittys
will
stop
to make radio and TV ap-
pearances, hold court at retail
outlet
autograph

and
meet
news-
paper and magazine people.
Stops scheduled thus far (after the
April 17-18-19 stint in

are
as follows: Chicago, April
20,
21, 22;
New York City, April 23, 24, 25, with
a return planned for April 28, 29, 30;

April
26,
27;
Boston,
April
27,
28;
Baltimore-Washington,
May
1,
2;
Cleveland, May
3,
4;
and
Detroit, May
5. After leaving Detroit
the group
will
jet to
Salt Lake
City
for May 6
activities and then return
to the West Coast.
The Nitty Gritty Dirt Band
is cur-
rently on the Top 100 with their “Buy
For Me The Rain”

their
first
LP,
titled
simply
“The
Nitty
Gritty Dirt Band,” is making a lot of
noise on the Coast.
UA Enjoys Hot
Singles Streak
NEW YORK—United
Artists
Rec-
ords
has
reported
its
best-selling
singles
sales
period
since
Oct.
1965
during the month of March.
The Spencer Davis Group and their
“I’m A Man,” and The Easybeats and
“Friday
On My
Mind,”

These
are followed by Bobby
Golds-
boro’s “Goodbye To All You Women,”
another fast-rising UA disk.
In
the C & W
field, Johnny Dar-
rell’s
“Ruby, Don’t Take Your Love
To Town,” Del Reeves and “Blame It
On My Do Wrong,” and Bobby Lewis
and his “Two Of The Usual,”
all
oc-
cupying niches
on
the
charts,
added
impetus to UA’s banner March.
United
Artists
executives
are
con-
fidently predicting that April will sur-
pass March,
in view of the fact that
the majority of their top
disks have
yet to reach
their peak. UA expects
great things of Ellie Greenwich’s out-
ing, “I Want You To Be My Baby”.
Joe Simone Named
Main Liner Manager
CLEVELAND—Joe Simone has been
named manager
of
the
independent
record division of Main Line Records,
the label affiliate of Main Line Cleve-
land.
Simone
returns
to
Cleveland
from
Los
Angeles
where
he
was
branch manager for Liberty Records.
He held the same post with Liberty in
Cleveland
before
his
move
to
the
West Coast. Main Line
is one of the
largest
record
distributors
in
the
United States.
Simone
replaces Ed
Rosenblatt
in
the position, who is leaving Main Line
and Cleveland for personal reasons.

Conley

anc

Casinos
The
Casinos, a nine-man group
ol
musicians,
have
recently
gained na
tional

with
their
singh
on
the
Fraternity
label, “Then Yoi
Can
Tell Me

tean

ag<

Pete Bolton, and Joe Patterson. The3

ai

j

Capitol's New
'Fringe' Merchandising
Dept. To Be Directed By Don Doughty
Disk Bootlegging Returns In Force
HOLLYWOOD—A
‘fringe’ merchan-
dising
department
has
been
created
by
Capitol
Records,
to be headed up
by Don Doughty, Cash Box learned last
week.
It
is understood that Doughty,
who has just joined
Capitol Records
Distributing
Corp.
as merchandising
project manager,
will
be
responsible
for the preparation of merchandising
and
advertising programs
on
behalf
of
selected
Capitol
pop LP
product,
with
special
emphasis
on
catalog
product not currently tied in with hit
singles
as
well
as
product
introduc-
ing new
acts. In his new role he will
report
directly
to CRDC vp and na-
tional merchandising manager Brown
Meggs.
Doughty
entered
the
record
busi-
ness in 1960 as a salesman for Decca
Records
in
upstate New York, Ver-
mont and Western Massachusetts. He
subsequently
joined
Capitol
in
a
similar
capacity
before
moving
to
Columbia,
first
as
a
salesman,
then
as a field promotion man. In 1963, he
moved
to Columbia’s headquarters
in
New York
City, where he worked
in
a number of capacities, including man-
ager
of
field
communications,
na-
tional promotion manager, and prod-
uct manager for pop-album catalog.
Doughty
left Columbia
in
October,
1966,
moving
to
California
and
be-
coming
national
promotion
director
for
GNP-Crescendo.

(2), Art Blakey, Jimmy Smith, Stan-
ley Turretine and the Three
Sounds.
Block believes the
additional concen-
tration on the juke box level is one of
the prime reasons for what has been
termed their great sales success. This
has
afforded
another
media
of
con-
sumer listening. Juke box operators all
over the country have
for
the most
part reportedly expressed gratification
in the introduction of Blue Note little
LP’s.
Jubilee Shows
Profit
At End
of
Fiscal '66
NEW YORK—In the
fiscal year end-
ed
Sept.
30,
1966,
Jubilee
Industries
had a net income of $41,231 and total
revenues
of
$4,959,684
as
compared
with
the
loss
sustained
in
1965
of
$300,729 on total revenues of
$3,919,-
483.
Figures
were
revealed
recently
by Jerry Blaine, president and
chair-
man of the board of Jubilee.
Blaine called fiscal 1966 one of “the
most
satisfying
in
the
company’s
history
in
light
of
its
reversal
of
three years of losses and the increase
in
total
revenues
of
approximately
26%
over
the
prior twelve months.”
How The Change Came About
The
rise
in
profits was
attributed
in part to Jubilee’s divestment of
its
distribution
facilities
with
the
ex-
ception of its interest in All-One-Stop
and Distributing Corp. of New York.
In
a
statement
to
shareholders,
Blaine
said,
“We
are
now
record
producers
in New York through
our
own
lines and
in joint ventures with
other
labels
and
manufacturers
of
recordings via our pressing plant and
auxiliary facilities in the greater Los
Angeles
area.
The
development
of
this
manufacturing
division
through
expansion
and
modernization was
a
major
factor
in reversing
the
losses
shown
in previous
years.
“Our New York
headquarters’
of-
fices
now
include
a
fully-equipped
recording studio that can produce both
stereo and monaural records, our own
cutting room and special facilities for
such
technical procedures
in master-
ing a finished record as mixing, over-
dubbing,
tracking,
etc. We augment
our own
creative
efforts by
signing
young, independent record
producers.
“Our record manufacturing facility
in
California
now
consists
of
four
plants
capable
of
turning
out
four
million units per month and perform-
ing every function from printing the
label
to
automatically
sealing
the
finished product
in a
skintight,
poly-
ethylene bag. We have our own elec-
tro-plating factory, warehouses and a
complete machine shop for
dies.
“One
of
our
subsidiaries,
Record
Labels,
Inc.,
is
a
printing
plant
ca-
pable
of
turning
out
sufficient,
full-
color labels for six million records per
month.”
Blaine indicated that Jubilee’s West
Coast
manufacturing
operation
(Monarch
Record
Division,
Etan
Products
Division,
Record
Labels,
Inc. and
A.F.M.
Engineering
Corpo-
ration)
enjoys
an
annual
volume,
eliminating
all
inter-company
trans-
actions, of approximately $4.2 million
and has over 300 customers.
The Jubilee President said that the
company has “advantageous arrange-
ments
with ITCC,
a vendor
of
tape
cartridges. Under the
terms
of
this
arrangement, ITCC
is releasing selec-
tions
from
our
catalog
of
recorded
material
on
stereo
tape
cartridges
for which we
will be reimbursed
on
a
royalty
basis. As
stereo
tape
car-
tridge
sales grow
in
both
auto
and
home
use,
this
contract
will assume
increasing
importance.”
Blaine also stated that Jubilee will
continue
“to
develop
its
tremendous
catalog
of comedy and spoken word
recordings, to seek acquisitions in re-
lated
areas
of
the
entertainment
industry,
and
to
enhance
its
music
|
publishing
activities.”

The broadcast restriction has now been removed from “Casino Royale” and
the Festival people have rush-released the hot single by Herb Alpert and the
Tijuana Brass on the A&M
label. The side should soon be grabbing
all kinds
of chart action.
Southern Music are
out with the
sheet copies on
“Epistle To Dippy” and
“Look At My Baby,” the latter recorded by local boy Russ Kruger.
Latest record production
figures
(to
the
end
of
February,
1967)
indicate
a dip in the roduction of 7" product, but albums rose nicely
all around. Some
idea of the growth of the industry in this country
is seen from the fact that
total record production figures for the eight months period ended February,
1967, are greater than that for the
entire twelve months period
of 1963/64.
There
is no doubt that when we examine
the
statistics
at
the
end
of June
(the
end
of
the
fiscal
year
in
Australia)
total
production
figures
for
the
twelve months will be the highest ever. In the area of albums, stereo product
is running at about 50% of total LP production.

“That’s What
I Want” and

Unlikely;”
the
Probe with

Never

the Elois with “I’m A Man” and “By My Side.”

WLIB—New
York,
the
Harlem
radio
outlet,
has
become
the
first
radio
outlet
programmed
for
the
Negro
community
ever
to
win
a
Peabody
Award,
the
highest
honor
available
to
broadcasters.
It
is
also
the only local New York radio or TV
outlet
to win
a Peabody Award
this
year. The Peabody Award plaque for
the
nation’s
outstanding
local
radio
[
educational program of 1966 was pre-
sented
to
WLIB
general
manager
Harry Novik on April 20 at a lunch-
eon
ceremony
at
the
Hotel
Pierre.
The
WLIB
program
honored
was
“Community
Opinion,” the
“hot-line”
program
moderated
by
Leon
Lewis,
which
broadcasts
the
telephoned
I
opinions and problems of the nation’s
largest Negro community.
The
Pea-
body Award
Citation
to WLIB
said:
“(The outlet), during the hot summer
of 1966, gave Harlem a ‘safety valve.’
“Community
Opinion”
.
.
.
(per-
mitted)
citizens
of Harlem
to
voice
their feelings, frankly and openly, via
a hot
line telephone
interview, heard
not only by the Negro community, but
by
the
entire
city.
In
addition,
the
station
provided
details
of how
lis-
teners could avail themselves of exist-
ing
vital
community
services. Many
national,
state
and
local
officials
in
the
highest capacities have appeared
as guests on the show,
to
be
on the
receiving end
of
calls from
listeners
asking pointed questions about activi-
ties
under
the
guests’
supervision.
Last
month,
the
New
York
Urban
League honored WLIB’s Leon
Lewis
and
Betty Granger
Reid
for
“excell-
ence
in news reporting during
1966”
in ceremonies
at
the Overseas
Press
Club.
Thirty-seven
pounds
of
entries
to
sixty-one pounds of money. That was
the
ratio
in
WIOD-Miami,
Fla.’s
“Sixtv-One
Pounds
of
Money”
con-
test,
won
by
Cy
Mitchell,
of
5134
N.W.
Second
St.,
Miami.
Mitchell
guessed within two cents of the exact
amount
of
money
contained
in
the
treasure
chest.
He
used
the
clues
broadcast for three weeks on WIOD
to
come
up
with
the
estimate
of
$375.96. The
actual
value
as
verified
by
officials
of
the
United
Banking
Group and Wells Fargo was
$375.94.
Officials of the United Banking Group
exchanged the chest with “Sixty-One
Pounds of Money” for a much lighter
cashier’s check, so that Mitchell would
not have to carry the 7,457 coins and
bills. The 37 pounds of entries
in the
contest
comprised
more
than
10,000
entries. The estimates ranged from a
quarter of a million dollars to a lowly
six
dollars and
ten
cents.
“Music
’Til
Dawn,”
the
concert
music program sponsored by Ameri-
can Airlines on KNX-Hollywood, cele-
brated
its
14th anniversary on
April
13.
The
all-night program was
first
heard on KNX on April 13, 1953 with
host
Mel
Baldwin, who
is
currently
on a two-year leave of absence. KNX
personality
George
Walsh
has
been
hosting the program
since Jan.
1966.
“Music
’Til Dawn”
is
aired Monday
through
Saturday,
11:30
P.M.—5:30
|
A.M.
WRKO-Boston motored into its new
pop
format
in
a
Candy
Apple
Red
Convertible
with
$680
in
the
glove
compartment.
This
was
the
grand
prize
that
the
outlet’s

vied
for
in
the
“Candy
Apple
Mustang”
contest.
Thousands
of

WRKO
listening
area
sent
in
their

and
phone
num-
bers,
and
then
called WRKO
when
they heard their names on the
air to
win
$60 and become
eligible
for
the
drawing for
the car and cash. After
four
weeks
of
intensive
promotion,
the
automobile was
awarded
to
Mr.
and
Mrs.
Robert
Plourde
of
Fall
River, Mass.
Alley
oops!
Right,
it’s
the
“Alley
Oops” of the KMPC Bowling League
who
have won
the

season

jay
Ira
Cook
and

outstanding

of

and

the

roll-off. Ira Cook
rolled a
168, a
160, and
a
192; while Niehaus
came through with a
171, a
156 and
final game 180 for the clincher. Phyllis
Carter and Marilyn Niehaus also con-
tributed
to
the
winning
effort.
The
KMPC
League
will
hold
its
annual
Bowling Banquet at
the
Sportsmen’s
Lodge on May 20.

WLIB—New

this

local

sented

eon

at

Hotel
Pierre.
The
WLIB

honored
was
“Community
Opinion,” the
“hot-line”
program
moderated
by
Leon
Lewis,
which
broadcast:;
the
telephoned
opinions and problems of the nation’s
largest Negro community. The
Pea-
body Award
Citation
to WLIB
said:
“(The outlet), during the hot summer
of 1966, gave Harlem a ‘safety valve.’
“Community
Opinion”
.
.
.
(per-
mitted)
citizens
of Harlem
to

their feelings, frankly and openly, via
a hot

provided

of how

ing

Talent On Stage:
Boston's American
BOSTON—Education,
innovation and
awareness
were
the
dominating
themes
of
Boston’s
first
American
Festival
of Music
(April
20-23). The
Festival
was
comprised
of
a
series
of
concerts
designed
to
trace
the
evolution and dramatize the influence
of present-day music. Its purpose was
unique
in
that
it attempted
to make
the
public
aware
of
their
musical
heritage, rather than simply display-
ing
a
conglomeration
of
diversified
talent.
This
creative
undertaking
is
hoped to be the
first of many annual
efforts presented by Unicorn Concert
Productions
and
sponsored
by
the
Boston
Herald
Traveler
Charities
Fund.
The
first
day’s
concert,
April
20,
was entitled “Music
of the Americas
(Our New World of Neighbors)”.
Its
aim was to expose the audience to as
fine and varied an international show
as possible. Impaired by several tech-
nical and organizational bugs
it was
not as enjoyable as it could have been,
but
it was moderately entertaining.
The concert opened with Babatundi
Olatunji and his company of African
dancers, drummers and
singers.
Ola-
tunji exhibited an array of primitive
African
instruments
and
explained
their cross-cultural significance. With
each explanation he demonstrated, in
heart-bursting
fashion,
the
various
ways each could be
played. Unfortu-
nately,
his African dancers
looked
a
bit too Americanized for realism and
detracted from
an
otherwise
exhila-
rating and
informative
performance.
Following Africa came
Israel, rep-
resented by Geula
Gill. Geula began
singing while serving her hitch in the
Israeli
army,
and
it
shows.
She
is
energetic and vibrant, like her young
country, and what she lacks in talent
she makes
up
in
spirit. Her Jewish
humor
and
audience
participation
songs high-lighted her act, along with
her
Israeli
hit
“Talk
to
Me
With
Flowers and Red Roses”.
From the Contrescarpe Cafe on the
Left Banke
of
Paris came
the
Con-
trescarpe
Singers.
Each member
an
accomplished
vocalist,
together
they
were
five times as
pleasurable. With
them they brought the new sound of
Paris:
classical
and
modern
poetry
put
to
music
and
spiced
with
a
comedy
routine
of
a human manne-
quin
done
by
Bernard
Haller,
that
forced you to wonder if he was really
alive. This combination of a new folk
sound and sharp comedy proved to be
a crowd
pleaser.
Ireland was the next stop, with the
rowdy, boisterous Irish Rovers. These
four
boys
with
their
bright
green
costumes and thick Irish brogue were
the most refreshing change of the en-
tire
night. They sang
down-to-earth
story-songs about the Irish Rebellion,
drinking,
and
life
in
general.
Willie
Miller describes the group as “a glass
of
fine
Irish
whiskey—smooth
and
happy,”
and
that’s
exactly
the way
they
were.
After an almost non-existent inter-
mission, Josh White
took
the
stage.
His distinctive singing style, message
songs and ultra-casual stage manner
made
him
a
rousing
hit. When
he
tried
to
leave,
a
resounding
“more,
more, more” went up from the crowd.
He came back on stage and did a song
called “The
Free And Equal
Blues,”
which
describes better than anything
else the thinking of Josh White.
From a primitive tribe deep in the
rain forests of Brazil came
the next
act.
Los
Indios
Tabajaras
and
two
guitar-playing Indian brothers whose
rough exteriors gave no sign of their
exceptional
musical
genius. They
in-
ject
a
rich,
lively sound
into
every-
thing they play, from Chopin’s Piano
Concertos
to
“Maria
Elena”
their
Mexican
smash.
Next, bringing some Jamaican beat
into
the
program
was
the
Islander
Steel Band. They did an excellent job
as
steel
bands
go,
except
for
their
over-zealous
leader who
tried
some
off-key
crooning,
which
tuned
the
audience
right
out.
The
beat
was
A HELPING HAND—Philips
recording
stars,
the
Four
Seasons,
recently
volunteered their services to the Job Corps as
unofficial ambassadors of good
will. They are now on a nationwide tour of Job Corps
centers. In
the photo
above,
Sargent
Shriver,
director
of
the
Office
of Economic
Opportunity,
is
shown
helping Four
Seasons’ Tommy
DeVito
into
his Job Corps
blazer
in
his
( Shriver ’s) Washington
office. Looking on are
the other members
of the
Four Seasons:
(from
left to right) Bob Gaudio, Frankie
Valli, and Joe Long.
Festival Of Music
good,
the
sound was
pure,
and
the
singer was
terrible.
The
low
point
of
the
show came
with
the
Mexican
Mariachi
Band.
Their
good
Tiajuana
sound
was
ruined
by
redundancy
and
amateur-
ish
stage
maneuvers.
The
over-
stretched act proved
to be exception-
ally noisy and boring.
The
closing
act,
the
Mothers
of
Invention, were,
if nothing
else,
ori-
ginal.
Frank
Zappa,
the
composer,
arranger and leader of the group has
started
a new
phase which
he
calls
“Mothers’
Music.”
Their
long,
disar-
ranged
hair and
tight
multi-colored
j
clothes are part
of this phase.
The
act
itself,
although
relatively
organized, appeared
to be an
off-the-
cuff
improvisation. Instruments were
used, but there was no distinguishable
sign of music. The audience screamed,
yelled
and
laughed,
but
I
think
it
was
at them
rather
than
for
them.
Thursday
night’s concert, although
reasonably entertaining, was extreme-
ly over-packed. A
scheduled two and
one-half hour show
lasted nearly
six
hours, which grew to be a
little tedi-
ous.
This
being
the
first
concert
of
the
first year’s
Festival,
it should be
excused,
but
should
be
taken
into
consideration next year.
There were
three
concerts
Friday,
one
afternoon,
one
evening, and
one
late
night.
The
afternoon
concert,
which
featured
the
Siegal-Schwall
Band,
Muddy
Waters,
and
Chuck
Berry
could
have
been
eliminated.
Those
three
acts
not
only
appeared
again
later
the same
day,
but were
considerably
better
at
night.
‘Frontier
Tradition’
Friday’s
concerts
were
designated
“The
Frontier
Tradition
(From
Ply-
mouth
Rock
to
Hullabaloo),”
and
|
stayed within the boundaries
of folk
music.
The
goal
of
these
concerts
was
to make
the
audience aware
of
how
music
was
born
and
nurtured
in
the
United
States.
Pete
Seeger
opened
the
evening
concert.
He
is
looked
up
to
by
all
folk
singers and cheered by
all
folk
music
lovers.
This
night
was
no
exception. Pete
is a feeling, sensitive
person who sings from the soul. This
was the perfect man
to
start a
con-
cert,
especially
this
one.
Frontier
tradition
is
family
tradi-
tion, and family tradition is the Beers
Family.
Bob,
Evelyne
and
their
daughter
Martha
sang,
danced
and
accompanied themselves with
several
interesting
frontier instruments. The
!
act was
enjoyable, but just
a
bit
to
stuffy
for a
hip Boston
audience.
Far
from
stuffy,
Arlo
Gunthrie
might be one of the most imaginative
young folk singers of this generation.
He was on stage for twenty minutes
and
did
one
witty,
sardonic
protest
song,
“Alice’s
Restaurant.”
It
was
invigorating
to
hear him
tear down
established
institutions that so many
people
swear
by.
His
unique
style,
the ragtime talking blues,
will make
Arlo Gunthrie an immortal someday.
Two years
is a painfully short time
to
become
a
folk
star.
Leonda
is
a
product of an age
in which failure
is
i
reserved for the old. She
is a dynamic
j
i
young
talent who
will
inevitably
be
(
j
great once she
is given time to devel-
1
j
op
all
of
her
tremendous
potential.
Josh White
Jr., a singer as young
as Leonda, has already gone through
the
mill
and
acquired an abundance
of
polish. He
demonstrated
this
by
doing
a
slow,
quiet
and
pure-toned
melody
in an almost whispered fash-
ion.
This
high-lighted
his
act
and
proved his credentials as
his
father’s
son.
After
the
second
night’s
abbrevi-
ated
intermission,
Dave
Van
Ronk
came
on. His voice was gravelly and
rough
but
had
a
powerful
quality.
He blasted out a song called “Legend
;
Of A Sailor” in an unusual vocal man-
ner. He frequently raised and lowered
1
his
voice, not
for emphasis, but
for
effect.
Dave’s
most
valuable
asset
is
not
his
voice
but
his
personality.
Of
all the entertainers on the pro-
gram, Tom
Paxton
would
probably
be
considered
the
most
successful.
He’s
been
in
the music
business
for
only
six
and
a
half
years,
but
is
rated
as one
of
the
very
best. Tom
does not sing a song, but experiences
it. He
relates
the
inner meaning
of
every word
almost
as
if
each
were
his own
child
and
he was
a
proud
father showing them
off. Tom
is one
of
the few
entertainers
you can
re-
fer
to as an
artist.
The Highwaymen
were
a
skillful,
experienced,
and
tuneful
group.
Re-
grettably,
their
skill
and humor
did
not
set them apart from a multitude
of
other very pleasant
groups. They
will never cease to entertain, but like-
wise
they
will
never
captivate
an
audience.
Closing
the
evening
concert
were
the
popular
Jefferson
Airplane.
Un-
like most of the
psychedellic groups
the music
of the
Airplane was
rela-
tively
conventional.
They
added
a
“free
spirit”
to
a
hackneyed
rock
sound and came up with a genuinely
modern
concert. The
vocalist, Marty
Baffin,
along with numerous
colored
spotlights, added the finishing touches
to an odd looking but peculiarly lucid
group.
‘Living
Blues’
After a
quick change
of audiences
the
late
night concert was
ready
to
go.
This
concert was
the
first
of
a
two-part
section
called
“The
Living-
Blues (From Mississippi to Chicago).”
Its main
objective was
to
trace
the
growth of blues and jazz
in America.
Leading off was John Lee Hooker, a
now legendary Mississippi blues sing-
er.
His
slow and easy chanting and
automatic
guitar
accompaniment
gently crept into the ears of the en-
tire
audience.
His melancholy Negro
work
songs
were
especially
popular.
One
of the biggest groups on
the
Chicago
scene
today
is
the
Siegal-
Schwall
Band.
Their
approach
was
novel
in
that they
did
folk-rock and
jazz
with
electric
instruments.
The
vocal was
sour, but the instrumental
was superb. Of the various
first-rate
nieces,
an
harmonica
solo by
Corky
Siegal was the outstanding high point.
The most disappointing
act
of the
entire
evening
was
Muddy
Waters.
He
was
poor
in
the
afternoon
and
improved
slightly
at
night,
but was
still a frustrating let-down. His band
was
tinny and
over-amplified. When
he finally broke through the noise, his
voice
was
harsh
and
projected
an
absence
of
emotion.
Muddy
Waters
is getting
old, but that
is no reason
to become
inferior.
Chuck
Berry,
a
rock
’n
roll
star
for
over
a
decade,
closed
the
show
with a smash hit. He started
off slow
and
gained
speed
singing
such
fa-
vorites
as
“Mabelline,”
“Johnny
Be
Good,”
“Sweet
16,”
“Roll
Over
Beethoven,”
and
many
other
self-
composed hits. For the first time dur-
ing
the
run
of
the
Festival
a
per-
former
received
a
standing
ovation.
Chuck Berry
is as good today as he
was twelve years ago.
Skip
James,
an
old
time
country-
blues
singer, started
off “The
Living-
Blues
Part
II”
concert
Saturday
night.
His
voice was
high and
thin,
with
a
sad,
moody
overtone.
Skip
sang about his own hardships
in
the
vernacular
of
the
Old
South.
His
different
singing
style
and
agile
guitar
playing
started
the
night
off
right.
The
next
act, The
Stevens
Gospel
Singers,
were
exceedingly
atrocious.
They
sang
loud
and
ineptly.
The
traditional
quality of the
fine South-
ern spiritual was lowered to a prayer-
meeting
type
mockery. The
“Gospel
Singers” should undoubtedly
be ban-
ned
in
Boston.
Carmen McRae
entered, and
order
was
brought
back
to
the
stage
by
her
mere
presence.
She
sang
each
word
of
every
song
distinctly,
and
occasionally drew one out to a breath-
less
summit.
Carmen
interpreted
every
song
into
electrical
impulses
felt by
all who
listened. Her closing
and most emotional number,
“Alfie,”
also was her biggest.
Sonny Terry and Brownie McGhee
were
mildly
entertaining.
They
of-
fered a respite between big acts, but
were cut short in the middle of their
own. The roughness with which they
were
handled
was
in
astoundingly
poor
taste and
should
be
avoided
in
the future.
Art Blakey and
the
Jazz
Messen-
gers
served up
a
slice
of good mod-
ern
jazz.
The
progressively
improv-
ing
solos
shifted
from
the
saxo-
phonist, but the big one was done by
Art
himself.
In
his
closing
piece
“Tunisia,”
Art
went
into
an
ear-
shattering drum solo that ended with
two
sticks
in
orbit
and
unbridled
cheers from the audience.
Buddy Rich’s new Big Band was a
thrilling
thing
to
hear.
Buddy,
ac-
claimed
to
be
the
greatest
living-
drummer, led the band by his skillful
drumbeat.
Among
his
best
efforts
were
selections
from
“West
Side
Story”
and
the
Beatles “Norwegian
Wood.” For the second and
last time
during
the
Festival
an
entertainer
received a standing ovation.
Sunday’s
concert was
the
last
of
the
Festival.
It
was
entitled
“The
Mountains and the Plains (The Nash-
ville Sound).” The country and west-
ern
headliners
for
the
last
concert
included
Archie
Campbell,
Webb
Pierce,
Dottie
West,
Carl
Smith,
Grandpa
Jones,
Flatt
and
Scruggs
and Tex
Ritter who
stole
the show
with
his
blue
grass
hit
“Hillbilly
Heaven.”
The
American
Festival
of
Music
was
an
overwhelming
success.
The
hall, the Commonwealth Armory, was
far
from
accoustically
perfect.
The
sound
system
was
referred
to
as
“cheesy” and the
seats were uncom-
fortably
hard, but
this was expected
for
the
first
year.
The
outstanding
calibre of talent dwarfed most of the
technical
and
organizational
difficul-
ties
and
produced
one
hell
of
a
Festival.
46
Cash Box—May
6, 1967

NEW YORK—Flowers,

The

LONDON—Louis

(2)

and a grandson, Nicholas Firth.

named
professional manager
of
Sat-
urday
Music,
it
has
been
announced
by Tom
Catalano,
vice
president
of
the Crewe Group
of Companies. Un-
der the
exclusive long-term
contract,
Weiss,
in
addition
to
his
duties
as
professional manager, will contribute
his talents as a songwriter.
Weiss entered the music business as
a free-lance writer. His first successes
were
with
Nat
“King”
Cole,
Timi
Yuro
and
Chuck
Jackson.
In
1965,
Weiss joined the A & R department of
Kapp Records.
Last
year,
Weiss
became
general
professional
manager
of
the
Claus
Ogerman
pubberies—Helios/Glamous
Music.
He
was
responsible
for
hit
records both here and abroad by the
Animals, the
Outsiders, Gene
Pitney,
Chris
Montez,
Bobby
Vinton,
the
Standells, Jerry Butler and the Toys.
Weiss’ last releases for Helios before
joining
Saturday
Music
were
Jeff
Beck’s “Hi-Ho
Silver Lining”,
Goldie
& the Gingerbreads’ “Walking In Dif-
ferent
Circles”
and
the
Montanas’
“Caio Baby”—all in current release.

Monument Acquires
bounds Of Babies
7
HOLLYWOOD—Monument
Records
has
acquired
the
rights
to
“The
Sounds
Of
Babies” LP from
Hutsh,
Ltd.
Especially
dedicated
to
new
and
expectant
parents,
the
“Sounds”
re-
cording
is devoted
to
“live” perform-
ances
by
babies,
with
hundreds
of
sounds taped over a period of months
and
endless
editing
sessions,
so
that
the
final
result could be explained
in
detail
by
Dr.
Harry
F.
Dietrich,
a
pediatrician
of
Beverly
Hills,
who
narrates
the
special
script
prepared
by Edward E. Hutshing.
Monument
plans
special
merchan-
dising of the unique LP according to
Bob Summers, vice president of sales
and
merchandising,
slanting
special
sales
efforts
at
the
maternity
and
baby
departments
of
large
chain
stores as well
as normal
record
out-
lets.
George
Durgom
produced
the LP
in

of
Hutsh,
Ltd.,
and
con-
cluded the contract negotiations with
Bobby
Weiss, Monument
vice

dent
and

International
Division, who
also
helms
the
Holly-
wood
office
for

Columbia's Chicago
Service Center Opens
NEW
T
YORK — Columbia
Records’
Chicago service center moves into
its
new headquarters on May
8.
The new service center
is located at
5410 W. Touhy Avenue in the Edens
Industrial Park
in
Skokie,
Illinois,
a
suburb of Chicago. The one-story cus-
tom
designed
structure
is
the
most
modern
of Columbia Records’
service
centers, the label claims.
The new facility is reportedly twice
as
large
as
the
old
Chicago
service
center.
It
will
house
sales and
ship-
ping installations, as well as facilities
for
phonograph
repairs.
Columbia
states that this
is the
first such oper-
ation
within
any
of
its
service
centers.
Among the
staff members who will
occupy the new premises are Colum-
bia’s
North
Central
regional
man-
ager; the operations manager for the
Chicago service center; the sales man-
ager of Columbia Records in Chicago;
field
promotion
managers;
the man-
ager of special markets;
the Chicago
field
credit manager;
and
Date
Rec-
ords’
Mid-West
regional
promotion
manager.
The new Chicago service center will
render greatly improved working
fa-
cilities
and
substantially
increased
space.
Situated
within
commercial
trucking zones, the new facility offers
easy access to all major roads. Among
the markets serviced by the new cen-
ter are
Illinois, Minnesota, Iowa, Ne-
braska,
North
and
South
Dakota,
and parts
of Indiana and Montana.
Columbia
Records inaugurated
the
service
center operations some
years
ago. Presently, the label has in-plant
service
centers
at
the
Pitman, New
Jersey,
Terre
Haute,
Indiana,
and
Santa Maria, California manufactur-
ing plants, as well as regular service
centers
in Chicopee
Falls, Massachu-
setts, Cleveland, and Dallas.
The
negotiations and planning
for
the
Chicago
service
center
were
handled by Warner
N.
Pagliara,
di-
rector of administration
of Columbia
Records
Sales
in
conjunction
with
Milton
Maier,
director
of CBS
real
estate
and
the CBS
real
estate
de-
partment.

FOCOS ON jazz
"n•lUll|lll'lHl|llWlll:nl^ r
FEGA
No
one
can
dispute
the
fact
that
jazz
is in the throes of a major revo-
lution,
perhaps
the most
violent
de-
parture
that
the
music
has
ever
known.
Knowing
people
would
also
acknowledge
that
this
is
in
keeping
with
the
socio-economic
upheaval
that
has
become
such
a
significant
aspect
of our society today. Much
is
being
written
about
the “now”
jazz
in the various
publications; much
of
it
is being played in clubs throughout
the country; most of the young jazz
players
are
oriented
to
this
“free”
jazz. But, by proportion to the amount
of
space
it
is
being
given
in
the
written
and
spoken
word,
there
are
relatively few record companies pro-
ducing this type of jazz.
It begs the
question, why?
With some minor exceptions, minor
in
the
quantitative
rather
than
the
qualitative
sense,
the
major
labels
have
declined
recording
the
young
rebels
in jazz. When we speak of the
major labels, we mean Columbia, EGA
Victor,
MGM-Verve,
each
of
which
has an abundant
roster
of
jazz
art-
ists, and from whom they enjoy huge
revenue.
It would seem
that
in
the
best
interest
of
perpetuating
jazz
these same
companies would
be
the
very
ones who
could
best
afford
to
give
voice and
exposure
to
the new
expressionists.
But
such
is
not
the
case! The task has fallen
to
the
les-
ser
labels, one
of which was
created
for the sole purpose of recording the
new breed of jazzman, confident that
this
is the
jazz
of the future,
or,
as
many believe, the jazz of the present.
Our mission
will be
to
discuss these
labels
that
have
chosen
to
pursue
this highly
speculative, but very
ex-
citing
course.
Who
Are The Champions
Of The New Jazz?
Impulse
Records,
the
jazz
subsid-
iary of ABC, under the aegis of Bob
Thiele,
has
produced
some
of
the
most exciting of the new jazz. Thiele,
a
young
veteran
of
the
recording
business,
has
an
illustrious
history
as a producer of good jazz recordings.
His
Signature
recordings
of
1943
with Coleman Hawkins, Oscar
Petti-
ford, Eddie Heywood,
Shelly Manne,
and
others
are
legend,
as
are
his
recordings of Ben Webster and Lester
Young.
In
the
years
between
then
and now. Bob has recorded many
of
the
greats, names
like
Louis
Arm-
strong, Duke
Ellington,
and Johnny
Hodges,
all
giants and
all
tradition-
alists.
So,
in the
light of these
asso-
ciations,
Thiele’s
affiliation
with
the
new jazz takes on added significance.
The heavyweight
in
Thiele’s stable
of
jazz
artists
is,
unquestionably,
John
Coltrane.
Perhaps
more
than
any
other
avant
gardist,
Coltrane’s
Impulse albums sell the best. It would
seem,
from
talking
to
young
jazz
fans,
that
John
Coltrane
is
con-
sidered
the
spiritual
leader
of
the
new movement
in
jazz. This,
in spite
of
the
fact
that
Ornette
Coleman
pre-dated
Trane.
Each
of Coltrane’s new
releases
is
anticipated
with
great
relish by
his
followers, and the more extended each
of
the
tracks
on
the album
is,
the
better the
Coltrane
disciples seem
to
like
it. The
philosophy
of
long
cuts
is indigenous
to the recording of the
new jazy, and as a consequence, pre-
cludes the possibility of much air play.
In spite of this lack of exposure, the
sales
of
Coltrane’s
albums
continue
to soar. Another of the new breed
in
jazz
is
Archie
Shepp,
who,
before
his
Impulse
affiliation,
was
a
com-
parative
unknown
to
jazz
fans.
Shepp’s
popularity
similarly
grows
with
each
successive
album
release.
Trombonist Roswell Rudd
is
yet an-
other of the new jazz exponents whom
Thiele
has
recorded
with
great
suc-
cess.
Blue Note Records, whose forte over
the years has been conventional jazz
recordings, has with increasing regu-
larity been releasing albums that fea-
ture
the
“outside”
jazz.
The
credit
for this departure must go to Alfred
Lion and Frank Wolff, the originators
of the Blue Note label. More than any
other
jazz
producers, these two men
have
recorded
the
giants
of modern
jazz.
Their
list
of
accomplishments
include Thelonius Monk, Fats Navar-
ro, Bud Powell, Miles Davis,
Clifford
Brown,
Art
Blakey,
Horace
Silver,
Tadd
Dameron,
and
so many
more.
So, Lion and Wolff come well recom-
mended,
too.
Today Blue Note
is recording such
“outsiders”
as
Andrew
Hill,
Bobby
Hutcherson,
Sam
Rivers,
Joe
Hen-
derson, Anthony Williams. Admitted-
ly,
these men have not achieved the
big
reputation
yet,
but
if
the
new
jazz
is
to
prosper,
they
are
in
the
vanguard of the movement and they
should enjoy the benefits. This
situa-
tion
is
identical
to
the
bop
revolu-
tion
of over twenty years ago when
the
aforementioned
titans
were
re-
corded.
And
herein
hangs
the
tale:
it
is the men of vision who continue
to infuse
jazz, or any art form, with
vitality
and
growth.
Bernard
Stollman,
The Boldest Of Them
All
Earlier
I
mentioned
a
man
who
formed
a
label
for
the
express
pur-
pose
of recording new
jazzmen.
His
name
is
Bernard
Stollman,
an
at-
torney
by
profession,
and
the ESP
label
is
his.
Prior
to
the
institution
of
the
ESP
label,
Stollman
func-
tioned exclusively as a legal
advisor,
often to performers. Stollman’s efforts
in
the
interest
of
the
“new”
jazz
players
is
especially noteworthy
be-
cause, unlike established labels which
have
their normal
output
to
sustain
them,
he
started
from
scratch
and
depended
on new
artists
exclusively
to
make
it
go.
Not
only
did ESP
feature
new
and
unknown
artists,
but
it
featured
a
completely
new
concept
in
packaging,
as
well.
For
one
thing, ESP albums
did not have
any
liner
notes;
for
another
thing,
the
artwork
embodied
in
the
pack-
aging was characteristic to the music
contained
in the album. The concept
was
constant,
completely
uncompro-
mising,
with
not
the
slightest
sug-
gestion
of
commercialism.
Because
I am intimately acquainted with Stoll-
man,
I can tell you that he had more
than
his
share
of
difficulty
in
insti-
tuting the ESP
label. In
spite of
all
the
trials,
distribution,
public
ac-
ceptance,
et
al,
Stollman
prevailed
and today the ESP label and
its ros-
ter of artists are generally considered
to be the true champions of the “new”
jazz.
For
their
perserverance
and
their strong
self-belief everyone con-
nected with
the ESP
label
is
to be
congratulated.
In
the
strictest
sense
of the word, they are pioneers!
There
are
others who
are worthy
of mention
in our exploration of the
development of the new thing in jazz.
Certainly,
we
should
commend
Les
Koenig
and
his
Contemporary
label
for the two Ornette Coleman albums
that he produced
in the
late
Fifties.
Nesuhi Ertegun
at
Atlantic,
for
his
further
efforts with Coleman
in
the
early
Sixties,
deserves
praise. RCA
Victor
recorded
several
exciting
al-
bums
with
Sonny
Rollins
upon
his
return
after
a two
year
retirement.
Prestige
gave
Eric
Dolphy
his
first
opportunity
to be heard
as a leader
when
he
departed
the
Chico Hamil-
ton
group.
Savoy
Records, when
it
was
active
in
recording
jazz,
gave
voice
to
new
players
like
Archie
Shepp,
Bill
Dixon,
and
Bill
Barron.
Even Decca Records, not known par-
ticularly
for
its
jazz
product,
re-
corded
George
Russell,
a
true
inno-
vator.
Riverside
Records,
in
its
hal-
cyon
days,
also
gave
expression
to
many jazz radicals. Columbia Records
deserves
mention
for
its
two
John
Handy albums, conceivably the finest
of
the new
jazz
that
has
been
re-
corded,
to
date.
In
my
recollections
I
obviously
have
overlooked
people
who
have
made
some
contribution
in
the
evo-
lution
of
the new
jazz.
For
this
I
have regrets. However,
to those peo-
ple,
in
fact
to
all
people
connected
with
the new
jazz movement,
I
say
revel
in
the
inner
satisfaction
that
comes from knowing
that you have
made
your
contribution.
You
are
among
the
lion-hearted,
that
special
breed who defy the gods.

THE CROONER — Steve Mason — Mason MLP
1003
i

sings a
set
of pop
outings that
were
popular
in
the
’20’s
and
’30’s.
Featured
on the LP are

Internotionol News Report
Liberty Completes British Entity
LONDON — Bob
Reisdorff,
who
ar-
rived
in
this
country
three
months
ago
to take up
his position as man-
aging
director
designate
of
the
Lib-
erty Records
Ltd.
British
operation,
reports that plans are now complete
and
Liberty’s
independent
onslaught
on the British market will get under-
way in July. Label’s existing contract
with EMI
expires
June
30,
as
re-
ported in last week’s
issue.
As
soon
as
negotiations
are
com-
pleted
the
company
will
move
into
their new headquarters at
11, Alber-
marle Street, London, W.
1. Meantime
both record and publishing
activities
will
be
carried
on from
the
Metric
Music
ofl5,ce
at
52,
Maddox
Street,
London. The aims
of
Liberty’s
inde-
pendent
record
operation
will
be
to
sign and produce
British
artists
for
U.S. and world wide release but with
the
accent
on
the
U.K.
In
London
Reisdorff will also be responsible for
the
selection
of
material
from
the
American Liberty catalog but will not
automatically issue either U.S. artists
or material in Britain unless he feels
it is right for the British market. The
first release tentatively scheduled for
July
will
feature
a
British
singer
name and
title
as yet undisclosed.
The new
British names
will
take
their place alongside such established
Liberty
talent
as
Del
Shannon,
P.J.
Proby and Cher whose British image
will also be boosted by the new com-
pany. A
strong promotional
depart-
ment headed by Ron Bell will be
set
up to work closely with A & R per-
sonnel as well as
deejays, radio and
TV producers etc. to ensure maximum
exploitation for all Liberty talent. Re-
leases by
artists from Liberty’s sub-
sidiary
labels,
Dolton,
Imperial
and
Minit will also be made on the Liberty
label. The Blue Note
product which
will continue
to be imported
will go
out on its own label. It was Reisdorff
who
founded
the
Dolton
label
and
Cornerstone
publishing
company
in
1959
discovering
such
talent
as
Vic
Dana, The Ventures, The Fleetwoods
etc. In 1964 he sold Dolton to Liberty.
Outlining his plans Bob Reisdorff told
Cash Box that
the company’s major
interest will be
in finding and
devel-
oping new singers with the talent and
sound
to
become
sustaining
record
stars. Liberty Records Ltd. has no in-
tention of rushing into the studios for
the sake of recording. Unless a record
is
worthy
of
release
it
will
not
be
issued.
Publishing
Build-Up
On
the
publishing
side,
an
all-out
drive
will be made
to seek and
sign
British composers whose material will
BOB
REISDORFF
be released both at home and abroad.
To sum up Reisdorff hopes that Lib-
erty Records Ltd. will, in due course,
become as important as Liberty Rec-
ords is in America and the rest of the
world. Pressing and distribution plans
have
yet
to
be
finalized.
However,
London will be the heart of Liberty’s
export
business
for
Europe,
Africa,
the Near and Middle East and Nordic
countries. The exceptions will be Ger-
many, where the company has
it own
distribution

Mercury Establishes London Office
Under Reiiner; 2- Way Ties Cited
CHICAGO—Dramatizing the
increas-
ing
importance
of
coordinating
the
European and American disk markets
Irving
Green,

of

Records, has appointed Lou
Reizner,

for the
firm
in Lon-
don.
Catalyst In Cooperation
“Reizner can become
a
vital
cata-
lyst in achieving the proper equation
for
the
smoothest,
quickest
coopera-
tion between these two strategic areas
which
represent
approximately 75%
of the world’s sales on many kinds of

product,” Green
stated.
Reiz-
ner’s

in
Europe
will
be multi-pronged. Green said. He will
work
closely
with
Philips
Phono-
graphic
Industries
to

that
American and European record prod-
uct from
either source gets the
ulti-
mate exposure in both sales areas. “I
feel
strongly that the presence
of
a
qualified
American
record
executive
like
Reizner, when coupled with
the
activity of a European record veteran
such as Herman Cats of PPI, can pro-
vide
the
essential teamwork
for
the
greatest mutual sales benefits,” Green
opined. “Cats and Reizner with their
extensive experience
in many phases
of our business insure continuous ex-
pert supervision of this essential liai-
son that
is
required by the growing
one-world concept in recorded sounds,”
Green said.
Green
pointed
to
Cats’
recent
lengthy
visit to the United States as
already bearing fruit toward a
closer-
link
between
the
cross-licensees
of
PPI and the
five
labels
in the Mer-
cury family. Smash, Fontana, Philips,
Limelight and Mercury. Green noted
Reizner’s
successful
track
record
as

poration, during which he brought to
the
United

Philips’
companies
in

such

as
The
Swingle

Horst Jankowski, The
Singing Nun,
The Mindbenders and Dave Dee, Dozy,
Beaky, Mick, and Tich among others.
Not only will Reizner work with prod-
uct already produced
in Europe, but
he
will work
directly with European
artists
in formulating product which
will be aimed for the American mar-
ket such as has been the case
in his
A&R contact with Jankowski, for ex-
ample.
.

Exirope

^^*<;germany^
It’s
all over but the
celebrating. Long, long
ago, the German GEMA, the
equivalent
to ASCAP-BMI
stateside,
sued
the
five major manufacturers
of
tape recorders here
for
a percentual
interest
in
their
sales
for
the
use
of
music controlled by GEMA. Now, the five firms—Telefunken, Grundig, German
Philips, Saba and Uher—have
agreed
to pay
4
million marks
(one
million
dollars)
yearly
in
royalties
for
the
right
to tape
records and
radio
shows.
GEMA has been trying for years to get a settlement in this case and started
back in 1963 with the first process. The demand was for 5% of the local sales
on
tape
recorders
for composers
and
authors.
The
manufacturers
declared
themselves ready to pay 1.5% for the rights but would not open their books
to inspection by GEMA as they felt that the competition would have too much
of an insight into their business.
The firms have now agreed on the round sum
of 4 million marks
so that
business
secrets
can
be
kept. Payment
is from
the
first
of January,
1966,
retroactive. Great news for authors and composers in this country!
Bad news for the record buyers also came this week as the tax authorities
decided
to
cut
the 5%
tax
reduction
for phonograph
records, and
it
looks
like
price
increases
will
be
carried
through
here.
With
the
single
record
already costing $1.19 (DM
4.75),
just how high can
prices go and
still
sell
product?
Switzerland has already cut the price
of singles back and turnover
has increased tremendously. The LP’s here are running from between DM
6
($1.25)
to the normal price
of DM
18
($4.50) which
is
fine and
sales show,
but the overpriced singles have really lost their impulse buying power through
the high prices, and sales have dropped tremendously since the price raise of
about 4 years ago.
Nobody can say that Hamburg
is not doing anything for music. The
city
will pay
out
21.5
million marks
(over
$5
million)
next
year
in
boosts
to
theatres, the state opera, the philharmonic,
etc. The
loss for the opera alone
will run about 13 million marks.
One of the most famous German operetta and pop composers and publishers.
Will Meisel, died at the age of
69. Will Meisel was born on the 17th
of Sep-
tember 1897 in Rixdorf. The famous composer wrote hundreds of evergreens
and top hits. Last year he celebrated his 40th year as a music publisher and
his 60th year as an artist. The popular music man
is survived by his wife and
Peter & Thomas Meisel who are
also very active in the music business. The
world of music
is one fine man poorer.

“Marne” star Angela Lansbury vis-
ited

Throughout the month of May,

“Marne” motif. In the New York store

vette

to

The entire “Marne” Month program

Subsequently,

to

of
Miss
Lans-
bury’s appearances and promote

“Marne” LP.
Columbia reports that

“Marne” LP
have

high thus far in May. The success of
“Marne” Month
is a result of the
co-
operative efforts of the E. J. Korvette
chain, the producers of the show, and
Columbia Records’ New York branch.

and “Funny, Familiar, Forgotten Feel-

Musicor

VTI
Records Bows
HOLLYWOOD—A
new
label,
VTI
Records, has been formed by Variety
Theatre International of Duluth, Min-
nesota, long-time bookers and promo-
ters of shows and concerts throughout
the country. The new
label, which
is
Variety
Theatre
International’s
first
venture in the recording business, will
be based here
in Hollywood and
will
be
under
the
direction
of Andy
Di
Martino as general manager.
The
parent
firm
has
long
range
plans for the label which include de-
veloping new acts through recordings
which
they
(the
acts)
will promote
nationally through
concert and show
appearances.
The first new act developed by the
firm
is the 7 Sons, whose first record-
ing, “Baby
Please Come Back,” was
released
recently. VTI has named 24
distributors nationally and Di Martino
leaves
today
(22)
on
a
tour
of
the
country
to
visit the
distributors and
radio stations on the new release.
A publishing firm, Minnesota Music,
has also been established and will op-
erate from
the
Hollywood
offices
of
VTI. Writers under contract
to Min-
nesota are John Gummoe, composer of
“Rhythm
Of
The
Rain,”
and
Gabe
Lapano.
Di Martino was most recently
en-
gaged
in independent record produc-
tion
and
personal
management.
He
produced
sessions
for
several
labels,
notably
the
Cascades’
hit
single,
“Rhythm Of The
Rain,” for Valiant.
He
still
produces the
Cascades, now
on
Smash, and he
also produces the
Wallers on Viva and Johnny Parris on
Dunhill. These three acts will now be
under the direction of Variety Theatre
International
for
management
and
bookings.
Prior
to
entering
the
independent
production
field,
Di
Martino was an
A&R man
for Liberty
Records, pro-
ducing sessions for such artists as the
Fleetwoods and the Accents. He was
also associated with Charter Records
as
vice
president
in
charge
of A&R
and promotion.
Martino’s
duties
as
general man-
ager of VTI Records will include audi-
tioning
talent
and
material
for
the
label.
Artists
signed
and
additional
personnel will be announced when he
returns from his present trip.

NY UJA Campaign
NEW YORK—Little more than two
weeks remain
before
reservations
to
the N.Y. UJA Coin Division’s testimo-
nial dinner in honor of MONY attor-
ney Teddy Blatt are closed complete-
ly. The
affair, the year’s
social high-
point for the metropolitan area
coin
machine industry, will take place June
10th at the Statler-Hilton Hotel.
1967 campaign chairman
Gil Sonin
strongly urges all operators who have
thus
far
neglected
to
reserve
their
seats
for
the
dinner and
those who
have
filed
reservations
but
require
additional
seats
to
contact
the com-
mittee NOW
before
time
runs
out
completely.
At an executive committee meeting
held last Tues. evening at UJA head-
quarters,
Sqnin announced
that
over
$46,000 has thus far been pledged by
the
industry
for UJA.
“This
is
an
amazing response from the trade for
In Home Stretch
UJA and
in honor
of Teddy
Blatt,”
Sonin declared, “but we’ll continue to
build upon
this
total right up
to the
very last minute.”
Sonin urged the entire committee_ to

TALENT ON STAGE
BOBBY VINTON
NEW CHART
ADDITIONS
There’s a rumor going ’round that
mama don’t allow no swinging cats at
the
Copa, but Bobby Vinton
doesn’t
care
what mama
don’t
allow—he’s
gonna swing anyhow, with the Jules
Podell’s blessing.
Vinton has come a long way from
the rock
'n
roller who wrote “Roses
Are Red, My Love”
in some
school-
girl’s graduation book, but wisely he
has not come so far that he can’t dip
into the rock bag to
flavor
his Copa
act.
The opening night show was high-
lighted by medleys, one following an-
other in a breezy, fast-paced perform-
ance which couldn’t help but charm at
least a good portion of the audience.
Most of the numbers were chosen for
their
brightness
and
long-standing
appeal,
with
an
A1
Jolson
medley
(“Rosie,” “Swanee,” “Rockabye Your
Baby” and “Anniversary Waltz”) and
an
international
potpourri
(“Cest
Si
Bon,” “Cuando
Caliente
El
Sol” and
“Havah
Nagila”)
highlighting
that
part of the evening.
There was also a sprinkling of Vin-
ton hit recordings, most of which fall
into a more melancholy classification.
His
“Roses
Are
Red”
and
“Blue
Velvet”
are
charming,
and
“Mr.
Lonely”
is touching
in
its
simplicity
and sincerity.
The evening was marred, however,
by
Bobby’s
apparent
difficulty
with
lyrics
at
several
points
during
the
show. Although there were fine recov-
eries
in
each
of
the
instances,
the
edge was taken off what would other-
wise
have
been
a
first-rate
show.
Bobby also gets plus and minus points
with
the
addition
of
two
“Georgie
Girls”
to
the
act. On the
plus
side,
both
girls
are
lovely,
and
both
are
talented.
They
provide
an
excellent
backing
to
Bobby
on
several
sets,
both musically and visually. There are
one or two spots, however when they
are a bit distracting to the audience.
Also worth a meritorious mention
was
Vinton’s
closing
number
of
“Gotta
Travel On,” when the
singer
had
the
finesse
to
call back
Bernie
Berns, the show’s comic, to help him
close out the show.

Epic
Sales Contest
Winners Announced
NEW YORK—Mort
Hoffman,
Epic
Records’
director of marketing,
last
week announced the three winners of
Epic’s four-month sales incentive pro-
gram.
In
the program, which began
on January 2 and ran
till
April
29,
distributors
competed
against
each
other,
earning
points based on
per-
formance
in the
sale of records dur-
ing the contest.
The
firet-place prize, a 1967 Cadil-
lac DeVille convertible, was awarded
to Don Dumont, Dumont Record Dis-
tributors,
Boston.
The
second
prize,
consisting
of
an
all-expense-paid,
week-long trip for two to Paris, was
won by Al Hirsch
of Malveme
Dis-
tributors
in New York. A week
for
two
in the Caribbean, the third-place
prize, was
capped by Joe
Stanzione
of
Campus
Record
Distributors
in
Miami.
All personnel within each
distribu-
torship
participated
in
the program.
Prizes
to other personnel
in the top
three
organizations
include
a
19"
table-model
color
television
set
to
each promotion manager and
opera-
tions manager, as well as to all sales-
men.
Female members
of
the
office
and warehouse staffs received Ronson
portable
hair
dryers,
and
the
men,
Ronson electric razors.

Elekf-ra Growth
(Continued from page 6)
Holzman
himself,

child, Siegel and Abramson have au-
thority
to

its
expanded

at
1855
Broadway in New York. All functions
operate out of an entire floor, includ-

to

man believes that one of the
critical
problems

label
is the retention of important acts.

Nevada Dist. Plans
Scandinavian Tour
RENO, NEVADA—Lane
G.
Fleis-
cher,
president
of
three
amusement
games
and gaming
device
distribut-
ing firms headquartered in Reno, has
announced
a
forthcoming
sales
trip
to
take
him
throughout
the
Scan-
dinavian
nations
and
the
Northern
European
countries.
Fleischer, who heads up the Nevada
Fruit Machine
Corp., Alman
Enter-
prises and
Mills
Sales
Co.
Ltd.,
will
depart
from
Vancouver,
Canada
on
June
29
and
arrive
in
Copenhagen,
Denmark on the
30. From Denmark,
the
games
distributor
will
motor
throughout the North countries touch-
ing upon
all the important coin ma-
chine markets from Olso to Stockholm
and eventually return to Europe.
Fleischer’s European itinerary will
include
Germany,
Holland,
Belgium
(he intends
to
hit Antwerp
on July
20)
and
finally back
to Copenhagen
Aug.
10.
In
all,
the
Reno
distributor
will
have
spent
seven
weeks
on
his
European sales junket. Accompanying
him
will
be
his
wife
and
daughter
(whose fiuent Norwegian and Danish
should help in business transactions).
Any
European
games
operators
wishing to contact Fleischer can leave
word
at
Skandinavish Motor
Co.
in
Copenhagen where he will be in con-
stant
touch.
Fleischer’s
firms
distri-
bute new and used equipment of both
amusement and gaming
varieties
in-
cluding
machines
manufactured
by
Bally, Mills, Jennings and other U.S.
based factories.
Operator's Son Gains
Annapolis Appointment
DICK MASSA
CHICAGO—Dick
Massa,
son
of
Mr.
& Mrs. Silvio Massa, owner of M & M
Music Company,
in Munster, Indiana,
was notified last week of his appoint-
ment
to
the
United
States
Naval
Academy at Annapolis, Maryland. He
is an appointee of Representative Ray
J.
Madden,
First
District
Congress-
man.
The proud father,
Silvio Massa,
is
a
veteran
coin
machine
operator
in
Munster. He and John Friend, director
of athletics at Munster High
School,
remarked
that
“Dick
is
a
dedicated
worker and we’re certain he will be a
credit
to the Naval Academy on the
athletic
field and
in the classroom.”
A three-sport athlete, young Massa
also excelled in the classroom at Mun-
ster High School, where he carried a
B-plus average in college preparatory
curriculum.
He
competed
in
wrestling
for
the
first time this season and turned in a
creditable
first
year
performance.
Massa was also a shot-putter on the
Mustang track team.
Columbia, S.C. Operator
Is
First
In The City
To
Install Two-Play-For-A-Quarter System
COLUMBIA,
S.C.— E. W.
Galloway,
operator of (Jalloway Music Co., paved
the way for
2-plays-for-a-quarter
in
this city by being the first to install a
phonograph in an open location on this
price
structure.
The Seeburg SS 160 was installed at
Goldie Garrett’s “The High Hat.” Mrs.
Garrett
said,
“I’ve had
a Seeburg
in
my
place
for 32
years
and
wouldn’t
have anything else. I am very proud of
my new Seeburg as the
first to have
two plays for two bits.”
The
2-play-for-a-quarter
idea was
conceived by
Bill Adair, president of
the phonograph
division
of the
See-
burg Sales Corp. back in 1966, accord-
ing to Bernie Inge, president of South-
western Music.
“Mrs. Garrett is to be congratulated
for her action in helping to bring this
promotion forward,” Inge
said. Most
operators
are
reluctant
to
introduce
this
relatively
new
concept
to
the
location
owners,
but
a
definite
im-
provement can be
seen not
only for
the operators and location owners, but
for the customers also, in as much as
Two
of
Galloway’s
me-
chanics,
Tom
Leitzsey
and
Jeff
Sykes
(right)
admire the new installa-
tion
along
with
Goldie
Garrett,
owner
of
the
“High Hat.”
the extra provided income
will allow
the
operators
to program the
latest
hit
tunes
sooner
while
providing
a
better selection for the customer.
The customer now pays
eight and
one-third cents per play as compared
to the twelve and one-half cents under
the 2-for-a-quarter system. The added
income
might
well
bring
the
coin
machine
operating
industry
on
a
closer par with the rest of the econ-
omy.

At Columbia:
June
Is 'Stravinsky Month'
NEW YORK—In tribute to the famed
composer/conductor
Igor
Stravinsky,
who
will
celebrate
his
eighty-fifth
birthday on June
17, Columbia Mas-
terworks has named June “Stravinsky
Month.”
Stravinsky has recorded exclusively
for Columbia Masterworks since 1945,
and
his
“Stravinsky
Conducts
Stra-
vinsky”
series
now
totals
nearly
thirty albums
in
the
label’s
catalog.
Recordings
by
Igor
Stravinsky
are
produced by
John
McClure,
director
of
Columbia
Masterworks’ A&R
de-
partment.
As part of a large birthday celebra-
tion, Columbia Masterworks will aug-
ment
its “Stravinsky Conducts
Stra-
vinsky”
series with
five new albums.
A
five-page
article
entitled
“Stra-
vinsky
and
the
Microphone,”
will
appear
in
the
June
issue
of
High
Fidelity.
In the July
issue, Columbia
Masterworks
will run
a full-page ad
featuring the five newly released Stra-
vinsky
LP’s,
as
well
as
the
entire
Columbia
catalog
of
“Stravinsky
Conducts
Stravinsky”
albums.
Full-
page
ads
saluting
Igor
Stravinsky
will
also appear
in the July issue
of
the Schwann Catalog and The Ameri-
can
Record
Guide.
Radio
stations
on
Columbia
Mas-
terworks’
subscription
service
will
receive “Stravinsky Month” packages,
which
include
the new
releases
and
timed
scripts
for
ease
in
program-
ming. As an aid to salesmen, Colum-
bia has
also prepared a
special issue
of
its
sales manual, “Buyways,”
out-
lining
in
detail
the
entire
effort
in
behalf of Igor Stravinsky.
In
addition,
feature
stories
on
Stravinsky
are
slated
to
appear
in
the New York
Times
and
Saturday
Review,
as
well
as
in
a number
of
music publications.
The world over, celebrations will be
held
in
honor
of
Igor
Stravinsky’s
85th birthday. In June, Menotti’s pro-
duction of “The Rake’s Progress” will
be
given by
the Hamburg Opera
at
the
Metropolitan
Opera
House,
and
Ingmar Bergman’s production
of the
same work will be performed at Mont-
real’s
Expo
’67
by
the
Stockholm
Opera. The Los Angeles Museum
of
Art will also take part in the celebra-
tion
by
presenting
a
special
concert
in honor of Stravinsky.
In England, the Oxford Bach Festi-
val
will present a
special
Stravinsky
series in June, and another Stravinsky
series will take place at the Edinburgh
Festive during August and Septem-
ber.
In France, the Paris Opera Bal-
let
is taping a color television film of
the
complete
“Firebird”
ballet
with
sets
by Marc
Chagall,
and
Stravin-
sky’s
new
Requiem
will
receive
its
French premiere
in Paris
in the near
future.

Island Bow

by

1. The Epitome Of Sound
is
currently

at

and

I AM—Johnny
Tillotson—MGM
E/SE
4452
Johnny
Tillotson
is featured
in
a
set
of rock
tunes.
The
efforts
include
“Make
This
Train.”
“Don’t
Tell Me
It’s
Raining,”
“Deafening Roar
Of
Silence,” and “Come Back When You Grow
Up.” The melodies rock
soft and hard;
the beat
is
pulsating; and the sound
is
satisfying. “Here
I Am” should establish itself as a winner in short
order.
I
CRIED
FOR YOU—Johnny
Watson—Cadet
LP/LPS 4056
Johnny Watson chants a group of pop ditties, in-
cluding “I Cried For You,” the title track. Other
songs
are
“I’ll
Remember
April,” “When
Did
You Leave Heaven,” and “Misty.” The artist dis-
plays
exceptionally good piano
playing,
refresh-
ing
phrasing,
and
professional
projection.
He
makes
very
old
songs
ring anew with
life and
meaning. The LP should do much to further the
reputation
of the
singer.

Quintet—Columbia CL 2649/CS
9449
Art Farmer plays trumpet and fluegelhorn on

is given able sup-

peting
e-vinces

combined
with
an
impec-
cable time and rhythm. The album
is
a superb
distillation of a brillant jazz
talent.
BIG SWING FACE—Buddy Rich—Pacific Jazz
PJ10117/ST 20117
The new Buddy
Rich Big Band
sets down a
solid set of jazz sessions. Rich gives driving and
tastefully refreshing renditions to some of today’s
best pop material, including “Norwegian Wood”
and “The Beat Goes On.” Other
excellent

ings are the title tune, “Big Swing Face,” “Wack
Wack,”
and
“Bugle
Call
Rag.”
The
package
should
find
its
quality rewarded
in the market-
place.

iAYDN
THE CREATION
HAYDN
: THE CREATION—Gunter Wand, Con-
ductor—Vanguard SRV 238/9 (SD)
Franz
Joseph
Haydn’s
magnificent
oratorio,
“The Creation,”
is brought to

involved
in
the
two-record
set,

artistry,
and the album should be a favorite with classical
music devotees.

Ties Ended Between
Verve & Folkways
NEW YORK—A distribution
deal,
in
effect
for
the
past
two
years,
has
been
terminated
between
the
Verve
label
and
Folkways
Records,
Cash
Box
has
learned. The
label
born
of
the
arrangement.
Verve /Folkways,
has been dropped and replaced by
a
new
tag.
Verve /Forecast.
Original
deal ran out last May, at which time
Verve
did not pick up
a
1
year
op-
tion
to
continue.
While Verve has a 9-month
sell-off
period,
it will no longer press Verve/
Folkways
masters,
and
will
event-
ually
return
all
masters
originally
released
on
Folkways.
Verve
will
keep
a
number
of
artists
it
has
signed to Verve/Folkways pacts over
the
past
two
years,
including
the
Blues
Project,
Tim
Hardin,
Laura
Nyro,
Janis
Ian and
Richie
Havens.
They now appear on Verve /Forecast.
Jerry Schoenbaum, who runs Verve/
Forecast, told Cash Box that the label
will continue to produce a commercial
“urban”-type folk sound.
Folkways, founded by Moe Asch,
is
still an active
label, with
its product
being marketed by
Scholastic Maga-
zine.
NEW YORK—A new agency for the
collection
of
mechanical
copyright
royalties has been established in Can-
ada. Smyth Copyright Services,
Ltd.,
the new Canadian
agency, bowed
to

(8)
attended by most of the leading
figures
in

lishing world.
At the luncheon, held in New York’s
Plaza
Hotel,
J.
B.
Smyth,
president
of the new agency, described the prob-
lems peculiar to the Canadian market
and the reasons for establishment of
a Canadian agency.
Smyth stated that mechanical roy-
alties
from
Canada
in
1966
should
have been
$3,200,000, but were
actu-
ally
$2,650,000,
due
to
many
unli-
censed
records, most
of them
unau-
thorized translations of English works
into
French.
He
pointed
out
that
many so-called translations were act-
ually entirely new titles and lyrics to
pop tunes, and could not be recognized
except by
actual
monitoring
of
the
French pop charts. Further, he stres-
sed the almost total absence of licens-
ing of synchronizations and transcrip-
tions
in Canada. These represent an
additional source of revenue to music

Otis To Consolidate
All His Pubberies
NEW
YORK— Effective
June
30,
Clyde Otis will consolidate
all of his
BMI firms into Eden Music and all of
his ASCAP
pubberies
into
Prentice
Music.
’The
affected BMI
companies
are Play Music, Music Products, Lily
Music,
Keblo
Music,
Edison
Music,
Brenda Music and Actual Music. The
ASCAP outlets are Asset Music, Tu-
lip Music and Vanessa Music.
The consolidation move will tighten
Otis’ various publishing activities by
centralizing their operations into two
major concerns and by
allowing
for
a
better
working
relationship
with
staff writers.
