DGG Phasing Out Mono IP's in U.5.
NEW YORK—Deutsche Grammophon
will
begin
to
phase
out
its
mono
albums
beginning
with
its
initial
autumn release due in August. In re-
sponse
to the record industry’s move
to
a
stereo-only
market,
all
future
classical
albums
on
both DGG
and
Archive labels will be issued in stereo
only.
Deutsche
Grammophon
has
long
had a $5.79 list in effect for both mono
or
stereo
disks
since
Jerry
Schoen-
baum became chief of MGM’s classical
division
in
Sept, of
1963.
Schoenbaum
said
that the
propor-
tion
of
stereo
to mono
sales
is
ex-
tremely high, especially in some areas
of
the
country
where
distributors
order in the ratio of ten stereo disks
to one mono. In many instances, the
re-order pattern for monaural albums
after their
initial release
is
insignifi-
cant.
The
major
factor
behind
Deutsche Grammophon’s high rate of
stereo
sales
is
attributed
to
be
the
long
established
equal
list
price,
though the special nature of the DGG
and
Archive
catalogues
is
no
doubt
a
point
not
to
be
overlooked.
The
decision
to
eliminate
the mono num-
bers
from
the
catalog,
the
label
states,
is not a new one;
it has been
under
consideration
during
the
last
season, when a study of sales figures
indicated
the huge growth
in
stereo
buyers.
All
future
issues,
according
to
FRONT COVER:
The Four Seasons, said to have sold
55
million
disks
since
1962,
continue
to ride the crest of great popularity.

ords
act
is nearing yet another Top
10
sound

Marianne.”

Off You.” The group

the album

with

LP,
“Gold Vault Of

the

for
the
team,
composed

Valli,
Bob

and

is

first concert
appearance on the west coast, at the
Santa

Civic
Auditorium
on
Sat.,
July

the Melodyland
in

3.
In
addition,
the
boys are making a TV film. Both the
Seasons
and
Valli
are
recorded
by
Bob Crewe.

Music. Under the

deal
with Acuff-Rose, B&B copyrights are
to revert to the Bryants after 10 years
they

year basis. This already includes “We

“Raining

and
“Let’s

About

The
Acuff-Rose
deal
involves
the
U.S. On

the

a
short-term

ment with Fred Foster of Moiiument
Records.

Broadway Musicals '66-67: Made
In America. Bat Not That Well
NEW YORK—The American musical
theatre
went
American
during
the
just-concluded 1966-67 season, and its
vaunted legacy wasn’t quite upheld.
England in recent seasons has sup-
plied
Broadway
with
a
number
of
hits (eg. “Oliver!,” “Stop The World.
.
.
.,” “Roar Of The Greasepaint”) and
if
not
hits,
a
series
of
oft-recorded
scores.
But,
the
spotlight
fell
solely
on
American
productions
with
less
than
historic
results.
Nine musicals were slated to open;
one of them, “Chu Chem,” closed out
of town and
another,
“Breakfast
at
Tiffany’s,”
never
got
past
opening
night. Another failure, “Sherry,” ran
for several months, but RCA Victor,
a heavy investor in the musical adap-
tation
of Kaufman &
Hart’s
“The
Man Who Came To
Dinner,” passed
up
its
rights
to produce an
original
cast
album.
“A
Joyful
Noise,”
in
which Liberty Records provided some
backing,
folded
shortly
following
opening
night,
also
failing
to
obtain
a
cast LP.
Two
1966-67
productions
seemed
headed
for
success.
They
are
“Ca-
baret” and
“I Do
I
Do.”
“Cabaret,”
winner
of
this
year’s
New
York
Drama Critics Circle and Tony awards
as the top musical of the season, has
developed
into
a
strong
caster
on
Columbia, while RCA and Broadway
are
doing
well
with
“I
Do
I
Do.’’
Columbia has also had moderate suc-
cess
with
“The
Apple
Tree”
and
“Hallelujah,
Baby,”
as
is
United
Artists
with
“Ulya
Darling,”
the
song-and-dance version of “Never On
Sunday.”
The
Off-Broadway
scene
can
still
boast
such
long-run
items
as
“The
“Fantasticks” (MGM)
and “Man Of
La
Mancha”
(Kapp),
but
nothing
really developed
last season.
Despite
rave
notices, “Man With A Load Of
Mischief”
is done with, and Kapp can
hardly
anticipate
worthwhile
sales
with
its cast LP version of the show.
Individual Songs
Easily the most popular singles hits
to develop out of a Broadway tune are
“I
Do,
I
Do’s” “My
Cup
Runneth
Over” by Ed Ames on RCA. The title
song from “Cabaret,” has a long
list
of recordings, with no sizeable singles
hit to show for
it.
Despite some published reports that
labels may
take
it
easy
as
far
as
cast LP rights are concerned, an early
check
of
labels
indicates
that
most
Broadway
shows
set
for
the
next
season are in the process of finalizing
deals
for
original
casters.

Seehurg Home Phono Stores, Plays
30 Albums On Dial Phone Basis
NEW YORK—The Seeburg Corp. has
entered the home phono market with
an innovation in album programming.
A console unit was unveiled
in New
York
last
week
containing
a
com-
pletely
automatic
unit
which
plays
both sides of an LP in a vertical po-
sition,
enabling
the
continuous
play
of
both
sides
of
50
LP’s.
Once
the
disks are placed in a vertical carrier,
a
device
scans,
selects,
plays
and
stores
records.
Bill Adair, vp of the Chicago-based
firm, largest producer
of commercial
musical equipment, described the new
phono unit at a special press showing
at the Plaza Hotel. He said the unit
would be
available
for consumers
in
about
four
to
six weeks.
Trade
dis-
play
will
be made
at
the
upcoming
NAMM Music Show
in Chicago, and
at the Electronics Show in New York.
Advertising
and
promotional
plans
will be unveiled in Sept., Adair noted.
‘Memory Bank’
The new mechanism
also
boasts a
memory
bank,
similar
to
that
used
in today’s computers, which can
call
forth up
to
100
sides
of
a
personal
record library, either stereo or mono.
By dialing numbers on a conventional
telephone
dial,
either on
the
unit or
from
a
remote
point,
the
user
can
make
the
instrument
perform
con-
tinuously
for
as many
as
40
hours
and
switch from
“pop”
or
classical
music
to
dramatic
readings
or
lan-
guage
study
records.
The
stored albums
are_ selected by
means
of
a
booklet,
which
contains
the LP
titles and
their
dialed
codes.
Louis
J.
Nicastro, president of the
company,
declared that the new sys-
tem
represented
a
major
break-
through
in home
entertainment.
“This
is
the
most
revolutionary
development in musical equipment for
the home since Edison’s perfection of
the phonograph, and Emile Berliner’s
invention
of the
flat
disk,”
Nicastro
said.
He
pointed
to
the
fact
that
until
now,
records
had
been
stacked
one
on top
of the
other
in home phono-
graphs
or when
not
in
use,
which
resulted
in
their
being
scratched,
thumb
printed or damaged.
“Now,
they
will
be
played
and
stored in an upright position in such
a
way
that
they
will
never
touch
each
other, and
will not be
_ touched
by human
hands,
safeguarding
rec-
ords against warpage and breakage,”
he
said.
Nicastro
indicated
that
the
com-
pany
holds
exclusive
patents on
the
revolutionary
record-playing
mecha-
nism.
The
unit
has
been
engineered
to
meet
the
technical
specifications
of
the Institute of High Fidelity.
It fea-
tures
a
solid
state AM/FM
stereo
tuner
and
plays
tape
cartridges
as
well
as
records. This makes
possible
separate
music
for
separate
rooms.
Through use of optional accessories,
as many
as
twelve remote
locations
around the home—from den to
patio
to swimming
pool—can produce mu-
sic
of
the
listener’s
choice
at
the
touch of a
button.
There
will
also
be
a
component
version available for those who have
an
existing sound equipment system
that will provide the automatic record
handling feature as well as the remote
capabilities.
The
new
record
playing
systems
will retail from $795
to
$1500.

retailer and one-stop requests, Cash Box
is providing data

of

the

Columbia Records.
Geared to the theme of “Ed Sullivan Presents,” a line of albums will be cre-
ated that will be based on holidays, Broadway, Hollywood and various countries
of the world. Sullivan told Cash Box last week that he will appear as a narrator
on a number of projects, although other releases may just bear his sponsorship
of the series.
About a decade ago, Sullivan lent his name to a line of low-priced albums that
re-created hit Broadway musicals.
Currently
in production for release later this year
is “Christmas with Ed
Sullivan.”

MGM To Produce Sat. Night
Pop Music Show On WABC-FM
NEW YORK—MGM Records has pur-
chased a weekly time spot—6-7 P.M.,
Saturday night—on WABC-FM Radio.
The
spot
will
be
used
to
present
a
pop
music
show
to
be
produced
by
Harvey Cowen, assistant ad manager
of MGM. The show will feature MGM
A&R exec Tom Wilson, who
will act
as
a
deejay
and
program
material
highlighting
today’s
popular
sounds.
Hip
and
witty,
Wilson
is
the
well-
known producer of hit disks for such
recording
names
as
Simon &
Gar-
funkel, Bob Dylan, the Animals,
the
Mothers
of Invention and the Velvet
Underground.
MGM
will
spotlight
its own prod-
uct on the show, but 10-20%
of ma-
terial
will come from
outside
labels.
The object of the show
is to create a
public
airing
in
the
most
exciting
manner possible of MGM, Verve and
Verve Forecast disks.
The show, which premiers June 24,
is being geared for eventual syndica-
tion. A 13 week pact has been signed
with WABC-FM, with options
to
re-
new at the end of that period.

Famed group the Swingle Singers whose
arrival was due
this month,
will
visit Ai’gentina in mid-July,
it was reported to Cash Box. The group will ap-
pear at the Gran Rex Theater and on TV Channel
11, with a probable
visit
to Montevideo, Uruguay. Phonogram, who has the representation
of
Philips
and thus
their records,
is planning a
strong campaign
in their behalf.
Inci-
dentally,
Channel
11
has
been
airing
frequently
video-tapes
recorded
by
the Singers in Italy and received by
this plant through
its connections with
Italian RAI.
Music Hall’s Luis Calvo feels enthusiastic about the
sales of the company,
something made more remarkable by the fact that May and June have been
considered bad months by the whole industry. MH
is
still selling strongly
its
Spanish Raphael recordings—and added a new
single, with “Yo Soy Aquel,”
previously available only on Compact 33—Little Tony, Sandie Shaw’s “Puppet
On A String” and a bunch of new releases including a version of “La Plaza,”
the big Brazilian hit. Frank & Nancy Sinatra’s new single, “Somethin’ Stupid,”
is
also showing reaction
in the market which may mean
a new
hit for the
Sinatra family.
Last week we
reported some
of
the arrangements made by RCA’s A&R
topper,
Adolfo
Pino,
in
Spain,
during
his
recent
trip
to
Europe. He
con-
tracted the
representation
of the Massiel (young lark currently a
sensation
in that country)
recordings for Argentina and
plans
to
release them
soon
here. In
Italy, Palito Ortega recorded Italian versions of “La Felicidad” and
“Un Muchacho Como Yo,” two of his biggest hits of recent times
in Argen-
tina, while Barbara &
Dick
cut
in
Italian
the
versions
of “El Funeral Del
Labrador”
(RCA’s
top
selling
record
during
the
past
twelve months)
and
“Facundo” which
will
be
titled
“Nicola”
in that market.
Mauricio
Brenner
of Fermata
infos
that
Beto Fernan
has
recorded
for
Music Hall
a version
of “La Carta” coupled with “Canta
Muchachita.” The
same tunes have been
cut by Claudia for Odeon Pops, and “La Plaza” has
still one more version by Os Garotos on the same label. Brenner believes that
this tune
will turn
into a
hit
as
strong
as “La Banda” which stormed
the
local charts a couple of months ago. On the tango
side, there
will be an
in-
strumental album devoted
to the
14 songs
of “14 With The Tango” on the
RCA
label. The Record Division of Fermata
is preparing a

Fia
and

Nicolai with
“Django” and
another
one
with
“Corazon De
Papel” by the
Silvery Boys, this one produced originally by RGE.
Odeon reports
that Rafael
Rossi, who has been recording for the
diskery
for more than 40 years
(his first record was released in May, 1927), has just
finished a new LP which
will be due soon. Other regional music
artists with
new recordings are Tarrago Ross and Ramon Mendez, whose
first LP will ap-
pear
soon. On
the
International
side
there
is
a new
single by Tom
Jones
(“Detroit City” and “Riders In The Sky”) and another one by Lucho Gatica
(“Bravo”), and
also
local
singles by Ramona Galarza and a new group Los
Rivera, already commented in this column.
A strong bunch of singles coming this week from Disc Jockey, starting with

newie
by

Veneto’s
carrying two

(“Pietre”

(jf A Thousand Dances”; and also a record by local group

“Trabajo

Microfon’s Mario Kaminsky feels happy with the initial success of “Summer

Four UCLA Students
Win Sinatra Awards
LOS ANGELES—At a ceremony and
concert held in Royce Hall auditorium
on
the UCLA
campus
on
Saturday
night, June
10, four UCLA
students
were named
the
first
year’s winners
of the
$5,000 Frank
Sinatra
Musical
performance
awards.
The
four
winners,
selected
from
among music majors
in UCLA’s
Col-
lege
of
Fine
Arts,
are
Gary
Gray,
clarinetist and jazz saxophonist,
first-
place winner
($2000)
in
the
instru-
mental category; Diana Sims, colora-
tura
soprano,
first-place
winner
($2000)
in
the
vocal
category;
Wil-
liam
Cosby,
second-place
winner
($500)
in the instrumental category;
and Andrew Belling, singer and com-
poser-arranger-pianist,
second-place
winner
($500)
in the vocal
category.
The
four
students
were
presented
cash prizes by Frank Sinatra follow-
ing
the
concert,
in which
each gave
solo performances and joined
in pop-
ular
and
classical
selections.
A
highlight
of
the
concert was
a
tribute to Frank Sinatra conducted by
Gray
and
arranged
by
Belling.
Ac-
companied by 18 instrumentalists, the
winners presented a medley of songs
made famous by
Sinatra.
Robert L. Tusler, assistant dean of
the
College
of
Fine
Arts,
declared
that
the
concert
was
a
major
per-
formance
opportunity
for
the
stu-
dents and characterized
it as a “Town
Hall
of the West’’
recital.
Sinatra
established the awards for
three
years
to
help
promising music
students develop their talents toward
professional careers.
Gray,
27,
has won
several
music
scholarships and awards.
In
1957 he
won the Indiana Young Artists Com-
petition
to become guest
soloist with
the
Indianapolis
Symphony
Orches-
tra. He
was
first
clarinetist
in
the
Indiana
University
Philharmonic
from 1960 to
1963. He
is presently a
teaching assistant in band and orches-
tra
at UCLA
while working toward
his Ph.D.
degree
in music
education.
Gray
is
the
son
of Delmer
Gay
of
Indianapolis.
Diana Sims is a 19-year-old soprano
from
Beverly
Hills who
is
currently
a sophomore
at UCLA. A winner of
many vocal awards, she has received
a summer
scholarship
to
the
Music
Academy of the West and a
scholar-
ship to attend Juilliard School of Mu-
sic in New York. She
is the daughter
of Mr. and
Mrs. Edward
S. Sims
of
320
S. Clarke
Dr., Beverly
Hills.

K-R To Produce
Brit-ish Walkers
NEW
YORK— Charles
Koppelman
and Don Rubin have announced that
the
British
Walkers, whose
last
re-
cording
was
“Shake’’,
will
now
be
produced by the Brothers Boylan for
Koppelman-Rubin
Associates
by
agreement
with
Chartbuster
Music.
The
first release under the new pro-
duction agreement, “Bring The Whole
Family’’,
which was
written by
the
Brothers
Boylan,
is due
out immedi-
ately
on Cameo/Parkway
Records.
Koppelman and Rubin have racked
up
a
total of twelve
top ten records
in less than two years. They currently
are
represented
on
the
charts
with
“She’d Rather Be With
Me,’’ by
the
Turtles.
In
addition
to
the
Turtles,
the
Lovin’
Spoonful
and
Gary
Lewis,
Koppelman-Rubin Associates also pro-
duce
Bobby
Darin,
the
Righteous
Brothers,
Connie
Francis
and
Dino,
Desi &
Billy, among others.
William Cosby, 21, begin his formal
music education at 7, when he finished
a
five-year accordion method
in
less
than two years. He entered accordion
competitions
at
nine
and now
holds
many regional,
national and
interna-
tional
titles. He has made two record
albums, for Impromptu and Neofonic
record companies. A second album for
Neofonic
is
soon
to
be
released. He
lives with
his parents, Mr. and
Mrs.
R. W. Cosby, at 911 Faysmith Ave. in
Torrance.
Belling,
who
performed
his
own
compositions
for
the
concert,
at-
tracted national
attention
at
17 with
his
musical
“Huckleberry”. He
was
author, composer, and aranger for the
2(4
hour show which was perfoi’med
at Washington
High
School
in
San
Francisco. He
has worked
in
televi-
sion
as
a
scriptwriter, composer and
performer. He
is
currently
assistant
conductor
of
the UCLA
Glee
Club.
He
is the son of Mr. and Mrs. Morris
Belling
of San
Francisco.
The Fourth of July weekend always
signifies
something
special
in
the
world
of
jazz,
the
staging
of
The
Newport
Jazz
Festival,
which,
by
virtue of
its thirteen year history
is
generally considered the top jazz
at-
traction of its kind in the world. New-
port’s major domo, George Wein, has
assembled another mammoth extrava-
ganza
which
will
run
from
Friday,
June
30,
through
Monday,
July
3.
There
will
be
four
evening
concerts
stai'ting at 8:00 P.M. and three after-
noon concerts, excluding Friday, start-
ing at 2:00 P.M. For the
third year,
the
site will be Festival Park, Wein’s
permanent
location
in Rhode
Island.
Some Pop Names
As has been his wont
in the more
recent yeaz’s, impresario Wein has not
only asembled most of the top names
in jazz
for The
Festival, but he has
also taken pains
to
flavor the shows
with a few
attractions
that are best
known
in pop
circles, but whose
ef-
forts are genuinely jazz
oriented. To
wit,
on
Sunday
night,
probably
the
biggest night of the
four, the crowd
will hear The Blues Project, a group
best known to followers of today’s pop
music. My
feeling
is
the The
Blues
Project will break
it up
at Newport,
not only with the many youngsters in
the audience, but with the many
die-
hard, rock-ribbed jazz patrons as well.
Each of the evening shows will have
a big band on stage. Friday
it will be
Count
Basie,
Saturday, Buddy
Rich’s
new band,
Sunday, Woody Herman’s
Herd, and Monday, Lionel Hampton’s
Alumni Orchestra. Similarly, each eve-
ning
show
will
feature
a
vocalist,
namely,
Joe
Williams, Nina
Simone,
Marilyn
Maye,
and
Sarah
Vaughan.
Everything about the programming is
conceived
to
assure
a
well
balanced
evening of top drawer entertainment.
The only thing that might make one
performance more attractive than an-
other
is
one’s
personal
tastes
and
one’s personal devotion to a particular
performer.
Naturally,
the
best thing
to do would be to try to attend every
performance, because each is rich with
the
best
to
be
seen
and
heard
in
today’s market.
Full Evening’s Sponsor
This year, for the
first time
to the
best of my knowledge, one entire eve-
ning is being sponsored by a national
product,
Schlitz
Beer.
The
opening
show on Friday
is called “Schlitz Sa-
lute To Jazz 1967” and, curiously, the
prices for this performance are scaled
down to one dollar from the prices of
the
other three
evening
shows. May
we assume that Schlitz is reimbursing
Wein
to
the
tune
of
one
dollar
per
person, or $15,000, which would be the
tap for a capacity crowd of 15,000?
If
this
sponsorship
begins
a
trend and
permits us to look forward to the time
when
each
of
the performances
will
have
a
commercial
benefactor,
it
should have a very salutary effect on
jazz matters. First, the wedding of a
national
sponsor
to
jazz
is
healthy
because
it opens
the
too-long
closed
doors of Madison Avenue to jazz. Sec-
ond,
it enables the jazz fan to enjoy
an incomparable evening of music at
a lower cost.
Anyone remotely familiar with the
history of the Newport Jazz Festivals
under the aegis of George Wein must
recognize
his loyalty and devotion to
a
small
cadre
of
veteran
musicians.
This year, as in years past, the people
who attend the Festival will have the
opportunity to hear players like Ruby
Braff,
Buck
Clayton, Bud
Freeman,
Pee Wee Russell, Buddy Tate, Illinois
Jacquet, and others of that ilk. Unlike
his colleagues in the field of jazz con-
certizing, Wein has remained resolute
in
his
determination
to keep
yester-
day’s
heroes
in
the
public
eye. For
this he
is to be highly commended be-
cause the Jacquets and the Braffs and
the
Claytons have
so much
to
offer.
Often,
impresario
Wein,
who
plays
very respectable piano, will join these
fellows for a happy, swinging set.
Workshop Series
The afternoon concerts at Newport
sometimes
offer
the
most
exciting
music of the entire program, the pity
being that these performances are no-
torious for their poor attendance. Of
special importance
is the “workshop”
series
that
had
its
inception
about
three years ago. This year’s workshop
will showcase the saxophone as exem-
plified by the playing of Bud Freeman,
Booker
Ervin,
John
Handy,
Illinois
Jacquet, Budd
Johnson, Buddy
Tate,
and
others.
Billy
Taylor,
a
very
knowledgeable
commentator,
will,
as
in years
past, conduct the workshop.
Billy has a great faculty for present-
ing,
in
lay
language,
just what
the
musicians
are
trying
to
accomplish
with their varied styles. Being an ex-
pert jazz pianist,
it’s not unusual for
Taylor to join in the playing, the bet-
ter that he might illustrate his point.
Father Norman O’Connor, along with
Billy
Taylor,
are
listed
as
the
co-
masters of ceremonies for the
entire
four day program.
New Faces Of
’67
Another
exciting
aspect
of
this
year’s Festival
is the number of new
faces
in
jazz
that
will be
presented.
Albert Ayler’s Quintet will be heard,
as will be the big band of Don
Ellis,
which is being flown in from the West
Coast, expressly for
this appearance.
Ellis’ band has won rave
notices for
its appearance at The Monterey Jazz
Festival of last Fall and
its more re-
cent UCLA
jazz
fete. Gabor
Szabo’s
“Jazz Raga”
is
another
exciting
ex-
ploration that will be heard. This will
be
Szabo’s
first Newport appearance
as a leader, having played here previ-
ously
as
a member
of Chico
Hamil-
ton’s ensemble. Gary Burton, too, will
be making his
first Newport showing
as
a
group
leader.
Burton
first
ap-
peared
there
in
1960
as
a seventeen
year old phenomenon, later as a vital
member
of
Stan
Getz’s
group.
This
year
Gary
will
be
leading
his own
quartet, though
still only twenty four

More
Atlantic
Gold
NEW YORK—Atlantic-Atco has con-
tinued
its
gold
record
streak
with
Arthur
Conley’s “Sweet
Soul Music”
on
Atco. The
disk has been
certified
by
the RIAA
as
a
million
seller.
This marks
the
eighth gold record
earned during June 1967 by Atlantic-
Atco. The other million
sellers were:
Aretha
Franklin’s
“Respect”
and
“I
Never
Loved A
Man
(The Way
I
Love
You)”;
the
Young

“Groovin’
Booker

“I Never Loved A

On

Shore.”

con-
tributed constructive
criticism
at the

its
need for 1200
feet of tape on a
con-
tinuous

that would
play
for an
hour. Later tape was used
for back-
ground
music
and
in
the
broadcast-
ing industry. In 1960 or
’61, Esch re-
called, Earl Muntz got the tape cart-
ridge
started
in the auto industry.

nilla Fudge), Dick Simpson (producer

was Bill Lear, Esch stated, who

Ray Rand subsequently defined the

MONO LP PRICE INCREASE
In answer to retailer and one-stop requests. Cash Box
is providing data
on those
labels which have announced price increases of
their mono LP's
to the
level of stereo.
This section should be detached and placed where
it can
inform
consumers
of the
price
rise.
Additions
will be made when
they
arise. Cash Box
urges
labels not represented, but which have made
similar moves to bring their moves to our attention.

ilu@ Note; A Sound
1st Yr. Under
Liberty
NEW YORK—The Blue Note label’s
first year of operation
as an acquisi-
tion
of
Liberty
Records
has
been
marked by an expansion
in the pro-
motion
and
distribution
of
product.
Bernie
Block
was
brought
in
as
sales manager,
leaving
Alfred
Lion
and
Frank
Wolff
to
concentrate
on
the A&R phase of the diskery, a func-
tion they have
directed for the past
25 years.
The
initial moves were in
the
dis-
tributor
changes
in
markets
which
have
Liberty
branch
distributors.
During the
label’s July 1966 conven-
tion,
an
outline
of
a
concentrated
method
for
the
distribution
of
Blue
Note
product
in
these markets was
made.
Part of this
outline was
pre-
preparing
a background
of data
on
the product that would best suit Blue
Note distributors designed to give all
involved a better working knowledge
of the Blue Note
catalog.
Product Successes
"Reaction
to
the
product
released
in the past 12 month period was of a
very
positive
nature,
and
this
was
very evident
in
sales and promotion
of albums such as ‘Search For A New
Land’ by Lee Morgan,
‘Got A Good
Thing Goin” by John Patton. ‘Bucket’
by
the
Incredible Jimmy Smith, and
‘Indestructible’ by Art Blakey and the
Jazz Messengers,” says Block. The re-
lease of “Rough ’N Tumble” by Stan-
ley Turrentine indicated
to the label
that some of its product falls into the
R&B category. Sales at the R&B level
have increased to a degree which Blue
Note had
not experienced with Tur-
rentine in the past. Blue Note’s initial
year under the Liberty management
team has
also seen the
re-unification
of The Three Sounds with the Blue
Note label. In their first offering back
at
the
label,
“Vibrations,”
a
new
sound was born for
this group. The
combination
of
organ
and
piano
proved
successful.
Pearson To A&R
Block
says that Blue
Note’s
direc-
tion
this
year
is
to
become
“more
expansive
in our
sound.” In
this
re-
gard, artist-writer Duke Pearson has
just been
hired on
a
full time A&R
basis.
“I
feel
certain
that
his
ideas
and
compositions
will
be
another
great
tool
in
the
continued
success
of Kue
Note.”_
Two innovations at the label in the
past
year.
Block
feels,
also
contrib-
uted
to the company’s growing
sales
pattern. These included the release of
the
label’s
first
Little
LP
product,
filling.
Block
explains,
“a
pipeline
sorely needed, to the juke box opera-
tor,” the creation of Blue Note Jazz
Classics,
and
a
compilation
of
the
best-selling
45’s. Last April saw the
release
of a “Gems of Jazz” Limited
Edition
album,
which
exposed
such
talents as Horace Silver, Miles Davis,
Art
Blakey,
Clifford
Brown,
Tadd
Dameron, Milt Jackson, Jay Jay John-
son,
James
Moody,
Fats
Navaroo,
Thelonious
Monk
and
Bud
Powell.
Also,
Horace
Silver’s
“The
Jody
Grind,” introduced the Blue Note line
to
the
double-fold package
concept.
Other
strong
artists
at
the
label
are
Lee
Morgan,
Ornette
Coleman
and Duke Pearson.
Bell Adopts Hot Line Concept Between
Distribs
NEW YORK—Now there’s a Hot Line
phone twist in the disk business. Bell
Records
has
installed
direct
phone
service between its office in New York
and
its
distrib
outlets
around
the
country.
According
to
sales
manager
Irv
BELL'S TELEPHONE
Biegel, the installation of these phones
has
eliminated
the
lengthy wait
for
operators
and
gives
Bell
an
instant
pulse
of today’s market.
Installed in the Bell
offices are two
card
dialer telephones, one on
Presi-
dent Larry Uttal’s desk and the other
on Biegel’s. The phones are the same
shade of blue as the Bell label and the
corresponding phones at the distribu-
tors
are
also
blue. Each
is equipped
with a
Bell
logo—“Bell Records Hot
Line.”
To
place
a
call from
Bell’s
offices,
all
that has
to
be
done
is
to
insert
special
cards
supplied by
the
phone
company. The phones are placed stra-
tegically
in
each
distributor’s
office
and only pre-designated personnel can
answer these
calls. Biegel says “these
phones
give
us
immediate
access
to
key
personnel
at
the
distributorship
such as the sales manager and promo-
tion man. So far we’ve only tried this
in
12
markets
but
the
results
have
been so favorable that we are now
in
the
process
of having them
installed
in every market in the country.”

the

ever produced by

record company in a major city. Hip and witty, Wilson is the producer of decks

ducers and artists and other such events. While recently out on the coast

is to create a

Song

SPAIN—THE PAST 12 MONTHS
The two-year boom
(1965-1966)
in
the Spanish record industry has very
largely come to an end. This
is due to
the general economic situation, whose
trend
is
now
towards
stabilization.
In
the
record
business,
as
in many
other
fields, the past two years were
years
of
optimism.
Sales
increased
highly,
and
the
quality,
technically
and
artistically,
increased
as
well.
Some new companies
(both
little and
big ones) entered the market in com-
petition with the already
established,
which
increased
the volume
of work
considerably.
In
order
to
get
information
about
the development of the market. Cash
Box spoke with Julio Sampedro, presi-
dent of the Spanish Group of the In-
ternational Federation of Phonografic
Industries.
This
is
the
main
trade
organisation
in Spain. There are two
other
organisations. One
of them
is
the “subgroup
of music
over
plastic
materials”
of
the
Institute
Espanol
del
Libro
(Spanish
Book
Institute).
The other
is the “subgroup of editors
of records” of the Sindicate of Paper
and
Grafic
Arts.
Publishers
and
authors are
affiliated with the SGAE
(Sociedad
General
de
Autores
de
Espana) “Spanish General Society of
Authors,” a member of BIEM.
As 'Sampedro
told
us, the
Spanish
group of the IFPI does not deal with
commercial
affairs,
and
their
meet-
ings
(generally
one
every
three
months)
are held for a
discussion of
impressions
and
general
considera-
tions about the business. For example,
the
last meetings were given over to
a
discussion
of
author
royalties,
which are
calculated from the global
price of the record. As this price
in-
cludes the price of the cover
(a
fifth
of the total in some cases), the group
is going to present a proposal to ask
that the
authors’ 8%
should be
cal-
culated
only from
the
price
of
the
record.
As
far
as we know,
there
are no
official
figures
of
record
sales
in
Spain,
but
the
approximate
estima-
tions
are
that
last
year
about
six
million records were
sold. To increase
this figure a great deal
is really
diffi-
cult
if you consider that there are no
more than a million record players in
the country. The figure does increase
about 75,000 every year, which
is not
too
much
according
to
the medium
economic
level. What
is
the reason?
Sampedro pointed out that Spain
is a
sunny country with good weather
al-
most the whole year. In winter, young
people (most of the record buyers are
youngsters)
are
inside
studying
or
working,
and
they buy
records
con-
stantly,
with
highest
figures
in
De-
cember.
But
as
soon
as
the
spring
comes people prefer the open air ac-
tivities.
Beside
this,
record
players
are not as essential to life as washing
machines,
cars, refrigerators,
etc.,
so
a
record
player
is
almost
the
last
thing a family buys. We can be opti-
mistic, because
the
increase
of
sales
of
record
players
is
constant
if not
spectacular.
Sampedro
thinks
that
sales
will be stabilized
in one or two
years after the boom of 1965-1966.
Another
question
is
the
price
of
records.
While
most
other consumer
products
have
been
increasing
their
prices,
record
prices
have
remained
the same
for almost four
years. On
the
other
hand,
costs
are
higher:
salaries,
higher
publicity.
The
mo-
ment
for
the
increase
of
prices
has
come. It is not yet confirmed, but it is
very probable that most of the com-
panies
are
going
to
sell
the EP
at
115 pesetas
(they are now sold at 95
pesetas),
singles
at 75
pesetas
(now
65),
(60 pesetas equals a
dollar). No
increase
is
expected
in
LP’s.
Spain
was in past years a definitive EP mar-
ket,
but now
things
have
changed.
More
singles and LPs
are
sold now.
The EP
will remain, but singles and
LP’s
will
continue
to
take
a bigger
part of the market.
Another
question
is
taxes.
The
Spanish record industry
is hoping for
an exemption from
taxes. They
say
that
since books,
as a
cultural prod-
uct,
have
no
taxes,
records
should
have none either. For the time being,
records
are
charged
with
a
15%
“luxury
tax,”
and
a
2.70%
“enter-
prises traffic tax,” as well as the 8%
that has
to be paid
to the SGAE as
“author rights.”
As
a
result
of
the bigger promo-
tion given to certain records, the past
12 months saw more of them pass the
100,000 mark. This
is not
too
usual,
but every time there
is a bigger
dif-
ference
in the
figures
of
hit records
and
those
of
the
records
nobody
knows. Some Spanish artists are con-
sistent best
sellers. Among them we
can
mention
Raphael. A
two
time
Spanish singer in the Eurovision song
contest, he has appeared on English
TV and in almost
all South American
countries. There are groups
that
hit
with
almost
every
record
they
pro-
duce.
This
is
the
case
with
the
Pekenikes,
an
instrumental
group
whose
records
appear
in
England
and
the
USA
(through
Pye
and
United
Artists)
and whose
self-com-
posed tunes have had
a good
recep-
tion here and abroad. Also we should
mention
Los
Brincos,
who
recently
recorded
in
England
for
Page
One
records
(the Larry Page label). Their
records appeared
in England, France
and
Italy.
Los
Bravos
are
the
best
internationally-known Spanish group,
due
to
the
big
succses
of “Black
Is
Black,”
that
also
sold
very
well
in
Spain,
(number
one
for
more
than
two months). Juan & Junior, former
members
of
the
Brincos,
are
also
planning to do international business.
Their
records
are
going
to
be
re-
leased on the CBS label in England^
Joan Manuel
Serrat
is
the
big
sur-
prise
of
the
year.
He
is
a
young
singer
and
sings
his
own
songs
in
“Catalan”
(a language spoken
in the
North
East,
the
part
of
Spain
of
a
higher level economically). Massiel
is
the
most
outstanding
female
artist.
She
sings
songs
of
a new
“author-
singer,”
Luis Eduardo Aute,
as
well
as her own songs. Two other groups
among the best sellers are
Losi Sirex
and
Los Mustang.
In
the
folk
field,
Manolo Escobar and Peret are gener-
ally accepted as the
artists that
sell
the most
records.
Other
artists
that
sell well are Bruno Lomas, Duo Dina-
mico,
Los
3
Sudamericanos,
Los
Pasos,
Luis
Aguile,
Micky
y
Los
Tonys, Los Relampagos, Los Salvajes,
Lone
Star,
Los
Angeles
and
Luis
Eduardo Aute.
Beside domestic
disks, foreign
rec-
ords
sell well here
if they have a big
promotion
or
have
been
recently
in
the USA
or
English
top
ten.
The
Four Tops, Nancy and Frank Sinatra,
The Beatles, The Rolling Stones, The
Turtles,
Adamo,
The
Troggs,
The
Spencer
Davis
Group,
The
New
Vaudeville
Band,
The
Monkees,
Iva
Zanicchi,
Little Tony, Donovan, Wil-
son Pickett, Manfred Mann, The Who,
Herman’s
Hermits,
James
Brown,
Michel Polnareff, and Tom Jones have
been
in
the
best
sellers
lists, among
others.
A number of new record companies
began
to
operate
here
during
the
past 12 months: Ekipo Records, with
a
folklore catalogue;
Sesion Records,
with
different
artists
(domestic);
Sonoplay
(with
domestic
artists and
foreign labels); Fidias and GEM, the
newest
of them
all.
In distribution, some foreign labels
have
changed
representatives
and
some
labels with no distribution here
are
now
handled
by
Spanish
com-
panies.
Atlantic,
previously
repre-
sented by Belter,
is now represented
by Hispavox. Festival and CGD, pre-
viously represented by Hispavox, are
now
represented
by
Tempo.
Tamla
Motown, whose
releases appeared
in
the
Stateside
label,
are now
repre-
sented
here
by
RCA.
Liberty,
pre-
viously represented by Odeon
(EMI)
is
now
represented
by
Hispavox.
Verve,
previously
represented
by
Odeon,
is now represented by Fono-
( Continued on page
62)

ENGLAND—
THE PAST 12 MOS.
(Continued from page 34)
poration
of
New
York,
previously
handled
in
the
U.K.
by
Chappells,
opened
its own independent
office
in
London
in
March
1967,
under
the
management of Andrew Heath. Since
that date, the catalogue has seen
its
single releases become more frequent,
with records such as
“I Think We’re
Alone Now” by Tommy James, and
The Shandelles on Major-Minor, “Too
Much
Of A
Good
Thing”
by
the
Shirellas
on
Pye,
and
“I
Like
The
Way” by Simon on RCA. Also a
lot
of Planetary titles have been recorded
in
England
with
releases
scheduled
for later in the year. This new activ-
ity
in
the
singles market augments
the consistent releases of album ma-
terial that the company enjoys. Some
of the artists to have released Plane-
tary-Nom
titles
in
the
past
few
months
include
Herb
Alpert,
Zoot
Sims,
Lulu,
Peaches &
Herb,
Mar-
garet
Whiting,
The
Searchers,
The
Righteous
Brothers and
Ike &
Tina
Turner. Andrew Heath
is
optimistic
about
the
year ahead now
that
the
new
set-up
is
firmly
established and
a regular flow
of material being
re-
ceived
from
the
States
and
from
young English
writers.

RCA Plant Strike Settled
WASHINGTON—A month-old
strike
of RCA
pressing

ended
last
Thursday
(6) when striking electrical
union

a new
con-
tract.
Plants
in
six
states
were
in-
volved.
Thirty-two
thousand
strikers
agreed
to pay raises
of 4%
annually
over
the
next
three
years.
Also
in-
cluded
is special
skill differential pay
increases ranging from 24
to 30^ an
hour. This covers skilled workers such
as machinists and tool and die makers.
The new contract takes
in the Hol-
lywood plant, where its employees had
voted
to continue working. The other
plants
are
located
in
Indianapolis,
Bloomington
and
Marion,
Ind.,
Lan-
caster
and
Meadowland,
Pa.,
West
Palm Beach, Fla., Rockaway, N.J. and
Finland,
Ohio. Besides
disk
pressing,
the
plants
also
manufacture
i-adio
and TV
sets, tubes and
electric com-
ponents.

Tie-In For Disk, Film Production

clusive

Dan
Crewe
of

panies.

of Pro-

at Paramount
Pictures,

liated with the

with

tribution

ple picture product agreement
in
as-
sociation with Paramount.
The

is
another

tion
to
Gulf & Westerns
diversifica-
tion program into leisure time
activi-
ties.
Gulf &
Western
is

of Paramount

Under

will continue to produce for The Four

are
under
contract
to
the
Philips’ label; Frankie Valli, also
of
Philips; and
Leslie Gore for Mer-
cury; and Ellie Greenwich for United
Artists.
Crewe
will be
actively
looking
for
new producers, artists, composers and
allied
talents
for DynoVoice
as
well
as bringing with him to the Dot fam-
ily a large
staff of experienced writ-
ers,

musicians
and A&R men.
From 1957 to 1967 Crewe has pro-
duced

has

ings.

HOLLYWOOD—The

A strong line of gatherings and cocktail parties took place last week start-
ing with ©deon’s press conference at
its recording studios under the “Odeon
Promotes Argentine Music All Through The World,” which initiates an adver-
tising and
public
relations campaign
to
help
the
diskery’s
locally
recorded
catalog.
The
campaign
is
being headed
by
Odeon
toppers
Edgar
Spinassi
(local A&R for folk and tango music) and Denis Dunn, A&R coordinator at
the EMI local branch. The different aspects of the move were explained at the
conference, which was attended by artists, press people and deejays.
Next
in
line was CBS’ meeting at the Hernan Figueroa Reyes folk music
“peha”
(clubs devoted
to
typical music, with amateur and
paid
singers
ap-
pearing)
to celebrate the release of his new LP, “A Winner.” Figueroa Reyes
(who some time ago, when recording for Odeon, smashed the charts with “El
Corralero,” a Chilean song) has once more a top notch song
in “Tendras Un
Altar,” currently number one in sales. Figueroa Reyes will also be present at
the Poncho Song Festival in the city of Catamarca in mid-July.
A few days later
it was CBS once more with a dinner at one of the down-
town restaurants
celebrating
the
second
golden
record awarded
to
tropical
music group Cuarteto Imperial which
is now nearing the three
million
sales
mark since the start of
its career three years ago. The Cuarteto has
several
albums, and many of its singles have reached the top twenty making them one
of the most successful groups of this country.
Arriving soon are the Swingle Singers, the well known classical-pop group
formed by Ward Swingle
in
Paris. The
octet
will reportedly appear
at the
Gran Rex Theater and on Channel
11, and Phonogram, who
distributes
their
records
here, has released a new album by them, “Rococo Au Go-Go,” with
their
latest
recordings.
Swingle &
Co.
are
selling
well
in
this market, and
Phonogram
expects
that
this
visit
will
up
even more
their
appeal
to
the
market. As we reported before, TV 11 has been airing tapes recorded by them
in Italy in one of its top evening programs, “Comienza El Show.”
RCA’s Adolfo Pino
infos that Spanish
lark Massiel, whose records
will be
released
in Argentina through this company
(she records in that country for
Novola),
will
arrive
in town next November. RCA has already released her
first single, “Rosas En El Mar” and “Hasta Manana,” and expects to turn her
into a consistent star in short time. Other news are the release of “Pastor De
Nubes,” winning song at the recent Odol Festival on Channel 13 recorded by
lark Ginette Acevedo coupled with a Mexican song penned by Jose Alfredo
Jimenez, “Arrullo De Dios,” a strong hit in that country. The diskery
is
also
launching new artist Rocky Andrews who already has a heavy TV schedule for
this winter’s season.

strong
seller
through the Brazilian Roberto Carlos waxing, while new artist Rocky Andrews,

miA Bills $5.2 Mil At Vegas Confab
LAS
VEGAS—MGM
Records
blos-
somed
out
with
impressive
flower-
power
and more
at
its
sales
confab
here last week (9-12). The label billed
$5.2 million for
its round-up
of more
than 70 new albums and
six
singles.
The company claimed
in
excess
of
2
million
album
units
sold
Signifi-
cantly, a spokesman for MGM noted,

Jesse Kaye, MGM west coast veep,
has viewed a number of screenings of

agers
attend
some

By

feels he
can determine those scenes with mu-
sic that have the most emotional im-
pact.
It’s

prior

of the soundtrack was prevented

in dual owner-

Pictures

0.
Selznick.

will

the

mikes,
p.a., and
a new custom-made
jtage wardrobe.
The Vagrants had
left their equip-
.-lent at Action House after a Sunday
night
(9)
performance.

were
scheduled
for
another appearance
at
the
club
on Wednesday
(12).
The cause of the
fire has not been
determined. The Nassau
Police Dept.
Arson Squad
is investigating.

guitarist

West,
commenting
upon
the

said,

is rebuild
the
act
as
if
from
scratch.

planning
a
complete
campaign
to
build ourselves a better sound system
and find instruments that will do the
most for our music.”
Changes At CROC
HOLLYWOOD — The following
changes in the national sales
staff of
Capitol Records Distributing were an-
nounced last week by William B. Tal.
lant, the firm’s VP and national sales
manager:
Joseph
F.
Okla
has
been
named
sales
coordinator,
replacing
Bob Setzer, who recently became dis-
trict sales manager in San Francisco;
Richard E. Green has been appointed
sales
service
analyst,
replacing Bob
Keels, who
resigned.
Okla
first came to work for CRDC
in
February,
1950
as
a
salesman
in
Cleveland.
In
July,
1957,
he became
sales
manager
in
Syracuse,
and
in
June, 1964, territory manager in Buf-
falo. He remained
in the last-named
post until receiving his new appoint-
ment.
Green, a new man who for the past
two years has been with Price, Water-
house and
Co.,
will make
statistical
analyses and reports for CRDC.
Both Okla and Green will work at
the Capitol Tower here in Hollywood,
reporting directly to CRDC’s assistant
national
sales manager,
Pete
Goyak.

Edison Award For
Philips' 'Messiah'
Philips Records has collected a 1967
Edison Award
for their recording
of
Handel’s “Messiah,” performed by the
London
Symphony
Orchestra
and
chorus conducted by Colin Davis.
The award, which was among those
announced
by
the CGCC
(Collective
Gramophone
Campaign
Committee)
of
Holland,
is
the
second
to be won
for
this
Philips
recording.
In March
this year it claimed the coveted Grand
Prix du Disque de I’Acadamie Charles
Cros 1967.
Correction
In the July 8 issue of Cash Box,
it
was
stated
that
CBS
International
had
negotiated
a
deal
with
Valando
Music
to
sub-publish
the
latter’s
catalog. CBS
has
informed
us
that
this deal covers only the Latin Amer-
ican countries.

PACIFIC—Broadening
its
international
marketing
outlet.
Liberty Records recently concluded negotiations
for the

of product
from

label’s
divisions

Barclay & Bovema Merge Branches
Barclay Netherlands and
the com-
panies
forming
the
Bovema
group
have
decided
to
unite,
as
of
Sept.
1,
their commercial branches in order to
increase
the
potential
of
their
dis-
tribution network.
The companies
will
keep
their
re-
spective head
offices but the dispatch-
ing and invoicing departments will be
situated
in
one
building, which
is
in
the course of being finished. Someone
from
each
of
the
respective
com-
panies
will
continue
to
look
after
promotion.
This agreement
is
seen
as
a
fore-
runner
of future
alliances which
are
destined to give a greater efficiency to
companies, on the eve of the opening
of
the
frontiers
of
those
countries
forming part of the Common Market
in
July,
1968.
CBS Cuts Bernstein, Stern
Concerts That Aided
Jerusaium
Leonard Bernstein and Isaac
Stern
in
Israel
for
concerts,
recorded
by
CBS, in aid of the rebuilding of Jeru-
salem.
The
Mayor
declared
July
9
“A
Day
of
Public
Celebration”
to
mark
the opening
of
the
old
city
of
Jerusalem.
Bernstein conducted three
concerts with the Israel Philhai'monic
Orchestra
in
the
Mann
auditorium
Tel
Aviv,
in
the Amphi
Theatre
on
the
slopes
of Mount
Scopus
and
in
the
Congress
Hall
in
Jerusalem
it-
self.
The
program
comprised
the
Israelie
national
anthem,
Mendel-
ssohn’s
Violin
Concerto
with
Issac
Stern
as
soloist
and
Mahler’s
2nd
Symphony. CBS perpetuated the occa-
sion by
‘live’ recordings
of
all works.
Proceeds from the
sale of the records
will be donated to Israel
charities.
McKuen In London
For RCA 'Warm' LP
HOLLYWOOD —
Singer-songwriter
Rod
McKuen,
in
Europe
since May
for a series of concerts and recording
dates
in
Spain,
Italy,
France
and
England, was
in London
for
a week
of
recording
on
a new RCA
Victor
LP
based
on
his
upcoming Random
House book, “Listen To The Warm.”
Both book and album
are due out
in
September.
Random House meanwhile
is said to
have
offered McKuen
a
healthy
ad-
vance
to take over
his current book,
“Stanyan
Street &
Other
Sorrows,”
now
published by
his own company,
Cheval-Stanyan.
No
deal
has
been
concluded
as
yet, though
representa-
tives
from
the
publishing
company
will meet with McKuen in Europe for
further
talks.

CBS/Group Decentralizes
NE"\V
YORK—Goddard
Lieberson,
president
of
the
CBS /Columbia
Group,
last week announced the
pro-
motion
of
John
J.
Lorenz
to
vice
president and
assistant
to
the
presi-
dent,
and
the
appointment
of
four
new controllers in the company’s pro-
gram
of
decentralization
of
financial
functions.
Lorenz
joined
CBS
in
1958
and
worked as senior and general auditor
until he became assistant controller in
’61 and
vice president
of the
finance
division
in
’62.
In
1965, Lorenz was
appointed
vice
president
of
develop-
ment and became responsible for the
exploration, study, evaluation, coordi-
nation
and
execution
of
the
major
development and diversification activi-
ties
of the CBS/Columbia
Group.
In
his new post, Lorenz will continue to
plan and
oversee
these
actions, and
he
will
be
responsible
for
directing
the complementary functions of mar-
ket and economic research. He
is also
to
assist Lieberson
in managing and
the fulfilling of present objectives
of
the firm plus formulating new
strat-
egies and
objectives.
Lieberson also noted that four new
controllers were
appointed, and
that
the
Group program
of
decentraliza-
tion
of
financial
functions had
been
completed.
The
plan
had
begun
in
1965.
The four new appointments went to
Theodore R. Sullivan, who will handle
the CBS
records
division,
Joseph
G.
Cucchia,
vice
president with
the
ad-
ministration
department
and
con-
troller
of the CBS
direct marketing
services division; Nicholas Cirillo with
the CBS
international
division;
and
Harold
Travis
at
the
CBS
musical
instruments division.

Mason
Records
Revives
Crosby-Like Crooning
NEW YORK—In
a
business where
new musical trends crop up with each
new
season, and gimmickery
is
con-
sidered standard operating procedure,
it
is somewhat rare
to
see the debut
of a new label aimed
at propagating
a
near-extinct
form
of
music—the
sound of the
30s. The
label
is Mason
Records and the owner (and sole art-
ist
at
this
point)
is
Steve Mason,
a
former
singing
waiter
whose
“bag”
is crooning the pop
ballads from an
era that saw Bing Crosby and Russ
Columbo holding down popularity po-
sitions much
akin to
those
currently
held by
the
Beatles and
the
Rolling
Stones. Not only does Mason feature
a
bill
of
fare
composed
strictly
of
classic pop
numbers, but he
delivers
them
in the
style
that
once
caused
flappers
to
flap
and bobby
soxers
to
bob.
His
vocal
efforts
aimed
almost
entirely at the 35-year-old plus audi-
ence, the erstwhile teeny-boppers who
were bopping
before bop became an
“in” art form.
At
this
point. Mason
Records
has
a
catalog
of two
albums
and
eight
singles,
with
distribution
limited
to
the New York
area. The
label
is
as
close
to a one-man operation
as
can
be found in the business, with Mason
constantly
changing
uniform
as
he
becomes
label
president, promo man,
salesman, arranger and
artist almost
simultaneously. To date Mason’s drive
to revive the past
is an
uphill
battle,
a
one-man
crusade
which
he
hopes
will spread beyond the confines of the
five
boroughs
here.
Word-of-mouth
was
the
basis
of
his
publicity
until
he
began
making
frequent
appear-
ances
on
the
New
York-based
Joe
Franklin
TVer, “Memory
Lane.”
As
interest begins
to grow
in
the
label.
Mason,
who
operates
out
of
2716
Decatur
Ave.
in
the
Bronx,
is
sending
out
feelers
to such
areas
as
Chicago, San Francisco and Los An-
geles
for
distribution
and
handling
of
the
label, with hopes
of
reaching
a
good
portion
of
that
limited,
but
certain
audience that
remembers
“I
Surrender,
Dear.”

===== PAGE 60 =====
Pollowing the Cash Box leader of a few weeks back concerning the ‘second
front’ invasion of the American charts by British
artists,
it
is interesting to
note that, vice-versa the British charts reflect a similar resurgence of stateside
talent on this side
of the
Atlantic. That the British Top Twenty of today
is
shared almost equally by English & American artists while the American pal-
ate
still hungers for the best Britain has to offer, confirms the healthy balance
of musical taste which has developed between our two
countries. A year ago
Britain had a weekly average of 17 - 20 entries in the American Top 100. Today
the level is around 12 - 17. On the other hand, the average number of Arnerican
entries
in
the
British
charts
is
slightly
higher than
a year
ago.
It
is
also
interesting

MEXICO
Last July 8, Enrique Guzman and Silvia Pinal, two of Mexico’s most popular
artists were married. The wedding took place in the city of Cuautla and only
very close friends of both assisted at the ceremony.
Silvia
is ten years older
than Enrique, and this
is her third marriage. Enrique
is 24 years old and says
he
is the happiest guy in the world.
Sergio Niinez Falcon resigned from his position as manager of public rela-
tions for Capitol Records. It is probable that Sergio will go back to working as
a TV animator and announcer.
Among the latest recordings made by Gamma records are “ ‘8’ Teen” and “I
Need Somebody” by
the Question Marks, “Baby
I Need You” and
“Gettin’
Ready For Tomorrow” by Johnny Rivers, and “Cuando Llegue El Amor” and
“El Libro De Magia” by Karina.
The
latest
Orfeon
productions
are
“Ven A Mi”
and “Palmeras” by Los
Hitters, “Piden Pan” and “Embrujado” by
the new
group,
Los
Stops, and
“Necesito Tu Amor” and “Sin Tu Corazon” by Los Escavadores. In extended
play on the Roulette label, Orfeon released “Mirage,” “I Like The Way,” “Let’s
Be Lovers” and “Run, Run Baby, Run” by Tommy James and the Shondells.
On
his own
label, “Acuario,” Enrique Guzman
released “El
Rock,” which
is
a potpourri of popular rock tunes, and “Caminar,” a new song on which
Guzman plays his guitar.
Jimmy Nicols and Eddie Quinn left town to go to the United States, where
they will promote the new album and single they made at the RCA studios.
New Capitol releases are “La Chica Y La Luna” and “Besa Mas Suave,” by
Lalo Duarte, “Hablame” and “Contigo Aprendi” by Lucho
Gatica,
(who
re-
cently
left town for Europe
to
fulfill several contracts he has there) and an
EP by European chanter Adamo, who
sings
in
Spanish
such
songs
as “Tu
Nombre,” “Era Una Linda Flor,” “Un Mechon De Tus Cabellos” and “Quiero.”
Capitol told us that they just signed French singer Jacqueline Fellay to do a
live LP of her night club show.
Musart records released a marvelous EP by
Spanish
singer
Gloria
Lasso,
who has been living for a long time in Mexico. On the EP Gloria sings “Ciao
Amore, Ciao,” “Los De Varsovia,” “Esta Es Mi Cancion” and “Vivo.”
RCA cut a new single by the popular composer Armando Manzanero. The
single features two new songs by Manzanero, “Esta Tarde Vi Llover” and
“Contigo Aprendi.”

of Argentina and
Brazil,

tiations were completed with Leben-
diger

vice-president and director

TEMPTATIONS
NEW YORK—First
there was some
fine old-fashioned entertainment, then
the Detroit hit machine brought extra
excitement to the show, and suddenly
—there was magic as the Temptations
paraded
in
splendid
revue
at
the
Copacabana in New York.
Opening
strongly with
a
series
of
blues
songs,
the Temptations
nearly
gave
the
impression
that
Copa
habituees had come to the wrong place
since they mark a departure from the
usual headline act type at the nitery;
but by the closing number there was
no doubt that viewers had been won
over by
the
sheer excitement
of
the
group and their material. Rather than
striking out by showing to the wrong
audience,
the
quintet
struck
a
blow
for the spread of Motown blues among
the
older,
somewhat
conservative,
people who frequent the club.
But
the
act
was
not
a
simple
smattering
of
one
musical
view;
it
was
a
presentation
of
the
many
faceted talents of the team, who per-
formed
with
equal
talent
selections
out
of the American show,
folk and
blues
bags,
as
well
as
a
combined
Anglo-French
pairing
of
“Yester-
day” and “What Now My Love.”
Spacing performances of their own
hits by including
softer material
be-
tween them, the crew allowed viewers
a
chance
to
catch
their
breath
and
see
another
side
of the
entertainers.
“Beauty
Is
Only
Skin
Deep,” “My
Girl” and “Ain’t Too Proud To Beg”
were broken up by a fine up-dating of
“Swanee”
and
the
team’s
tribute
to
“some
of
the
groups who
guided us
along
the way”—a
showing
of
im-
personations
of
the
Freshmen,
Ink
Spots and Mills Brothers, whose styles
are
blended
into
the
sound
that
is
only the Temptations.
In the encore segment of the almost
hour-long
performance,
the
group
scored with the audience on a brilliant
reading of “Ole Man River” and broke
up
the
entire
evening’s
gathering
with an indescribable “Losing You.”
Enthusiastic applause for many
of
the sone-s was nowhere near the shat-
tering ovation that poured out during
the
fina’e
a
version of “Losing You”
that
ca T'
only
be
called
a
jazz-like
session developing and is altering the
show by the singers’ building emotion
and
ability
to
swing
into
the mood
read
in the crowd.
HERMAN'S
NEW
YORK—Remember
Saturday
afternoons
at
the
movies when
the
kids
screamed
through
all
the
car-
toons
and
pelted
the
screen
with
empty (and sometimes not so emptv)
popcorn and candy boxes?
Well,
the
same atmosphere,
if not precisely the
same
spirit,
nrevailed
at
the
West-
bury Music
Fair
in Westbury, Long
Island
last
Monday
afternoon
(7)
when MGM’s
top
rock
group,
Her-
man’s
Hermits,
pitted
their strength
against
that
of
a
crowd
composed
mostly
of frenzied teenage
girls. Of
course
the
Hermits, who have
been
similarly
received hundreds
of times
before,
did
not
really
expect
to
be
heard
clearly. Having
little wads
of
paper thrown at them by their ador-
ing
fans was
probably
nothing new
either.
But
the
few
people
in
the
HERMITS
audience
who
wanted
to
hear
the
Hermits perform rather than worship
them were denied that pleasure.
What
could
be
heard,
sounded
good, and judging by the very nature
of
the
audience’s
apnroval,
the Her-
mits are
still one of the most ponular
grouns
around.
Leading
off with an
infectious reading of the Beatles’ “A
Little
Help From My
Friends,”
the
boys
offered
a
wide
variety
of
pop
tunes including the Bee
Gees’ recent
hit,
“New
York
Mining
Disaster
1941,”
and
their
own
hits,
“Mrs.
Brown. You’ve Got A Lovely Daugh-
ter,” “Henry VIII,” “There’s A Kind
Of A
Hush,”
and
others. No
doubt
about the Hermits’ talent. But
if you
really want
to hear them, buy
their
records.
JIMI HENDRIX EXPERIENCE
NEW YORK—One
of the most aptly
named groups
on
the modern
blues-
rock scene, the Jimi Hendrix Experi-
ence, closed their New York stay with
a frantic set at Salvation marking the
night spot’s opening last Tuesday
(8).
Titling
the
team
“Experience”
is
appropriate
because
that
is
exactly
what their shows
are. The act
is
en-
thralling on
records, as may be
wit-
nessed by
the
ranid
recention
given
“Are You
Experienced?,”
the
trio’s
first American release LP on Renrise;
but even more engrossing
in person.
Music aside, and that
is hardly the
way
it
effects
audiences,
the
act
is
really
something
to
behold.
Hendrix
himself
is not satisfied to perform as
one
of
the
finest blues
guitarists on
the
current
scene,
and
he
goes
to
great lengths to prove his capabilities
by carrying on
in
a number
of con-
torted
positions
losing
none
of
his
artistry,
and
even
(at
one
point
in
the
act)
by
picking
a
melody
with
his teeth
or his toes.
Visually exciting, audially a delight,
the
Jimi Hendrix Experience proved
a worthy talent to mark the premiere
to the public of Salvation.
CANDY MEN
NEW YORK—Long a back-un group
for Roy Orbison, the Candy Men are
out on
their own now
and,
just
last
week, were
packing
’em
into
Steve
Paul’s
the
Scene.
The
group
is
as
tight
as any we’ve
ever seen and
is
a sort of “musicians group,” drawing
members
of
other
rock
a^-ts
to
the
cavernous
nitery
night
after
night.
The Candy Men
offer material from
just about every bag imaginable, from
middle-fifties
rock
’n’
roll
to
slices
from
the
“Sgt.
Pepper’s
Lonely
Hearts Club Band” LP.
They do other people’s material ex-
tremely well and we look forward to
hearing them
do some more
original
stuff somedav. Thev are
particularly
good and well worth seeing whenever
the opportunity arises.

ME. WE

FROM
SCRATCH.’
I
AND THAT’S HOW

MAN.”

Hollywood, Vox Dealers
In Nationwide Talent Hunt
HOLLYWOOD — The motion picture
industry,
always
on
the
alert
for
talent,
has
called
on VOX
musical
instrument dealers from coast to coast
to
assist
in
finding
the
top
musical
group
in the country.
Movie producer Sam Katzman and
Joe Benaron, president of the Thomas
Organ Company, VOX
division, have
launched
jointly “Win
a Movie
Con-
tract”—the VOX Band
Battle—to be
held through
September
10. The top
winner will be flown to Hollywood to
appear
in
a
Sam
Katzman
motion
picture.
Talent headquarters throughout the
country will be the hundreds of VOX
dealerships. Every group must regis-
ter at a VOX dealer
in order to enter
“Win
a
Movie
Contract”—The VOX
Band
Battle.
After signing an application at the
dealership,
each
group
will
be
re-
quired
to
send
a tape or disk
to the
VOX
plant
in
Sepulveda,
California,
along with a photo of the group and
biographies of each member.
Judging will be done by outstanding
people
in the entertainment
field.
The winning group will be flown to
Hollywood with
all expenses paid and
will appear in a future Sam Katzman
(movie
to
be
produced
at MGM. The
name of the group will appear in the
screen credits.
Thousands of dollars in VOX equip-
ment will be distributed as prizes.
|
VOX
is
the
equipment
used
by
major
musical
groups
all
over
the
world
including
the
Beatles,
the
Monkees,
and
Paul
Revere
and
the
Raiders.

Henry
B. Clay & Wife
Die In Plane Crash
NEW YORK—Henry B.
Clay, execu-
tive
vice president and general man-
ager of KWKH-Radio
in
Shreveport,
Louisiana, was killed with his wife on
Aug.
3
when
their
private
plane
crashed
near
Nevada,
Missouri.
The
Clays
were
enroute
to
the
fishing
camp of Charles T. McCord of Shreve-
port on McCord Island in Nestor Falls,
Canada.
Mr.
Clay
was
piloting
the
plane
when
it went down
during
a
light
rainstorm
at
approximately
7:10
p.m.
The
exact
cause
of
the
crash
is unknown,
but witnesses
say
that the plane broke up as
it
fell
to
earth.
Some
heard
a
noise
which
sounded
like
an
explosion
or
the
engines being reved up at
full speed.
The
plane
did
not
burn
after
it
crashed.
Mr. Clay was 48 and Mrs. Clay, 44
at the time of their death. Both were
prominent citizens of Shreveport. Both
served as directors of the Shreveport
Times. Both were active in social and
civic
organizations.
Mr. Clay came
to KWKH
as man-
ager at the age of 28. He was head of
the National Broadcasters Association
in
1955,
and
in
1958
the
Louisiana
Broadcasters
Association
elected him
to
its
board
of
directors.
The LBA
named him “Broadcaster of the Year”
in
1965. Mr. Clay founded the famed
“Louisiana
Hayride.”
The
Clays
are
survived
by
four
children. Mr. Clay
is also survived by
four
brothers
and
four
sisters,
and
Mrs. Clay by one brother.
Lester
Flatt Hospitalized
NASHVILLE —
Lester
Flatt,
lead
singer
and
rhythm
guitarist
of
the
famed bluegrass duo, Flatt & Scruggs,
is currently undergoing treatment
at
the
White
City
Hospital
in
Sparta,
Tenn. for a blood clot which developed
in
his
heart.
Flatt became aware
of
his ailment when he almost collapsed
after
an
appearance
at
Constitution
Hall
in Washington, D.C.
British C&W Music
(Continued from page
54)
“However,” Smith states, “the aver-
age
British
listener
still
does
not
necessarily
identify
with
country
music. He identifies with a particular
artist such as Jones or Humperdinck.
This is the major reason why we must
try to build an image of C&W music
as a form unto itself.
“We
are
not,
however,
trying
to
build
a
picture
of
country
music-
American
style
but
country
music-
English
style.
In
America,
the
em-
phasis
is on the
lyric. Generally, you
look
for
either
a
strong message
or
a clever lyrical content as a basis for
a
hit C&W
song.
In
England,
the
emphasis
is on the sound, and we are
hoping
to
develop
our
own C&W
sound.”
When
asked
to
comment
on
the
future
of country music
in
England,
Smith told Cash Box, “Country music
is
moving
in
England now
just
as
R&B music
did
a while
back.
People
said R&B wouldn’t go here, but when
groups
like the Rolling Stones began

Cedarwood
Fetes
Tillis & Walker
NASHVILLE—On August
15, Cedar-
wood
Publishing
will
hold
a
special
reception
at
St.
Clair’s restaurant to
honor two of its and Nashville’s most
famed
songwriters,
Mel
Tillis
and
Wayne
Walker.
Cedarwood
chief
J.
William
Denny
will
host
the
event.
During their long careers, Tillis and
Walker
have
each
composed
more
than 400 songs. Walker, who has won
16 BMI
Writer’s
Awards,
has
been
writing
for Cedarwood
for
11
years.
Tillis,
who
has
received
15
of
the
same awards, has penned for the pub-
bery
for
10
years.
Walker
and
Tillis
co-cleffed
Jack
Green’s recent smash, “All The Time.”
Walker
is
currently
represented
on
the C&W
scene by
“In Your Heart”
(recorded
by
Red
Sovine),
“Sweet
Misery”
(recorded by Jimmy
Dean),
and a
co-cleffing, “Fairweather Love”
(recorded by Arlene Harden). Current
tunes to Tillis’ credit include “Goodbye
Wheeling”
(which
he
also
waxed),
“Ruby,
Don’t
Take
Your
Love
To
Town”
(which
he
cut
with
Johnny
Darrell), “Mental Revenge” (recorded
by
Waylon
Jennings),
and
two
co-
cleffings,
“Detroit
City”
and
“The
Snakes Crawl At Night.”

LONDON—Philips
Records
Limited
recently staged
its
1967 annual
sales
conference
in
London,
during
which
future
releases
on
Philips,
Fontana
and Mercury were presented.
Top
executives
from
Liberty
Rec-
ords,
whose
product
is
distributed
here by
Philips, were
also
in attend-
ance.
Present were Alvin
S. Bennett,
president,
Seymour
Zucker,
vice-
president,
Bob
Scaff,
vice-president,
Ronald
Kass
European
director
and
Robert
Reisdorff, managing
director,
Liberty Records Landon.
The Philips Group has enjoyed con-
siderable success
in recent years with
an
above
average
number
of
chart
entries, and
the
organization’s
inten-
tion
of achieving even higher ratings
in
the
future was
evidenced
by
the
very high standard
of future releases
presented at the conference.
Musicassette Plans
Managing
director
Leslie
Gould
said that after a rather slow summer
sales
period, he was
looking forward
to
a
very
successful
selling
season
with
a bumper
release
schedule
con-
taining an unusual number of “block-
busters.”
Looking
further
ahead,
Gould
prophesied
that
1968/69 would
be
“Musicassette
Year,”
with
new
machines,
new
manufacturers
and
new
programs
in
this
field.
Philips’
plans
for
musicassettes
cover
all
facets of music and
will be aimed
at
all markets including many new ones
where records have not yet been sold.
Playback equipment will be within the
reach
of
all
buyers, ranging
in
price
from £10-£50 a machine. Car cassette
machines
will
also
be
available
in
more
compact
designs,
which
will
revolutionize the concept of music
in
cars. Over one hundred different pro-
grams,
catering
to every
taste, have
been
specially
designed
for cars and
will soon be on the market.
Gould
announced
the
forthcoming
release
(October
1st)
of
a
special
charity record of Christmas carols by
the
Gregory
Orchestra,
which
has
been produced by
Philips
for Oxfam.
Entitled
“David
Frost
Introduces A
Christmas
Record
for
Oxfam,”
the
album
will
sell
for
£1.
Dealers
will
take a reduced profit, and
all proceeds
will go
to Oxfam.
Darcy
Glover,
Philips’
marketing
manager, was responsible for organiz-
ing
yet
another
highly
successful
sales
conference.
‘Campaign’ Presentation
An innovation of this year’s confer-
ence was the presentation
of product
to
the
sales
force
by
‘campaigns’
rather than by the usual label by label
method.
Presenting
the
future
prod-
uct, Glover
first announced plans for
the
company’s
Double
Album
re-
leases, which, for the

These

will
also

for

time
classical
and

word

Philips
has

and

of
sale
mer-
chandising. A

Glover announced
that
due

line popu-
lar
jazz

(retailing

21/9d)
the

would

extended
as

to include not only jazz,

“Super

three record sets selling for the price

a combined campaign.
It was

will

re-

set, featuring the L.S.O. conducted by

Fickwick Buys Southtown
NEW YOEK—Pickwick International,
in
a
further
step
to
accelerate
its
position
in
the
publishing
field,
has
purchased Southtown Music. The
an-
nouncement was made by Cy
Leslie,
president
of
Pickwick
International.
Joseph
Abend,
vice
president
of
Pickwick, concluded the acquisition of
the
Nashville-based
operation
which
included
such
outstanding copyrights
as
“Charleston
Railroad
Tavern”
(Bobby
Bare);
“How Long
Has
It
Been?”
(Bobby
Lewis);
“I
Didn’t
Jump
The
Fence”
(Red
Sovine)
&
“Seven
Days
of
Crying”
(Harden
Trio), which
all
attained
top
ratings
on the charts during the
first part of
1967.
Pickwick’s
Barmour
Music,
also
based
in
Nashville,
and
headed
by
general manager Tony Moon, has two
top
hits
on
the
charts
currently,
“Promises & Hearts” and “Love Me
And Make
It All Better”.
Leslie
stated
that Barmour
Music
and
Southtown
Music would
operate
under one roof and would also include
in this operation the Weiss & Barry
catalog
which
Pickwick
acquired
3
years ago. Tony Moon will function as
general manager
of these companies
and Ralph Davis has been retained to
supervise the Southtown activities re-
porting
directly
to
Moon.
Barmour,
which has exclusive writing pacts with
several
top
writers
including
Gene
Crysler and Larry Lee, has the plug
side
of
the new
Epic
single by
the
“Lemonade Charade” and four tunes
in the can by a group called “We The
People” on RCA. Both
of these
acts
are produced by Moon
exclusively.
Waiting
for
release
are
songs
re-
corded by such artists as Jimmy Dean,
Wanda
Jackson,
Little Jimmy
Dick-
ens, Porter Wagoner, Stonewall Jack-
son,
Ray
Pillow,
David
Houston,
Anita Carter and Jim Ed Brown.
Leslie
indicated
that
Pickwick
is
now negotiating to acquire additional
music publishing companies.
HERE IT IS—Arthur Jacobs
(stand-
ing,)
producer
of
the
film
“Doctor
Dolittle”
for
20th
Century
Fox,
ac-
cepts the first original cast LP of the
press from
Larry Newton,
president
of ABC
Records,
distributors
of
the
set.

DiMinno Upped At TRO
NEW YORK—The Richmond Organ-
ization
has
added
Nick
DiMinno
to
its
professional
staff,
in
its
current
pi’ogram
of
expansion
and
new
di-
rections in publishing. DiMinno, whose
special
interest
is comtemporary and
rock music,
joins TRO’s
professional
team
of vice-president A1 Brackman,
Larry
Coleman,
and
vice-president
Marvin
Cane,
director
of TRO’s
tal-
ent
development
division.
DiMinno
will work closely with Cane
in relat-
ing
to
artists,
songwriters, and
pro-
ducers, helping to develop new mate-
rial, and
in
staging
special
exploita-
tion
projects
for TRO
material.
Since coming to TRO in May, 1966,
DiMinno has
been
in charge
of
tap-
ing
and
dubbing
operations. He
has
also
served
as TRO’s
representative
to New York radio
stations, and will
continue
to
work
in
supplementing
record company promotion of record-
ings
of TRO-published
songs. A pro-
fessional musician himself (who
reg-
ularly plays with groups
in the met-
ropolitan
area)
DiMinno
is
a
gradu-
ate
of
Christopher
Columbus
High
School
in
the
Bronx.
TRO,
publishers
of
the
interna-
tional
big
one, “A Whiter Shade
of
Pale,”
is
also
publisher of songs by
the Who
and
other
hit pop
groups,
and has potential pop
hits
in “Paper
Sun,”
by
Traffic,
and
“See
Emily
Play,” by the Pink Floyd. Bob Cam-
eron,
Epic
recording
artist managed
by Marvin Cane,
is currently scoring
with two singles from his new album,
“For
the
First
Time.”

West Coast Stations Hum To
Bill Drake Tuning
LOS ANGELES—Programming
con-
sultant Bill Drake can drive down the
full length of the California coast and
listen
to one
top
radio
station
after
another and pride himself in the fact
that
he’s
a
consultant
for
each
of
these
top
outlets.
The
four
in
California
include
KFRC
in
San
Francisco, KYNO
in
Fresno, KHJ in Los Angeles and KGB
in San Diego. But these are only four
of
the
stations
presently
employing
the services and advice of the Drake-
Chenault
Organization.
Others
in-
clude KAKC
in Tulsa, CKLW
in De-
troit, WRKO
in Boston, WOR-FM
in
New York and WHBQ
in
Memphis.
All
in
the
record
industry
familiar
with call letters that attract audiences,
recognize the aforementioned stations
as
leaders
in
their
cities.
Although
many
record
industry
reps
point to
the tremendous
strides
made
by
the
Bill
Drake
service,
during the past 4 years, those familiar
with
the
tall,
soft-voiced
exec
are
aware
of the fact that
his
ability
as
a
programming
consultant
is
based
on more than two decades
of experi-
ence in radio, production and program
direction.
Bill
started
in Bambridge,
Ga.,
in
1955
as
a DJ
on WMGR,
a
station
playing
rural C&W
and
Pop C&W
;
the more commercial acts at the time
such as the Everly Bros., Elvis Pres-
ley,
Jerry
Lee
Lewis
and
the
like.
After a short stay here, he returned
to college.
In 1959 he got the midnight to
six
spot on WAKE
in Atlanta. And as a
result
of
his
success
with
contests,
commercial production, jingle produc-
tion,
etc., he was named the
station’s
program director within a year.
From
’61 to
’63 he served as PD at
KYA
in San Francisco. That’s where
he met radio magnate Gene Chenault
and with him
set up Drake-Chenault
Enterprises
providing
sales and
pro-
gramming know-how for
stations
in-
terested
in subscribing to
his
service.
The Drake-Chenault operation
just
recently
took
over
as
programming
consultants for the whole RKO chain
of stations. The deal
is reported to be
in excess of seven figures.
Van-Jak, Bates
Pubberies Bow
NEW YORK —
.
Madelyn
(Maddy)
Segal, in partnership with Herman D.
Gimbel,
has
formed
two new
music
companies,
Van-Jake
Music
Corp.
(ASCAP)
and
Bates
Music
Publish-
ing Corp.
(BMI). The two firms
will
have
their
base
at
221
West
57th
Street.
Miss
Segal
is
no newcomer
to
the
music
business.
As
singer
Madelyn
Russell, she worked with the orches-
tras
of Vaughn Monroe,
Skitch Hen-
derson, Gene Krupa and many others.
She
has
appeared
in
theatres
and
nightclubs
throughout
the
country
and
abroad, and has
also had
a few
disks
marketed
by
recording
com-
panies.
She has
also made radio and
TV
appearances
on
the Gary Moore
and Steve Allen Shows, among others.
As
a
writer.
Miss
Segal
is
a mem-
ber
of ASCAP
and AGAC
and
has
penned many
popular
songs
as
well
as
the
scores
for
an NBC
musical
titled
“A
Man’s
Game”
starring
Nanette
Fabray,
and
for
the
Paul
Winchell show with guest star Janet
Blair.
The
firm
is
open
to
all
kinds
of
music
including Rock and
Roll,
Folk
Rock,
ballads,
novelties
and
Bossa
Novas.
Miss
Segal
will
run
both
companies.
Bill attributes the success his oper-
ation
has
experienced
to
the
key
personnel at the stations he advises
people who he calls astute, capable pro-
gram
directors. He points with pride
to: Ron Jacobs at KHJ
in
L.A., Tom
Rounds
at KFRC
in
San
Francisco;
Mark Dennis
at KEB
in San Diego;
Nick Anthony
at KYNO
in
Fresno;
Scooter Seagrave at KAKC
in Tulsa;
Mel
Phillips
at WRKO
in
Boston;
Paul
Drew
at CKLW
Detroit;
and
Gary Mack
at WOR-FM
in
N.Y.
In
his own home
office,
people
re-
sponsible
for keeping
the show
run-
ning
smoothly
are
Les
Turpin
and
Bill Watson, Programming Assistants,
and
Administrative
Assistant
Bernie
Torres.
One
of
the
key
reasons
for
suc-
cessful
programming
at
the
above
mentioned
stations
is,
according
to
Drake,
“our
constant
communication
with
all
our
P.D’s. around the coun-
try.”
With
9
different
P.D’s exchanging
ideas
with
Drake
and
with
one
an-
other,
a
great many
successful
for-
mulas
are
discussed.
Bill
says,
“If we
try
just two
left
field
records
on
each
station
every
week we can get a weekly reading of
audience
reaction
and
response
to
18 different titles, an excellent testing
ground
for
new
releases.
In
this
manner we
find
out
about
audience
acceptance
to
a
great many
titles
without cramming
all of the 18 titles
in
one week on
one
station,
thereby
diluting that station’s exciting sound.”
The
Drake-Chenault
operations
home
office
is
in Los Angeles.

Cash Box—August
26, 1967
57

===== PAGE 54 =====
GouA
COUNTRY
ROUNDUP
Six weeks ago we reported on the
opening
of
New
York’s
very
own
country
nightclub,
Nashville
at
the
New Yorker (Country Roundup,
Jul.
15),
and
we
expressed
our
opinion
that the club could make
it big with
the
right support from
the industry.
While
it
still may
be
too
early
to
give an honest
(and
correct)
evalu-
ation
of the
club’s
status, and while
six
weeks may
not
provide
enough
of
a
yardstick
to
gauge
the
future
possibilities
of
the
club, we
feel
it
necessary
to
report
the
progress
of
the
Nashville
club
to
the
hundreds
of
artists,
bookers, managers,
musi-
cians,
etc.
whose
livelihoods
depend,
to some
degree, on
such
clubs.
Cash Box has
visited
Nashville
at
the New Yorker
almost
every week
since
its opening (we regret that we
missed Roy Drusky and Wilma Bur-
gess when
they
teamed
up
to
play
the
house),
but
has
held
back
on
giving a status report until such time
as
the
situation
cleared
sufficiently
to give a more vivid
picture. For the
first few weeks
the
club was
a
pic-
ture of confusion—highlighted by the
fact
that
in
successive
weeks
coun-
try
fans
were
shuffled
from
the
hotel’s
coffee
house
to
the Manhat-
tan Room, back
to
the
coffee
house,
then on, finally, to the Terrace Room.
The club has certainly had
its grow-
ing
pains—but
let’s
not
forget
that
the
keyword
there
is
“growing.”
From
our vantage
point
there
have
definitely
been
strong
forward
steps
made
by
the
club,
aided
by
a
good
deal of cooperation from other coun-
try
music
business
entities.
Of
course,
there
is
only
one way
to
measure
success
in
this
type
of
business—by
counting
up
the
dol-
lars
at
the end
of the week. And
it
seems that the
dollars are continual-
ly
taking
longer
to
count.
Granted,
there
were
ups
and
downs
in
the
initial
weeks,
but
over
the
last few
weekends
things have begun
to
jell,
and the club seems to be on
its way.
One of the reasons for the success
has
been,
naturally,
the
talent
em-
ployed
by
the
house.
Another
rea-
son,
as we
have
repeatedly
pointed
out,
is
that
there
is
a
definite mar-
ket
in
this
area
for
country
music.
Crowds
have
been
pouring
into
the
club
in SRO
numbers
lately,
with
each
week
seeing
a
larger
number
of turnaways. For the owners
of the
Nashville room these results must in-
deed
be
gratifying—to
say
nothing
of
all the other
folk who are finding
another
lucrative
market
at
their
disposal.
Artists
like Tammy Wynette, Hank
Thompson,
the
Hardin
girls,
the
Flatt & Scruggs crew, Ferlin Husky,
David
Houston,
Jan
Howard,
the
Geezinslaw
Bros.,
Wanda
Jackson,
Dick
Curless
and
Connie
Smith,
in
addition
to
the
aforementioned
Roy
Drusky and Wilma Burgess, have ven-
tured
north-by-northeast
for
first-
hand
looks
at
the
strange
natives
who
dwell
in
the
concrete-and-steel
island
of Manhattan, and the natives
are
beginning
to
respond
lustily.
Now’s
the
time
to
hit
’em
even
harder.
By
continuing
to
hit
hard
and
fast,
country
music
people
can
wrap
up,
if
not
the
entire
city,
at
least
a
sizeable
portion
of
its
en-
tertainment-hungry
populace.
LeRoy Van Dyke and his “Auction-
eers” are currently on a tour
of the
East
Coast
and
Midwest.
The
tour,
which
includes
dates
in
Michigan,
Maryland, Indiana,
Illinois and Iowa,
runs
from
August
10
through
Sep-
tember. ...
On
September
1, Key
Talent
will
open
a
branch
office
in
Las Vegas at 2419 Las Vegas Boule-
vard
South.
The
office
will
handle
Key’s
West
Coast
operations.
.
.
.

Red
Foley
is
on
a
country-
wide tour which began August 19
in
Charleston, West Virginia, and which
will take him
to Disneyland
in
Cali-
fornia;
Anchorage,
Alaska;
Seattle,
Washington; and Elkhorn, Wisconsin.
In
addition
to
personal
appearances,
Red
will make promotional
visits
on

Internotioniil News Report
Paramor Shines With Yugoslavian
Rest
LONDON—A
first hand report from
EMI A & R manager, Norrie Para-
mor and British group, the Shadows,
both home again
after appearing
at
‘ the
recently-held
3-day
National
Song
Festival
at
Split,
Yugoslavia,
-^confirms
that
the
event was
a
big
success.
Paramor, who
is
EMI’s
controller
of international music publishing and
manager
of
EMI’s
international
“pop” A & R
division,
devised
and
produced
the
festival
and
directed
* the forty-piece accompanying orches-
tra.
-
The festival was both national and
international.
All
the
songs
entered
were
Yugoslavian
compositions
and
were
rendered
by
artists
from
the
east and the west. Paramor was
full
of praise for the very high standard
of
eastern
performers,
and
the
< Shadows were most impressed by the
genuine
comeraderie between
artists
^from
the west and
the
east.
The Shadows
themselves were
ac-
corded
an
excellent
reception
and
were
successful
in taking one
of the
competing songs into
first place, tak-
ing themselves no
less than
10
cur-
tain
calls.
*
There were two winning songs
at
the Festival—one
of them voted
into
y first
place
by
the
members
of
the
audience, the
other voted
to
the top
by a panel of judges. Each song was
performed twice—once by a Yugoslav
artist or group, and once by a
visit-
ing
artist
or
group.
The
Shadows’
winning
song
(on
the
judges’
vote)
' was
entitled
“Running
Out
Of
World”—with
lyrics
written
by
^ Great Britain’s Don Black. The music
was by
Yugoslavia’s
Mario
Bogliani
—its
Yugoslav
title
is
“Beat
Na
Moru”—and
it
was
performed
also
by the
Split group, the
Delfini.
The song voted
into
first place by
the
audience
was
entitled
“Pismo
Cali”
and
was
performed
by
the
Yugoslav
artist.
Vice
Vukov
and
Germany’s
Heino.
An
LP
of
the
Festival
is
to
be
released
by
the
Jugoton
record company
of
Zagreb.
After voting had taken
place, the
Shadows
gave
a
special
40-minute
show
which
was
also
televised.
As
a result of the Festival, the Shadows’
single, “Running Out Of
World,”
is
to
be
released
throughout
the
east-
ern
block.
EMI
has
a
licensing
deal
with
Jugoton, and
since
it came
into
op-
eration at the end of 1966, a number
of EMI
masters
have
been
success-
fully
released. As
a
direct
result
of
the
Festival
the
demand
for
EMI
disks
should
increase
both
rapidly
and
considerably.
It was interesting to note that the
Festival marks
the
first time
that a
major
western
international
record-
ing
company
(EMI)
has
so
fully
collaborated
with
their
eastern
counterparts. The immediate and mu-
tual admiration and respect for each
other’s
talents
is
evidence
of
the
growing one-world music concept be-
tween
east and
west.
Besides
the
Shadows,
other EMI
artists
taking
part
in
the
Festival
were the Lords
(Electrola, Germany),
Heino
(Electrola
Germany),
Bjorn
Tidmand
(EMI
(Dansk-Engelsk),
Denmark),
Gerard
Brevant
(Pathe
Marconi,

(EMI,

Betina
(EMI,

by Monument up and director of the

in
